interpretation: This verse condemns the eagerness and competitive nature of certain people in pursuing forbidden acts, emphasizing that their rush toward sin—encompassing both moral transgressions and material exploitation through illicit means—reflects a deep spiritual corruption, with the divine disapproval marking such behavior as fundamentally wretched and worthy of censure.

translation: Why do not the rabbis and the learned men forbid them from uttering sin and from eating unlawful gains? Wretched indeed is what they have been doing.
interpretation: This verse condemns the religious scholars and leaders of the Jewish community who failed in their moral and spiritual duty to guide their people away from wrongdoing. The verse specifically identifies two major sins: uttering false words and consuming unlawful wealth. The rhetorical question format (beginning with 'Why do they not...') functions as a strong reproach, emphasizing that these learned men bear responsibility not only for their own sins but also for their failure to prevent the corruption of their community. The verse underscores the critical role that religious scholars play as moral custodians and the grave consequences when they neglect this responsibility or become complicit in wrongdoing themselves.

translation: And the Jews said, 'The hand of Allah is chained.' Chained are their hands, and cursed are they for what they said. Rather, both His hands are extended; He spends as He wills. And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. And We have cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection. Every time they ignite the fire of war, Allah extinguishes it. And they strive throughout the land [causing] corruption, and Allah does not love the corrupters.
interpretation: This verse condemns the false belief of some Jews who blasphemously attributed stinginess to Allah by saying His hand is chained, implying He is miserly. The verse establishes that Allah's attributes are perfect and unlimited—His hands (representing His power and generosity) are fully extended, and He gives liberally according to His wisdom. The punishment for such rejection of truth is that it becomes a means of increasing their rebellion and disbelief, creating a cycle where rejection breeds further rejection. The verse also illustrates the inevitable consequence of opposing divine truth: division, enmity, and perpetual conflict characterize those who reject Allah's signs, as their internal discord and outward mischief-making continue until the Final Day, despite Allah's constant intervention against their destructive endeavors.

translation: And if the People of the Book had believed and been God-fearing, We would have expiated their evil deeds from them and would have admitted them into the Gardens of Bliss.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates that salvation and divine forgiveness are not based on religious identity or ancestry alone, but rather on genuine faith and righteous conduct. Allah is teaching that despite their prior rejection, if the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) had truly embraced faith and practiced piety, they would have received the same mercy and reward as believers. The verse emphasizes the universal nature of Allah's justice—that redemption is available to all who sincerely believe and guard themselves against disobedience, regardless of their background or previous spiritual condition.

translation: And if only they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what had been revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet. Among them is a moderate community, but many of them - evil is what they do.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of divine cause and effect, showing that adherence to revealed guidance brings material and spiritual abundance ('eating from above and below'), while neglect of such guidance leads to deprivation and moral corruption. The mention of a 'moderate community' acknowledges that even among those who received revelation, there exists a distinction between the righteous who follow the guidance and the majority who deviate from it, emphasizing personal responsibility in choosing obedience or disobedience to divine law.

translation: O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord. And if you do not do so, then you have not conveyed His message. And Allah will protect you from the people. Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute obligation and sacred responsibility of the Prophet Muhammad to proclaim the complete message of Allah without any omission, modification, or fear of human opposition. The clause 'if you do not do so, then you have not conveyed His message' underscores that partial or selective preaching would constitute a failure of the prophetic mission itself, making the conveyance of the entire message—not merely portions of it—the essential definition of fulfilling prophethood. The promise that 'Allah will protect you from the people' serves both as reassurance against persecution and as a divine guarantee enabling fearless proclamation. The concluding statement about Allah not guiding the disbelieving people indicates that the Prophet's duty is to convey clearly, while guidance remains ultimately within Allah's domain; thus the Prophet is absolved of responsibility for those who reject despite clear communication.

translation: Say, 'O People of the Scripture, you are not upon anything until you establish the Torah and the Gospel and that which has been revealed to you from your Lord.' And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. So do not grieve over the disbelieving people.
interpretation: This verse establishes that adherence to revealed scripture requires living according to its teachings, not merely possessing it. The statement that following the revealed text will increase many in transgression and disbelief reflects the reality that knowledge of truth without sincere intention and humility can lead to greater spiritual arrogance and rejection—as those who know better yet choose to deny face greater accountability. The concluding instruction not to grieve emphasizes that the Prophet's responsibility is only to convey the message; ultimate belief is determined by God's will and people's internal dispositions, so sorrow over their rejection is neither obligatory nor productive.

translation: Indeed, those who have believed and those who are Jews and the Sabians and the Christians - whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds, there is no fear upon them, nor will they grieve.
interpretation: This verse establishes that righteous belief and action, centered on faith in Allah and accountability in the afterlife, are the criteria for salvation and divine favor, transcending external religious labels and tribal affiliations. It emphasizes that God judges people by the sincerity of their hearts and the quality of their deeds rather than by their nominal religious identity alone.

translation: Indeed, We took a covenant from the Children of Israel and sent to them messengers. Every time a messenger came to them with that which their souls did not desire, a group among them denied him and a group among them killed him.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the persistent pattern of human resistance to divine guidance when it conflicts with personal desires and worldly inclinations. It demonstrates that rejection of truth is not due to lack of evidence or messengers, but rather stems from the soul's attachment to its own preferences and the community's unwillingness to submit to standards that challenge their established ways, whether through denial or violent suppression of those who call them to righteousness.

translation: And they thought there would be no trial (for them), so they became blind and deaf. Then Allah turned to them in mercy, but then many of them became blind and deaf again. And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do.
interpretation: This verse describes the state of those who persist in denial and rejection despite receiving guidance and clear signs. The blindness and deafness are metaphorical, representing spiritual heedlessness and deliberate disregard for truth. The verse illustrates a cyclical pattern of those who reject Allah's message: they are given an opportunity through Allah's mercy to perceive and understand, yet they choose again to turn away from guidance. This demonstrates that continued rejection of truth hardens the heart and seals the faculties of perception, making one insensitive to signs and warnings. The verse concludes by reminding that Allah's complete awareness encompasses all human actions and intentions, suggesting an ultimate accountability for such persistent choices.

translation: Indeed, those who have said, 'Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary,' have disbelieved. And the Messiah has said, 'O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord. Indeed, he who associates partners with Allah—Allah has forbidden him Paradise, and his refuge is the Fire. And there are not for the wrongdoers any helpers.'
interpretation: This verse condemns the Christian doctrine of the divinity of Jesus Christ, emphasizing that such belief constitutes disbelief (kufr) in Islamic monotheism. The verse powerfully uses the testimony of Jesus himself—commanding worship of Allah alone and warning against shirk (associating partners with Allah)—to establish that Jesus himself rejected any claim to divinity. The consequence of shirk is eternal exclusion from Paradise and consignment to the Fire, with no one to aid those who persist in this fundamental error. The verse thus establishes that monotheism (tawhid) is the central requirement of faith, and any deviation into polytheism, including the elevation of created beings to divine status, represents a grave violation that severs one from Divine mercy.

translation: Those who say, 'Indeed, Allah is the third of three,' have disbelieved. And there is no deity except one Deity. If they do not desist from what they are saying, there will surely afflict the disbelievers among them a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse refutes the Christian concept of the Trinity by emphasizing God's absolute oneness (Tawhid). The passage condemns associating partners with Allah in His divinity and warns that those who persist in this belief—specifically the Christian doctrine that God is three persons—will face severe punishment. The verse underscores that monotheism is not negotiable in Islam, and polytheistic beliefs, whether explicit or theological, represent a fundamental rejection of faith. The warning of painful punishment is directed at those who, despite understanding the message, stubbornly refuse to abandon their false beliefs about God's nature.

translation: Then will they not repent to Allah and ask His forgiveness? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse presents a rhetorical call to repentance, emphasizing both the urgency of turning back to Allah and His readiness to forgive. The phrase 'Afala' (then will they not) expresses reproach and wonder at those who persist in wrongdoing despite having the opportunity to seek forgiveness. The verse underscores that repentance and seeking forgiveness are always open pathways available to humanity, and concludes by affirming Allah's essential attributes of forgiveness and mercy as a source of hope and encouragement for the repentant, regardless of the severity of their sins.

translation: The Messiah, son of Mary, is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him. And his mother was a woman of truth. They both used to eat food. Look how We make clear to them the signs; then look how they are deluded.
interpretation: This verse establishes the humanity of Jesus Christ and refutes the Christian doctrine of his divinity by emphasizing that he was merely a messenger like all the prophets before him, subject to the same human needs and limitations such as eating food. The reference to Mary as 'a woman of truth' establishes her righteousness without elevating her to divine status. The verse concludes by highlighting the contradiction in those who deny the clear signs of God's oneness—despite the evidence being plainly presented, they continue to turn away from the truth, which is a remarkable manifestation of human obstinacy in the face of clear guidance.

translation: Say, 'Do you worship besides Allah that which possesses for you neither harm nor benefit? And Allah - He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.'
interpretation: The verse challenges the logical inconsistency of worshipping idols or entities other than Allah by appealing to reason: if these beings cannot control outcomes in one's life, neither protecting nor benefiting the worshipper, then the act of devotion to them is fundamentally irrational and devoid of purpose. The reference to Allah's attributes of hearing and knowing at the verse's conclusion emphasizes that only the Almighty, who is fully aware of all things and listens to His servants, deserves worship and devotion.

translation: Say, 'O People of the Scripture, do not exaggerate in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the desires of a people who went astray before and led many astray, and strayed from the right path.'
interpretation: This verse warns against religious extremism and blind following of human desires masquerading as divine guidance. The 'People of the Scripture' refers to Christians and Jews who had deviated from their original teachings through innovations and exaggerations—such as deifying Jesus or creating forbidden practices. The verse emphasizes that true faith lies in adhering to objective truth rather than the subjective whims of religious leaders who have themselves been misguided. It calls believers to independent discernment and a return to the straight path, implicitly positioning Islam as the authentic continuation of monotheistic faith and warning the Muslim community against repeating the same patterns of deviation that afflicted previous religious communities.

translation: Those who disbelieved from the Children of Israel were cursed by the tongue of David and Jesus, son of Mary. That is because they disobeyed and were transgressing.
interpretation: This verse indicates that the disbelievers among the Children of Israel incurred divine curse through the pronouncement of the righteous prophets David and Jesus, who called down judgment upon those who persistently violated God's commands and exceeded the bounds of obedience. The curse is presented as a consequence of their rebellion against divine guidance and their transgressive behavior, emphasizing that rejection of God's message and refusal to obey His prophets results in divine disapproval and condemnation.

translation: They did not forbid one another from the evil they committed. How evil was what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse condemns the failure of a community to collectively discourage and prevent evil practices among themselves. The verse emphasizes that moral responsibility is not merely individual but communal - a society that permits wrongdoing to persist unchecked without mutual admonishment shares in the blame for that evil. The strong censure ('labbisa') highlights how this passivity compounds the sin, as the community's silence becomes complicit in perpetuating transgression. This teaches that believers have a duty to enjoin good and forbid evil, and that the absence of this collective moral courage is itself a grave moral failure.

translation: You see many of them taking the disbelievers as allies. Wretched is what their souls have sent forward for them, that Allah has become angry with them and in the punishment they will abide eternally.
interpretation: This verse exposes the spiritual danger of choosing association with those who reject Allah over loyalty to the faith community. The phrase 'what their souls have sent forward' refers to their sinful choices and actions which precede them on the Day of Judgment, emphasizing that every individual is ultimately accountable for their own decisions. The consequence—Allah's anger and eternal punishment—demonstrates that aligning oneself with disbelief compromises one's relationship with the Divine and invokes divine displeasure. The verse serves as a warning about the irreversible nature of conscious rejection of truth and the necessity of maintaining loyalty to the correct path rather than being swayed by worldly considerations or social pressures.

translation: And if they had believed in Allah and the Prophet and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies, but many of them are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: The verse reveals that the rejection of the believers' enemies and their adoption of other allies as protectors is fundamentally rooted in a lack of true faith. The condition 'if they had believed' indicates that genuine belief in Allah and His messenger necessitates loyalty to them and their guidance. The consequent clause shows that the enemies' choice to ally with others and distance themselves from the believers is not a matter of mere preference or circumstance, but rather a manifestation of their spiritual rebellion and refusal to submit to divine truth. This demonstrates that apostasy and wrongdoing are not isolated actions but symptoms of a deeper rejection of faith itself.

translation: You will surely find that the most hostile people towards the believers are the Jews and those who associate partners with Allah. And you will surely find that the closest in affection to the believers are those who say, 'We are Christians.' That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they do not show arrogance.
interpretation: This verse indicates that among the People of the Book and polytheists, the Christians demonstrated greater spiritual humility and intellectual openness compared to the Jews and idolaters of that time. Their proximity to the believers stems from their institutional structure of ascetic scholars (priests and monks) who cultivated spiritual discipline and freedom from arrogance, qualities that enable receptiveness to divine truth. The verse is not making a blanket theological statement about these groups for all times, but rather describing a historical observation about the relative attitudes toward the believers during the Qur'anic period—their freedom from stubborn pride made them more inclined toward understanding and peaceful coexistence with the Muslim community.

translation: And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of what they have recognized of the truth. They say, 'Our Lord, we have believed, so write us down among the witnesses.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the emotional and spiritual response of believers—particularly those among the People of the Book—who recognize divine truth when they encounter the Qur'an. Their tears signify genuine faith and deep emotional connection to God's message, while their prayer to be written among the witnesses demonstrates their desire to align themselves with the community of believers and to have their testimony recorded in the sight of God. The verse emphasizes that true belief produces visible signs of devotion and transforms the heart to seek proximity to God.

translation: And why should we not believe in Allah and in what has come to us of the truth, while we hope that our Lord will admit us among the righteous people?
interpretation: This verse reflects the sincere desire of believers to embrace faith and righteous deeds as a means of attaining closeness to Allah and joining the company of the virtuous. It conveys that accepting truth and having hope in divine mercy motivates believers toward continuous striving for righteousness, as they recognize that belief combined with righteous action is the pathway to being counted among Allah's favored servants.

translation: So Allah rewarded them for what they said with gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they will abide eternally. And that is the reward of those who do good.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of divine recompense based on righteous action and speech. The reward of Paradise with its eternal gardens and flowing rivers is not arbitrary but is directly linked to what the believers said—referring to their sincere testimony of faith and their righteous words. The phrase 'that is the reward of those who do good' (جزاء المحسنين) emphasizes that this ultimate reward is reserved exclusively for those who combine both sincere speech and virtuous deeds, demonstrating that true excellence (ihsan) in the sight of Allah encompasses both the inward faith expressed through words and the outward manifestation through righteous conduct.

translation: And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs - those are the companions of the Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse establishes a fundamental principle of divine justice: that the ultimate consequence of persistent disbelief and deliberate rejection of God's clear signs is eternal punishment in the Hellfire. The dual action of disbelieving (kufr) and denying (takdhib) indicates a willful and obstinate rejection rather than mere ignorance, emphasizing personal accountability for turning away from divine truth despite its clarity.

translation: O you who have believed, do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love those who transgress.
interpretation: This verse warns against unnecessary self-imposed restrictions and excessive asceticism that go beyond what Allah has prescribed, encouraging believers to enjoy the permissible blessings Allah has provided while maintaining moderation and not exceeding the divinely set boundaries. It teaches that piety lies in obedience to Allah's actual commands, not in self-invented prohibitions or imbalanced extremism.

translation: And eat from that which Allah has provided for you, lawful and good; and fear Allah in whom you are believers
interpretation: This verse instructs believers to sustain themselves through permissible and wholesome provisions while maintaining consciousness of Allah. The juxtaposition of eating lawful sustenance with piety suggests that righteous consumption—awareness of the source and nature of one's food—is an expression of faith and obedience, establishing that material provision and spiritual responsibility are inseparable. By reminding them that they are believers in Allah, the verse appeals to their commitment to align their actions, even in the mundane act of eating, with divine guidance.

translation: Allah will not hold you accountable for unintentional oaths, but He will hold you accountable for oaths you have deliberately made binding. Its expiation is the feeding of ten poor people from the midst of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. And whoever finds not the means shall fast for three days. That is the expiation of your oaths when you have sworn. And guard your oaths. Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs so that you may give thanks.
interpretation: This verse establishes a distinction between careless, unintentional utterances and deliberate, binding oaths, teaching that Divine accountability is proportionate to human intention and will. The graduated expiation—feeding, clothing, or freeing slaves, with fasting as an accessible alternative—demonstrates Divine mercy while simultaneously emphasizing the seriousness of oath-taking through a meaningful obligation. The command to guard oaths serves not merely as legal instruction but as a moral teaching that truthfulness in word and fidelity in commitment are essential qualities that cultivate consciousness of God (taqwa) and gratitude (shukr), making one's words and promises reflections of one's inner spiritual state.

translation: O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrifices to] idols, and divining arrows are, in fact, uncleanness from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you might succeed.
interpretation: This verse establishes that intoxicants and gambling are not merely harmful habits but spiritual pollutants originating from Satan's influence, making their avoidance a fundamental part of sincere faith and moral purification. The condition 'that you might succeed' indicates that success in this life and the afterlife is contingent upon distancing oneself from these corrupting influences, emphasizing that true prosperity comes through obedience to divine guidance and resistance to satanic temptations.

translation: Satan only wants to sow enmity and hatred among you through intoxicants and gambling, and to divert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. Will you then not desist?
interpretation: This verse reveals Satan's strategy of exploiting worldly temptations—specifically intoxicants and gambling—as vehicles to corrupt human relationships and disconnect people from their spiritual obligations. The verse emphasizes that these vices are not merely individual moral failings but weapons deliberately employed to fracture community bonds and sever the connection between humans and their Creator. The rhetorical question at the end serves as a powerful call to consciousness, inviting the believers to recognize this satanic scheme and choose the path of abstinence, thereby preserving both their spiritual relationship with Allah and their social harmony with one another.

translation: And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that upon Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance [of the message].
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that obedience to Allah and His Messenger is essential for believers, while warning them of the consequences of disobedience. The reassurance that follows—that the Messenger's responsibility is only to clearly convey the message—serves to remind believers that while guidance is their choice, rejection of the message places the burden of accountability upon those who reject it, not upon the Messenger. The verse thus establishes both the obligation of obedience and the Messenger's fulfilled duty in clear communication, leaving the final choice to the people themselves.

translation: There is no blame upon those who have believed and done righteous deeds for what they have eaten, if they fear Allah and believe and do righteous deeds, then fear Allah and believe, then fear Allah and do good. And Allah loves the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse conveys that sincere believers who maintain piety (taqwa) and righteous conduct are absolved of minor transgressions or ambiguous matters of lawfulness, as their consistent commitment to faith and good works demonstrates their underlying sincerity and proper intention. The repetition of the conditions—fearing Allah, believing, and doing good—emphasizes that the path to spiritual security lies in continuous vigilance, unwavering faith, and the pursuit of excellence in conduct, with Allah's love and approval being the ultimate consequence of such steadfast righteousness.

translation: O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and spears can reach, so that Allah may know who fears Him unseen. So whoever transgresses after that for him is a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse establishes that Allah tests the believers' righteousness and god-consciousness through their restraint and obedience to His commands, specifically regarding the hunting of game during the state of ihram (ritual consecration in pilgrimage). The test reveals one's true fear of Allah and submission to His will when removed from the scrutiny of others, demonstrating that genuine piety is demonstrated in private obedience. The warning of severe punishment for those who transgress after understanding Allah's command emphasizes that the test is designed to distinguish between those whose faith is genuine and those whose obedience is merely outward, thereby establishing that divine guidance depends upon sincere internal commitment to Allah's laws.

translation: O you who have believed, do not hunt game while you are in a state of ihram (pilgrimage sanctity). And whoever among you kills it intentionally, then the penalty is an equivalent from livestock, to be judged by two just men among you, as an offering reaching the Ka'bah; or alternatively, expiation by feeding the poor, or an equivalent in fasting, so that he may taste the evil consequences of his deed. Allah has pardoned what is past; but whoever returns to it - then Allah will take retribution from him. And Allah is Mighty and Owner of Retribution.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the sanctity of the pilgrimage state demands respect for all life within the sacred precinct, imposing accountability through restorative justice rather than mere punishment. The emphasis on deliberation ('mutamadan'), the requirement of just arbitration, and the multiple pathways for expiation—livestock, feeding the poor, or fasting—demonstrates that Islamic law seeks to reform the transgressor and restore balance through meaningful consequences that connect the offender's own deprivation to the harm caused. The phrase 'so that he may taste the evil consequences of his deed' reveals that the purpose of these penalties is not retributive satisfaction but rather experiential learning and moral transformation, enabling the believer to internalize the gravity of violating sacred boundaries and to develop piety through disciplined restitution.

translation: Lawful to you is the catch of the sea and its food as provision for you and for travelers, but forbidden to you is the hunt of land animals as long as you are in the state of ihram. And be mindful of Allah to whom you will be gathered.
interpretation: This verse establishes a balanced set of divine regulations for pilgrims in the sacred state, permitting the bounties of the sea as sustenance while restricting hunting on land as a spiritual discipline. The permission for sea provisions reflects Allah's mercy in providing sustenance even during sacred observance, while the prohibition on land hunting is a test of devotion and a means of cultivating taqwa—the consciousness of Allah that compels obedience not through hardship but through mindful awareness of divine judgment.

translation: Allah has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, an establishment for the people, and [has made sacred] the sacred month, the offerings, and the garlands. That is so that you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth, and that Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the sacred symbols and rituals of pilgrimage—the Ka'bah, the sacred months, sacrificial offerings, and the ritual garlands—are divinely ordained institutions that serve as a means for humanity to recognize and acknowledge Allah's absolute knowledge and sovereignty. By instituting these visible, tangible signs on earth, Allah demonstrates that His knowledge encompasses all of creation, both the seen and unseen realms, and this awareness of His omniscience should inspire reverence, submission, and proper observance of His sacred ordinances.

translation: Know that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse establishes a balance between two fundamental divine attributes: Allah's justice and His mercy. It warns believers that transgression carries serious consequences, while simultaneously emphasizing that repentance and seeking forgiveness are always possible. The juxtaposition of these contrasting attributes is meant to instill both reverence and hope in the believer's heart—fear of divine justice should deter from sin, while faith in divine mercy should encourage turning back to Allah with sincere repentance.

translation: There is nothing upon the Messenger except to convey [the message]. And Allah knows what you disclose and what you conceal.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the limited responsibility of the Prophet Muhammad - his duty is only to communicate the message of God clearly to people, not to force them to believe or guarantee their acceptance. The statement that Allah knows both what is openly displayed and what is hidden in hearts serves as a reminder that while humans may hide their intentions or reject the message outwardly, God is fully aware of all states of the soul, implying that ultimate judgment belongs to God alone, not to the Messenger or any human authority.

translation: Say, 'The foul and the pure are not alike, even though the abundance of the foul might please you.' So fear Allah, O people of understanding, that you might succeed.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the fundamental principle that moral and spiritual distinctions are absolute and immutable regardless of worldly success or popularity. The mention of 'abundance of the foul' pleasing observers warns against being swayed by the outward prosperity or prevalence of vice and corruption in society. True discernment—the quality of those with understanding ('ulul-albab')—requires recognizing that quantity and worldly appeal do not determine moral worth. The call to fear Allah connects this recognition to piety and obedience, suggesting that genuine success and prosperity derive from adhering to what is pure and morally sound, not from following what merely appears attractive or prevalent in the material world.

translation: O you who have believed, do not ask about matters which, if they are made clear to you, will trouble you. And if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be made clear to you. Allah has pardoned that which is past, and Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.
interpretation: This verse teaches believers to refrain from raising unnecessary questions about religious matters that are not explicitly addressed in revelation, as pursuing such inquiries may lead to confusion or distress. The verse warns against speculative questioning during the time of revelation, as such questions could complicate the faith of the community. Instead, believers should accept what Allah has already pardoned and clarified, trusting in His wisdom and forbearance rather than burdening themselves and others with exhaustive questioning about matters that are not central to the faith.

translation: A people before you had already asked about it, then they became disbelievers in it (the she-camel).
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of Thamud who demanded a she-camel as a sign from their prophet Salih, and when Allah provided it as a clear miracle, they rejected it and became disbelievers, ultimately leading to their destruction. The verse serves as a warning that asking for signs is not enough without sincere faith, and that rejection of clear divine miracles results in divine punishment.

translation: Allah has not made for you any prohibition regarding Bahira, nor Saiba, nor Wasila, nor Hami. But those who disbelieve invent lies about Allah, and most of them do not use reason.
interpretation: This verse rejects the false practices and superstitions that pre-Islamic Arabs had invented, falsely attributing them to divine law. The verse clarifies that Allah never ordained these arbitrary restrictions on livestock, thereby condemning the attribution of human inventions to the Divine. It emphasizes that disbelief fundamentally consists of fabricating falsehoods against Allah while lacking the intellectual capacity to recognize truth, highlighting how false religious practices stem from spiritual blindness rather than authentic divine guidance.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger,' they say, 'Sufficient for us is that upon which we found our fathers.' Even if their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?
interpretation: This verse exposes the fallacy of blind adherence to ancestral traditions as a substitute for truth. Those who reject divine guidance rationalize their rejection through inherited customs, yet the verse challenges this reasoning by highlighting the absurdity of following the example of those who themselves lacked knowledge and spiritual guidance. The rhetorical question implies that following the ignorant is unjustifiable, establishing that truth must be evaluated on its own merit rather than validated merely by its antiquity or ancestral practice. This addresses the human tendency to defer moral and spiritual responsibility to tradition rather than engage in sincere, critical investigation of divine revelation.

translation: O you who have believed, upon you is [responsibility for] yourselves. Those who have gone astray will not harm you when you have been guided. To Allah is your return all together, and He will inform you of what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes personal accountability and spiritual independence, instructing believers to focus on their own faith and conduct rather than becoming preoccupied with the misguidance of others. It establishes that individual salvation depends on one's own commitment to guidance, not on the failures of others, while simultaneously reminding believers that all will ultimately answer to Allah for their deeds. The verse thus balances personal responsibility with the consolation that believers need not despair over the straying of others, provided they themselves remain steadfast on the path of righteousness.

translation: O you who have believed, testimony [is required] among you when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest - [let there be] two just men of your people or two [just men] from outside if you are traveling through the land and the misfortune of death should befall you. Detain them after prayer and let them both swear by Allah, [saying], 'We will not exchange it for any price, even if he were a near relative, and we will not withhold the testimony of Allah. Indeed, we would then be among the sinners.'
interpretation: This verse establishes the legal requirement for witnesses in cases of testamentary bequest, emphasizing that justice and truthfulness must override all worldly considerations, including familial ties or financial incentives. The verse teaches that bearing false witness or concealing testimony is a grave sin that corrupts not only individual character but also the fabric of society's judicial integrity, and that believers must prioritize their duty to Allah and truth above all else.

translation: But if it is discovered that the two were guilty of sin, then two others from those who have a better claim shall take their place, and they shall swear by Allah, 'Our testimony is more truthful than their testimony, and we have not transgressed. Indeed, if we did, we would then be among the wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse establishes a judicial mechanism for correcting false testimony in cases of inheritance disputes. It emphasizes that when two witnesses are found to have committed perjury, they are replaced by other qualified witnesses from among the heirs who have a greater right to speak truthfully. The verse underscores the gravity of bearing witness by requiring the replacement witnesses to invoke Allah's name, affirming the supremacy of truthful testimony over false testimony and acknowledging that transgression in this matter constitutes a serious wrongdoing. The passage highlights the Islamic legal system's commitment to justice and the sanctity of truth-telling under oath.

translation: That is more likely so that they will give testimony in its proper form, or fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths. And fear Allah and listen. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that establishing proper procedures for testimony - particularly the rules of evidence and oaths in legal matters - serves the purpose of ensuring truthfulness and accountability. By fearing that false oaths may be exposed and their own credibility destroyed in return, people are more likely to speak truthfully. The verse teaches that fear of Allah's justice and willingness to obey His laws are prerequisites for guidance, while those who knowingly turn away from Allah's commands and persist in transgression cut themselves off from divine guidance. The phrase 'fear Allah and listen' represents the complete submission required of believers - both inward reverence and outward obedience to what is commanded.

translation: On the Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, 'What response did you receive?' They will say, 'We have no knowledge. Indeed, You alone are the Knower of the unseen.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the ultimate limitation of human knowledge, even among the most honored creation - the messengers. Despite their divine mission and proximity to Allah, the messengers will acknowledge complete ignorance about certain matters on the Day of Judgment, specifically regarding how their messages were ultimately received and the true states of people's hearts. This humbles all knowledge and redirects absolute understanding exclusively to Allah, emphasizing that complete knowledge of hidden realities belongs only to Him, and serves as a reminder that even the greatest among humanity must defer to Allah's infinite wisdom and knowledge.

translation: When Allah said, 'O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My favor upon you and upon your mother when I supported you with the Holy Spirit. You spoke to people in the cradle and in maturity. And when I taught you the Scripture, wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel. And when you fashioned from clay the form of a bird by My permission, then you breathed into it and it became a bird by My permission. And you healed the blind from birth and the leper by My permission. And when you brought forth the dead by My permission. And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you when you came to them with clear proofs, those who disbelieved among them said, "This is not but evident magic."'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the comprehensive nature of divine support granted to Jesus, establishing that all his miracles and abilities were performed by Allah's permission and authority, not through his own power. The repetition of "by My permission" (بإذني) underscores that Jesus was a servant of Allah through whom Allah manifested His will and signs, thereby refuting any notion of Jesus possessing independent divine power or being a deity. The verse establishes Jesus as a messenger and servant who was honored with extraordinary abilities to confirm his message, while maintaining the absolute sovereignty and authorship of all miracles with Allah alone.

translation: And when I inspired the disciples to believe in Me and in My Messenger, they said: 'We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the immediate and wholehearted acceptance of faith by the disciples when they received divine guidance. Their affirmation demonstrates the proper response to revelation—not mere intellectual assent, but a complete submission to God's will (Islam). The phrase 'bear witness' emphasizes their public declaration and commitment, showing that true belief necessitates both inner conviction and outward testimony. Their willingness to submit entirely to both God and His Messenger exemplifies the ideal of unconditional obedience to divine instruction.

translation: When the disciples said, 'O Jesus, son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?' He said, 'Fear Allah, if you are believers.'
interpretation: Jesus responds to the disciples' request for a miraculous sign not with immediate fulfillment, but with spiritual redirection. By invoking taqwa (God-consciousness and fear of Allah), he teaches that true faith should not be contingent upon witnessing extraordinary miracles, nor should believers make demands of God based on their desires. This response reveals that the test of genuine belief lies in submitting to God's will and maintaining conscious obedience, rather than in pursuing sensational proofs. The disciples' question itself reflects a weakness in their understanding of faith—they seek material validation rather than spiritual certainty—which Jesus corrects by emphasizing that authentic believers must first establish their relationship with God through consciousness of His majesty and compliance with His guidance.

translation: They said: 'We wish to eat from it, and let our hearts be at peace, and that we may know that you have told us the truth, and that we may be witnesses to it.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the disciples' request for a tangible sign - a meal from heaven - to strengthen their faith and serve as evidence for others. It demonstrates how even believers may seek physical manifestations of divine power to deepen their certainty and provide them with compelling proof they can share with others, revealing the human need for sensory evidence alongside spiritual belief.

translation: Jesus, son of Mary, said: 'O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table from heaven that will be a feast for us—for the first of us and the last of us—and a sign from You. And provide for us, for You are the best of providers.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates how Jesus, despite possessing miraculous powers, directed his followers to seek their sustenance directly from Allah rather than relying solely on material provisions or his own authority. The request for a table from heaven symbolizes the need for divine provision and blessing, emphasizing that true sustenance—both physical and spiritual—comes from Allah alone. The designation of the table as an 'Eid' (festival/feast) and a 'sign' demonstrates that provision is not merely about survival but about the mercy and communication of Allah with His servants, transforming daily sustenance into a manifestation of divine care and a reminder of Allah's generosity toward His creation.

translation: Allah said: 'Indeed, I will send it down upon you. But whoever among you disbelieves after that, then I will surely punish him with a punishment the likes of which I have not punished anyone among the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse conveys a profound warning about the severity of rejecting divine guidance after it has been clearly made available. The punishment promised is not merely severe, but uniquely suited to the gravity of the transgression—it represents a punishment greater than any inflicted upon previous peoples who rejected their messages. This emphasizes that rejection of divine signs becomes increasingly culpable when clarity and knowledge are present, and that Allah's justice is calibrated according to the degree of one's understanding and deliberate turning away from truth.

translation: And when Allah said, 'O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as deities besides Allah?"' He said, 'Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say. If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen.'
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute transcendence of Allah and the limits of human knowledge, while demonstrating Jesus's complete innocence of the false claim attributed to his followers. Through Jesus's response, the Qur'an emphasizes that only Allah possesses complete knowledge of all hidden matters and human intentions, and that Jesus himself did not claim divinity nor would he dare attribute partners to Allah. The exchange illustrates the principle that while Jesus knows his own thoughts and intentions, only Allah possesses omniscience of all secrets and the unseen, thereby addressing the Christian doctrine of the Trinity and affirming strict monotheism.

translation: I told them nothing except what You commanded me: 'Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.' And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them. But when You took me up, You became the watcher over them, and You are a witness over all things.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of prophetic integrity and the transference of divine oversight—a prophet's responsibility is limited to conveying the message without alteration or addition, and upon his departure from the community, Allah alone assumes the role of witness and guardian of their affairs, emphasizing that ultimate accountability rests with God rather than with the messenger.

translation: If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants. And if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the complete sovereignty of Allah over His creation, emphasizing that all beings are His servants regardless of whether they face punishment or forgiveness. The phrase demonstrates that both justice and mercy are manifestations of Allah's ultimate power and wisdom—punishment does not diminish His authority over His servants, nor does forgiveness compromise it. Rather, both divine actions flow from His supreme wisdom and might, establishing that all outcomes in the divine plan serve the purposes of an all-knowing and all-powerful God.

translation: Allah said: 'This is a Day on which the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness. For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they shall dwell forever. Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him. That is the great attainment.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that truthfulness and sincerity in faith are rewarded with eternal paradise and the highest favor of Allah. The mutual satisfaction between Allah and the righteous servants represents a reciprocal bond of love and approval that transcends the transactional nature of deeds and rewards, indicating that the ultimate success lies not merely in entering paradise but in achieving complete harmony and contentment with the Divine.

translation: To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is within them. And He is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute sovereignty and ownership of Allah over all creation. It emphasizes that nothing exists outside of Allah's domain or control, and that His power extends comprehensively to every aspect of existence. The verse is foundational to Islamic theology, affirming that Allah's dominion is not limited by time, space, or any condition, and that His power to create, sustain, and command all things is complete and without restriction.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darkness and the light. Then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord.
interpretation: This verse establishes that despite Allah's clear signs of creative power evident in the ordered universe—where darkness and light exist in perfect distinction and harmony—those who reject faith persist in associating partners with Him. The progression from praising Allah's creation to condemning disbelievers' actions highlights the inexcusability of shirk (associating partners with Allah) in the face of such manifest evidence of His oneness and majesty. The verse underscores that rejecting monotheism is not due to lack of evidence but to willful denial and spiritual blindness.

translation: He is the One Who created you from clay, then decreed a term for you, and there is another term appointed with Him. Yet you still doubt.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes human accountability for our disbelief and hesitation regarding Allah's predetermined plan for our lives. The progression from creation to appointed terms highlights that Allah has set both a natural lifespan and a specific moment of reckoning known only to Him, yet despite this clear divine framework, people remain in doubt and denial about the reality of the afterlife and divine judgment. The verse critiques this willful skepticism as unreasonable given the manifest signs of our creation and the evidence of divine wisdom in the ordering of all affairs.

translation: And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth. He knows your secrets and what you reveal, and He knows what you earn.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's omniscience and omnipresence as the ultimate reality and authority in all creation. By stating that Allah is God in both the heavens and the earth, it establishes His supreme dominion over all realms of existence. The subsequent clause about knowing secrets and what is revealed underscores that no aspect of human conduct—whether hidden thoughts or public actions—escapes His knowledge, and the mention of knowing what we earn (our deeds and their consequences) reinforces personal accountability before Allah on the Day of Judgment. The verse thus serves to instill consciousness of divine watchfulness as a foundation for moral responsibility.

translation: And there never comes to them a sign from the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it.
interpretation: This verse describes the spiritual blindness and obstinate rejection of those who refuse to acknowledge divine guidance despite clear evidence. Their persistent aversion to God's signs demonstrates that their disbelief stems not from lack of evidence but from deliberate choice and hardened hearts; the problem lies within themselves, not in the clarity or sufficiency of the signs presented to them.

translation: So they have denied the truth when it came to them. Soon there will come to them news of that which they used to mock.
interpretation: This verse conveys a warning of divine retribution against those who reject the truth and ridicule it. The structure suggests an inevitable consequence: those who turn away from divine guidance and scoff at it will eventually face the reality of what they mocked, serving as a lesson that mockery of truth is not without consequence in the sight of God. The phrase 'news of that which they used to mock' suggests that they will witness the fulfillment of what they dismissed, thereby experiencing regret and understanding the gravity of their rejection.

translation: Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established in the earth with capabilities We have not given to you, and We sent down upon them rain in abundance, and We made rivers flow beneath them? Yet We destroyed them for their sins and created after them another generation.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that previous nations possessed greater material resources and power than the current generation, yet their transgression led to their destruction. The reference to rain and rivers symbolizes divine provision and blessing, indicating that material abundance is not a guarantee of safety; rather, it is adherence to divine guidance that ensures salvation. The message warns the listener's community that they too can face destruction if they persist in disobedience, regardless of their current status or advantages.

translation: And if We had sent down to you a book upon parchment so they could touch it with their hands, those who have disbelieved would still say, 'This is nothing but obvious magic.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates that the disbelievers' rejection is not based on rational examination or material evidence, but rather stems from a pre-existing spiritual blindness and hardness of heart. Even if God provided them with tangible, physical proof—a book written on parchment that they could feel with their own hands—they would still attribute it to sorcery rather than acknowledge it as divine revelation. The verse demonstrates that the fundamental barrier to belief is not the availability of signs or evidence, but the willful refusal to accept the truth that comes from arrogance, stubbornness, and spiritual heedlessness.

translation: And they said, 'Why has not an angel been sent down to him?' But if We had sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and then they would not be reprieved.
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers' demand for angelic confirmation of the Prophet's message, while divine wisdom determines that such a miraculous intervention would remove human free choice and hastily execute judgment upon them. God's mercy delays decisive punishment to allow time for reflection and belief, demonstrating that the natural process of prophethood through a human messenger is more conducive to genuine faith and accountability than coercive miraculous signs.

translation: And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have confused them in the same way they are confused.
interpretation: This verse addresses the objection of the disbelievers who demanded that the Prophet Muhammad be an angel rather than a human. The interpretation reveals that even if Allah had sent an angel, He would have given it a human form to communicate with humans on their level. The phrase 'We would have confused them' indicates that the disbelievers' fundamental problem is not the form of the messenger but their own spiritual confusion and resistance to truth—changing the messenger's form would not resolve their obstinate rejection, as their confusion stems from their own hearts, not from the nature of the revelation or the messenger.

translation: And certainly, messengers before you were mocked, but those who scoffed at them were enveloped by what they used to mock.
interpretation: This verse provides historical consolation to the Prophet Muhammad by reminding him that previous messengers also faced ridicule and mockery from their people. The deeper meaning is a warning about divine justice: those who mock the messengers ultimately face the very punishment they ridiculed—whether in this life through humiliation and defeat, or in the Hereafter. The verse emphasizes that mockery of divine guidance is not without consequences, as Allah's justice inevitably catches up with the mockers, turning their derision into their own destruction.

translation: Say: 'Travel through the earth and then see how was the end of those who denied (the truth).'
interpretation: This verse invites reflection through empirical observation of history. The Qur'an directs believers to travel and witness the ruins and remnants of previous civilizations that rejected their prophets, thereby understanding that rejection of divine guidance inevitably leads to destruction and ruin. This serves as a powerful argument for the truthfulness of the message, as the pattern of divine punishment for denial is observable in the historical record of destroyed nations, encouraging believers to avoid the same fate and to have confidence in the Qur'anic narrative.

translation: Say: 'To whom belongs all that is in the heavens and the earth?' Say: 'To Allah.' He has prescribed for Himself mercy, that He will surely gather you unto the Day of Resurrection, in which there is no doubt. Those who have lost their souls - it is they who do not believe.
interpretation: This verse establishes Allah's absolute ownership and dominion over creation as the foundation for faith and moral responsibility. The emphasis on Allah's self-prescribed mercy toward His creatures demonstrates His justice in gathering all people on the Day of Judgment where they will be held accountable. The concluding statement about those who lose themselves reveals that disbelief is ultimately a form of self-destruction - those who reject the truth despite Allah's clear signs and manifest mercy are the ones who forfeit their souls, choosing destruction over salvation.

translation: And to Him belongs whatever rests during the night and the day. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's complete sovereignty and ownership over all creation at all times. The phrase 'whatever rests' (ma sakana) refers to all creatures and things that settle or remain in existence throughout day and night, indicating nothing escapes His dominion regardless of when or where it exists. The conjunction of His attribute as 'All-Hearing' and 'All-Knowing' reinforces that His ownership is not merely titular but actively exercised through His complete awareness of all that occurs within His creation, suggesting that divine sovereignty is inseparable from divine vigilance and knowledge of all affairs.

translation: Say, 'Shall I take as a protector other than Allah, the Creator of the heavens and the earth? And He feeds but is not fed.' Say, 'Indeed, I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit [to Allah], and do not be among those who associate partners with Allah.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the logical impossibility and irrationality of seeking protection or reliance (wilayah) from anyone other than Allah, the Creator who sustains all existence. By highlighting that Allah alone feeds all creation without needing sustenance, the verse demonstrates His absolute self-sufficiency and complete power. The Prophet is then commanded to declare his firm submission to this monotheistic principle, establishing himself as the foremost exemplar of Islamic surrender to Allah's oneness, and is warned against any form of shirk (associating partners with Allah). The verse thus serves as a call to reject all false gods and loyalties, and to anchor one's trust exclusively in the Divine sustainer.

translation: Say: 'Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great Day.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the Prophet's sincere fear of Allah and his complete submission to divine commands. It conveys that obedience to Allah is not merely a matter of external compliance, but stems from genuine reverence and awareness of accountability on the Day of Judgment. The Prophet's expressed fear serves as a model for believers, teaching that true piety is rooted in consciousness of Allah's majesty and the ultimate consequences of disobedience, rather than in blind ritual or social conformity.

translation: Whoever is turned away from the Fire on that Day, He has indeed had mercy upon him; and that is the clear triumph.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that salvation on the Day of Judgment is fundamentally an act of divine mercy rather than something earned by human effort alone. The 'turning away' from the Fire represents deliverance from punishment, which is presented as the direct result of God's mercy. By describing this deliverance as 'the clear triumph,' the verse teaches that true success is not measured by worldly gains but by being spared from Hell and achieving Paradise, which is entirely dependent on God's merciful will and grace.

translation: And if Allah touches you with hardship, there is no remover of it except Him. And if He touches you with good, then He is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute sovereignty and power of Allah over all affairs, emphasizing that neither harm nor benefit comes except by His will, and that reliance must be placed entirely in Him alone, as no created being possesses the ability to change one's condition without His permission.

translation: And He is the Subduer over His servants, and He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute sovereignty and control over all His creation, coupled with His perfect wisdom and knowledge of all hidden matters. The combination of divine supremacy with divine wisdom suggests that Allah's dominion is not arbitrary or tyrannical, but exercised with perfect knowledge and wisdom in all circumstances, ensuring that His governance serves the ultimate good and justice for His servants.

translation: Say, 'What thing is greatest in testimony?' Say, 'Allah is witness between me and you. And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby and whoever it reaches. Do you indeed testify that there are with Allah other deities?' Say, 'I do not testify.' Say, 'Rather, He is only one God, and indeed, I am free from whatever you associate with Him.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Allah alone is the ultimate witness and authority in all matters, and the Qur'an itself serves as evidence of the truth of the message. The Prophet is instructed to firmly reject the polytheistic claims of the Meccan disbelievers and to clearly dissociate himself from their practice of associating partners with Allah, establishing absolute monotheism as the foundation of Islamic belief and practice.

translation: Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize it as they recognize their own children. Those who have lost themselves - they do not believe.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the People of the Book possess clear knowledge of the truth about Prophet Muhammad and the Qur'an, similar to how a parent recognizes their own child with absolute certainty. Their disbelief is not due to lack of clarity or evidence, but rather stems from their own spiritual loss and self-deception—they have knowingly rejected the truth despite their clear recognition of it, thereby harming their own souls.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who fabricates lies against Allah or denies His signs? Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the greatest injustice is twofold: to fabricate false claims about Allah's nature, commands, or revelations, and to reject His clear signs. The rhetorical question implies there is no one more unjust, emphasizing that lying about Allah represents the ultimate transgression against truth and justice. The declaration that wrongdoers will not achieve success conveys both a moral principle—that injustice contains within itself the seeds of its own failure—and a divine decree that such people are cut off from true flourishing in this life and the next, as success is contingent upon alignment with divine truth.

translation: And on the Day We gather them all together, then We will say to those who associated partners (with Allah): 'Where are your partners whom you used to claim?'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the ultimate accountability and exposure on the Day of Judgment, where those who committed shirk (associating partners with Allah) will be confronted with the falsity of their claims. The rhetorical question poses a moment of realization and shame, revealing that the false deities they worshipped have abandoned them, and they will have no intercession or support. It serves as a powerful deterrent against polytheism by highlighting the futility of relying on anything other than Allah alone, and underscores the inevitability of divine reckoning where all pretenses are stripped away.

translation: Then their only excuse will be that they say: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not those who associated partners with Allah."
interpretation: This verse reveals the futile defense that polytheists will offer on the Day of Judgment. Despite their clear rejection of monotheism in this life, they will attempt to deny their shirk (associating partners with Allah), showing the desperation and delusion of the disbelievers when confronted with divine justice. Their denials will be hollow and unconvincing, as their deeds and the testimony of their own faculties will bear witness against them.

translation: Look how they lied against themselves, and lost from them was what they used to fabricate.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the self-destructive nature of fabricating falsehoods. The phrase 'lied against themselves' conveys that when people invent lies about divine matters or truth, they ultimately harm their own souls and spiritual condition. The consequence is that 'what they used to fabricate' becomes lost to them—their invented falsehoods provide no benefit, no guidance, and no spiritual sustenance. This demonstrates a profound principle: that deception and false claims about religion do not grant the deceiver any advantage, but rather leave them devoid of the very truth they rejected.

translation: And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed coverings over their hearts so they do not understand it, and in their ears is deafness. And even if they see every sign, they will not believe in it. Until when they come to you, they argue with you. Those who disbelieve say, 'This is nothing but legends of the former peoples.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the spiritual and intellectual obstruction that Allah places upon those who persistently reject faith. The 'coverings' and 'deafness' represent not physical impediments but the sealing of hearts and minds that results from repeated rejection of truth. The verse demonstrates that miraculous signs alone cannot compel belief when the soul has turned away—belief requires receptivity of the heart. The subsequent argument with the Prophet exemplifies how those whose hearts are sealed respond to divine guidance with dismissal and accusation, attributing the Qur'an to human fabrication rather than acknowledging its divine origin. This conveys the principle that Allah's guidance reaches all, but only those with sincere hearts willing to understand can truly comprehend and believe.

translation: And they forbid others from it and keep away from it themselves, yet they destroy no one but themselves, and they do not perceive it.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the consequences of hypocrisy and contradictory behavior. Those who forbid others from something while practicing it themselves, or who discourage people from a matter while engaging in it, ultimately harm only themselves. The phrase 'they do not perceive it' indicates a spiritual blindness where the wrongdoers fail to recognize that their own disobedience and duplicity are the true sources of their destruction, not external forces. This reveals a fundamental spiritual principle: that one's own actions are the measure of accountability, and self-deception about one's failings leads to ultimate ruin.

translation: And if you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire and say: 'Oh, would that we could be sent back! We would not deny the signs of our Lord, and we would be among the believers.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the tragic reality of regret in the Hereafter—those who rejected God's signs in life will desperately wish for a return to the worldly life to correct their course, but their plea reveals the impossibility of sincere belief after witnessing the reality of Divine punishment. The verse emphasizes that true faith must be embraced in this world where the test remains genuine and the choice remains free, for belief born from the fear of Hell in the afterlife lacks the moral value of voluntary faith. Thus, the verse warns believers about the folly of procrastination in faith and the consequences of rejecting clear divine guidance while opportunity exists.

translation: Rather, there has become apparent to them what they had been concealing before. And if they were returned, they would surely return to what they had been forbidden from, and indeed, they are liars.
interpretation: This verse reveals the hypocrisy of those who deny the truth; their concealed disbelief and rejection, which they had tried to hide, becomes manifest on the Day of Judgment. The verse emphasizes that their claims of faith and repentance are false, for given another chance in this world, they would inevitably return to their forbidden transgressions, exposing that their inner state has never truly changed—they are liars in their professions of belief and remorse.

translation: And they said, 'This is not but our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the denial of the afterlife by those who reject divine guidance. Their statement reveals a materialistic worldview that limits reality to the present temporal existence and denies accountability beyond death. This denial serves as a rejection of divine justice and the consequences of one's deeds, which forms a central motivation for their disbelief and immoral conduct in this life.

translation: And if you could see when they will be made to stand before their Lord. He will say, 'Is not this the truth?' They will say, 'Yes, by our Lord!' He will say, 'Then taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the moment of divine confrontation on the Day of Judgment when disbelievers are brought before Allah and their denial of truth is made undeniable to them. Despite their acknowledgment of the truth in that supreme moment, they are condemned to punishment because their disbelief during their earthly life was a deliberate rejection of clear signs. The verse emphasizes that knowledge of truth alone does not absolve one of responsibility; rather, it is the intentional refusal to believe and obey during one's lifetime that merits punishment, demonstrating that accountability is based on one's choices in the world, not on forced acknowledgment in the afterlife.

translation: Those who denied the meeting with Allah have indeed lost. When the Hour comes upon them suddenly, they will say, 'O our regret for what we neglected therein!' And they will be bearing their burdens upon their backs. Unquestionably, evil is that which they carry.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the spiritual devastation of rejecting accountability before Allah and the afterlife. The sudden arrival of the Hour catches deniers unprepared, transforming their negligence into overwhelming regret. The metaphor of bearing burdens on their backs symbolizes the inescapable consequence of their actions in life—their sins become a tangible weight they must carry, from which there is no escape or relief. The verse emphasizes that denial of the Day of Judgment does not prevent its occurrence, and those who lived heedlessly will face the full weight of their accumulated transgressions.

translation: And the worldly life is not but amusement and diversion. And indeed, the home of the Hereafter is better for those who are righteous. Then will you not reason?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the temporal and trivial nature of worldly pursuits compared to the eternal and meaningful reality of the Hereafter. By contrasting the fleeting nature of this life with the lasting benefits reserved for the God-conscious, the verse calls believers to reassess their priorities and values, urging them to invest their efforts in spiritual righteousness rather than becoming preoccupied with worldly entertainment and temporary pleasures that ultimately lead to no lasting benefit. The rhetorical question at the end serves as an appeal to human intellect and discernment, implying that reason itself should guide one toward this higher understanding.

translation: We certainly know that what they say grieves you. But indeed, they do not deny you; rather, it is the signs of Allah that the wrongdoers reject.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad's emotional distress at the people's rejection and mockery, offering him consolation by clarifying the true nature of their opposition. The grief he experiences is not due to a lack of credibility or trustworthiness in his message delivery, but stems from the willful rejection of Allah's clear signs by those whose hearts are corrupted by injustice and wrongdoing. This reframing serves to redirect the focus from personal rejection toward the deeper spiritual reality that the disbelievers are rebelling against divine truth itself, not against the Prophet as an individual, thereby providing solace and perspective during times of mockery and resistance.

translation: And indeed, messengers were denied before you, but they were patient over what they were denied and harmed until Our help came to them. And there is no changing of the words of Allah. And there has certainly come to you from the news of the messengers.
interpretation: This verse provides consolation to Prophet Muhammad by reminding him that rejection and persecution are not unique to his message, but are rather a recurring pattern in human history where the righteous endure trials until divine assistance arrives. The emphasis on 'no changing of Allah's words' signifies the immutable nature of God's promise—that patience in faith and steadfastness through adversity will ultimately result in divine support and vindication, thereby establishing a universal and unalterable principle of God's covenant with His prophets and believers.

translation: And if their turning away is grievous to you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel through the earth or a ladder to the sky to bring them a sign... And if Allah had willed, He would have gathered them all upon guidance. So be not of the ignorant ones.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet's emotional burden regarding the disbelief of his people, acknowledging his human distress while paradoxically using hyperbolic imagery (tunnels in earth, ladders to sky) to illustrate the impossibility of forcing belief through miraculous signs. The verse teaches that ultimate guidance is in Allah's hands alone, and the Prophet's responsibility is only to convey the message, not to compel faith. The final admonition warns against adopting the ignorant approach of those who respond to rejection with impatience or despair, emphasizing that wisdom lies in accepting the limits of one's role and trusting in Allah's divine will regarding who receives guidance.

translation: Only those who hear will respond, and the dead - Allah will resurrect them, then to Him they will be returned.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the spiritual divide between those receptive to God's message and those who are spiritually dead. The 'dead' refers not merely to physical death, but to those whose hearts are sealed and unresponsive to divine guidance. The verse emphasizes that true acceptance of God's message requires an active willingness to listen and understand, and that all souls will ultimately be held accountable before God regardless of their state in this life. The resurrection is presented as the moment when the truth becomes undeniable and all are brought before their Lord for judgment.

translation: And they said, 'Why has not a sign been sent down upon him from his Lord?' Say, 'Indeed, Allah is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know.'
interpretation: The verse reveals that the deniers' demand for miraculous signs stems from their ignorance rather than a lack of divine power. Allah emphasizes that the ability to produce signs is not the issue—He is fully capable—but rather that most people lack the knowledge or understanding to recognize signs even when presented to them. This suggests that the problem lies not with the absence of evidence, but with the spiritual blindness and lack of discernment of those who refuse to believe.

translation: There is not an animal on earth, nor a bird that flies on its wings, except that they are communities like you. We have not neglected anything in the Book. Then to their Lord they will be gathered.
