The messenger clarifies that he seeks no material compensation, that his purpose is purely to convey the divine message, and that he will not reject believers out of deference to the disbelievers. The emphasis on the coming meeting with the Lord underscores the ultimate accountability that awaits all souls, implying that the disbelievers' rejection stems not from rational deliberation but from ignorance of this fundamental truth and the consequences of their denial.

translation: And O my people, who will help me against Allah if I were to drive them away? Will you not then remember?
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the prophet's profound trust in God's sovereignty and His ultimate power. By rhetorically asking who could help his people against Allah if he expelled the angels or believers, the speaker emphasizes that God's will is absolute and inescapable. The rhetorical question serves to awaken the people's consciousness about their dependence on divine protection and mercy, urging them to reflect upon their relationship with God rather than relying on worldly alliances or material power. The appeal to remembrance (tذكرون) calls them to acknowledge this fundamental spiritual reality through conscious reflection.

translation: And I do not say to you that I possess the treasures of Allah, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I say that I am an angel, nor do I say to those upon whom your eyes look down that Allah will never give them any good. Allah knows best what is in their souls. Indeed, if I did so, I would then be among the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse establishes the boundaries of the Prophet's knowledge and authority, emphasizing his humanity and disclaiming supernatural powers or divine prerogatives. The Prophet rejects any claim to possess divine secrets, knowledge of the future, or the right to judge people's worth based on outward appearance or social status. The reference to not disparaging those whom people look down upon reflects the Islamic principle that true worth comes from piety and character, not social rank, and that only Allah knows the inner state of hearts. The verse reinforces that to make such false claims would constitute a grave injustice against both Allah and His creation.

translation: They said, 'O Noah, you have disputed with us and multiplied your dispute with us. So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful ones.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the people's rejection of Noah's message through their demand for immediate divine punishment. Rather than engaging sincerely with his warning, they mockingly challenge him to produce the threatened punishment as proof of his truthfulness, revealing their arrogance and spiritual blindness. Their dismissal of his lengthy preaching as mere 'dispute' shows how those who reject divine truth can reframe sincere warning as argumentativeness, using rhetorical demands as a means to evade accountability and avoid contemplating the reality of their disobedience.

translation: He said: 'Allah will bring it to you if He wills, and you will not be able to escape Him.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of Allah over all creation and events. The speaker affirms that the fulfillment of any matter rests entirely with Allah's will and divine decree, not with human effort or capability alone. Furthermore, it conveys a warning that no one can escape or thwart the will of Allah, establishing that human power is ultimately limited and subordinate to Divine power.

translation: And my advice will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah intends to lead you astray. He is your Lord, and to Him you will return.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the ultimate sovereignty of Allah's will over human guidance and misguidance. The speaker (Nuh) conveys that despite his sincere desire to counsel his people, his words cannot avail them if Allah has determined their state of misguidance, emphasizing that neither human effort nor good intentions can override divine will, and that all accountability ultimately returns to Allah as the final judge and master.

translation: Or do they say, 'He has fabricated it'? Say, 'If I have fabricated it, upon me is my crime, and I am innocent of what you commit.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the Prophet's willingness to bear full responsibility for his claims about revelation, thereby establishing his sincerity and moral confidence. By declaring that any falsehood would be his crime alone while absolving himself of their misconduct, the Prophet emphasizes that his mission is separate from and uncontaminated by the sins of those who reject it. This response serves as evidence of his truthfulness, as a fabricator would fear such accountability, whereas the Prophet's assurance reveals his certainty in the divine truth of the Qur'an.

translation: And it was revealed to Noah that none of his people will believe except those who have already believed, so do not grieve over what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse teaches that divine decree determines the outcome of human free will in matters of faith. Noah is instructed not to despair despite the apparent futility of his prophetic mission, as God has already revealed that only those destined to believe will do so. This provides comfort to the messenger by shifting the burden of responsibility from the outcome of his preaching to the faithful discharge of his duty to convey the message, while submission to God's wisdom brings peace in the face of human rejection.

translation: And construct the ark before Our eyes and [according to] Our revelation. And do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they will be drowned.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Noah's construction of the ark was done under divine supervision and guidance, stressing that every aspect of this monumental task was accomplished through Allah's direct oversight and instruction. The prohibition against interceding for the wrongdoers serves to highlight the absolute nature of divine justice and the futility of seeking mercy for those whose hearts have been sealed in rejection and arrogance. It establishes the principle that there are limits to human compassion and intercession when it comes to those who persistently deny the truth and oppress others.

translation: And he constructed the ark, and whenever a group of his people passed by him, they ridiculed him. He said, 'If you ridicule us, then we will ridicule you just as you ridicule [us].'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the steadfastness and spiritual conviction required to stand alone against overwhelming social pressure and mockery. Noah's response demonstrates that the believer's dedication to divine truth cannot be shaken by ridicule or derision from the disbelievers. His words convey that while he acknowledges their mockery, he remains unmoved in his purpose and warns them that their scorn will ultimately result in their own humiliation, as the consequence of rejecting truth is degradation in this life and the hereafter. The verse teaches that patience in the face of persecution, coupled with clear communication of consequences, is the proper response of the believer to those who mock the message of Allah.

translation: So you will come to know who will receive a punishment that will disgrace him and upon whom will descend a punishment that will remain.
interpretation: This verse is a warning directed at those who reject the truth, informing them that they will eventually witness the consequences of their disbelief. The 'punishment that disgrace him' refers to the humiliation and shame that befalls the disbeliever in this life through their spiritual blindness and loss, while the 'punishment that remains' alludes to the eternal torment of the Hereafter. The verse emphasizes that this knowledge will not come through mere intellectual understanding but through direct experience and witnessing, serving as a powerful deterrent against arrogance and rejection of divine guidance.

translation: Until when Our command came and the oven overflowed, We said: Load into it from every kind two pairs, and your family except those against whom the word has already gone forth, and whoever has believed. But none had believed with him except a few.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the urgency and finality of divine judgment through the metaphor of the overflowing oven, signifying that the moment of reckoning had arrived. It demonstrates that even when given explicit command and clear signs, the majority of people rejected Noah's message, with only a handful choosing faith. The phrase 'those against whom the word has already gone forth' emphasizes that some were already judged to disbelieve due to their persistent rejection and hardened hearts, highlighting the principle that divine decree encompasses those whom Allah knows will turn away from truth. This teaches that patience in preaching truth is met with ingratitude, and that salvation comes only to those whose hearts are open to receive guidance, however few they may be.

translation: And he said, 'Embark upon it in the name of Allah—its course and its mooring are both in the name of Allah. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of trust in Allah (tawakkul) combined with practical action. Noah instructs his followers to board the Ark and to invoke Allah's name, recognizing that while they take the physical step of boarding, ultimate control over the vessel's movement and safety belongs to Allah alone. The mention of Allah's forgiveness and mercy at the conclusion emphasizes that despite the coming flood as punishment for the disbelievers, Allah's mercy remains available to those who obey Him and place their trust in His wisdom and protection.

translation: And it (the ship) was sailing with them amid waves like mountains. And Noah called out to his son, who had kept apart (from the believers): 'O my son! Embark with us and do not be with the disbelievers.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the moment of ultimate spiritual separation within a family—despite sharing blood ties and physical proximity during the flood, the son's disbelief creates an unbridgeable spiritual distance. Noah's plea to his son represents the powerlessness of even the most righteous prophets to compel faith in those closest to them, teaching that belief is a matter of individual choice and divine guidance, not inheritance or parental authority. The imagery of towering waves emphasizes the magnitude of the trial and the urgency of the moment, while the son's deliberate separation ('معزل') foreshadows his rejection of salvation despite his father being the messenger of God himself.

translation: He said, "I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water." Allah said, "There is no protector today from the command of Allah except for whom He has mercy upon." And the waves came between them, and he was among the drowned.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the futility of relying on worldly means or one's own intellect when faced with Allah's decree and divine punishment. The son of Noah believed his physical strength and the mountain would save him, yet neither could avail him against Allah's command. The verse teaches that true protection and safety come only through Allah's mercy, not through material defenses or personal efforts. The drowning of the son despite his attempt to escape demonstrates that when Allah's judgment comes, no refuge or barrier—whether physical, intellectual, or material—can stand against it. This underscores the complete dependence of all creation upon Allah's will and His sole authority over life, death, and salvation.

translation: And it was said, 'O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, cease [your rain].' And the water subsided, and the matter was concluded, and the ark came to rest on al-Judi, and it was said, 'Away with the wrongdoing people.'
interpretation: This verse describes the miraculous end of the Great Flood, emphasizing divine control over natural forces through the personification of earth and sky obeying God's command. The settling of the ark on Mount al-Judi symbolizes God's mercy toward the believers while the curse upon the wrongdoing people underscores the justice of divine judgment - those who rejected God's message faced destruction, while those who believed found salvation. The verse demonstrates the absolute authority of God over creation and the inevitable consequences of rejecting divine guidance.

translation: And Noah called out to his Lord, saying: 'My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the Most Just of judges.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the profound internal struggle of Prophet Noah as a father confronting the consequence of his son's rejection of faith. Despite his righteous plea appealing to familial bonds and God's justice, Noah's invocation reveals the doctrine that worldly kinship cannot supersede obedience to God's command. The verse teaches that even the most beloved relationships must yield to divine will, and that divine promises and judgments transcend human sentiment and expectation. Noah's acknowledgment of God's justice even while supplicating demonstrates the ultimate submission (islam) required of believers—accepting God's wisdom even when it contradicts human desire.

translation: He said, 'O Noah, indeed he is not of your family; indeed, he is of unrighteous work. So do not ask Me for that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, I advise you lest you be of the ignorant.'
interpretation: This verse conveys that one's spiritual status and righteous character, not merely blood relation, determine true family bonds with the believers. Those who persist in disobedience separate themselves from the community of the faithful, regardless of kinship. The verse also establishes a fundamental principle that human reason and understanding have limits, and one should not question or petition God concerning matters beyond their comprehension or knowledge, as doing so reflects ignorance of God's wisdom and sovereignty. The warning against ignorance emphasizes the importance of accepting divine judgment with submission rather than presumption.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, indeed I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy upon me, I will be among the losers.'
interpretation: This verse expresses the principle of intellectual humility and the recognition of human limitations in knowledge. The speaker (Prophet Nuh) demonstrates that asking about matters beyond one's understanding is a form of transgression against divine wisdom, and that salvation ultimately depends on God's forgiveness and mercy rather than on one's own righteousness or questioning. It teaches that restraint from inquiring into matters of divine mystery, combined with reliance on God's grace, is the path to deliverance from spiritual loss.

translation: It was said, 'O Noah, descend in peace from Us and with blessings upon you and upon nations from those with you. But (there will be) other nations to whom We will grant enjoyment, then a painful punishment from Us will touch them.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine mercy shown to Noah and his believing followers upon their safe arrival after the flood, while simultaneously establishing the principle of divine justice that extends to all humanity—those who receive blessings are tested by responsibility, and those who reject guidance face inevitable consequences. The contrast between 'peace and blessings' and 'painful punishment' emphasizes that Allah's judgment is comprehensive and inescapable, applying to all generations and nations according to their choices and deeds.

translation: These are from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. You did not know them, nor did your people, before this. So be patient. Indeed, the good outcome is for the righteous.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the Prophet Muhammad receives knowledge of future events and hidden matters through divine revelation, which neither he nor his community possessed before. The instruction to be patient serves as reassurance that despite the hardships and opposition he faces, ultimate victory and success belong to those who maintain piety and trust in God. The verse underscores the unique nature of prophethood as a source of supernatural knowledge, not derived from human reasoning or prior cultural knowledge, and affirms that righteousness and faith are the true measures of ultimate triumph.

translation: And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud. He said, 'O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. You are not but inventing [lies].'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the fundamental message of all the prophets: the call to monotheism and the rejection of idolatry. Hud's statement that his people are 'inventing lies' refers to their fabrication of false deities and their stubborn denial of the truth despite possessing innate knowledge of Allah's oneness. The verse emphasizes that the rejection of divine guidance in favor of invented gods is a form of willful deception and intellectual dishonesty, not mere ignorance.

translation: O my people! I ask you no reward for it. My reward is only from the One Who created me. Will you not then use reason?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the selfless dedication of the messenger to his calling. By declaring that he seeks no worldly compensation and that his true reward comes solely from Allah, the speaker establishes the purity of his mission and appeals to his people's rationality. The rhetorical question at the end serves as an invitation to reflect on the logical consistency of accepting guidance from someone who stands to gain nothing materially from their message, thereby challenging them to recognize the truth through rational contemplation rather than worldly suspicion or doubt.

translation: And O my people, ask forgiveness of your Lord and then repent to Him. He will send upon you rain from the sky in abundance and add strength to your strength, and do not turn away as criminals.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the inseparable link between spiritual reform and material prosperity: repentance and seeking divine forgiveness are not merely spiritual acts but are the foundational causes of earthly blessings such as abundant rain and increased strength. The passage implies that turning away from God (represented by criminal behavior) severs one from these blessings, while turning toward Him through repentance reopens the channels of divine grace and provision. The sequence—first seeking forgiveness, then repenting, then receiving blessings—demonstrates that material abundance follows moral rectification, not the reverse.

translation: They said: 'O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof, and we will not abandon our gods because of your saying, nor will we believe in you.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the stubborn rejection of Hud's message by his people, revealing their triple refusal: they deny the validity of his evidence, they are unwilling to renounce their idols regardless of his call, and they refuse to accept him as a messenger. Their response demonstrates how people prioritize their inherited customs and desires over the truth, and how they demand physical proof while remaining closed to spiritual signs, highlighting the fundamental barrier of spiritual blindness that prevents faith when the heart is already committed to falsehood.

translation: They said, 'Nothing afflicts us except that some of our gods have touched you with harm.' He said, 'Indeed, I make Allah witness, and you bear witness, that I am innocent of what you associate with Him.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the rejection and false accusation faced by a messenger when calling people to monotheism. The disbelievers attribute the messenger's misfortunes to their gods as punishment for abandoning them, revealing their spiritual blindness and refusal to acknowledge the true cause of events. The messenger's response demonstrates unwavering conviction and clarity of purpose, invoking Allah as witness to his disassociation from idolatry, emphasizing that his mission is grounded in absolute monotheism rather than any personal interest, and inviting others to recognize this fundamental reality alongside him.

translation: other than Him; so devise a plot against me all of you, then do not give me respite.
interpretation: This verse represents the defiant challenge of Prophet Yusuf to the king and his court, asserting his absolute trust in Allah's protection and power. By calling them to plot against him while he worships only Allah, Yusuf demonstrates supreme confidence that no earthly scheme can harm him, thereby affirming the principle that reliance on Allah alone renders human machinations powerless. The verse illustrates how true faith transcends fear of worldly opposition and punishment.

translation: Indeed, I have relied upon Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is not an animal except that He holds it by its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is upon a straight path.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes absolute trust in God's sovereignty and control over all creation. By declaring reliance on Allah and stating that He holds every creature by its forelock (a metaphor for complete dominion), the speaker affirms that all beings are under Divine command and none can act except by His will. The statement that 'my Lord is upon a straight path' reinforces that God's governance is just, purposeful, and guided by wisdom, assuring believers that trusting in this Divine order and justice is the correct course of action. This teaches that true security and guidance come from recognizing and accepting God's absolute authority over all existence.

translation: So if you turn away, I have conveyed to you that with which I was sent to you. And my Lord will replace you with another people, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed, my Lord is over all things a Guardian.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the finality of the Prophet's message delivery and the insignificance of human rejection in the face of divine purpose. The Prophet's responsibility ends with faithful transmission of the message; the people's choice to accept or reject it does not diminish God's power or alter His plans. The verse conveys that God's purpose will continue regardless of any particular generation's response, as He can always raise up other peoples to fulfill His will. This serves as both a reassurance to the Prophet and a warning to those who reject the message that their disobedience cannot harm God or prevent the establishment of His religion.

translation: And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe punishment.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine principle of deliverance through faith and obedience: when God's judgment manifests, those who maintain sincere belief and adherence to the messenger are spared from destruction. The verse emphasizes that salvation is not achieved through human effort alone but through God's mercy granted to the faithful, while the stubborn resisters face the inevitable consequences of their rejection. This establishes the pattern that faith combined with God's grace provides protection from divine retribution.

translation: And those were the people of 'Ad. They rejected the signs of their Lord and disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every stubborn tyrant.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the pattern of destruction that befalls nations who combine three grave sins: rejecting divine signs, disobeying the prophets, and yielding to the authority of arrogant oppressors. The emphasis on "every stubborn tyrant" suggests that their fundamental error was abandoning divine guidance in favor of following human despotism, demonstrating how idolatry of power and rejection of prophetic truth are interconnected causes of a society's downfall.

translation: And they were followed by a curse in this worldly life and on the Day of Resurrection. Behold, 'Ad disbelieved in their Lord. Behold, away with 'Ad, the people of Hud.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the consequence of rejecting divine guidance: those who persistently deny their Lord's signs face both temporal punishment in the form of divine curse affecting their affairs and circumstances in this life, and eternal punishment on the Day of Resurrection. The repeated phrase 'Ala (Behold) emphasizes the certainty and finality of their fate, establishing that disbelief leads inevitably to divine estrangement and destruction, serving as a grave warning to all who witness the example of 'Ad's rejection of the message brought by their prophet Hud.

translation: And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said, 'O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. It is He who has created you from the earth and made you settle upon it. So ask forgiveness of Him and then repent to Him. Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the fundamental principle of divine unity (tawhid) and humanity's accountability to God as their Creator and Sustainer. Salih's message underscores that worship belongs exclusively to Allah, and his reminder that humans are created from earth and entrusted with stewardship therein implies a covenant of responsibility. The call to seek forgiveness and repent is not merely about acknowledging past sins, but represents a complete reorientation of the soul toward its Lord. The concluding statement that 'my Lord is near and responsive' conveys the profound mercy of Allah—that He is always accessible to those who sincerely turn to Him, offering hope that sincere repentance will be answered. This reflects the principle that divine mercy precedes and enables human repentance, and that God's closeness is both immediate and responsive to genuine human intention.

translation: They said, 'O Salih, you were among us a man of promise before this. Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped? And indeed, we are in grave doubt concerning that to which you call us.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the fundamental obstacle to faith: when a person's message challenges established cultural practices and ancestral traditions, people reject it not primarily due to logical reasoning but because it threatens their inherited beliefs and social continuity. The people's reference to Salih's former good reputation yet their simultaneous dismissal shows how cognitive dissonance can cause even respected individuals to be rejected when they champion transformative spiritual change. Their doubt is not intellectual inquiry but willful skepticism rooted in attachment to tradition, revealing that spiritual resistance often stems from cultural conditioning rather than genuine uncertainty about the truth.

translation: He said, 'O my people! Have you considered: if I stand upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He has given me mercy from Himself, who then could help me against Allah if I disobeyed Him? You would only increase me in loss.'
interpretation: This verse expresses the futility of worldly support when one possesses divine guidance and mercy. The speaker emphasizes that having clear evidence from Allah and His mercy is superior to any human aid, and conversely, disobeying Allah cannot be compensated for by human assistance. The rhetorical question underscores that those offering mere worldly help cannot protect against divine consequences, making their opposition ultimately detrimental rather than beneficial—hence they only add to his loss by their rejection of truth.

translation: And O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah - a sign for you. So leave her to eat in the land of Allah and do not touch her with harm, lest there seize you a punishment soon.
interpretation: This verse conveys the principle that divine signs and miraculous manifestations are granted as tests of human faith and obedience. The she-camel serves as a tangible evidence of Allah's power, and respecting it becomes a measure of the community's willingness to submit to divine guidance. The warning of imminent punishment emphasizes that rejection of clear signs brings swift divine consequences, teaching that deliberate harm to what Allah has designated as sacred or miraculous constitutes a grave transgression against the divine order.

translation: So they hamstrung her. Then he said, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied."
interpretation: This verse illustrates the consequence of rejecting divine signs through the example of Thamud who hamstrung the she-camel sent by Allah as a miracle. The three-day respite granted before punishment represents Allah's justice in giving the people time to reflect upon their transgression and repent, while also demonstrating that even when divine punishment is decreed due to persistent disobedience, it does not come immediately but according to Allah's wisdom and with clear warning.

translation: So when Our command came, We saved Salih and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and [saved them] from the disgrace of that day. Indeed, your Lord - He is the Mighty, the Powerful.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine pattern of salvation and humiliation: those who submit to God's message receive His mercy and protection from shame, while those who reject it face destruction. The emphasis on God's strength and might at the verse's conclusion underscores that this outcome reflects the absolute power of the Divine, who determines the fate of believers and disbelievers according to His justice and wisdom.

translation: And the blast overtook those who wronged, and they became in their dwellings fallen dead.
interpretation: This verse describes the divine punishment that befell those who rejected the prophets and persisted in wrongdoing. The 'blast' (as-Sayhah) represents God's overwhelming power to destroy those who defiantly reject His signs and oppress others. The imagery of them remaining lifeless in their homes emphasizes both the completeness of their destruction and the permanence of their disgrace—they receive no proper burial or respect, serving as a warning to those who come after them about the inevitable consequences of arrogance and denial of the truth.

translation: As if they had never dwelt in their midst. Verily, Thamud disbelieved in their Lord. Verily, away with Thamud!
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the completeness of the destruction that befell the people of Thamud - they were annihilated so thoroughly that it was as if they had never existed in their dwellings. The repetition of 'verily' (ala) at the beginning of successive clauses serves as a solemn affirmation of both their rejection of their Lord and their deserved curse, highlighting how the consequences of disbelief and arrogance manifest in complete obliteration from the earth.

translation: And indeed Our messengers came to Abraham with good news. They said, 'Peace.' He said, 'Peace,' and hastened to bring them a roasted calf.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the virtue of hospitality as a sacred duty and expression of faith. Abraham's immediate and generous response to his guests—preparing food without hesitation or inquiry—demonstrates the proper conduct toward visitors and the importance of welcoming others with warmth and dignity. His greeting and reciprocation of 'peace' also exemplifies respectful courtesy and spiritual awareness, setting a noble example of how believers should treat those who come to them, particularly those bearing divine messages.

translation: So when he saw their hands not reaching toward it, he denied them and conceived from them a fear. They said, 'Do not fear. Indeed, we have been sent to the people of Lot.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates Abraham's initial mistrust when the angels arrived at his home and failed to eat the food he had prepared, a sign that something was unusual about these guests. His fear was natural and human—he did not recognize them as angels at first, and their refusal to eat caused him anxiety about their true nature and intentions. The angels then reassured him and revealed their divine mission to destroy the people of Lot, which explains their arrival and unusual behavior. This moment demonstrates that even the greatest prophets experience natural human emotions like fear and suspicion when facing the unknown, though they ultimately trust in God's guidance when the truth is revealed to them.

translation: And his wife was standing, and she laughed. So We gave her good tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the transformation of doubt into faith through divine reassurance. Sarah's laughter, born from the incredulity of bearing a child in her advanced age, becomes the occasion for God's explicit promise, suggesting that even uncertainty and hesitation can be met with divine compassion and confirmation. The mention of both Isaac and Jacob emphasizes the continuity of God's covenant across generations, demonstrating that the promise extends beyond the immediate blessing to encompass an entire lineage, thereby transforming a moment of human weakness into a foundation for spiritual legacy.

translation: She said, 'O woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman, and this is my husband in old age? Indeed, this is a strange thing.'
interpretation: This verse captures Sarah's expression of disbelief and wonder at the divine promise of bearing a child in her advanced age. Her exclamation reflects the natural human reaction of recognizing the impossible becoming possible through God's will, demonstrating how belief is tested at the boundaries of human expectation and the laws of nature we perceive.

translation: They said, 'Do you wonder at the decree of God? The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, O people of the household. Indeed, He is the Praised, the Glorious.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the angels' affirmation of God's sovereignty and their recognition that Sarah's conception, despite her advanced age, is a manifestation of divine power deserving no amazement. The invocation of blessings upon Abraham's family is the angels' acknowledgment that this miraculous event testifies to God's perfect wisdom and glory, emphasizing that what seems impossible to human comprehension is entirely within God's dominion and reflects His praise-worthy nature.

translation: So when fear departed from Abraham and the good tidings reached him, he began to dispute with Us concerning the people of Lot.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the human tendency to advocate for mercy and justice even in the face of divine judgment. Abraham's willingness to argue with God about Lot's people demonstrates that faith does not preclude questioning or intercession on behalf of others. It shows that righteous servants of God are emboldened by receiving good news and reassurance from the divine, which gives them the confidence to present their moral objections and plead for leniency toward sinners, reflecting the noble character of seeking God's clemency for humanity.

translation: Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, devoutly obedient, and turning back to Us in repentance.
interpretation: This verse describes the essential spiritual and moral qualities of Abraham (Ibrahim) that made him a model of faith and righteousness. His forbearance (hilm) reflects his patience and clemency in facing trials and adversity, his devotion (awwah) indicates his constant remembrance of God and concern for others' spiritual welfare, and his turning in repentance (munib) shows his unwavering submission and return to God's guidance. Together, these attributes portray Abraham not as someone who attained perfection through his own strength, but as a servant whose humility and reliance on God were the foundations of his spiritual station, making him worthy of being described as the Friend of God (Khalil Allah).

translation: O Abraham, turn away from this. Indeed, the command of your Lord has come, and indeed, there will come upon them a punishment that cannot be repelled.
interpretation: This verse conveys God's command to Prophet Abraham to cease his supplication on behalf of the people of Lot, as their punishment is now inevitable and irreversible. It teaches that divine justice ultimately prevails despite the intercessor's compassion, and that when God's decree is established, no amount of pleading can alter it. The verse emphasizes the limits of intercession and the certainty of God's punishment for those who persist in transgression.

translation: And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed for them and felt straitened in his breast, and he said, 'This is a difficult day.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates Lot's profound anxiety upon receiving the divine messengers, not out of disbelief but from awareness of the danger his people posed to the messengers and from his anticipated confrontation with the people of Sodom regarding their immoral practices. His distress reflects the burden of being a prophet among a corrupt and hostile nation, highlighting the psychological and emotional toll of prophetic mission when surrounded by those who reject divine guidance.

translation: And his people came to him, rushing toward him. And before that, they had been doing evil deeds. He said, 'O my people, these are my daughters—they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me regarding my guests. Is there not among you a single man of sound judgment?'
interpretation: This verse reveals the prophet's profound moral dilemma and the hierarchy of Islamic ethics: he prioritizes the sanctity of hospitality and the protection of guests over the protection of his own family members, implying that the covenant of hospitality is sacred and inviolable, while simultaneously demonstrating that his appeal to reason ('Is there not among you a man of sound judgment?') represents an attempt to awaken their conscience and remind them that moral wisdom should guide human behavior away from transgression.

translation: They said, 'You have certainly known that we have no claim on your daughters, and indeed you know what we want.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the people's explicit acknowledgment of their sinful intentions and desire for Lot's male guests, while their reference to having 'no claim on your daughters' exposes the perversity of their request - they are rejecting what is lawful (women) and demanding what is forbidden and unnatural. Their admission that Lot 'knows what we want' indicates both their shamelessness in their desires and Lot's awareness of their deviant nature, setting up the moral confrontation between divine guidance and human depravity.

translation: He said, 'If only I had against you some power, or could take refuge in some strong support!'
interpretation: This verse expresses Shu'ayb's lament of powerlessness in the face of his people's rejection and hostility. His statement reveals that when divine guidance is resisted by a community, the messenger becomes vulnerable without external support. The mention of 'strong support' alludes to the protection and backing from Allah that ultimately sustains the message, highlighting the lonely struggle of the prophets who must rely on God's strength rather than worldly power or human alliance. It demonstrates the human limitation of the messengers and their dependence on divine assistance when facing opposition.

translation: They said, 'O Lot, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So take your family and depart in a part of the night, and let not anyone of you look back—except your wife. Indeed, she will be struck by that which strikes them. Their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates divine protection and urgency in salvation. The messengers' assurance that the people 'will never reach you' indicates that God's plan for saving the righteous cannot be thwarted by the wicked. The command to depart at night without looking back symbolizes the necessity of complete separation from corruption and severing all ties with the past. The wife's exception reveals that those who choose disbelief through their hearts cannot be saved against their will, even if they share the same household with the faithful. The repeated emphasis on the proximity of dawn—first through its mention as the appointed time, then through the rhetorical question—conveys that divine judgment arrives swiftly and inevitably, allowing no lingering in places of sin.

translation: So when Our command came, We made its highest parts its lowest, and We rained upon it stones of baked clay, arranged in order.
interpretation: This verse describes the destruction of the people of 'Aad, demonstrating Allah's absolute power to overturn the natural order when His command is executed. The reversal of high and low signifies the complete devastation and overturning of their civilization, while the rain of stones represents a punishment that is both material and overwhelming. The phrase 'stones of baked clay, arranged in order' emphasizes the systematic and purposeful nature of Allah's punishment, leaving no escape or refuge, and serves as a warning to all peoples that defiance of Allah's message inevitably leads to destruction.

translation: Marked (distinguished) with your Lord, and it (the punishment) is not far from the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the Divine punishment is predetermined and well-known to Allah, and that those who commit injustice should not assume they can escape accountability. The 'marking' signifies that this punishment is specifically designated by Allah's knowledge and justice, and serves as a warning that wrongdoers cannot evade the consequences of their actions, for punishment is always within reach of those who transgress against divine commands.

translation: And to Madyan, We sent their brother Shu'ayb. He said, 'O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. And do not diminish the measure and the weight. Indeed, I see you in prosperity, but I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing Day.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the comprehensive nature of prophetic guidance, showing that spiritual reform (monotheism) is inseparable from social and economic justice. Shu'ayb's warning against cheating in weights and measures, despite the people's material prosperity, teaches that material wealth without moral integrity invites divine punishment. The juxtaposition of acknowledging their goodness while warning of impending doom emphasizes that prosperity itself does not exempt people from accountability—rather, it increases their responsibility to maintain justice and honor their covenants with God.

translation: And O my people, give full measure and weight in justice, and do not deprive people of their things, nor spread corruption in the land.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the ethical imperative of honesty and fairness in all transactions and dealings with others. By addressing his people directly, the messenger calls them to practice justice in commerce and interpersonal relations, warning against the twin evils of cheating through false measures and spreading chaos. The verse teaches that integrity in business matters is not merely a commercial concern but a moral and religious obligation, and that such honesty is foundational to social stability and obedience to God's will.

translation: The remnant of Allah is better for you, if you are believers. And I am not a guardian over you.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that reliance upon what Allah provides and preserves (the remnant of His blessing) is superior to pursuing worldly gain through dishonest means, and that the Prophet's role is not to compel faith or police the believers' actions, but rather to convey the message and leave the consequences to Allah, thereby teaching that true success comes from faith and obedience, not from external coercion or the pressure of leadership.

translation: They said, 'O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we should forsake what our fathers worshipped, or that we should not do what we please with our wealth? Indeed, you are the forbearing, the wise.'
interpretation: The people of Madyan are sarcastically mocking Shu'ayb's religious convictions, using mockery as a weapon to deflect from the serious moral corruption he addresses. Their rhetorical questions reveal their fundamental rejection of spiritual guidance, as they conflate obedience to Allah with the loss of ancestral traditions and personal autonomy over wealth. The irony in their praise—calling him forbearing and wise—underscores their arrogance and refusal to acknowledge that true forbearance and wisdom lie in submitting to divine commandment rather than clinging to custom and worldly desires. This verse illustrates how those who reject prophetic truth often resort to sarcasm and ridicule rather than engage with the substance of the message.

translation: He said, 'O my people, have you considered: if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord and He has provided me with good provision from Him, and I do not wish to oppose you by doing that which I forbid you from - I only wish to reform [matters] as much as I am able. My success is not but through Allah. Upon Him I have relied, and to Him I turn in repentance.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the sincere motivation of the reformer who seeks to establish justice and virtue among his people despite their rejection. The speaker emphasizes that his call is grounded in divine guidance and supported by Allah's blessings, yet he acknowledges the limits of human effort and places complete reliance upon Allah. The statement that he does not wish to contradict his own message by engaging in the forbidden acts he warns against reflects the principle that moral authority derives from moral consistency - one cannot call others to righteousness while practicing the opposite. The repeated assertion of dependence upon Allah ('my success is not but through Allah') underscores that all reformation and guidance ultimately emanate from the Divine, not from human capability alone.

translation: And O my people, let not your enmity towards me entice you to sin, lest there befall you the like of that which befell the people of Noah, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih. And the people of Lot are not far from you.
interpretation: The speaker (a messenger) warns his people that their opposition to him should not lead them to commit sin and rejection of divine guidance, for doing so would result in divine punishment similar to what befell the previous nations who rejected their messengers. The mention of Lot's people being 'not far' suggests that the consequences of rejecting divine signs are imminent and inevitable for those who persist in their defiance, serving as a timely reminder of the proximity of divine accountability.

translation: And ask forgiveness of your Lord and then repent to Him. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the completeness of repentance through two stages: seeking forgiveness (istighfar) for past sins and turning back (tawbah) to obedience. The mention of Allah's attributes—Merciful (Raheem) and Loving (Wadood)—reassures believers that sincere repentance is always accepted, for Allah's compassion and affection for His servants is boundless and encourages them not to despair but to return to Him with hope.

translation: They said, 'O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and indeed, we see you among us as weak. And if not for your family, we would have stoned you. And you are not to us mighty or honored.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the arrogance and contempt of the people of Madyan toward the prophet Shu'ayb, revealing how those who reject truth often resort to attacking the messenger's character and status rather than engaging with the message itself. Their refusal to understand his preaching, combined with their threats of violence and their only restraint being his family's strength rather than respect for justice, demonstrates how spiritual blindness leads people to rely on power and intimidation while dismissing the messenger as insignificant—a commentary on how rejection of divine guidance is rooted in pride and worldly considerations rather than rational discourse.

translation: He said, 'O my people, is my family more mighty to you than Allah? And you have taken Him behind your backs with disregard. Indeed, my Lord encompasses what you do.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the prophet's appeal to his people's sense of priorities and accountability. By questioning whether their fear of his family's power exceeds their fear of God, he exposes the irrationality of their disbelief—they have abandoned God's authority and relegated it to insignificance, treating it as something to be dismissed. The statement 'my Lord encompasses what you do' serves as a reminder that despite their negligence of God's authority, His knowledge and justice encompass all their actions, and they will ultimately be held accountable regardless of their current rejection.

translation: And O my people, work according to your ability; indeed, I am working. You will soon know who will be afflicted with a punishment that will disgrace him and who is a liar. And wait; indeed, I am with you, watching.
interpretation: This verse represents a moment of ultimate confrontation between a righteous messenger and his defiant people, where the speaker asserts both his commitment to his mission and his certainty in divine justice. The phrase 'work according to your ability' suggests that each party will expend their utmost effort in their respective paths—the messenger in calling to truth and the people in their opposition. The declaration 'I am with you, watching' serves as a final warning that carries both a threat of divine oversight and an implicit comfort to believers, establishing that God's awareness encompasses all actions and will ultimately distinguish between truth and falsehood through concrete punishment and vindication. The verse's force lies in its presentation of an inescapable accountability where the outcomes will become manifest, and no one can hide from the consequences of their choices.

translation: And when Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him through a mercy from Us. And the blast seized those who wronged, so they became in their dwellings fallen down dead.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine principle of differentiation between the righteous and the wrongdoers at the moment of God's judgment. When the predetermined time of punishment arrives, God's mercy becomes a protective shield for the believers and their prophet, preserving them from destruction, while simultaneously the disbelievers face inevitable divine punishment. The 'blast' (al-sayhah) represents the overwhelming nature of God's punishment that leaves no room for escape or resistance, emphasizing that divine justice is both merciful to the faithful and inescapable for those who persist in wrongdoing.

translation: As if they had never dwelt therein. Away with Madyan, just as Thamud went away!
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the complete obliteration of the people of Madyan from their land, as if they had never inhabited it at all. The repetition of the fate of Thamud serves as a powerful reminder that just as Thamud was destroyed and utterly removed from their dwelling place by Allah's punishment, so too did Madyan face complete annihilation. The verse underscores the severity and decisiveness of Allah's judgment against those who reject His messengers, leaving no trace of their civilization or prosperity behind.

translation: And We sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Prophet Moses was commissioned by Allah with both miraculous signs (ayat) that demonstrated divine power and a manifest authority (clear proof and legitimacy) that validated his message. The phrase 'clear authority' indicates that Moses possessed undeniable evidence of his prophethood - not merely miraculous acts, but rational and demonstrable proof that he was a genuine messenger from Allah, which served to establish his credibility among the people of Egypt and those who believed in him.

translation: To Pharaoh and his chiefs, so they followed the command of Pharaoh. And the command of Pharaoh was not right guidance.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the spiritual danger of blind obedience to human authority figures. The chiefs' unquestioning adherence to Pharaoh's orders despite their inherent wrongness demonstrates how collective compliance with unjust leadership can entrench people in error and distance them from divine guidance. The verse serves as a warning that following the commands of those in power is only legitimate and beneficial when those commands themselves are aligned with truth and wisdom, not merely because of the authority or position of the commander.

translation: He will lead his people on the Day of Judgment and then he will have led them to the Fire. And evil is the destination to which they are led.
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of a leader (referring to the Pharaoh and leaders like him) who misguided his people away from God's truth during their worldly life. On the Day of Judgment, this leader will be forced to guide or lead his followers directly into the Fire of Hell as a consequence of his misguidance. The verse serves as a grave warning about the accountability of those in positions of leadership and influence - they will be held responsible not only for their own sins but for leading others astray. The emphatic conclusion 'and evil is the destination to which they are led' emphasizes the severity and finality of this punishment, highlighting the danger of following false leaders and the paramount importance of seeking guidance from God alone rather than relying on human leaders who turn away from divine truth.

translation: And they were followed in this life with a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection. What a terrible provision those who were in agreement with them will have.
interpretation: This verse describes the consequence for those who followed the transgressors mentioned in the preceding context. The 'curse' (la'nah) signifies divine displeasure and separation from mercy in this world, which continues into the afterlife on the Day of Resurrection. The phrase 'terrible provision' (bies al-rafd al-marfud) emphasizes the severe punishment and wretched recompense that awaits such people. The verse warns that following wrongdoing does not escape accountability; rather, it brings humiliation in both worlds, and one becomes bound to the same fate as those who led them astray, demonstrating that complicity in transgression carries its own divine punishment.

translation: That is from the news of the cities which We relate to you; some of them are still standing, and some are reaped/destroyed.
interpretation: This verse refers to the ruins and remnants of past civilizations that Allah mentions in the Qur'an. The phrase suggests that among the communities whose stories are being narrated, some continue to exist (whether physically as ruins or through memory), while others have been completely obliterated or forgotten. This emphasizes how Allah preserves knowledge of these historical events and their remains as signs for those who reflect, demonstrating both divine mercy in preservation and divine justice in destruction.

translation: And We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. And their gods to whom they called upon instead of Allah availed them not a thing when the command of your Lord came. And they did not increase them in anything but ruin.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Allah's punishment is just and not oppressive, as the polytheists' destruction came entirely from their own choices and rebellion. The verse illustrates the futility of shirk (associating partners with Allah) by showing that when divine punishment arrives, the false gods they relied upon cannot help them at all, nor do they provide any benefit—only adding to the ruin and destruction already incurred through disbelief. This serves as a profound warning that one's own moral choices and beliefs determine one's outcome, and that turning away from the truth to false sources of power and hope leads inevitably to complete loss.

translation: And thus did your Lord seize the cities while they were committing injustice. Indeed, His seizing is painful and severe.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of divine justice and accountability, emphasizing that Allah's punishment of nations that persist in wrongdoing is both inevitable and severe. The seizing (taking) of cities refers to their destruction and ruin as a consequence of their collective injustice and rejection of divine guidance. The verse serves as a warning that oppression and disbelief do not go unpunished, and that Allah's grip on the wrongdoers is inescapable, combining both the aspect of pain (عذاب - punishment) and strength (شديد - might), suggesting that divine retribution leaves no room for escape or mitigation.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter. That is a day for which all people will be gathered, and that is a witnessed day.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the signs of God's power and justice in this world serve as evidence and warning specifically for those who possess genuine consciousness of God and fear His accountability in the Hereafter. Those who take heed of such signs do so because they understand that all humanity will ultimately be brought together on the Day of Judgment where every deed will be witnessed and accounted for. The verse thus connects the perception of divine signs in the present with one's eschatological awareness—suggesting that the ability to recognize God's signs depends upon one's sincere concern for the ultimate reckoning.

translation: And We do not delay it except for a specified term.
interpretation: This verse refers to Allah's decree regarding the postponement of punishment or the final Hour. The divine wisdom behind any delay in the manifestation of Allah's will is always tied to a specific, predetermined time known only to Him. This teaches that there is no randomness in creation - every event, including consequences for actions, unfolds according to divine knowledge and measured purpose, demonstrating that Allah's decisions are not arbitrary but based on wisdom and predetermined timing.

translation: On the Day when it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission. Then among them will be the wretched and the blessed.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of Allah over all speech and communication on the Day of Judgment. The phrase 'no soul will speak except by His permission' signifies that in that momentous day, human free will regarding speech is entirely suspended—every word spoken will be by divine permission alone. The division of humanity into 'the wretched' (those destined for punishment) and 'the blessed' (those destined for reward) indicates that this silencing of unauthorized speech serves to prevent the desperate pleas, arguments, or excuses that souls might otherwise attempt to make, thereby establishing divine justice without the confusion of human words or defenses.

translation: As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire. For them in it is sighing and loud respiration.
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of those who have chosen wretchedness through their disbelief and disobedience. The mention of 'sighing and loud respiration' (zafir and shahiq) symbolizes the intense suffering and anguish experienced by the inhabitants of the Fire - the sounds represent their desperate, labored breathing as they endure torment, emphasizing the severity of their punishment and the complete loss of peace or comfort in their eternal abode. The verse reinforces that the consequences of spiritual wretchedness in this life are dire and irrevocable punishment in the next.

translation: Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills. Indeed, your Lord is the Doer of what He intends.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the eternal nature of punishment or reward in the afterlife, while simultaneously affirming Allah's absolute sovereignty and will. The clause 'except as your Lord wills' serves as a reminder that nothing is permanent except by Allah's permission, establishing that even concepts of eternity are ultimately subject to His divine will and power. The concluding statement affirms that Allah executes His plans perfectly and is not constrained by any force, reinforcing His complete control over all matters and outcomes.

translation: As for those who are blessed, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills. An uninterrupted gift.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the eternal and unceasing nature of Paradise for the blessed believers. The phrase 'as long as the heavens and the earth endure' conveys perpetual duration, while the exception 'except as your Lord wills' acknowledges Allah's absolute sovereignty and power over all creation. The final description of Paradise as 'an uninterrupted gift' (عطاء غير مجذوذ) underscores that the blessings of Paradise are continuous, inexhaustible, and cannot be cut off, highlighting the boundless generosity and mercy of Allah toward those who achieve salvation.

translation: So do not be in doubt about what these people worship. They do not worship except as their fathers worshiped before. And indeed, We will give them their share undiminished.
interpretation: This verse reassures the Prophet Muhammad that the idolatrous practices of the Meccan polytheists are merely blind imitation of ancestral customs without any rational basis or divine guidance. The divine promise that God will grant them their full portion (whether of punishment or worldly consequence) emphasizes God's justice—they will face the full consequences of their choices, neither augmented nor diminished. This serves to strengthen the Prophet's conviction in his message and to clarify that the people's persistence in idol worship stems from cultural tradition rather than any legitimate spiritual understanding, and that divine justice will ultimately prevail over their stubborn adherence to baseless customs.

translation: And indeed, We gave Moses the Scripture, but disagreement arose concerning it. And if not for a word that had preceded from your Lord, it would have been judged between them. And indeed, they are in doubt about it, a disquieting doubt.
interpretation: This verse illustrates how the clarity of revelation does not guarantee unanimous acceptance among those who receive it. Despite the divine gift of the Scripture to Moses, people's differing predilections, cultural biases, and spiritual inclinations caused them to disagree about its meaning and implementation. The verse points to God's forbearance and mercy in delaying judgment between the disputing parties, allowing time for reflection and guidance rather than immediate punishment. The mention of their troubling doubt emphasizes that this disagreement stems not from intellectual difficulty but from a restless uncertainty rooted in their hearts—a spiritual condition that prevents them from accepting the truth even when it is clearly presented to them.

translation: And indeed, your Lord will surely repay each of them for their deeds. Indeed, He is fully aware of what they do.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the Divine principle of accountability and recompense in the afterlife. Allah assures that no action, whether good or evil, goes unnoticed or unrewarded. The phrase 'fully aware' (خبير - khabir) underscores that Allah's knowledge is not merely distant observation but intimate and comprehensive understanding of the intentions, circumstances, and nature of human actions. This serves as a powerful moral deterrent and encouragement - those who do good should not despair of reward, and those who do evil should not think themselves hidden from Divine justice.

translation: So direct yourself to the faith as you have been commanded, and [do so] with those who have repented with you. And do not transgress. Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine requirement for steadfastness in following the straight path that Allah has ordained. The Prophet is commanded to remain firm in his convictions and to lead those who have believed alongside him with the same commitment. The warning against transgression serves as a reminder that true obedience consists not only of adherence to the prescribed way, but also of restraint and moderation, while the concluding assertion of Allah's complete awareness reassures the believers that their efforts are witnessed and their accountability is certain, thereby providing both motivation for righteousness and deterrent against deviation.

translation: And do not incline towards those who have wronged, lest the Fire should touch you. And you have no protectors other than Allah, then you will not be helped.
interpretation: This verse warns believers against aligning with or relying upon those who commit injustice and transgress against Allah's law. The prohibition against 'inclining' (rokun) encompasses both physical association and spiritual compromise with the unjust. The consequence of such alignment is divine punishment represented by the Fire, emphasizing that proximity to wrongdoers spiritually endangers one's faith and salvation. The verse reinforces absolute dependence on Allah alone, signifying that no earthly ally or intercessor can rescue a believer from the consequences of abandoning divine guidance, thus establishing the principle that the pursuit of justice and righteous association are essential to maintaining one's protection under Allah's sovereignty.

translation: And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and at some hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that prayer at prescribed times throughout the day and night serves as a spiritual discipline that purifies the soul from transgressions. The statement that good deeds erase bad deeds teaches that righteous actions possess a transformative power to cancel the effects of wrongdoing, encouraging believers to repent through beneficial works while maintaining constant connection with Allah through regular prayer. The concluding phrase addresses those with mindful hearts who understand and internalize this spiritual principle.

translation: And be patient, for indeed Allah does not waste the reward of those who do good.
interpretation: This verse encourages believers to endure hardship and maintain their commitment to righteousness with the assurance that Allah will never allow the efforts and sacrifices of the righteous to go unrecognized or unrewarded. The promise serves as spiritual motivation during times of difficulty, emphasizing that patience and virtuous conduct are never in vain in the sight of Allah.

translation: If only there had been among the generations before you those of virtue who forbade corruption in the land, except for a few whom We saved from among them. But those who wronged followed what they were given of luxuries, and they were criminals.
interpretation: This verse presents a moral reproach to humanity's historical tendency toward spiritual decline and corruption. It suggests that throughout history, righteous individuals who possessed understanding and wisdom were always a minority, and their absence or ineffectiveness in preventing societal corruption is lamented. The verse reveals that those who perpetrated wrongdoing and sin were specifically those who indulged in worldly luxuries and comforts without moral restraint, showing that material abundance without spiritual rectitude inevitably leads to transgression and criminality. The passage thus teaches that corruption is not inevitable but rather results from the conscious choices of those who prioritize worldly indulgence over ethical responsibility, while simultaneously indicating that divine salvation comes to those who resist such temptations, demonstrating that moral strength and divine favor are intertwined.

translation: And your Lord would never destroy the cities in injustice while their inhabitants were righteous.
interpretation: This verse establishes a divine principle that God does not punish communities unjustly or destroy them while they still contain righteous people who are working to reform society. It emphasizes God's justice and mercy, implying that divine punishment only comes after clear signs have been given and the majority have turned away from righteousness, or when corruption becomes so widespread that even the righteous have abandoned their efforts to reform. This provides moral reassurance that God's judgment is never arbitrary and always measured according to the actual spiritual and moral state of a people.

translation: And if your Lord had willed, He could have made mankind one nation, but they will not cease to differ,
interpretation: This verse establishes that human diversity and disagreement are part of Allah's deliberate design for creation. Rather than viewing disagreement as a flaw or aberration, the verse teaches that Allah has given humans free will and varying capacities, and this difference is intentional and part of the divine plan. The continuous state of disagreement mentioned reflects the reality that humans will naturally hold different beliefs, values, and perspectives due to their exercise of choice—which is essential to human moral responsibility. This implies that unity cannot be imposed mechanically but must be achieved through guidance and choice, and that the diversity itself serves purposes within Allah's wisdom.

translation: Except those upon whom your Lord has mercy. And for that He created them. And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: 'I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men, all together.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's ultimate wisdom and purpose in creation: while most of jinn and mankind will earn punishment through their rejection of faith and disobedience, God's mercy remains available to those who turn to Him. The verse reconciles divine predestination with human responsibility, indicating that God's knowledge and decree (that Hell will be filled) does not negate His offer of mercy to those who seek it. The phrase 'for that He created them' suggests that God created them aware of their ultimate destinies, yet this foreknowledge includes the possibility of mercy for the believers among them, demonstrating that God's justice encompasses both consequence and compassion.

translation: And each of these stories of the messengers, We relate to you so that We may strengthen your heart thereby. And there has come to you, in this, the truth and an exhortation and a reminder for the believers.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes the dual purpose of narrating the accounts of previous prophets: the psychological and spiritual strengthening of Prophet Muhammad's resolve and faith in the face of opposition and hardship, while simultaneously serving as moral instruction, wise counsel, and a means of remembrance for those who believe. The repetition of these narratives is not merely historical but therapeutic and pedagogical, designed to fortify the messenger's heart and guide the believers toward righteousness.

translation: And say to those who do not believe: 'Act according to your position; indeed, we are acting.'
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet to respond to the disbelievers with a declaration of confident resolve rather than despair. The phrase 'act according to your position' is not a concession to their disbelief, but rather a challenge and warning—each party will proceed with their own course of action, and the believers will continue steadfastly with their faith and mission while the disbelievers persist in their rejection. It reflects unwavering conviction that ultimately God's purpose will prevail, and serves as a reassurance to the believers that they should not be intimidated or swayed by opposition, but rather maintain their commitment to God's way.

translation: And wait; indeed, we are waiting.
interpretation: This verse represents a challenge and declaration of defiance, where Allah commands the Prophet and believers to wait for Allah's judgment and support, while simultaneously declaring that Allah and His believers are also waiting to see the outcome of the disbelievers' actions and plots. It reflects the ultimate confidence in divine justice and the certainty that Allah's promise will be fulfilled, suggesting that the believers need not fear the threats and schemes of their enemies, as Allah is fully aware and will ultimately triumph. The mutual act of waiting emphasizes that both sides are aware of the confrontation, but only one—those who trust in Allah—will prevail.

translation: And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and to Him will be returned the matter, all of it. So worship Him and rely upon Him. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse establishes divine omniscience and sovereignty as the foundation for absolute trust in Allah. By emphasizing that all hidden knowledge belongs to Allah and that all affairs ultimately return to Him, the verse teaches that believers should surrender completely to Allah through worship and reliance, knowing with certainty that Allah is fully aware of their actions and intentions. This awareness serves as both a comfort for the faithful and a reminder of accountability, making taqwa (God-consciousness) the rational response to the reality of divine knowledge and control.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Clear Book.
interpretation: The invocation of God's names establishes the divine source and merciful nature of revelation. The Quranic initials (Alif, Lam, Ra) point to the miraculous nature of the Qur'an, composed of ordinary Arabic letters yet inimitable in its composition. The description of the Book as 'Clear' (Mubin) emphasizes that despite the mystery of the letters, the Qur'an's message is evident and unambiguous in its guidance, accessible to those who sincerely seek understanding.

translation: Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an so that you may understand.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes that God revealed the Qur'an in the Arabic language specifically to facilitate comprehension and rational understanding among its addressees. By using their native language, the message becomes accessible and the people are able to grasp its meanings through their intellect, rather than having the obstacles of linguistic barriers prevent them from understanding God's guidance. This underscores the wisdom in divine revelation being suited to the capacity and context of those who receive it.

translation: We relate to you the best of stories through what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an, and indeed, before it you were among those unaware.
interpretation: This verse establishes the Qur'an as a source of moral and spiritual edification through its narratives, while simultaneously affirming the divine origin of the Prophet Muhammad's message. The phrase 'best of stories' emphasizes that the Qur'an's accounts are superior in their ethical teachings and spiritual guidance compared to other narratives. The reference to the Prophet's former state of unawareness before revelation demonstrates the transformative power of divine guidance and serves to authenticate his message—he could not have produced such elevated wisdom from his own knowledge, thereby proving the Qur'an's divine source.

translation: When Yusuf said to his father, 'O my father, indeed I have seen eleven stars and the sun and the moon - I saw them prostrating to me.'
interpretation: This verse presents Yusuf's recounting of his dream to his father Ya'qub, which serves as the initiating event for the entire narrative. The dream is divinely-inspired guidance revealing Yusuf's elevated destiny and predestined leadership. The celestial bodies symbolize his family members and their acknowledgment of his authority and honor. The prostration imagery signifies both literal submission and the recognition of his superiority in wisdom, character, and station. Ya'qub's subsequent warning to Yusuf not to tell his brothers demonstrates paternal wisdom in protecting his son, as such a revelation would provoke their jealousy and resentment - foreshadowing the trials that will test and ultimately perfect Yusuf's faith and character.

translation: He said, 'O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers, for they will plot against you with deception. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the wisdom of discernment in speech, teaching that not all knowledge should be shared indiscriminately, especially with those who may be jealous or envious. The father's counsel reflects understanding of human nature and the vulnerability of revealing one's advantages or aspirations to potential adversaries. By warning against sharing the dream, the verse emphasizes prudence in discretion and acknowledges how Satan exploits human weaknesses like jealousy and malice to incite harm against others. The verse serves as guidance on protecting oneself through wise conduct and awareness of those around us.

translation: And thus your Lord will choose you and teach you from the interpretation of narratives/dreams, and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Jacob, as He completed it upon your fathers before you, Abraham and Isaac. Indeed, your Lord is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse establishes the continuity of divine grace and wisdom through the lineage of the prophets, demonstrating that Joseph's selection and gifting with the ability to interpret dreams is part of a purposeful divine plan that connects him to the spiritual legacy of Abraham and Isaac. The emphasis on God's completeness of favor (ta'mam al-ni'mah) suggests that prophetic knowledge and spiritual discernment are divine gifts bestowed according to God's perfect wisdom and knowledge, establishing that Joseph inherits not just a name but a sacred trust and capability passed through the prophetic tradition.

translation: Indeed, in Joseph and his brothers were signs for those who ask questions.
interpretation: This verse introduces the story of Prophet Joseph (Yusuf) as a narrative containing divinely inspired lessons and evidential signs for those who inquire and seek understanding.
