The Qur'an rejects this claim because it implies dependence, imperfection, and corporeality—attributes incompatible with the eternal and self-sufficient nature of the Creator. The verse emphasizes that such beliefs stem from ignorance and rejection of monotheistic truth.

translation: Indeed, you have come with something terrible/dreadful.
interpretation: This phrase expresses severe disapproval of a grave transgression. The word 'idda (إِدًّا) intensifies the gravity of the wrongdoing, suggesting that what has been committed is not merely wrong but shockingly and extraordinarily evil. The verse conveys divine condemnation of conduct that crosses a fundamental moral boundary, emphasizing how certain sins are so heinous that they defy normal categories of wrongdoing and provoke the strongest possible disapproval.

translation: The heavens are almost rent asunder thereat, and the earth is split asunder, and the mountains fall to pieces thereat.
interpretation: This verse describes the catastrophic cosmic reaction to the attribution of partners to Allah (shirk) or to His revelation, emphasizing the enormity of this transgression through vivid natural imagery. The near-destruction of the heavens, earth, and mountains symbolizes how fundamentally opposed creation itself is to polytheism and disbelief, illustrating that even the physical laws of nature recoil at such grave disobedience and that it provokes the anger of Allah to a degree that threatens the very stability of creation.

translation: That they claim that the Most Merciful has taken a son
interpretation: This verse refers to the false claim made by some polytheists and disbelievers who attributed offspring to Allah. The interpretation centers on the absurdity and blasphemy of this claim: Allah, in His absolute oneness and transcendence (tawhid), is beyond all human characteristics and limitations, including the need for or ability to have children. This statement emphasizes the fundamental Islamic principle that Allah has no equal, no partner, and no offspring, and such claims contradict the essential nature of His divinity and perfection.

translation: And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute uniqueness and transcendence of Allah, asserting that His nature is fundamentally different from His creation. Taking a son would imply procreation, physical need, or succession—all attributes of contingent beings that contradict Allah's status as the Eternal, Self-Sufficient, and Complete. The verse refutes false doctrines that attribute offspring to Allah, while affirming that such an act would be incompatible with His perfect attributes of mercy and wisdom. The emphasis on 'the Most Merciful' suggests that a merciful God would not burden Himself or others with such relationships, highlighting instead His transcendent nature and absolute sufficiency.

translation: Indeed, everyone in the heavens and the earth will come to the Most Merciful as a servant.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of Allah and the universal submission of all creation to His dominion. It conveys that without exception, every being—whether in the heavens or on earth—will ultimately approach Allah on the Day of Judgment as His servant, acknowledging complete dependency and obedience. This underscores the inevitability of divine judgment and the futility of any claim to independence or defiance against Allah's authority.

translation: He has enumerated them and counted them with a [precise] count.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's infinite knowledge and awareness of all things. The repetition of counting terms (أحصاهم - enumerated them, and عدهم عدا - counted them with a count) stresses the completeness and precision of Allah's knowledge. It conveys that nothing escapes Allah's awareness, whether it concerns people, deeds, or creation. This absolute knowledge is presented as evidence of Allah's perfect attributes and His dominion over all things, serving to remind humans of their accountability before an all-knowing Creator.

translation: And all of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the complete isolation and individual accountability that each person will experience on the Day of Judgment. Despite whatever wealth, family, followers, or power one possessed in the worldly life, no one can accompany or help another in the afterlife. Each soul stands alone before Allah to answer for their deeds, highlighting that ultimate responsibility and judgment are entirely personal matters where no intercession from others can change one's fate without divine permission.

translation: Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds - the Most Merciful will grant them love.
interpretation: This verse expresses that true faith coupled with righteous action generates divine grace that translates into human hearts showing love and affection toward the believers. The promise is that sincere believers who act righteously will find acceptance and favor among people, as Allah places in the hearts of others a natural inclination to love and respect them. This reflects the principle that outward righteousness and inner faith create a spiritual magnetism that draws people toward goodness and virtue.

translation: So We have made it easy in your language that you may give good tidings thereby to the righteous and warn thereby a people who are stubborn/contentious.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the revelation was given in the Prophet's native Arabic tongue specifically to facilitate his mission of spreading the message to both believers and disbelievers. The divine ease (yusruna) refers to both the clarity of the Qur'anic language and the accessibility it provides for effective communication. The contrast between 'the righteous' (al-muttaqin) who receive glad tidings and 'a stubborn people' (qawman lidda) highlights how the same message serves different purposes depending on the spiritual state of the recipients—guidance for those who are receptive and a warning for those who resist. This reveals the universal applicability of the Qur'an while acknowledging that receptivity to its message depends on the listener's own disposition.

translation: And how many generations We destroyed before them? Can you perceive from them anyone, or hear from them any sound?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the futility of the idolaters' resistance by reminding them of the countless civilizations that came before them and were utterly annihilated for their defiance. The rhetorical questions about perceiving or hearing anything from the destroyed peoples serve to illustrate the complete and utter destruction that befalls those who reject Allah's message—they are erased from existence so thoroughly that no trace of them remains perceptible to the living. This is meant to be a sobering warning to the Quraysh and all deniers that defiance leads not merely to defeat, but to total obliteration and erasure from the world.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Ta Ha.
interpretation: This verse opens Surah Ta Ha with the Basmala (invocation of God's names) before presenting the mysterious letter combination 'Ta Ha,' which scholars interpret as either letters of the alphabet whose meanings are known to Allah alone, or as an invocation meaning 'O man,' serving to capture the reader's attention for the spiritual guidance that follows in the surah.

translation: We have not sent down the Qur'an upon you that you should be in distress.
interpretation: This verse reassures the Prophet Muhammad that the revelation of the Qur'an was not meant to burden him or cause him hardship, but rather to guide humanity. It emphasizes that the divine message is a mercy and a means of ease, not an instrument of suffering. The verse conveys Allah's compassion toward the Prophet and serves as a reminder that religious guidance should alleviate human struggle rather than compound it.

translation: Except as a reminder for those who fear [Allah]
interpretation: This phrase emphasizes that the Qur'an's primary benefit is for those who possess God-consciousness and fear Him. Its teachings and warnings are most effective for the spiritually receptive and conscientious, suggesting that spiritual receptivity and reverence for God are prerequisites for deriving true benefit from the Qur'an's guidance. Those lacking this foundational attitude may hear the message but fail to internalize or act upon it.

translation: A revelation from the One who created the earth and the highest heavens
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine origin and authority of the Qur'an by attributing it to Allah, who possesses the ultimate creative power over all existence. The mention of creating both the earth and the highest heavens establishes God's absolute sovereignty and dominion, thereby affirming that the Qur'an comes from the One with supreme knowledge and wisdom over all creation, making it a revelation worthy of full acceptance and obedience.

translation: The Most Merciful has established Himself upon the Throne.
interpretation: This verse affirms Allah's supreme authority and dominion over creation. The establishment upon the Throne (istawa) represents Allah's absolute sovereignty and control over all affairs of the universe. The emphasis on 'Ar-Rahman' (The Most Merciful) at the beginning suggests that this supreme power is exercised with mercy and justice, not arbitrary cruelty. This doctrine teaches that despite Allah's transcendence and majesty, His rule is fundamentally characterized by compassion toward His creation.

translation: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is under the soil.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute and comprehensive sovereignty of Allah over all creation - both the visible and invisible realms, the heavens, the earth, and everything in between and beneath. It conveys that nothing exists outside of God's dominion, ownership, and control, establishing the foundational principle of divine omnipotence and the complete dependence of all creatures upon their Creator. This assertion of Allah's universal sovereignty serves to humble creation before its Lord and to establish the basis for submission and worship.

translation: And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is even more hidden.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's complete and all-encompassing knowledge that extends beyond what humans can perceive or control. It serves as a reminder that attempting to hide one's true thoughts, intentions, or secrets from Allah is futile, as His knowledge penetrates all levels of reality—from the spoken word to the deepest, most concealed thoughts and feelings. This is meant to instill consciousness of Allah (taqwa) and accountability in believers, encouraging them to maintain sincerity and integrity in both public and private conduct, knowing that nothing escapes Allah's awareness.

translation: Allah - there is no deity except Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names.
interpretation: This verse establishes the core principle of Islamic monotheism by affirming that Allah alone is worthy of worship, and emphasizes His perfect attributes and qualities known as the ninety-nine names, which represent His divine perfection and sovereignty. The mention of His beautiful names underscores that all His actions and characteristics are guided by wisdom, mercy, and justice, serving as a foundation for understanding His relationship with creation.

translation: And has there come to you the story of Moses?
interpretation: This rhetorical question invites the listener to engage with the narrative of Moses that follows, emphasizing the importance and relevance of this historical account as a lesson for understanding God's guidance and the trials faced by His messengers. The question creates anticipation and draws attention to a significant example of divine wisdom and prophetic patience.

translation: When he saw a fire, he said to his family, 'Stay here; indeed, I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I can bring you a burning brand from it, or find at the fire some guidance.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates Prophet Musa's (Moses) human need and his initiative to seek provision for his family. His immediate concern for their welfare and comfort, combined with his hope to gain guidance from the fire, demonstrates the virtue of combining practical action with spiritual openness. The reference to seeking 'guidance' at the fire alludes to his subsequent encounter with the Divine at the burning bush, teaching that Allah often guides us through circumstances that begin as ordinary needs or searches.

translation: So when he reached it, he was called: 'O Moses!'
interpretation: This verse marks the moment of divine encounter where Moses, approaching the sacred fire, is addressed directly by name by God, establishing a personal relationship and indicating that he has been chosen for a special purpose. The act of being called by name emphasizes God's knowledge of Moses and His intentional selection of him for prophethood.

translation: Indeed, I am your Lord, so remove your sandals. Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa.
interpretation: This verse represents the moment of divine revelation to Prophet Moses at the burning bush, where God commands him to remove his sandals as a sign of reverence and sanctity. The removal of sandals symbolizes the need for spiritual purification and humility when standing before the Divine, emphasizing that the sacred valley demands a state of ritual and spiritual cleanliness. This act of obedience marks the beginning of Moses' transformation into a messenger and establishes the proper manner of approach to the Divine Presence.

translation: And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed to you.
interpretation: This verse conveys Allah's special selection of the Prophet Moses for a divine mission, imposing upon him the responsibility to attentively receive and obey the revelations (Wahi) that Allah will communicate to him. The command to listen emphasizes the necessity of complete attention, acceptance, and submission to divine guidance, establishing the foundational principle that Allah's chosen messengers must be fully receptive to His word and willing to implement His instructions without hesitation or alteration.

translation: Indeed, I am Allah - there is no deity except Me. So worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.
interpretation: This verse encapsulates the core of Islamic monotheism and the purpose of human existence. Allah asserts His absolute uniqueness and the exclusivity of His right to worship, emphasizing that servitude and devotion must be directed to Him alone. The command to establish prayer specifically 'for His remembrance' indicates that the primary function of ritual prayer is not merely a mechanical act of obedience, but rather an intentional means of maintaining consciousness of God, strengthening the bond between the servant and the Creator, and keeping the divine presence alive in the believer's heart and mind throughout their life.

translation: Indeed, the Hour is coming - I almost conceal it - so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the hidden nature of the Day of Judgment and God's divine wisdom in keeping its exact timing secret. The phrase 'I almost conceal it' conveys that God has kept the knowledge of the Hour nearly imperceptible to humanity, revealing only signs of its approach. This concealment serves a profound purpose: it ensures that people are judged based on the sincerity of their deeds and efforts rather than out of fear of imminent punishment. By hiding the exact time, God tests the genuine commitment of believers and prevents them from delaying their righteousness until the last moment. Thus, the concealment of the Hour becomes a mechanism of perfect divine justice, wherein each soul receives its recompense based on authentic striving and sincere intention.

translation: So let not those who do not believe in it turn you away from it, those who follow their desires and thus become ruined.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet (and by extension, the believers) to remain steadfast in faith and not be swayed by the disbelief and base desires of those who reject the message. It emphasizes that following one's whims and abandoning the truth leads to spiritual destruction and ruin, while staying the course despite opposition is the path to success. The verse teaches that conviction must be maintained regardless of external pressure from those driven by worldly desires rather than divine guidance.

translation: And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?
interpretation: This question, posed by Allah to Moses at the burning bush, is meant to draw Moses' attention to the staff in his hand as a means of understanding his divine mission. By asking this rhetorical question, Allah is initiating Moses into the purpose of the staff as an instrument through which he will perform miracles to convince Pharaoh and the people of Israel of his prophethood. The question serves as a transition from Moses' personal calling to his practical preparation as a messenger, establishing that ordinary objects can become extraordinary means of divine communication when placed in the hands of a prophet obedient to Allah's will.

translation: He said: 'It is my staff. I lean upon it, and with it I beat down branches for my sheep, and I have other uses for it.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates how Allah accepts and values sincere engagement with one's current responsibilities and resources. Musa (Moses) was present and occupied with the humble work of shepherding, yet he was fully present and purposeful in his duties. The mention of multiple uses for his staff suggests that even ordinary tools and circumstances can serve multiple functions in God's plan. This teaching emphasizes that one need not wait for extraordinary circumstances to demonstrate devotion or capability; excellence in present duties and mindful stewardship of what one possesses are themselves forms of readiness for greater responsibilities that Allah may call upon one to undertake.

translation: He said, 'Cast it down, O Moses.'
interpretation: This divine command represents the moment when Allah instructs Prophet Moses to throw down his staff as a sign of His power. The imperative form 'Alqaha' emphasizes the immediacy and authority of God's instruction, testing Moses' obedience and faith while demonstrating that what appears ordinary in human terms becomes extraordinary when placed in service of God's will. The direct address 'Ya Musa' reinforces the personal nature of this covenant between God and His prophet, establishing a foundational moment of trust in divine commands even when they seem unclear or fearful.

translation: So he cast it down, and thereupon it became a serpent moving swiftly.
interpretation: This verse describes the miraculous transformation of the staff into a living, moving serpent as a sign from Allah to Moses, demonstrating divine power over creation. The sudden change ('fa-idha' - 'thereupon') emphasizes the immediate and complete nature of the miracle, establishing that what appears to be an ordinary object can become something entirely different through Allah's command. This sign served to strengthen Moses' certainty and to provide him with evidence of divine support for his mission to Pharaoh.

translation: He said, 'Take it, and do not fear. We will return it to its former state.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates Allah's power to restore and transform, as exemplified when Moses cast down his staff and it became a serpent. The divine assurance 'do not fear' emphasizes that Allah's miracles serve to strengthen the believer's heart and establish certainty (yaqin) in His absolute control over all creation, transforming what appears as a threat into a sign of divine mastery and reassurance.

translation: And press your hand to your side; it will come out white, free from illness - another sign
interpretation: This verse describes one of the miracles granted to Prophet Moses as a sign of his prophethood. When Moses places his hand against his body and then withdraws it, it emerges radiantly white, yet healthy and unaffected by any disease or defect. This miraculous transformation serves as an undeniable proof of God's power and validation of Moses' divine mission, demonstrating that the whiteness is a supernatural phenomenon, not a pathological condition. The sign is meant to convince Pharaoh and those who witness it of the truth of Moses' message.

translation: So that We may show you some of Our greatest signs
interpretation: This verse expresses Allah's purpose in guiding the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) - namely, to grant him witness to the manifestation of His divine power and miracles. The 'greatest signs' refer to the wonders and extraordinary events that would confirm the truth of the message, serving as evidence of divine authority and demonstrating that Allah's promises are certain and His power is absolute.

translation: Go to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed.
interpretation: This verse represents Allah's command to Moses to confront Pharaoh despite Pharaoh's arrogance and tyranny. The phrase 'he has transgressed' emphasizes that Pharaoh's rebellion against Allah's guidance and his oppression of people have reached a level that demands direct confrontation. The instruction highlights the divine mission of prophets to challenge unjust rulers and call them back to monotheism, regardless of the ruler's power or defiance. It underscores that even the mightiest earthly powers cannot escape Allah's judgment when they persist in wrongdoing.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, expand for me my breast'
interpretation: This is Musa's (Moses) supplication to Allah requesting an expansion of his heart and mind to accept and understand his divine mission, and to be granted the capability to face the challenges of delivering the message to Pharaoh and the Children of Israel with patience, clarity, and inner peace.

translation: And make easy for me my affair
interpretation: This phrase, part of a supplication, expresses the human need for divine assistance in facilitating the complexities and difficulties of life's matters. It reflects the Islamic teaching that while humans must strive and plan, ultimate ease and success come from Allah's will and grace. The request acknowledges human limitation and dependence on divine support to overcome obstacles and achieve objectives with wisdom and clarity.

translation: And untie the knot from my tongue
interpretation: This is part of Prophet Moses's supplication to Allah, expressing his request for help in overcoming his speech impediment so that he can communicate clearly and effectively with Pharaoh. The phrase reflects the human tendency to seek divine assistance in removing obstacles that hinder the fulfillment of one's mission and the need for clarity in delivering God's message. The 'knot' is both literal (referring to a speech defect) and symbolic of any barrier preventing clear communication of truth.

translation: They may understand my speech
interpretation: This phrase, spoken by Prophet Musa in Surah Ta-Ha (20:28), expresses his prayer that Allah remove a speech impediment so that his message to Pharaoh will be clearly comprehended. The verse illustrates the importance of clear communication in conveying divine truth, and demonstrates that even prophets sought Allah's assistance in overcoming obstacles to effective preaching. The underlying meaning emphasizes that understanding of divine guidance requires not only the speaker's clarity but also Allah's grace in facilitating comprehension among the listeners.

translation: And appoint for me a minister from my family
interpretation: This supplication, spoken by Prophet Moses, represents a request for supportive leadership and shared responsibility in the divine mission. The request for a minister from his family indicates a desire for someone trustworthy and close to him—his brother Aaron—to assist him in delivering God's message and bearing the burden of guiding the people. This reflects the spiritual principle that prophets and leaders should seek capable helpers to strengthen their efforts, and that familial bonds combined with shared purpose create a foundation for effective collaboration in righteousness.

translation: Aaron is my brother
interpretation: This phrase expresses a familial relationship and reflects Moses' acknowledgment of his brother Aaron. In the context of Qur'anic narrative, this statement emphasizes the bond between the two prophets and is used to invoke Aaron's support and assistance in Moses' mission to Pharaoh, demonstrating how family ties and mutual support are valued in fulfilling divine responsibilities.

translation: Strengthen with him my back (or, my arm/power)
interpretation: This phrase expresses a request for divine assistance and support. The speaker seeks to be empowered and strengthened through the help of another person, typically understood in context as a supplication for God to provide aid and solidarity in fulfilling a difficult mission or responsibility. It reflects the human need for partnership and divine facilitation when facing challenging tasks.

translation: And make him my partner in my affair
interpretation: This phrase reflects the supplication of Prophet Musa (Moses) to Allah, requesting that Allah grant his brother Harun (Aaron) a share in his prophetic mission and responsibility. It demonstrates the importance of seeking assistance from capable individuals and recognizing that sharing responsibility with trustworthy companions strengthens one's ability to carry out important duties. The phrase emphasizes the principle of collaborative leadership and mutual support in fulfilling divine commands.

translation: So that we may glorify You abundantly
interpretation: This phrase expresses the purpose of divine guidance and blessings - to enable the servants of Allah to engage in frequent and continuous praise and glorification of Him. It emphasizes that the ultimate purpose of creation and the granting of faculties is to direct human consciousness toward the remembrance and exaltation of the Divine, recognizing that glorifying Allah abundantly is both the highest aspiration and the most fitting response to His greatness and mercy.

translation: And we remember you frequently / And we mention you often
interpretation: This verse reflects the human tendency to frequently invoke and remember the name or memory of someone significant. In Islamic context, it emphasizes the importance of remembrance (dhikr) of Allah and His guidance, suggesting that constant and repeated remembrance is a spiritual practice that reinforces faith and connection to the Divine.

translation: Indeed, You have always been seeing of us (aware of us).
interpretation: This verse expresses the acknowledgment that Allah's knowledge and awareness encompass all creation at all times. It affirms that nothing escapes God's sight or cognition, establishing the foundational Islamic principle that Allah is All-Knowing and All-Seeing, which serves to instill consciousness of divine accountability in believers' hearts and encourage moral responsibility in their actions.

translation: He said: "You have been granted your request, O Moses."
interpretation: This verse represents Allah's affirmative response to Moses' supplication. The granting of the request signifies Allah's mercy and acceptance of the righteous servant's plea, demonstrating that sincere and humble supplication to Allah from those of noble character is answered. This reflects the principle that Allah listens to and responds to His servants' genuine calls for guidance and assistance.

translation: And indeed, We have bestowed favor upon you another time.
interpretation: This verse acknowledges a previous act of divine grace bestowed upon the Prophet Muhammad, likely referring to earlier blessings and deliverances mentioned in prior Qur'anic passages. The phrase 'another time' suggests a repetition of God's favor, emphasizing the continuous and renewed nature of divine mercy toward the Prophet. This serves to reinforce the Prophet's position as one specially chosen and protected by Allah, reminding him of God's consistent support throughout his mission, which provides reassurance and encouragement during times of difficulty.

translation: When We inspired to your mother that which is inspired
interpretation: This verse refers to the divine revelation given to Mary, the mother of Jesus, instructing her regarding the miraculous birth and the special nature of her son. The phrase emphasizes the direct communication from Allah to Mary through revelation, establishing her as a recipient of divine guidance and elevating her status as the chosen mother of a prophet. It underscores that the extraordinary events surrounding Jesus's birth were part of Allah's predetermined plan and divine wisdom.

translation: Cast him into the chest, then cast it into the river. Let the river cast him upon the shore, where an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his shall take him. And I have cast upon you love from Me, that you may be brought up under My eye."
interpretation: This verse illustrates how Allah's providence works through natural and ordinary means to achieve His divine purposes. Though Moses's mother was instructed to place her infant son in a basket and entrust him to the river—an act that appears to involve great risk and uncertainty—Allah had already determined the outcome: the river would deliver him safely to shore where Pharaoh's household would find and raise him. The final phrase emphasizes that Allah's special mercy and protection over Moses was already established through His love, which guided all events according to His perfect wisdom. The verse teaches that true reliance on Allah does not mean passivity, but rather taking reasonable action while trusting that Allah directs all circumstances toward His intended ends.

translation: When your sister walked forth and said, 'Shall I direct you to someone who will take care of him?' So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve. And you killed a soul, so We saved you from distress and tried you with trials. Then you stayed years among the people of Midian. Then you came at the appointed time, O Moses!
interpretation: This verse illustrates Allah's divine providence in orchestrating the events of Moses' life toward a greater purpose. Each trial and apparent misfortune - his separation from his mother, the killing of the Egyptian, his flight to Midian - served as necessary tests that refined Moses' character and prepared him for his ultimate mission as a messenger to Pharaoh. The verse emphasizes that Allah's testing and guidance work together seamlessly, where even difficult circumstances are instruments of divine wisdom leading the chosen servant toward his destined role.

translation: And I have chosen you for Myself
interpretation: This verse expresses the divine selection and special favor granted by God to Moses, indicating that he was chosen for a unique and intimate relationship with the Divine. The phrase conveys that Moses was specifically crafted and prepared by God to fulfill a special purpose and mission, highlighting the honor and responsibility of being God's elect messenger. The use of 'for Myself' emphasizes the direct relationship between God and Moses, suggesting an exclusive bond of service and guidance that sets him apart from others.

translation: Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and do not slack in remembering Me
interpretation: This verse, spoken to Prophet Moses, commands him and Aaron to proceed with divine miracles and clear proofs to Pharaoh's people while maintaining constant remembrance of Allah. The prohibition against 'slacking' (taani) emphasizes that the mission of calling people to Allah requires unwavering commitment and vigilance—the messengers must not become negligent, forgetful, or lazy in their devotion to Allah and in their duty to convey His message, serving as a model of dedication for believers in their religious responsibilities.

translation: Go both of you to Pharaoh. Indeed, he has transgressed.
interpretation: This verse represents Allah's command to Moses and Aaron to convey His message to Pharaoh despite his arrogance and defiance. The phrase 'he has transgressed' serves as both a description of Pharaoh's spiritual state and a justification for why the mission is necessary—his rebellion against divine truth has reached such heights that a direct confrontation with Allah's message through His prophets is required. The dual form 'go both of you' emphasizes the importance of the mission and provides mutual support for the messengers in their challenging task of calling the most powerful ruler of their time to submit to Allah.

translation: So speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he will remember or fear [Allah].
interpretation: This verse teaches that persuasion and kind communication are the most effective means of calling people towards truth and belief. Even when addressing someone who may be obstinate or resistant, maintaining gentleness and softness in speech preserves their dignity, opens their heart to receive the message, and increases the likelihood that they will reflect upon it or develop God-consciousness. The verse emphasizes that harshness closes doors to understanding, while kindness opens the possibility for spiritual awakening and moral transformation.

translation: They said: 'Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will commit injustice against us or that he will transgress.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the human concern with fairness and balance in leadership. The speakers fear two extremes: that their leader might be lenient or negligent in upholding justice ('yafrit' - to neglect or fall short), or that he might abuse his authority through tyranny ('yatghaa' - to transgress or exceed bounds). This dual concern demonstrates the importance of moderation and justice in governance, and reflects the human need for rulers who neither abandon their responsibilities nor exceed their rightful authority. The fear of both extremes shows that true leadership requires maintaining equilibrium between protecting rights and maintaining order.

translation: He said, 'Do not fear. Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see.'
interpretation: This verse conveys divine reassurance and protection, emphasizing that God's presence transcends physical proximity—His awareness and vigilance are constant. The promise 'I am with you' signifies not merely spatial presence but active intervention and support, while 'I hear and I see' underscores God's comprehensive knowledge of all circumstances and needs, implying that He will respond appropriately to His servants' situations. This addresses the human tendency to feel alone in difficulty, reminding believers that divine attention never wavers.

translation: So go to him and say, 'Indeed, we are messengers of your Lord, so send with us the Children of Israel and do not punish them. We have come to you with a sign from your Lord. And peace be upon those who follow guidance.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine mission of the messengers and their appeal to authority based on their representation of God's will rather than personal persuasion. The phrase 'we are messengers of your Lord' establishes that their demand carries divine backing, making obedience a matter of religious obligation. The closing phrase about peace being upon those who follow guidance suggests that submission to God's messengers is inseparable from the path of righteousness, implying that rejection of the messengers' call is a deviation from the straight path.

translation: Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment is upon those who disbelieve and turn away.
interpretation: This verse affirms the divine reality of consequences for rejection of truth and arrogance. The revelation being emphasized ('إنا قد أوحي إلينا') indicates a firm certainty in the speaker's understanding that accountability is an inevitable divine principle—those who actively deny the truth and stubbornly turn away from guidance will inevitably face Allah's punishment. This establishes that rejection combined with turning away (willful abandonment) is what incurs divine justice, emphasizing both the intellectual and volitional dimensions of kufr.

translation: He said, 'Then who is your Lord, O Moses?'
interpretation: This verse represents Pharaoh's arrogant and defiant challenge to Moses, demanding that Moses identify his Lord. Pharaoh's question reveals his ultimate rejection of monotheism and his desire to assert his own supremacy and godhood. The verse demonstrates Pharaoh's spiritual blindness and his refusal to acknowledge any power beyond himself, despite the clear signs and miracles that Moses has presented to him.

translation: He said: 'Our Lord is He Who gave to everything its creation, then guided it.'
interpretation: This verse expresses the Islamic concept that Allah is the ultimate Creator and Guide of all existence. The 'creation' refers to the inherent nature, form, and function that Allah bestowed upon everything in the universe. The subsequent 'guidance' signifies that Allah not only brought things into existence but also provided them with the means, instincts, and faculties to fulfill their purpose and function in accordance with their created nature. This represents the divine wisdom in both creation and sustenance, demonstrating Allah's complete knowledge and sovereignty over all things.

translation: He said, "Then what is the matter with the former peoples?"
interpretation: This question expresses curiosity and concern about the fate of previous generations and civilizations. The speaker is asking for clarification about why earlier peoples were destroyed or punished, suggesting a desire to understand God's justice and the consequences of rejecting divine guidance. The question implies that if people before were held accountable for their disbelief, then the current generation should also expect similar accountability, highlighting the consistency of God's justice across all ages.

translation: He said, 'The knowledge of it is with my Lord in a record. My Lord does not go astray, nor does He forget.'
interpretation: This verse expresses the absolute omniscience and infallibility of Allah, emphasizing that all knowledge, particularly that which is hidden from human perception, is preserved in divine records and protected by Allah's perfect memory and unwavering guidance. The speaker acknowledges human limitations while affirming that forgetting and error are impossible attributes of God, thus establishing complete trust in Divine wisdom and the certainty of divine justice and accountability in the Hereafter.

translation: The One who made the earth a cradle for you and made pathways for you therein and sent down water from the sky, by which We brought forth pairs of various plants.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Divine providence and the intricate system of provision that Allah has established for humanity. The metaphor of the earth as a 'cradle' (mihad) conveys both security and nurturing care, suggesting that the earth has been precisely designed for human sustenance and comfort. The mention of pathways, water, and vegetation in sequence demonstrates the interconnected natural systems—pathways enable movement and commerce, water is the essential medium of life, and diverse vegetation sustains all creatures. The phrase 'pairs of various plants' (azwaj min nabat shatta) points to the complementary nature of creation and the biodiversity through which Allah maintains ecological balance, inviting reflection on how every element of creation serves a purposeful function in sustaining life.

translation: Eat and graze your livestock. Indeed, in that are signs for people of understanding.
interpretation: This verse encourages humans to consume the sustenance provided by their livestock and to tend to them properly through grazing. The deeper meaning points to the existence of signs (ayat) in the natural provision of livestock for those who possess intellect and reason. God is directing believers to observe and reflect upon how livestock serve as evidence of divine provision and careful design, demonstrating God's mercy and wisdom in creating animals that sustain human life. The verse invites contemplation on the relationship between human stewardship of nature and divine bounty, emphasizing that reflection on these natural provisions leads to greater understanding of God's power and benevolence.

translation: From it We created you, and into it We return you, and from it We will bring you forth once more.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the cyclical relationship between humanity and the earth, reflecting the humbling truth that we originate from earthly matter and ultimately return to it in death, only to be resurrected for the final judgment. It underscores human insignificance relative to God's dominion and the certainty of resurrection, dismantling any illusion of permanence or independence from divine will in our earthly existence.

translation: And indeed We showed him all Our signs, but he denied them and refused.
interpretation: This verse refers to Pharaoh who, despite witnessing all the miracles and clear signs from Allah through Prophet Moses, stubbornly rejected the truth and refused to believe or submit. The verse illustrates how human obstinacy and pride can cause one to reject even the most evident proofs of Allah's existence and power, emphasizing that mere exposure to truth is insufficient without a willing heart to accept it.

translation: He said, 'Have you come to us to drive us out of our land with your magic, O Moses?'
interpretation: Pharaoh's accusation reveals his fear that Moses poses a threat to his political power and control over Egypt. By attributing Moses's signs to magic rather than acknowledging them as divine miracles, Pharaoh resorts to dismissing the truth and delegitimizing Moses's mission in the eyes of his people. This response demonstrates the typical resistance of those in power when confronted with a message that challenges their authority, choosing denial and false accusations over honest reflection on the evidence presented to them.

translation: So let us bring you magic like it. Then set between us and you an appointment which we will not fail to keep, nor will you, [at] a place suitable [for us both].
interpretation: This verse reflects the arrogance and false confidence of Pharaoh's magicians when confronted with Moses' miraculous staff. They are proposing a public contest, believing their magical skills can match or overcome the divine sign. Their willingness to set a specific time and place for the confrontation demonstrates their conviction in their own abilities and their dismissal of the threat posed by Moses. However, their confidence is built on illusion and deception rather than truth, which will ultimately be exposed when they witness the clear distinction between magic and divine miracle.

translation: He said, 'Your appointment is the Day of Adornment, and let the people be gathered at forenoon.'
interpretation: This verse refers to Pharaoh's challenge to Moses regarding a confrontation between them. The 'Day of Adornment' (Yawm al-Zīnah) likely refers to a festival day when Egyptians would dress in their finest and gather in public display. Pharaoh arrogantly proposes this day for their contest, expecting his people and their finery to impress and intimidate Moses and the Israelites. By specifying the 'forenoon,' Pharaoh seeks the brightest time of day to showcase his power and grandeur. The verse illustrates Pharaoh's pride and his attempt to turn a spiritual confrontation into a display of worldly magnificence, revealing his fundamental misunderstanding of the nature of the encounter with God's prophet.

translation: So Pharaoh turned away, gathered his strategy, then came [with his forces].
interpretation: This verse illustrates Pharaoh's response to Moses' message by first rejecting it and then mobilizing all his resources and cunning to oppose Moses and his followers. The phrase 'gathered his strategy' (جمع كيده) signifies that Pharaoh consolidated his power, intelligence, and deceptive tactics with deliberate intent. This demonstrates how those who reject the truth often respond not with reflection but with active opposition, using whatever means and influence they possess to resist the divine message. Pharaoh's turning away represents the hardening of hearts against truth, while his gathering of strategy shows the human tendency to rely on worldly power rather than submission to God.

translation: Moses said to them: 'Woe to you! Do not forge a lie against Allah, lest He destroy you with punishment. Indeed, whoever forges a lie has failed.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the grave spiritual danger of fabricating falsehoods about Allah and His religion. Moses warns his people that inventing lies about Allah's commands or attributes is not merely a social or ethical violation, but an act that invites divine punishment and spiritual ruin. The phrase 'has failed' (khaaba) indicates that those who resort to such fabrication have lost both their moral standing and their ultimate success in the Hereafter. The warning serves to establish that truthfulness in religious matters is foundational to one's relationship with Allah, and deception in religious discourse severs one from divine favor.

translation: Then they disputed among themselves regarding their matter, and they concealed the secret talk.
interpretation: This verse depicts the internal discord and hidden deliberations of those who rejected the truth. The dispute among themselves shows the confusion and disagreement that arise when people abandon divine guidance, while their concealment of secret conversations reveals their awareness of wrongdoing and their attempt to hide their deception from others. This illustrates how those who turn away from God's signs become fragmented in their opposition, resorting to clandestine schemes rather than open and honest discourse.

translation: They said, 'Indeed, these two are magicians who want to drive you out from your land through their magic and take away your best way of life.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates how those who reject divine truth resort to personal attacks and false accusations against the messengers rather than engage with their message on its merits. By attributing Moses and Aaron's miracles to mere sorcery, the Egyptians reveal their spiritual blindness and their attempt to manipulate the masses through fear and misrepresentation, demonstrating that rejection of truth often stems from the human tendency to defend established power structures and worldly interests rather than from any rational basis.

translation: So gather together your plot, then come in a line. And indeed, he has succeeded today who has overcome [me].
interpretation: This verse captures the defiant challenge issued by Pharaoh to the magicians, commanding them to unite their magical abilities and present themselves in organized formation against Moses. The phrase 'he has succeeded today who has overcome me' reflects Pharaoh's arrogant belief that victory belongs to whoever can defeat him, revealing his profound spiritual blindness—for he fails to recognize that true success lies not in overcoming him, but in submission to Allah and His truth. This statement demonstrates how the disbelievers measure success by worldly dominance rather than by divine guidance, and their measures of achievement are fundamentally inverted from the truth.

translation: They said: O Moses, either you throw [your staff] or we will be the first to throw [our staffs].
interpretation: This verse reflects the magicians' challenge to Moses, displaying their confidence and arrogance in their magical abilities. Their words reveal their defiance and unwillingness to submit to Moses' message - they seek to intimidate him by suggesting they are capable of matching or surpassing his miracles through their own magical arts. The verse illustrates how those who rely on falsehood often attempt to overcome truth through intimidation and displays of apparent power, yet this challenge ultimately led to their humiliation and Allah's vindication of Moses' truth.

translation: He said, 'No, throw!' And suddenly their ropes and sticks appeared to him from their magic as though they were moving.
interpretation: This verse illustrates how deception and illusion, even when convincingly presented, cannot overcome truth and divine protection. Moses's calm response in the face of the magicians' stunning display demonstrates unwavering faith in God's support. The phrase 'yakhyal ilayhi' (appeared to him) emphasizes that what seemed real was merely an optical illusion created by skilled deception, teaching that the apparent power of falsehood is ultimately insubstantial when confronted with truth backed by divine will. This moment exemplifies how believers should remain steadfast and not be swayed by impressive but ultimately hollow tricks of those who oppose God's message.

translation: Then Moses felt fear within himself.
interpretation: This verse describes Moses' internal state of apprehension when he witnessed the miraculous transformation of the staffs into serpents during his confrontation with Pharaoh's sorcerers. Despite Moses' faith and his role as a messenger, he experienced natural human fear and anxiety in the face of this seemingly overwhelming display of sorcery. This demonstrates that even the greatest prophets are not immune to emotional responses and worldly concerns, and that experiencing fear in difficult circumstances is a part of the human condition—what matters is how one responds to that fear with faith and trust in God.

translation: We said, 'Do not fear; indeed, you are the superior one.'
interpretation: This verse (Taha 20:68) is spoken to Prophet Musa, assuring him of his triumph over Pharaoh despite the apparent power disparity. The interpretation conveys that Allah grants victory to the truthful and steadfast, and that ultimate superiority rests not in worldly might or sorcery, but in divine support and righteousness. The reassurance teaches believers that alignment with divine will elevates one above all opposition, regardless of the enemy's material strength or apparent dominance.

translation: And cast down what is in your right hand; it will swallow up what they have made. Indeed, what they have made is only a magician's trick, and the magician will not succeed wherever he goes.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the ultimate futility of falsehood and deception when confronted by divine truth. The staff of Moses, representing God's power and truth, effortlessly overwhelms the illusory tricks of Pharaoh's magicians, demonstrating that no matter how convincingly deception is presented or how many may practice it, it cannot ultimately prevail against the reality of God's message. The magician's failure is not accidental but inevitable, for truth by its nature supersedes all forms of artifice and illusion.

translation: So the magicians fell down in prostration. They said, 'We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the moment when the Egyptian magicians, after witnessing the clear miracle of Moses' staff consuming their magical illusions, experienced a spiritual transformation that transcended their worldly interests and fear of Pharaoh. Their immediate prostration and declaration of faith demonstrates that when truth becomes undeniable through divine signs, sincere hearts are moved to submit to God's will, abandoning their attachment to status, power, and material reward in favor of genuine belief in the One God.

translation: He said, 'Have you believed in him before I gave you permission? Indeed, he is your leader who taught you magic. So I will surely cut off your hands and feet on alternate sides, and I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees, and you will surely know which of us is more severe in punishment and more lasting.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the tyrant's desperate resort to threats and brutal punishment when confronted with his subjects' faith. By attributing Moses' miracles to 'magic' and positioning himself as the source of their knowledge and authority, Pharaoh attempts to maintain control through intimidation. His escalating threats—amputation and crucifixion—reveal how those who reject divine truth, despite witnessing clear signs, resort to violence and cruelty as their final recourse. The verse demonstrates that tyranny, when faced with the truth, becomes increasingly brutal and irrational, exposing the pathological nature of those who cling to falsehood and power at any cost.

translation: They said, 'We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us and over the One Who created us. So decree what you will decree. You can only decree concerning this worldly life.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the steadfast rejection of those who cling to divine truth despite pressure and threats from an unjust ruler. The phrase 'the One Who created us' emphasizes their consciousness of a higher authority than any earthly power, suggesting that true obedience belongs only to Allah. By stating 'You can only decree concerning this worldly life,' they acknowledge the fundamental limitation of tyrannical authority—it has no power over the eternal reality beyond this transient existence. This affirms that material punishment and threats lose their power over those whose conviction is rooted in recognition of the divine and awareness of the afterlife.

translation: Indeed, we have believed in our Lord so that He may forgive us our sins and the sorcery to which you compelled us. And Allah is better and more lasting.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle that sincere faith in Allah is the pathway to forgiveness and spiritual redemption. The speakers acknowledge that despite being forced to participate in sorcery against their will, their genuine belief in Allah supersedes their coercion, emphasizing that Allah judges the heart's true condition rather than outward actions performed under duress. The statement that 'Allah is better and more lasting' affirms that reliance upon Allah's justice and eternal nature is superior to any worldly power or temporary authority that attempts to compel people away from the truth.

translation: Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal - for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the eternal torment of those who meet Allah while burdened with disbelief and major sins, particularly shirk. The phrase 'neither die nor live' conveys the idea of an existence marked by perpetual suffering without the mercy of death or the peace of life - a state of continuous consciousness experiencing punishment, which is more dreadful than death itself. This teaches that accountability before Allah is absolute, and the consequences of meeting Him in a state of guilt without repentance are irreversible and unimaginably severe.

translation: And whoever comes to Him as a believer having done righteous deeds - those will have the highest ranks.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the highest stations in Paradise are reserved exclusively for those who combine two essential qualities: sincere belief in Allah and the consistent performance of righteous deeds. It establishes that true success is not achieved through either faith or works alone, but through their integration - one's inner conviction must manifest in outward righteous actions. The term "Al-Darajat Al-Ulaa" (the highest ranks) signifies the proximity to Allah and supreme honor in the Hereafter, which serves as motivation for believers to persevere in both faith and virtuous conduct throughout their lives.

translation: Gardens of Eden beneath which rivers flow, where they will abide forever. And that is the reward of those who purify themselves.
interpretation: This verse describes the ultimate reward in Paradise for those who engage in spiritual and moral purification (tazkiyah). The phrase 'those who purify themselves' refers to individuals who cleanse their souls from sin, pride, and worldly attachments through righteous deeds and obedience to Allah. The eternal nature of the gardens and the perpetual rivers symbolize the infinite blessings and continuous bounty that await the purified in the Hereafter, emphasizing that spiritual purification in this life is the gateway to eternal felicity and God's favor in the next.

translation: And We indeed revealed to Moses: 'Travel by night with My servants and strike for them a dry path through the sea. Do not fear being overtaken, nor be afraid.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's direct communication with Moses and His miraculous intervention on behalf of the believers. The command to travel by night represents the concealment and protection of the believers from their pursuers, while the parting of the sea demonstrates Allah's absolute power over creation. The reassurance against fear of being overtaken serves to strengthen the hearts of the believers with certainty that Allah's protection supersedes all earthly threats, teaching that reliance upon Allah's promises brings safety even in seemingly impossible circumstances.

translation: So Pharaoh pursued them with his soldiers, and the sea overwhelmed them with that which overwhelmed them.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the consequence of Pharaoh's arrogance and defiance of Allah's signs. Despite witnessing the parting of the sea, Pharaoh's pride compelled him to pursue the believers into the sea with his army, resulting in their destruction. The repetition of 'what overwhelmed them' emphasizes the inevitability and completeness of Allah's punishment upon those who persist in denying the truth and oppressing the faithful, demonstrating that Divine justice cannot be escaped by those who choose rebellion over submission.

translation: And Pharaoh led his people astray, and did not guide [them].
interpretation: This verse illustrates the consequences of rejecting divine guidance and the responsibility of leaders in their charge. Pharaoh's misguidance of his people serves as a warning about how those in positions of authority can lead entire nations away from truth through pride, denial of God's signs, and adherence to falsehood. The verse emphasizes that true guidance comes only from God, and those who reject it and lead others away from it will face accountability for their actions and the corruption they spread.

translation: O Children of Israel, indeed We saved you from your enemy, and We promised you the appointment at the right side of the Mount (Sinai), and We sent down upon you manna and quails.
interpretation: This verse reminds the Israelites of God's favors toward them: their deliverance from Pharaoh's oppression, the covenant made with them at Mount Sinai where they would receive divine law and guidance, and the miraculous sustenance provided during their wilderness journey. The verse serves as an appeal to their conscience and gratitude, establishing the basis for their obligation to fulfill the covenant and obey God's commandments, implying that rejection of these blessings would be a grave ingratitude deserving of punishment.

translation: Eat from the good things We have provided for you, and do not transgress therein, lest My anger descend upon you. And whoever My anger descends upon has indeed fallen.
interpretation: This verse establishes the principle that divine provision is a mercy meant to be enjoyed in moderation and gratitude. Transgression in consumption—whether through excess, ingratitude, or using blessings for forbidden purposes—constitutes a rebellion against the divine order that inevitably invokes divine punishment. The verse teaches that true ruin comes not from poverty but from spiritual corruption manifested through the misuse of bounty, emphasizing that obedience and restraint in the enjoyment of lawful things is the path to maintaining divine favor and spiritual well-being.

translation: And indeed, I am the Forgiving One for whoever repents and believes and does righteous deeds, then remains guided.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Allah's forgiveness is not merely a single act of acceptance, but rather encompasses a continuous process of spiritual transformation. The progression from repentance (tawbah) to faith (iman) to righteous works (amal salih) to remaining on guidance (ihtida) indicates that true forgiveness requires a sustained commitment to moral and spiritual rectitude. The phrase 'then remains guided' suggests that forgiveness is preserved through perseverance in righteousness, meaning that merely turning to Allah is insufficient without accompanying it with consistent righteous action and unwavering adherence to the straight path.

translation: And what has made you hasten away from your people, O Moses?
interpretation: This question, posed by Allah to Moses when he was coming down from Mount Sinai, reproves Moses for his excessive haste in leaving his people to receive the divine tablets. The verse illustrates that despite Moses' noble purpose in ascending the mountain for the revelation, his failure to arrange proper guidance for his people during his absence left them vulnerable to spiritual corruption—they subsequently fell into idolatry. The question thus emphasizes the obligation of a leader and prophet to balance spiritual duties with temporal responsibilities toward their community, teaching that zeal for religious knowledge must be tempered with prudent care for those under one's charge.

translation: He said: 'These are my followers. I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the speaker's (Musa/Moses) declaration of his commitment to following Allah's guidance and his earnest effort to fulfill His commands quickly and sincerely, motivated by the desire to earn Allah's approval and satisfaction. It demonstrates complete submission and obedience, prioritizing divine pleasure above all else.

translation: He said: 'Indeed, we have tested your people after you, and As-Samiri has led them astray.'
interpretation: This verse reveals that during Moses' absence on Mount Sinai, Allah tested the Israelites by allowing them to be misled by As-Samiri, who crafted the golden calf. The verse emphasizes how trials and temptations are part of Allah's divine testing of humanity, and that even a chosen people can fall into error when they abandon their guidance and follow the false promises of deceivers. It illustrates the consequence of straying from true faith when leadership is absent and people are vulnerable to manipulation.

translation: So Moses returned to his people angry and grieved. He said, "O my people, did not your Lord promise you a fair promise? Then did the time seem long to you, or did you desire that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you, so you broke your promise to me?"
interpretation: This verse illustrates the emotional and spiritual struggle of a leader witnessing his followers' abandonment of faith. Moses' anger and grief reflect not mere personal disappointment but a profound concern for his people's spiritual well-being and their violation of the covenant. His rhetorical questions expose the illogic of their transgression: they had witnessed God's promises and mercy, yet chose to abandon their commitment, thereby inviting divine punishment upon themselves. The verse emphasizes the consequence of breaking one's word to God through the medium of His messenger, and suggests that such betrayal stems from either impatience with divine timing or a reckless disregard for the consequences of disobedience.

translation: They said, 'We did not break our promise to you by our will, but we were burdened with ornaments of the people, so we cast them into [the fire], and thus the Samiri threw [something else].'
interpretation: This verse illustrates how those who worshipped the golden calf attempted to justify their transgression by claiming they were compelled by the weight of the people's jewelry and ornaments. The passage reveals the human tendency to deflect responsibility for sin by blaming external circumstances or peer pressure. The mention of the Samiri casting something (his own contribution to the idol) suggests individual culpability even within collective wrongdoing, emphasizing that despite external influences, each person bears personal responsibility for their choices and actions. The verse conveys that excuses rooted in material temptation and social conformity do not absolve one of accountability before God.

translation: So he brought out for them a calf, a body which had a lowing sound. Then they said, 'This is your god and the god of Moses, but he forgot.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the profound spiritual blindness and idolatry of the Israelites. Despite witnessing countless miracles through Moses, they immediately abandon their faith when Moses is absent, preferring a tangible, lifeless creation over the invisible God. The phrase 'but he forgot' suggests they excuse Moses for not remembering their 'true god,' revealing how people can rationalize and justify their own departures from truth when they are spiritually heedless. The calf becomes a symbol of how base desires and the attraction to the material and visible can overwhelm the faculty of reason and spiritual discernment, even among a people specially chosen and guided.

translation: Do they not see that it (the idol) does not return to them any word, and does not possess for them any harm nor benefit?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the futility of idolatry by highlighting the fundamental incapacity of idols to communicate, protect, or provide any form of benefit to their worshippers. The multiple negations ('does not return...does not possess') serve to establish the absolute powerlessness of these false gods, thereby exposing the irrationality of directing worship toward objects that are devoid of any agency or will. The verse calls the believers to recognize this obvious reality through reason and observation, challenging the idolaters to contemplate the logical absurdity of their practice.

translation: And indeed Aaron had said to them before, "O my people, you have been tested by it. And indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command."
interpretation: Aaron attempts to guide his people away from idolatry by reminding them that their deviation through the golden calf is a test or trial from God, not something to be pursued. His appeal to God's mercy (al-Rahman) serves as a counterpoint to their materialistic temptation, suggesting that true benefit lies in submission to God's guidance rather than in worldly fabrications. Aaron's call for obedience to his command reflects the divinely-appointed authority of prophetic leadership in guiding the community toward monotheism and away from misguidance.

translation: They said: 'We will not cease to cling to it [the calf] until Moses returns to us.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the weakness of human resolve and susceptibility to idolatry when leadership is absent. The people's attachment to the golden calf reveals how quickly they abandoned their covenant with Allah during Moses' absence, suggesting that spiritual steadfastness requires continuous guidance and that communities can easily regress into polytheism when deprived of righteous leadership and divine reminders.

translation: He said: 'O Aaron, what prevented you when you saw them going astray?'
interpretation: This verse reflects Moses's profound disappointment upon discovering that the Israelites had fallen into idolatry by worshipping the golden calf during his absence. Moses's question to Aaron emphasizes the responsibility of leadership in preventing moral deviation and the importance of active intervention when witnessing those under one's care straying from the path of God. The question implicitly conveys that even in the absence of the primary leader, the secondary leader bears a duty to firmly resist and prevent deviation from divine guidance, suggesting that spiritual leadership is not merely about passive observation but requires courageous action and unwavering commitment to God's principles.

translation: Will you not follow me? Have you then disobeyed my command?
interpretation: This verse reflects the profound despair of a believer (Prophet Nuh) who has devoted his life to calling his people to the oneness of Allah, only to witness their persistent rejection and defiance despite his sincere efforts and warnings. The rhetorical questions convey both the speaker's anguish at their refusal to accept divine guidance and the reproach toward those who reject the truth that has been clearly presented to them. It serves as a reminder of the challenge faced by prophets and sincere believers when confronted with human arrogance and the hardening of hearts against divine truth.

translation: He said, 'O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or my head. Indeed, I feared that you would say, "You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word."'
interpretation: This verse reveals Haroon's (Aaron's) emotional and psychological state when confronted by Musa (Moses) upon his return from Mount Sinai. Haroon's plea to not be physically grabbed demonstrates his vulnerability and fear of being blamed, while his stated reason for fearing accusation of causing division shows his awareness of the gravity of what occurred during Musa's absence. His concern reflects the human tendency to prioritize one's reputation and social standing, and it illustrates how even righteous individuals can be moved by fear of judgment from those they respect, revealing the internal conflict between duty and self-preservation.

translation: He said, 'What is your excuse, O Samiri?'
interpretation: This verse represents Allah's question to Samiri through Moses, demanding accountability for his grave transgression of leading the Israelites to idolatry by fashioning the golden calf. The inquiry challenges Samiri to explain his actions and motivations, emphasizing that there is no valid justification for such a serious violation of monotheistic belief. The question serves to establish clear moral culpability and divine disapproval of innovation in religion that contradicts revealed truth.

translation: He said: I have seen what they have not seen, so I took a handful from the track of the Messenger, and I cast it away. Thus my soul made it fair for me.
interpretation: This verse reveals the psychology of those who reject truth despite having direct perception of it. The speaker claims superior knowledge ('I have seen what they have not'), yet this very self-perception becomes the source of his corruption. By casting away the golden calf dust he seized from the Messenger's trail, he demonstrates how human intellect divorced from submission to divine guidance becomes a vehicle for self-deception. The phrase 'thus my soul made it fair for me' exposes how pride and unchecked desires rationalize disobedience—one's own ego becomes the ultimate authority, replacing obedience to God's messenger. This is a profound warning that knowledge and perception alone, without humility and acceptance of revelation, inevitably lead to misguidance.

translation: He said, 'Then go, for indeed, you have [the sentence]: 'Do not touch [anyone].' And indeed, you have a promise that will not be broken. And look at your god to which you remained devoted. We will surely burn it and then scatter it as dust into the sea.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates Allah's absolute power and authority over those who reject His signs. The phrase 'do not touch' is presented as a punishment reflecting the exile of the one who worships the calf—he becomes isolated and separated from society. The promise of a meeting with Allah emphasizes the inevitable accountability in the afterlife. The destruction of the golden calf symbolizes the ultimate futility of idolatry and false worship; no matter how much devotion is given to false gods, they are powerless and will be utterly annihilated. This serves as a profound lesson that only Allah deserves worship and devotion, as all false deities are destined for complete destruction.

translation: Your God is only Allah, there is no deity except Him. He has encompassed all things in knowledge.
interpretation: This verse establishes the core principle of Islamic monotheism (tawhid) by affirming that Allah alone is worthy of worship and that no other being deserves to be called upon as a god. The statement that He has encompassed all things in knowledge emphasizes His infinite wisdom and omniscience, which serves as the foundation for why He alone should be worshipped—His complete knowledge and perfect understanding qualify Him exclusively for divinity, whereas all creation is limited and dependent on Him.

translation: Thus We relate to you from the accounts of what has preceded. And We have given you from Us a Reminder.
interpretation: This verse establishes the Qur'an as a divine gift that combines historical narratives of previous events and prophets with spiritual guidance and remembrance of Allah. The phrase 'from Us' emphasizes the direct divine origin of the Qur'an, distinguishing it as a mercy and mercy-giving instrument rather than a mere historical record, meant to guide humanity and remind them of their relationship with their Creator and the eternal truths that transcend time.

translation: Whoever turns away from it will carry a burden on the Day of Resurrection
interpretation: This verse warns that those who deliberately reject or disregard the message of guidance (the Qur'an or the message of the Prophet) will bear the full weight and consequence of their rejection on the Day of Judgment. The 'burden' (wizr) symbolizes the accountability and punishment for willful ignorance and turning away from the truth, emphasizing that rejection of divine guidance is not without consequence and each person is responsible for their choice to accept or deny the message.

translation: Abiding therein eternally, and how evil shall be their burden on the Day of Resurrection
interpretation: This verse describes the eternal punishment of the disbelievers in Hell, emphasizing both the permanence of their punishment and the additional shame and burden they will carry on the Day of Judgment when their evil deeds are revealed and weighed against them. The verse underscores the gravity and severity of divine punishment for those who reject faith.

translation: The Day when the Trumpet will be blown, and We shall gather the criminals on that Day with eyes blue [from weeping].
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Judgment when the Trumpet is sounded by Israfil, marking the resurrection of all people. The gathering of criminals with 'blue eyes' signifies their state of anguish and despair—their eyes turned blue or darkened from the intensity of fear, tears, and the punishment they anticipate. This vivid description emphasizes the terror and hopelessness that will befall those who rejected faith and committed sins, contrasting with the salvation of the righteous, and serves as a powerful warning about the consequences of transgression on the Day of Judgment.

translation: They whisper among themselves, 'You remained only ten days.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the inhabitants of Paradise whispering to one another about the duration of their worldly life, realizing that their time in the material world was only ten days compared to the eternal duration of their existence in Paradise. This conveys the profound perspective shift that occurs when souls perceive the insignificance of earthly life in relation to the infinite afterlife, emphasizing how brief and fleeting the worldly existence appears when compared to eternity.

translation: We are most knowing of what they say when their most prudent among them says: 'You have not remained but a day.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's complete knowledge of the hidden thoughts and private conversations of disbelievers, even their most carefully reasoned arguments. When they deny the resurrection and claim they only spent a brief time in the world, Allah's knowledge encompasses all of this, suggesting that their denial stems from weakness of conviction and limited perception, while Allah's comprehensive awareness surpasses their understanding of reality and the ultimate truth of the afterlife.

translation: And they ask you about the mountains, so say: My Lord will blow them away completely.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Qur'anic theme of the Day of Judgment and the transformation of creation. When the disbelievers question the Prophet about the ultimate fate of the mountains—which they see as immovable and eternal—the response emphasizes Allah's absolute power and sovereignty. The mountains, symbols of permanence and solidity in human perception, will be completely obliterated and scattered like dust on the Day of Judgment. This serves to humble those who deny resurrection and the afterlife, demonstrating that nothing in creation is beyond Allah's control, and that the resurrection is as certain as the annihilation of these seemingly permanent structures. It also conveys that believers should not be deceived by the apparent stability of the material world, as all creation will be transformed according to Allah's divine will.

translation: And leaves it barren and desolate
interpretation: This phrase describes the devastating consequences of severe drought or divine punishment, depicting a landscape stripped of all vegetation and life. The use of two Arabic words for emptiness ('qa'a' and 'safṣafa') emphasizes the complete desolation and utter barrenness of the land, highlighting the magnitude of destruction and the total absence of any fertility or sustenance.

translation: You will not see in it any crookedness nor any unevenness.
interpretation: This verse describes the perfect creation of the heavens, emphasizing the flawless design and harmony of the celestial bodies in their orbits and structure. It serves as evidence of Allah's perfect wisdom and power, with no defects, irregularities, or imperfections in His creation, thereby refuting polytheism and affirming divine perfection and excellence in all of creation.

translation: On that Day, they will follow the Caller with no deviation from him. And voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful, so you will not hear except a whisper.
interpretation: This verse depicts the Day of Judgment when all creation will respond obediently to the call of the Angel Israfil without any deviation or resistance, signifying the absolute power of Allah over all beings.
