The phrase 'We were protecting them' indicates that despite their enslavement and humiliation through forced servitude, Allah maintained their existence and capability to function—they were preserved as instruments of Solomon's dominion as a manifestation of divine favor and power granted to Solomon. The verse demonstrates how even the rebellious spiritual creatures were brought under divine control to benefit the righteous servant of Allah.

translation: And [remember] Job, when he called upon his Lord, saying, 'Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the profound faith and humble supplication of Job even in his deepest suffering. Despite experiencing severe affliction, Job does not despair or lose hope, but rather turns directly to his Lord with confidence in His mercy. The phrase 'You are the Most Merciful of the merciful' reveals that true servitude involves acknowledging God's attribute of mercy even while experiencing hardship, demonstrating that faith is not contingent upon ease of circumstance, but rather is rooted in unwavering trust in God's compassionate nature and His ability to alleviate suffering when He wills it.

translation: So We responded to him and removed the harm that was upon him, and We gave him his family and the like of them with them as a mercy from Us and a reminder for those who worship.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of divine mercy and responsiveness to sincere supplication. When a person turns to Allah in genuine distress with humility and faith, Allah not only removes the suffering but abundantly restores what was lost, multiplying His favors beyond the original state. The addition of 'the like of them with them' emphasizes Allah's generosity in exceeding expectations. The phrase 'a reminder for those who worship' conveys that such acts of divine intervention serve as a lesson for believers about the efficacy of sincere devotion and prayer, demonstrating that patience combined with faith in Allah yields both spiritual and material restoration, and that witnessing such divine mercy should deepen one's commitment to worship and remembrance of Allah.

translation: And Ishmael, Enoch, and Dhul-Kifl - each was among the patient ones.
interpretation: This verse highlights the virtue of patience (sabr) as the defining characteristic that united these righteous prophets. The naming of Ishmael, Enoch, and Dhul-Kifl specifically in this context emphasizes that patience in facing trials, maintaining faith, and persisting in obedience to God is the essential quality that elevates the servant in God's sight, suggesting that true nobility and honor in the eyes of God are achieved through steadfastness and endurance rather than through worldly status or ease.

translation: And We admitted them into Our mercy. Indeed, they were among the righteous.
interpretation: This verse describes the reward that Allah grants to those who are righteous and upright in their faith and deeds. The phrase 'admitted them into Our mercy' signifies that divine mercy encompasses and protects the righteous, serving as their reward in both this life and the hereafter. By identifying them as 'among the righteous,' the verse emphasizes that inclusion in Allah's mercy is directly connected to one's moral and spiritual conduct, suggesting a cause-and-effect relationship where righteousness is the means by which believers attain Allah's comprehensive mercy and favor.

translation: And [remember] the man of the whale, when he departed in anger and thought that We would have no power over him. Then he called out within the darknesses, 'There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the consequence of abandoning trust in God's wisdom and plan. When Jonah (the man of the whale) left his mission in anger, thinking he could escape God's knowledge and power, he found himself alone in darkness. His call of repentance—affirming God's absolute oneness and his own transgression—shows that recognition of one's error and sincere submission to God's sovereignty is the path to redemption. The verse teaches that no one can flee from God's control, and that despair transforms into hope through genuine repentance and acknowledgment of God's transcendence.

translation: So We responded to him and saved him from the distress. And thus do We save the believers.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates Allah's principle of responding to the sincere supplication of the believers and delivering them from hardship and anxiety. The phrase 'thus do We save the believers' indicates that this is not merely an isolated incident, but rather an established pattern of divine mercy whereby those who believe and call upon Allah with sincerity will be granted relief from their difficulties, establishing that faith itself is a source of deliverance from spiritual and worldly distress.

translation: And Zachariah, when he called upon his Lord, "My Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors."
interpretation: Zachariah's supplication reflects the human anxiety about leaving no progeny and the fear of being forgotten after death. His invocation of Allah as "the best of inheritors" suggests his trust that Allah alone will preserve his legacy and memory, transcending the need for earthly descendants. This reveals the spiritual principle that true inheritance and permanence come through divine providence rather than material succession, expressing submission to Allah's wisdom while acknowledging human vulnerability and dependence.

translation: So We responded to him and granted him Yahya, and reformed for him his wife. Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds and supplicate Us in hope and fear, and they were humbly devoted to Us.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle that sincere devotion to God, combined with active pursuit of righteousness and earnest supplication, attracts divine mercy and blessing. The reform of Zachariah's wife and the gift of a son in advanced age exemplify how God rewards those who balance fear and hope in their relationship with Him, demonstrating that true servanthood encompasses both eager action toward goodness and complete submission to God's will.

translation: And [mention] the one who guarded her chastity, so We blew into her from Our Spirit, and We made her and her son a sign for the worlds.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Mary's virtue and moral integrity were the foundation for the miraculous conception of Jesus. Her preserved chastity was not merely a physical state but a manifestation of her spiritual purity and devotion to God. The 'blowing of the Spirit' into her represents God's direct intervention in the natural order, making her pregnancy a manifestation of divine power that transcends ordinary biological processes. By making Mary and Jesus together a 'sign for the worlds,' the verse indicates that their relationship and the circumstances of his birth serve as evidence of God's omnipotence and as a guidance for humanity throughout history, demonstrating that God's will operates beyond human comprehension and natural laws.

translation: Indeed, this religion of yours is one religion, and I am your Lord, so worship Me.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the fundamental principle of divine unity (tawhid) by establishing that all believers across time share one universal faith centered on the exclusive worship of Allah alone. The verse underscores that despite outward differences in practices and time periods, the essential message revealed to all prophets is identical: monotheism and obedience to God. By stating 'I am your Lord,' Allah asserts His absolute sovereignty and the obligation of all humanity to direct worship exclusively to Him, rejecting all forms of polytheism and idolatry. This unity of purpose transcends sectarian divisions and calls believers to recognize their common spiritual bond rooted in the worship of the One God.

translation: And they have cut off their matter among themselves, each one is returning to Us.
interpretation: This verse describes how the disbelievers have divided themselves into different sects and groups, each following their own whims and opinions regarding the message. The phrase 'each one is returning to Us' serves as a reminder that despite their divisions and disagreements in this worldly life, all people ultimately return to Allah on the Day of Judgment where He will judge their actions and resolve all their disputes. This conveys that their fragmentation and divergence are temporary, and the ultimate truth and justice will be established when they return to Allah.

translation: So whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer, there is no denial of his effort, and indeed We are recording it for him.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Allah acknowledges and preserves every righteous action performed by a sincere believer, ensuring that no good deed goes unrecorded or unrewarded, no matter how small or insignificant it may seem to others. The divine recording of deeds serves as a guarantee of God's justice and merciful attentiveness to the believer's efforts.

translation: And it is decreed for a town which We have destroyed that they will not return.
interpretation: This verse establishes a divine decree regarding the destroyed communities: once Allah destroys a population for their disbelief and corruption, that destruction is final and irreversible in this worldly life. They will not be restored to their former state, signifying the absolute and permanent nature of divine punishment in the temporal realm. This serves as a warning that the consequences of rejecting Allah's message are not temporary setbacks that can be overcome, but rather represent a final severing of that community's chance at redemption in this world, emphasizing both the gravity of divine justice and the importance of heeding revelation while one still has the opportunity.

translation: Until, when Gog and Magog are released and they swarm down from every hill,
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Judgment when divine barriers holding back Gog and Magog are broken, releasing them upon the earth as a sign of the Last Hour. Their emergence from every direction represents the overwhelming nature of this trial and the chaos that precedes the final judgment, signifying that the Hour is imminent when this occurs.

translation: And the True Promise has drawn near, then suddenly the eyes of those who disbelieved will be staring in horror. 'O woe to us! We were indeed in heedlessness of this; rather, we were wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment of reckoning when disbelievers witness the reality of the Day of Judgment they denied. Their shocked expression and confession reveals that their previous denial stemmed not from genuine doubt but from willful negligence and moral injustice—they knew the truth but chose to ignore it and suppress it, making them accountable not merely for disbelief but for conscious rejection and transgression against their own souls.

translation: Indeed, you and whatever you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell. You will enter it together.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute futility of associating partners with Allah in worship. The phrase 'fuel for Hell' (حصب جهنم) conveys that both the idolaters and their idols will become the combustible material of Hell fire, signifying complete annihilation and utter destruction. The verse is a stern warning about the ultimate consequence of shirk (polytheism), communicating that those who reject monotheism will experience the same fate as the false objects of their worship. The use of 'you will enter it together' underscores the inseparability of the worshippers from what they worshipped, illustrating that their misguided devotion will bind them together in punishment. This serves as a profound deterrent against idolatry and a call to recognize that only Allah deserves worship, as all other objects of devotion are worthless and will lead to perdition.

translation: If these (idols) were gods, they would not come to it; and all of them will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: This verse presents a logical argument against polytheism by pointing out the absurdity of idolatry. If the idols that people worship were truly divine, they would not enter Hell alongside their worshippers on the Day of Judgment. The fact that all who associate partners with Allah will be condemned to eternal torment in Hell serves as proof of the falsehood of idol-worship and the impossibility of anything being a god alongside Allah. The verse uses reason to demonstrate that true divinity must necessarily possess attributes of protection and deliverance, not debasement and destruction.

translation: For them therein is sighing and wailing, and they therein do not hear.
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the people of Hell, emphasizing the profound isolation and despair of their condition. The 'sighing and wailing' (zafir) represents their anguished cries of distress and regret, while the statement that 'they do not hear' suggests a complete breakdown of communication and connection—they cannot hear each other's pleas, cannot hear any mercy or relief, and are utterly alone in their suffering despite being surrounded by others in similar torment. This captures the essence of Hell as a state of complete alienation and hopelessness, where suffering is compounded by the inability to find solace or connection with others.

translation: Indeed, those for whom the good [decree] has preceded from Us - those will be kept far away from it [Hell].
interpretation: This verse refers to those whom Allah has predetermined for paradise and good fortune. They are protected and separated from Hell due to Allah's prior knowledge and decree of their righteousness. The 'good' (al-husna) signifies both the good outcome in this life and admission to paradise in the next. The verse emphasizes Allah's foreknowledge and His protection of the righteous, assuring believers that those destined for goodness by divine decree will be safeguarded from punishment and damnation.

translation: They will not hear its sound, and they will abide eternally in whatever their souls desire.
interpretation: This verse describes the condition of the inhabitants of Paradise, emphasizing that they will be isolated from all suffering and hardship (not hearing the sound of Hell), while simultaneously enjoying eternal satisfaction in the fulfillment of their deepest desires. The phrase 'whatever their souls desire' suggests a state of complete contentment and wish-fulfillment that is both permanent ('abiding eternally') and divinely granted, indicating that Paradise is not merely the absence of torment but an active state of joy and perfection tailored to each individual's righteous aspirations.

translation: Grief shall not touch them at the Greatest Terror, and the angels will meet them [saying], 'This is your Day which you were promised.'
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the righteous on the Day of Judgment when they encounter the angels at their death. The 'Greatest Terror' (al-faza' al-akbar) refers to the overwhelming fear and shock that will strike humanity on the Day of Resurrection. The righteous will be spared from this terror, indicating their security and peace of mind due to their deeds in life. The angels greeting them with the announcement that 'this is your Day which you were promised' emphasizes the fulfillment of divine promises to the believers and their anticipation of reward, highlighting the contrast between the righteous who find comfort and the wicked who experience fear.

translation: On the Day when We shall roll up the sky like the rolling up of a scroll for books. As We began the first creation, We shall repeat it. This is a promise binding upon Us. Indeed, We shall do it.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the cyclical nature of creation and the certainty of the Day of Judgment. The metaphor of rolling up the sky like a scroll conveys the dramatic transformation of the universe at the end of time. By stating that Allah will repeat creation as He initiated it, the verse underscores that the resurrection is not something extraordinary beyond His power, but rather a straightforward repetition of what He has already accomplished. The phrase 'wada'an 'alaina' (a promise binding upon Us) stresses the absolute reliability and inevitability of this divine promise, reinforcing that the Hereafter is not merely possible but certain and will definitely occur.

translation: And We have already written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants.
interpretation: This verse affirms that God's promise of ultimate dominion belongs to the righteous believers, indicating that despite worldly challenges and trials, those who remain steadfast in faith and righteousness will ultimately inherit and possess the earth, both spiritually through triumph of faith and practically through God's control of events. The mention of the Psalms and the Reminder establishes continuity of this divine promise throughout the sacred scriptures.

translation: Indeed, in this is a clear message for a worshipping people.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the Qur'anic message is not merely informational but serves as a profound spiritual guidance specifically for those who dedicate themselves to worship and obedience of Allah. It suggests that the effectiveness of the Qur'an's message depends on the spiritual receptivity and commitment of the audience—those who are devoted to worship are best positioned to understand and benefit from the divine guidance being conveyed.

translation: And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds
interpretation: This verse establishes the fundamental purpose of Prophet Muhammad's mission - his role is to bring Divine compassion and guidance to all of humanity. The universality expressed in 'the worlds' (al-'alamin) emphasizes that the Prophet's message transcends tribal, national, and cultural boundaries, offering spiritual healing and moral guidance to all people. The verse communicates that prophethood itself is an act of Divine mercy, not punishment or severity, highlighting that the Prophet's character and teachings are meant to rectify human hearts and societies through compassion rather than harshness.

translation: Say: 'Indeed, it has been revealed to me that your God is only one God. So will you submit (to Him)?'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Prophet Muhammad's message is grounded in divine revelation, not personal opinion or convention. By framing the affirmation of monotheism as something 'revealed to me,' the Qur'an establishes that tawhid (belief in God's oneness) is not merely an intellectual concept but a divinely mandated principle that demands active submission and obedience from humanity. The rhetorical question 'will you submit?' transforms the statement of belief into a call for committed action and surrender to God's will, making faith inseparable from dutiful practice.

translation: But if they turn away, say: 'I have announced to you equally, and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the Prophet's role as a messenger who has conveyed the message plainly to all people without distinction. His responsibility ends with clear communication; the outcome of acceptance or rejection is beyond his control. The declaration that he does not know when the promised punishment will come reinforces his human limitation and humility, while also serving as a warning that the threat of divine judgment is real even if its timing remains unknown to mankind.

translation: Indeed, He knows the open declaration of speech, and He knows what you conceal.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute and comprehensive knowledge that encompasses both the manifest and the hidden—all words spoken openly and all thoughts and intentions kept secret. It serves as a reminder of divine omniscience and accountability, conveying that humans cannot hide anything from God, whether their statements are public or their inner thoughts remain private, thus encouraging sincerity and moral consciousness in both external conduct and internal intention.

translation: And I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and enjoyment for a time.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Prophet Nuh (Noah) regarding the worldly possessions and lifespan granted to his people, conveys the principle that material blessings and prolonged life are not necessarily signs of divine favor, but may rather be tests from Allah to see whether people will remain grateful and obedient, or whether they will become arrogant and turn away from faith. The phrase 'enjoyment for a time' emphasizes the temporary nature of worldly pleasures, serving as a reminder that true success lies not in the accumulation of material goods but in one's relationship with the Divine and preparation for the afterlife.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, judge with truth. And our Lord is the Most Merciful, the One whose help is sought against what you describe.'
interpretation: This verse expresses the speaker's appeal to God for just judgment while simultaneously affirming their reliance upon God's mercy and help against the false accusations or claims made by their opponents. It reflects a profound submission to divine justice combined with a recognition that ultimate assistance comes only from God, demonstrating that true strength lies not in one's own power but in trusting God's judgment and seeking His aid against falsehood.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing.
interpretation: This verse opens Surah Al-Hajj with an urgent call to humanity to develop consciousness of God (Taqwa) by reminding them of the Day of Judgment, whose cataclysmic upheaval will be so overwhelming and terrifying that it serves as the ultimate motivation for moral accountability and righteous conduct in this life. The 'convulsion' symbolizes both the physical devastation at the end of time and the spiritual reckoning each soul will face, emphasizing that no earthly power or distraction can protect one from this inevitable reality.

translation: On the Day when you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from that which she nurses, and every pregnant woman will deliver her burden, and you will see the people drunk, yet they are not drunk—but the punishment of Allah is severe.
interpretation: This verse describes the profound terror and shock of the Day of Judgment, where the intensity and horror of that day will be so overwhelming that it will override the most fundamental human instincts and bonds. Even a mother's natural concern for her nursing child will be eclipsed by the magnitude of the events unfolding. The imagery of people appearing drunk while not being intoxicated illustrates their complete bewilderment and disorientation in the face of divine judgment, emphasizing that this confusion and loss of reason stems not from intoxication but from the absolute severity and terrifying nature of Allah's punishment, which leaves people mentally and spiritually shattered.

translation: And of the people is he who disputes concerning Allah without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil
interpretation: This verse condemns those who engage in religious argumentation and debate about matters of faith without possessing true knowledge or understanding. The phrase 'follows every rebellious devil' indicates that such people are susceptible to misguidance and easily swayed by deceptive ideas and false doctrines, as they lack the foundation of sound knowledge to distinguish truth from falsehood. The verse emphasizes that disputation in religious matters should be grounded in wisdom and evidence, not in ignorance and conjecture.

translation: It has been written upon him that whoever takes him as a guardian, he will lead him astray and guide him to the punishment of the Blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse refers to Iblis (Satan) and establishes that misguidance is his defining nature and predetermined role. The phrase 'written upon him' indicates that leading humans astray is his inherent characteristic and purpose. Taking Iblis as a guardian means following his whispers and desires instead of God's guidance. The consequence is twofold: immediate spiritual misguidance in this life and ultimate torment in the Hereafter, emphasizing that alliance with Satan inevitably results in loss in both realms.

translation: O mankind! If you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then [consider that] We created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, that We may clarify for you. And We settle in the wombs what We will for an appointed term, then We bring you out as infants, then [develop you] so that you reach your full strength. Among you are those who die, and among you are those who are returned to the most feeble age so that they know nothing after [having possessed] knowledge. And you see the earth barren, but when We send down upon it rain, it stirs and swells and produces every beautiful kind [of plant].
interpretation: This verse uses the observable natural phenomena of human creation and the earth's seasonal renewal as logical evidence that Resurrection is entirely possible. The progression from non-life to complex life, and the earth's transformation from barrenness to flourishing vegetation, mirror the possibility of mankind's revival after death. The mention of those who regress to helplessness in old age further illustrates the cyclical nature of existence and divine power over life stages, demonstrating that the One capable of such transformations in this life is fully capable of restoring life after death. The verse appeals to reason and empirical observation to persuade those who harbor doubts about the Hereafter.

translation: That is because Allah is the Truth, and because He gives life to the dead, and because He is Able to do all things.
interpretation: This verse establishes that Allah's absolute nature as the Truth (al-Haq) is the foundation for all His other attributes and actions. The phrase connects His truthfulness to His power over life and death, emphasizing that since Allah alone possesses ultimate reality and infinite capability, His dominion extends over all creation, including the resurrection of the dead. The verse is meant to reinforce belief in the Hereafter and divine omnipotence by grounding them in the fundamental principle of Allah's truthfulness—He cannot fail in His promises, and His word regarding resurrection and resurrection will certainly come to pass.

translation: And indeed, the Hour is coming—there is no doubt about it—and indeed, Allah will resurrect those who are in the graves.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the certainty of the Day of Judgment and Allah's absolute power over resurrection. The phrase 'no doubt about it' is not merely an assertion of the Hour's inevitability, but a call to absolute certainty of faith and conviction in this fundamental Islamic belief. By connecting the certainty of the Hour with Allah's power to resurrect from graves, the verse demonstrates that the resurrection is not speculative but an established reality as certain as the knowledge of Allah himself. The resurrection of those in graves symbolizes total divine authority over life and death, serving as grounds for moral accountability in this life.

translation: And among the people are those who dispute concerning Allah without knowledge, nor guidance, nor an illuminating scripture.
interpretation: This verse condemns those who engage in religious arguments and debates about Allah's nature, commands, and divine matters while lacking three essential foundations: knowledge ('ilm) based on evidence and understanding, guidance (huda) from divine inspiration and right direction, and the light of a revealed scripture (kitab munir) to illuminate their path. Such disputation without these three pillars is futile and spiritually harmful, as it represents arrogance and ignorance masquerading as intellectual inquiry. The verse serves as a warning against dogmatic argumentation divorced from sincere seeking of truth through proper sources of knowledge, divine guidance, and scriptural foundation.

translation: He pairs with him [another] to mislead [people] from the way of Allah. For him is disgrace in this world, and We will make him taste the punishment of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the severe consequences of those who deliberately associate partners with Allah and use their influence to lead others away from His guidance. The mention of disgrace in this worldly life and eternal torment in the Hereafter emphasizes that such misguidence carries both immediate spiritual and social consequences, as well as ultimate divine punishment, serving as a stern warning against shirk (associating partners with Allah) and leading others astray.

translation: That is because of what your hands have sent forward, and indeed Allah is not unjust to the servants.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes personal accountability and divine justice. It teaches that the consequences people face are directly tied to their own actions and deeds. The phrase 'what your hands have sent forward' refers to one's prior actions, suggesting that our present circumstances are the natural result of what we have done before. The second part affirms Allah's perfect justice, clarifying that any suffering or hardship people experience is not due to divine cruelty or unfairness, but rather a consequence of their own choices. This establishes the principle that Allah's justice is absolute and that individuals bear responsibility for their deeds.

translation: And among the people is he who worships Allah upon an edge. If good befalls him, he is content with it; but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He has lost this world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the weakness of superficial faith that lacks deep roots and conviction. The person who worships 'upon an edge' (حرف) represents one whose belief is unstable and conditional—dependent entirely on worldly prosperity and ease. Such a person cannot endure the trials that test faith, revealing that his commitment to God was never genuine but merely instrumental. The verse emphasizes that true worship requires unwavering commitment regardless of circumstances, and that those who abandon their faith when faced with hardship forfeit both worldly benefit (by losing divine protection and guidance) and eternal salvation, which constitutes the greatest and most obvious form of loss.

translation: He calls upon besides Allah that which neither harms him nor benefits him. That is the far straying.
interpretation: This verse condemns the futility of idolatry and associating partners with Allah by highlighting the irrationality of worshipping deities incapable of affecting human welfare. The phrase 'far straying' emphasizes that such polytheism represents not merely error, but profound spiritual deviation from the path of truth, as it contradicts the basic human logic that one should only rely upon and petition that which can genuinely help or harm—attributes belonging to Allah alone.

translation: He calls upon one whose harm is closer than his benefit. What an evil master and what an evil companion!
interpretation: This verse describes the spiritual condition of those who worship idols or false deities instead of Allah. The interpretation emphasizes that turning to anything other than Allah for help or reliance is fundamentally foolish because such false objects of worship cannot provide true benefit and their potential for harm far exceeds any advantage. The verse teaches that only Allah deserves to be called upon and relied upon as the true Master and Companion, while all other objects of worship fail in these roles entirely. This serves as a warning against associating partners with Allah and highlights the supreme wisdom of monotheistic devotion.

translation: Indeed, Allah will admit those who have believed and done righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed, Allah does what He wills.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Paradise is the reward for those who combine sincere faith with righteous action. The mention of rivers flowing beneath the gardens is a Qur'anic image of abundance, beauty, and eternal blessing. The closing clause 'Indeed, Allah does what He wills' reinforces that this reward is solely within Allah's discretion and power, reminding believers that they cannot guarantee Paradise through their own efforts alone, but must rely on Allah's mercy while striving to fulfill their obligations.

translation: Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him in this world and the Hereafter, let him extend a rope to the sky and then cut it, and let him see if his action will remove that which enrages him.
interpretation: This verse uses vivid imagery and a seemingly impossible action to illustrate the futility and absurdity of those who deny Allah's help and protection. By commanding the disbeliever to extend a rope to the heavens and cut it as a means to remove his anger and distress, Allah is highlighting the utter helplessness of mankind without divine aid. The verse emphasizes that rejecting Allah's support and relying solely on one's own efforts is not only foolish but fundamentally ineffective in achieving peace and resolution. It serves as a powerful rebuke to those who doubt Allah's sovereignty and capability, demonstrating that separation from Allah's mercy leads to despair and impotence, while also affirming that genuine salvation and relief come exclusively through reliance upon Allah in both this life and the Hereafter.

translation: And thus We have revealed it as clear verses, and indeed Allah guides whom He wills.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the Qur'an has been revealed with clear and unambiguous signs as guidance for humanity, yet its benefit is ultimately conditional upon Allah's will and guidance. The verse teaches that while the message itself is manifest and evident, receiving guidance from it depends on Allah granting guidance to those He wills - indicating that both the clarity of the message and receptiveness to it are expressions of divine will, placing ultimate responsibility with Allah rather than suggesting arbitrary deprivation but rather that guidance requires both the clarity of revelation and the preparedness of the heart which Allah alone determines.

translation: Indeed, those who have believed and those who were Jewish and the Sabians and the Christians and the Zoroastrians and those who associated partners with Allah - Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is, over all things, a Witness.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that despite the diversity of beliefs and religions in the world, Allah alone possesses complete knowledge and will render final judgment between all people on the Day of Resurrection based on their deeds and hearts, not on their mere claims or outward affiliations. The mention of various groups highlights that no one escapes Allah's knowledge or judgment, and the ultimate determination of who is rightly guided and who is misguided belongs solely to Allah, not to human opinion or preference.

translation: Have you not seen that to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the animals, and many of the people? But many have the punishment justified upon them. And whoever Allah humiliates - for him there is no bestower of honor. Indeed, Allah does what He wills.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the universal submission to Allah's will and divine authority that permeates all creation, demonstrating that obedience to Allah is inherent in the natural order of existence. The mention that many people still incur punishment despite this universal prostration serves as a reminder that conscious human choice and accountability differ from the instinctive obedience of creation, and that those who reject Allah's guidance will face disgrace that no one can prevent or remedy, illustrating the absolute nature of Allah's power and justice in determining the outcomes of human conduct.

translation: These two groups are adversaries who have disputed concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieved, garments of fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured down upon their heads.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the ultimate consequences of rejecting faith and divine guidance. The 'two groups' represent believers and disbelievers, whose fundamental disagreement about their relationship with God leads to radically different outcomes in the afterlife. The vivid imagery of fire garments and scalding water emphasizes that the punishment of disbelief is not merely the absence of reward, but active, sensory torment specifically designed to correspond to and reflect the nature of their transgression—they rejected the truth despite its clarity, and thus their punishment involves the stripping away of all comfort and protection, replaced by that which brings only pain and destruction.

translation: Therein is melted that which is in their bellies and their skins
interpretation: This verse describes the punishment of the disbelievers in Hell, where molten metal is poured over them, causing the contents of their stomachs and their skin to melt together. This depicts an extreme form of torture that represents the total destruction and suffering that awaits those who reject God's signs, emphasizing both the physical agony and the comprehensive nature of divine punishment - affecting their inner being and outer form alike. The imagery conveys that there is no escape from the consequences of disbelief, as even the most vital parts of the body cannot be spared from the torment.

translation: And for them are hammers (or maces) of iron
interpretation: This verse refers to the instruments of punishment that the inhabitants of Hell will wield against one another or that will be used against them. The hammers of iron symbolize the harsh and unrelenting nature of divine punishment in the afterlife, emphasizing the severity and painfulness of the consequences for those who reject faith and commit grave sins. The specific mention of iron underscores the unbreakable and overwhelming force of this punishment, leaving no possibility of escape or relief.

translation: Whenever they wish to exit from it due to anguish, they are returned into it; and taste the punishment of the Fire.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the eternal nature of punishment in Hell, emphasizing that the inhabitants will experience no escape or respite from their torment. The repetitive cycle of suffering—attempting to flee from the agony, only to be thrust back into it—demonstrates that Hell is an inescapable punishment where there is no possibility of release or diminishment of pain. This underscores the severity and permanence of divine retribution for those who reject God's message.

translation: Indeed, Allah will admit those who have believed and done righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their garments therein will be of silk.
interpretation: This verse describes the ultimate reward for believers who combine faith with righteous action, emphasizing that both inner conviction and outer conduct are essential for entering Paradise. The specific descriptions of gold, pearls, and silk represent the incomparable nature of divine reward—depicting not mere material luxury, but rather the exquisite beauty and excellence of Paradise that transcends earthly imagination, indicating that the rewards of the Hereafter are of a completely different and superior quality to anything experienced in this world.

translation: And they were guided to good speech, and they were guided to the path of the Praised One (Allah).
interpretation: This verse describes the spiritual elevation of the righteous who are divinely guided toward two essential aspects of righteousness: the mastery of righteous speech and adherence to the path that leads to Allah, who is worthy of all praise. The repetition of 'guided to' (hudū ilā) emphasizes the divine grace that directs believers away from harmful discourse toward constructive and truthful communication, while simultaneously keeping them steadfast on the straight path of submission to Allah's will and commands.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve and prevent [people] from the way of Allah and [from] the Sacred Mosque, which We made for the people - equal are those who stay therein and one from outside. And [for] whoever intends therein [to commit] injustice in disbelief - We will make him taste of a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse establishes that Allah's judgment and punishment apply universally without exception to those who commit disbelief and obstruct others from the path of Allah and the Sacred Mosque. The equality between the resident and the visitor in the Mosque emphasizes that the sanctity of this place belongs to all humanity, and the specific mention of 'injustice in disbelief' indicates that the severest punishment is reserved for those whose actions combine both disbelief and intentional transgression against the House of Allah, teaching that deliberate corruption within sacred spaces merits divine retribution.

translation: And [remember] when We designated for Abraham the site of the House, [saying], 'Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate it, those who stand [in prayer], and those who bow and prostrate.'
interpretation: This verse establishes that the foundation of the sacred sanctuary and its worship is built upon absolute monotheism and spiritual purification. The sequence of commands—from the prohibition of shirk (associating partners with Allah) to the purification of the physical House—reveals that the purification of the heart from idolatry is the prerequisite for the proper veneration of sacred spaces and the acceptance of all acts of worship performed therein. The House of Allah becomes a manifestation of divine unity and a beacon for those who seek to submit themselves entirely to Allah alone.

translation: And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage: they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, coming from every distant pass,
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the universal call to Hajj and its profound accessibility across all social classes and geographical boundaries. The mention of coming "on foot and on every lean camel" symbolizes that both the poor and wealthy, those with abundant resources and those with scarce means, are equally commanded and able to fulfill this obligation. The phrase "from every distant pass" indicates that distance and difficulty of terrain are no barriers to those whom Allah has decreed should perform Hajj, highlighting the divine facilitation and the spiritual magnetism of this sacred duty that draws believers from the remotest corners of the earth.

translation: That they may witness benefits for them and mention the name of Allah on specified days over what He has provided for them of livestock. So eat from it and feed the poor in misery.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the pilgrimage to Hajj and the associated sacrifice of animals is ordained so that believers may gather together in worship, acknowledge Allah's provision, and fulfill a divine command. The permission to consume the sacrificial meat alongside the obligation to feed the poor and destitute teaches that divine blessings are meant to be shared communally, transforming a ritual act into an exercise in gratitude, obedience, and social responsibility toward those in need.

translation: Then let them complete their prescribed duties, and let them fulfill their vows, and let them perform the circumambulation around the Ancient House.
interpretation: This verse describes the final acts of pilgrimage in the Hajj ritual. After the main days of Hajj, pilgrims must complete their religious obligations (tafath) which includes removing the pilgrim's state through grooming and changing clothes, fulfill any vows or promises they made to Allah during their pilgrimage, and perform the final circumambulation (Tawaf al-Ifadah) of the Kaaba. The verse emphasizes the completion of the Hajj ritual in its proper order, reminding believers that pilgrimage is not merely a physical journey but a structured series of sacred acts that culminate in renewed devotion and the fulfillment of one's commitments to Allah.

translation: That is [the ruling]. And whoever honors the sacred rites of Allah - that is better for him in the sight of his Lord. And there have been made lawful to you the grazing livestock, except for what is recited to you. So avoid the filth of idols and avoid false statement.
interpretation: This verse establishes that reverence for Allah's sacred ordinances (His commands, prohibitions, and rituals) reflects true piety and brings reward from the Lord. The passage then permits the consumption of livestock while excluding certain categories outlined in Islamic law, and commands believers to abstain from idolatry and falsehood. The underlying interpretation is that obedience to Allah's boundaries regarding what is sacred demonstrates genuine fear of Allah, while the avoidance of idols and false speech constitutes the practical manifestation of this reverence in daily conduct.

translation: As people of pure faith, not associating partners with Allah. And whoever associates partners with Allah - it is as though he has fallen from the sky and the birds snatch him away, or the wind carries him down into a distant place.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute necessity of exclusive monotheism and warns against the spiritual devastation of shirk (associating partners with Allah). The metaphor of falling from the sky depicts how the person who commits shirk experiences a catastrophic spiritual collapse - they lose all moral foundation and protection. The imagery of birds snatching or wind carrying them to a distant place illustrates how such a person becomes spiritually lost, helpless, and utterly abandoned, cut off from divine guidance and mercy. The verse conveys that monotheism is not merely a belief but the essential foundation upon which all spiritual safety and dignity rest, and that departing from it results in complete ruin and desolation.

translation: That is so, and whoever honors the rites of Allah - indeed, that is from the piety of hearts.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the reverence and proper observance of Allah's sacred rituals and symbols are not merely external actions, but rather they reflect and emanate from genuine piety and God-consciousness rooted in the heart. The verse teaches that true religiosity is measured by the sincerity of one's inner devotion, of which the honoring of sacred rites is an outward manifestation and evidence.

translation: For you therein are benefits until an appointed term; then their place of return is to the Ancient House.
interpretation: This verse refers to the ritual benefits and spiritual purposes of sacrificial animals used during Hajj. The phrase 'until an appointed term' indicates the limited time during which these animals serve their purpose in the pilgrimage rites. The 'Ancient House' (the Kaaba) represents the ultimate spiritual destination and focal point of Islamic worship, signifying that all acts of devotion and sacrifice are oriented toward pleasing Allah at His most sacred sanctuary. The verse emphasizes that worldly benefits are temporary and transient, while the true purpose of all righteous deeds is to draw closer to Allah's house and fulfill His commandments.

translation: And for every community We have appointed a rite [of sacrifice] that they may mention the name of Allah over what He has provided them of livestock. So your God is one God, so to Him submit. And give good tidings to the humble,
interpretation: This verse establishes the principle of divine unity in worship through prescribed rituals. By commanding each community to invoke Allah's name during sacrifice, the Qur'an emphasizes that worship practices are divinely ordained means to remember and glorify God. The transition from specific rites to the declaration of monotheism ('your God is one God') reveals that beneath the diversity of forms across communities lies a fundamental unity in purpose: submission to the one Allah. The final clause about giving good tidings to the humble conveys that those who genuinely humble themselves before God and recognize His oneness are the true recipients of divine mercy and glad tidings, suggesting that ritual observance must be accompanied by spiritual humility and sincere submission.

translation: Those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and those who are patient over what has befallen them, and those who establish prayer, and from what We have provided them, they spend.
interpretation: This verse describes the characteristics of the righteous believers: their hearts are filled with reverence and awe of Allah, demonstrating a living connection to the Divine; they endure life's trials with patience and steadfastness, accepting Allah's wisdom in their afflictions; they fulfill their religious obligations through consistent prayer; and they practice generosity by giving from their wealth in charity and good causes. Together, these qualities form a holistic portrait of piety that encompasses both spiritual devotion and practical righteousness in dealing with others.

translation: And the cattle We have made for you as part of the rituals of Allah; for you there is good in them. So mention the name of Allah over them when they are lined up (for sacrifice). Then when they fall on their sides, eat from them and feed the needy who asks and the one who does not ask. Thus We have subjected them to you so that you may be grateful.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the ritual of animal sacrifice is ordained by Allah as a means of worship and gratitude, while emphasizing the social responsibility to share the meat with those in need. The instruction to mention Allah's name before sacrifice sanctifies the act and redirects focus from the animal to obedience to the Divine command. The explicit command to feed both the asking and non-asking poor transforms sacrifice from a mere ritualistic act into a vehicle for establishing social justice and demonstrating gratitude to Allah through service to humanity, thereby linking submission to God with compassion toward His creatures.

translation: Neither their meat nor their blood reaches Allah, but the piety from you reaches Him. Thus He has made them subservient to you so that you may magnify Allah for having guided you. And give good tidings to those who do good.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the value of sacrifice lies not in the physical offerings themselves, but in the spiritual state of the person making the sacrifice. The meat and blood are merely material remnants, while what truly matters to Allah is the sincerity, piety, and consciousness of the worshipper. By connecting the subservience of sacrificial animals to the glorification of Allah, the verse teaches that obedience to divine commandments should flow from genuine gratitude and recognition of Allah's guidance, transforming ritual acts into expressions of authentic faith. The final phrase promises reward specifically for those who combine right action with inner virtue, indicating that true excellence in worship encompasses both outward compliance and inward righteousness.

translation: Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed. Indeed, Allah does not love any treacherous disbeliever.
interpretation: This verse assures believers that Allah actively protects and shields them from harm and evil, emphasizing His constant support for the faithful. The second clause establishes a contrast: while Allah defends the believers, He withdraws His protection and love from those who combine treachery (betrayal of trust and covenant) with disbelief and ingratitude, indicating that turning away from Allah's guidance while breaking oaths and trusts places one beyond the reach of His mercy and protection.

translation: Permission is given to those who fight because they have been wronged, and indeed Allah is capable of granting them victory.
interpretation: This verse marks the first Quranic permission granted to the Muslims to fight in defense against persecution and oppression. It establishes that armed resistance is permissible when people have been unjustly wronged and oppressed, grounding the justification not in aggression but in the restoration of justice. The emphasis on Allah's power to grant victory provides reassurance to the believers that their struggle against tyranny is supported by divine might, offering them both moral legitimacy and spiritual confidence in their defensive struggle.

translation: Those who were expelled from their homes without right except for saying 'Our Lord is Allah.' And if not for Allah's repelling of people, some by means of others, there would have been demolished monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques in which the name of Allah is much mentioned. And Allah will surely support those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is Powerful and Exalted in Might.
interpretation: This verse establishes the principle that religious freedom and the protection of all places of worship are interconnected divine purposes. The repulsion of oppression through righteous struggle is not merely permissible but necessary to preserve the sanctuaries where God is remembered across different faiths. The verse underscores that supporting God's cause—which includes defending religious liberty itself—is a mutual covenant wherein God guarantees support to those who uphold justice and protect the sacred spaces of belief, demonstrating that the defense of one community's right to worship protects the worship rights of all communities.

translation: Those to whom We give power in the land establish prayer, give zakah, and command what is right and forbid what is wrong. And to Allah belongs the final outcome of all matters.
interpretation: This verse describes the characteristics of righteous leaders and those given authority by Allah: they fulfill their spiritual obligations through prayer and zakah, and they exercise moral leadership by promoting virtue and preventing vice in society. The final clause emphasizes that despite their earthly authority, all affairs ultimately rest in Allah's hands, reminding leaders of their accountability before Him and that true success depends on divine will rather than human power alone.

translation: And if they deny you, then indeed there denied before them the people of Noah and 'Ad and Thamud.
interpretation: This verse provides the Prophet Muhammad with historical consolation by reminding him that rejection of prophetic messages is not unprecedented. The message is that false denial of truth has always existed throughout human history - the people of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud all rejected their respective prophets. By referencing these ancient nations, the Qur'an teaches that the Prophet's burden of facing denial is not unique to him, but is a consistent pattern that righteous messengers have endured. This serves as both reassurance that he is in good company with previous prophets and as a reminder that divine punishment ultimately befell those who rejected the truth, implying a similar fate awaits those who reject the final message.

translation: And the people of Abraham and the people of Lot
interpretation: This phrase refers to the communities that were guided by the prophets Abraham and Lot. In context, it highlights those who rejected their prophets' messages and faced divine punishment as a result. The mention of these two peoples together emphasizes the historical pattern of humanity's rejection of divine guidance and the consequences that follow such rejection, serving as a warning to believers about the importance of heeding the prophets' calls to monotheism and righteousness.

translation: And the people of Madyan. And Moses was denied, so I extended respite to the disbelievers; then I seized them. So how was My rejection!
interpretation: This verse illustrates the pattern of divine justice wherein those who reject God's messengers are granted a period of respite during which they may repent, but when they persist in denial, they are ultimately overtaken by divine punishment. The rhetorical question 'how was My rejection' emphasizes the terrible nature of God's punishment and serves as a warning to the contemporary audience about the inevitable consequences of rejecting divine truth, while also demonstrating God's patience and His ultimate sovereignty over all affairs.

translation: So how many a city have We destroyed while it was unjust, and it lies in ruins with its roofs fallen in, and [how many] a well abandoned and a castle standing tall?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the inevitable consequences of injustice and transgression, demonstrating that no civilization, regardless of its material grandeur or fortifications, is immune to divine punishment. The imagery of ruined cities alongside intact structures serves to illustrate the totality of destruction that befalls those who persist in wrongdoing, warning humanity that wealth, power, and architectural achievement cannot protect against the consequences of moral corruption and oppression.

translation: Have they not traveled through the earth so that they might have hearts to understand with, or ears to hear with? For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but the hearts within the chests that are blind.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that true blindness is not physical but spiritual and intellectual. The Qur'an is calling the disbelievers to reflect upon the signs of Allah evident in creation and history through travel and observation. However, the real impediment to understanding these signs is not lack of sensory organs, but the blindness of the heart—a willful refusal or spiritual incapacity to comprehend and acknowledge the truth. This points to the distinction between having physical faculties and actually using them with genuine sincerity and openness to recognize divine guidance.

translation: And they urge you to hasten the punishment, but Allah will not fail in His promise. Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of those you count.
interpretation: This verse addresses the human tendency to demand immediate divine retribution while remaining impatient with God's timeline. The emphasis on Allah's faithfulness to His promise affirms that punishment will certainly come, but according to God's infinite wisdom and time scale, not human urgency. The comparison of a divine day to a thousand earthly years illustrates the fundamental incommensurability between human temporal experience and divine eternity, teaching that what appears delayed from our limited perspective is perfectly timed within God's ultimate plan. This serves to console the believers and remind them that divine justice operates beyond the constraints of human impatience.

translation: And how many a city did We give respite to while it was committing wrongdoing, then We seized it, and to Us is the final destination.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's patience and forbearance toward unjust societies, allowing them time to repent and correct their ways before divine punishment. However, the inevitable seizure of such cities demonstrates that wrongdoing ultimately leads to destruction, serving as a reminder that no nation's arrogance or transgression escapes God's justice, and that all affairs ultimately return to God's judgment and control.

translation: Say: 'O people, I am only a clear warner to you.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the Prophet Muhammad's role as a messenger sent with clear warnings to humanity. The phrase 'only a clear warner' indicates that his primary function is to communicate divine guidance and warnings about the consequences of disbelief, not to force belief or compel obedience. The use of 'only' (إنما) establishes the limits of his authority and responsibility—he is a messenger whose duty is to convey the message clearly, while the choice to accept or reject it remains with the people themselves.

translation: So those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is forgiveness and a noble provision.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that faith combined with righteous action is the foundation for receiving God's mercy and generous sustenance. The pairing of belief with good works indicates that sincere faith must manifest itself through moral conduct, and when this occurs, believers are promised both divine forgiveness for their shortcomings and an abundant, honorable provision in both worldly and spiritual dimensions.

translation: And those who strive against Our signs to render them ineffective - those are the companions of Hell.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who actively work to nullify or contradict the signs of Allah with the intent of challenging His authority and truth. The phrase 'معاجزين' (mu'ajizin) carries the meaning of those who seek to render something ineffective or who compete defiantly against God's signs. The verse emphasizes that deliberate, persistent rejection and active resistance to Allah's clear guidance - not mere disbelief, but willful striving against His truth - results in their ultimate abode being Hell. This reflects the principle that those whose hearts are sealed in defiance and whose actions demonstrate enmity toward divine guidance will face the final consequence of their choice.

translation: We did not send before you any messenger or prophet except that when he recited (his message), Satan cast (something) into his recitation. But Allah abolishes what Satan casts, then Allah establishes His verses. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse addresses the reality that even the greatest prophets face Satanic temptation and distraction in their call to Allah, but Divine protection ensures that only truth remains. The verse demonstrates that human struggle against evil inclinations is universal, even among the most righteous, while ultimately Allah's will and message are preserved intact and cannot be corrupted. It reassures the Prophet Muhammad that his experience of Satanic interference is not unique but a trial common to all prophets, and that Allah's wisdom guarantees the purity of His revealed message.

translation: So that He may make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is disease and those whose hearts are hardened. And indeed, the wrongdoers are in extreme discord.
interpretation: This verse reveals that Allah permits Satan's whispers and deceptions to become a test that exposes the spiritual condition of people's hearts. Those with spiritual sickness—doubts, desires, and spiritual weakness—and those with hardened hearts devoid of mercy and faith are susceptible to these trials and will fall into them. The verse indicates that wrongdoing is characterized by fundamental separation from truth and guidance, manifesting as discord and conflict both within themselves and with others. The trial itself serves as a distinguishing mechanism, separating the spiritually healthy from the spiritually diseased, thereby making manifest what was hidden in the hearts.

translation: And those who have been given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord, so they believe in it and their hearts become humble before it. And indeed, Allah guides those who have believed to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the Qur'an's truth is recognizable to the learned, whose intellectual and spiritual understanding leads them to genuine belief characterized not by mere intellectual assent but by heartfelt submission and humility before God's guidance. The verse emphasizes that knowledge itself becomes a means of drawing closer to God and that guidance is a continuous divine mercy extended to those who genuinely believe.

translation: And those who disbelieve will remain in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them suddenly, or there comes to them the punishment of a barren day.
interpretation: The verse illustrates the stubborn persistence of disbelievers in their rejection of the truth, emphasizing that their doubt will only be dispelled through one of two inevitable events: either the sudden arrival of the Day of Judgment itself, or the destruction they experience in this world—a punishment so comprehensive and devastating that it leaves no room for recovery or respite, described as 'a barren day' (yawm aqeem) because it bears no fruit, mercy, or benefit for those who encounter it. This conveys both the certainty of divine consequences and the tragic reality that some reject faith until it becomes too late for repentance.

translation: The dominion that Day will be entirely for Allah; He will judge between them. So those who believed and did righteous deeds will be in Gardens of Bliss,
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of Allah on the Day of Judgment, highlighting that all earthly power and authority are temporal and will be stripped away. The judgment of Allah is presented as the ultimate reality where justice will be perfectly administered. The verse then contrasts the outcome for the believers and righteous—they will receive eternal reward in Paradise—thereby reinforcing that true success lies not in worldly dominion but in faith combined with righteous action, and that this pairing of belief and good works is what matters for one's final destination.

translation: And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs - for those there is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that rejecting Allah's signs and denying the truth that has been made clear constitutes a grave transgression that will result in severe divine punishment. The use of 'humiliating' (mهين) conveys not merely physical torment but a punishment that strips away dignity and honor, reflecting the spiritual degradation inherent in the choice to turn away from divine guidance. The verse serves as both a warning about the consequences of willful rejection of faith and a reminder of divine justice - that Allah's judgment is absolute and inescapable for those who choose disbelief despite clear evidence.

translation: And those who emigrated in the way of Allah and then were killed or died - Allah will surely provide for them a good provision. And indeed, Allah is the best of providers.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that those who sacrifice their lives in the path of Allah, whether through martyrdom or natural death after emigration, will be abundantly rewarded by Allah in the Hereafter. The verse conveys that Allah honors such sacrifices and ensures that the families and dependents of these individuals are cared for, establishing a Divine guarantee of provision and sustenance for those who prioritize their faith and obedience to Allah above all worldly concerns.

translation: He will surely admit them into a place of which they will be pleased. And indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Forbearing.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's perfect knowledge and wisdom in preparing an entrance into Paradise that will fully satisfy the righteous believers. The mention of Allah being 'All-Knowing and All-Forbearing' indicates that His admission of believers reflects both His complete understanding of what will bring them contentment and His clemency in overlooking their shortcomings in this life, thus assuring believers that their entry into Paradise will be precisely what they could hope for.

translation: That is so; and whoever retaliated with the like of that with which he was harmed, and then was transgressed against, Allah will surely help him. Indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse establishes the principle of just retaliation while emphasizing divine support for those who exercise restraint. When someone retaliates proportionately against harm done to them and then faces further aggression or injustice, Allah guarantees His aid to them. The verse's emphasis on Allah being 'Pardoning and Forgiving' suggests that while just retaliation is permissible, transcending vengeance through forgiveness is spiritually superior, and either way, the oppressed will ultimately receive divine justice and protection.

translation: That is because Allah merges the night into the day and merges the day into the night, and indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.
interpretation: This verse illustrates Allah's supreme power and control over the natural world through the continuous, imperceptible transition of day and night. The repetition of 'yulij' (merges/interpenetrates) emphasizes the seamless, gradual process by which daylight yields to darkness and vice versa—a phenomenon so smooth that we perceive it as natural yet cannot define its exact moment. The conclusion that 'Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing' grounds this cosmic order in Divine awareness and intentionality, suggesting that this precise regulation of day and night is not mechanical but reflects Allah's perfect knowledge and observation of all creation. The verse thus invites reflection on how apparent constancy in nature is actually the result of continuous Divine management, reinforcing human dependence on and accountability to an ever-watchful Creator.

translation: That is because Allah is the Truth, and whatever they invoke besides Him is falsehood. And indeed, Allah is the Most High, the Most Great.
interpretation: This verse establishes the fundamental principle that all reality and authority belong exclusively to Allah alone. The designation of truth and falsehood serves as a divine epistemological criterion - whatever aligns with Allah's guidance and monotheistic worship is truth, while idolatry and polytheism are inherently baseless. The closing attributes of 'Al-'Aliyy' (The Most High) and 'Al-Kabir' (The Most Great) emphasize Allah's absolute supremacy in rank and magnitude, which necessitates that all devotion and trust be directed toward Him alone, making the worship of false deities not merely mistaken but logically and spiritually impossible in light of His transcendent nature.

translation: Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky and thereupon the earth becomes green? Indeed, Allah is Subtle and All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse illustrates Allah's divine wisdom and power through the observable phenomenon of rainfall reviving barren land. The greening of the earth after rain demonstrates Allah's subtle yet all-encompassing knowledge and control over the natural world. The phrase 'Latif Khabir' (Subtle and All-Knowing) suggests that Allah's management of creation operates through intricate, delicate mechanisms that are perfectly orchestrated by His complete knowledge. The verse invites reflection on how Allah sustains life through seemingly simple natural processes, emphasizing His providential care and the profound wisdom underlying creation's renewal cycle.

translation: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And indeed, Allah - He is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute sovereignty and ownership of all creation, establishing that everything in existence ultimately belongs to Him and is under His dominion. The mention of His attributes as al-Ghani (the Self-Sufficient) and al-Hamid (the Praiseworthy) conveys that despite His complete ownership and control, Allah is entirely independent of any need from His creation, while remaining worthy of all praise and worship for His perfection and generosity - a fundamental teaching on tawhid that should inspire humility and gratitude in the believer.

translation: Have you not seen that Allah has made subject to you whatever is on the earth and the ships that sail through the sea by His command? And He withholds the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission. Indeed, Allah is to the people most Kind and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's comprehensive power and tender mercy toward humanity. By highlighting the subjugation of earthly resources, the regulation of ships at sea, and the suspension of the heavens, the verse demonstrates that all of creation operates under divine command and wisdom. The connection between these displays of divine might and the closing statement about God's kindness and mercy suggests that this awesome power is exercised not as a means of oppression, but as an expression of benevolence—God maintains the order of creation precisely to sustain and benefit humanity. The verse thus calls believers to recognize that their dependence on divine governance is not a burden but evidence of God's compassionate care for their welfare.

translation: And He is the One Who gives you life, then causes you to die, then gives you life again. Indeed, mankind is most ungrateful.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the cyclical nature of human existence—from non-existence to life to death to resurrection—as evidence of Allah's complete power and sovereignty. The statement that 'mankind is ungrateful' serves as a profound moral commentary, suggesting that despite this clear demonstration of divine power over life and death, humans fail to recognize and appreciate this favor, and instead turn away from gratitude and obedience to their Creator. The verse implicitly criticizes human negligence in acknowledging the ultimate dependence of all creation upon Allah's will.

translation: For every nation We have appointed a rite which they observe. So let them not dispute with you in the matter; and call to your Lord. Indeed, you are upon straight guidance.
interpretation: This verse establishes that Allah has ordained specific religious practices and rituals for each community, and they have the right to practice them according to their tradition. The Prophet Muhammad is instructed not to be troubled by disputes over these differing practices, as his responsibility is simply to call people to worship Allah and follow the straight path that he himself has been guided to. The emphasis is on maintaining resolve in the core message of monotheism and righteous guidance rather than being diverted by arguments over ceremonial details.

translation: And if they dispute with you, say: 'Allah knows best what you do.'
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet to respond to those who argue with him about Islamic teachings by appealing to God's ultimate knowledge and judgment rather than engaging in endless disputation. It emphasizes the futility of debating with those who dispute the truth and redirects accountability to God's all-encompassing knowledge of human actions and intentions, suggesting that God alone will judge the truth of matters and the sincerity of people's deeds, thereby providing the Prophet with a dignified and final response that acknowledges human limitations in resolving such disputes.

translation: Allah will judge between you on the Day of Judgment concerning that in which you used to differ.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes divine justice and ultimate accountability, indicating that all disputes and disagreements among people in this life—whether about faith, law, ethics, or worldly matters—will be resolved definitively by Allah on the Day of Judgment. The verse serves as a reminder that human judgment is fallible and temporary, while God's judgment is absolute and final, which should encourage believers to seek truth and avoid stubborn disputation, knowing they will ultimately answer for their positions and conduct.

translation: Do you not know that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Indeed, that is in a Book. Indeed, that upon Allah is easy.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute and comprehensive knowledge of all creation, both the seen and unseen realms. The reminder that this knowledge is preserved in a Book (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz - the Preserved Tablet) underscores the certainty and immutability of divine decree. The final phrase conveys that such infinite knowledge and recording of all things presents no difficulty for Allah, establishing His supreme power and perfect awareness as foundational to understanding His justice, wisdom, and dominion over all affairs.

translation: And they worship besides Allah that for which He has not sent down any authority, and that of which they have no knowledge. And there is no helper for the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse condemns the act of worshipping objects, idols, or concepts that lack any divine authorization or rational basis. The dual emphasis on 'no authority' (sulṭān) and 'no knowledge' underscores that such worship is both unfounded in divine revelation and baseless in human understanding. The final clause serves as a warning that those who persist in this wrongdoing—who are thus unjust (ẓālimīn)—will have no one to aid them on the Day of Judgment, suggesting that their self-imposed delusion in this life will leave them defenseless in the hereafter.

translation: And when Our clear verses are recited to them, you recognize denial in the faces of those who disbelieve. They almost attack those who recite Our verses to them. Say, 'Shall I inform you of something worse than that? The Fire—Allah has promised it to those who disbelieve, and wretched is the destination.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the intense hostility of disbelievers toward the divine message, manifested both in their visible expressions of rejection and their violent impulses. The passage emphasizes a critical reorientation of perspective: while the immediate threat of physical violence from the disbelievers appears formidable, it pales in comparison to the eternal consequence awaiting them. By directing the believers to proclaim this truth—that the punishment of Hell is far more severe than any temporal harm—the verse strengthens the resolve of those preaching Islam and invites reflection on the asymmetry between temporary worldly persecution and permanent spiritual consequences.

translation: O mankind, a parable has been set forth, so listen to it. Indeed, those whom you call upon besides Allah will never create [even] a fly, although they may gather for that purpose. And if the fly should steal away from them a thing, they could not recover it from it. Weak are the seeker and the sought.
interpretation: This verse uses the metaphor of a fly to demonstrate the complete powerlessness of idols and false deities.
