The parable illustrates that those who are worshipped besides Allah lack the most basic creative power—they cannot even create a fly, the smallest and most insignificant creature. Furthermore, if something as trivial as a fly were to take something from them, they would be utterly helpless to retrieve it. By this vivid comparison, the Quran establishes the absurdity of associating partners with Allah and seeking help from those who possess no real power or agency. The phrase 'weak are the seeker and the sought' encapsulates the futility of both those who worship idols and the idols themselves—both are equally powerless and dependent. This serves as a call to reason, inviting people to recognize the logical impossibility and spiritual danger of polytheism.

translation: They did not esteem Allah with the esteem that is His due. Indeed, Allah is Powerful and Mighty.
interpretation: This verse rebukes those who fail to recognize and honor Allah's true nature and attributes. The phrase 'did not esteem Allah with the esteem that is His due' refers to humanity's inadequate comprehension and acknowledgment of Allah's majesty, power, and sovereignty. The verse then emphasizes that this human shortcoming does not diminish Allah in any way—He remains absolutely mighty and powerful, independent of human recognition. This serves as a reminder that our failure to properly glorify Allah stems from the limitations of human understanding, not from any deficiency in His divine attributes.

translation: Allah chooses from the angels messengers and from mankind. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.
interpretation: This verse establishes that divine selection of messengers is an act of God's sovereign will and wisdom, not based on human preference or qualification. The phrase 'from the angels' and 'from mankind' indicates that messengers come from both categories of creation, chosen according to God's knowledge. The concluding attribute that 'Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing' emphasizes that God's choice is made with perfect knowledge of all circumstances, hearts, and capabilities, making His selection infallible and beyond human comprehension or questioning.

translation: He knows what is before them and what will come after them, and to Allah are all matters returned.
interpretation: This verse affirms Allah's complete omniscience encompassing all dimensions of time and existence - the past (what is behind) and the future (what is ahead) - demonstrating that human knowledge and control are limited, while ultimate authority and judgment rest exclusively with Allah, before whom all affairs must ultimately be brought to account.

translation: O you who have believed, bow down and prostrate yourselves, and worship your Lord and do good that you may succeed.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that true success (falah) in this life and the hereafter is achieved through a combination of spiritual devotion and righteous action. The mention of bowing and prostrating represents ritual prayer as the foundation of the believer's relationship with Allah, while the command to 'do good' encompasses moral behavior and service to others. The conditional phrase 'that you may succeed' indicates that prosperity is not merely a matter of outward religious observance, but rather the synthesis of sincere worship with virtuous conduct toward humanity.

translation: And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him. He has chosen you and has not placed upon you in the religion any difficulty. [It is] the religion of your father, Abraham. He named you 'Muslims' before [in former scriptures] and in this [revelation] so that the Messenger may be a witness over you and you may be witnesses over the people. So establish prayer, give zakah, and hold fast to Allah. He is your Protector; and excellent is the Protector, and excellent is the Helper.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that true struggle in the way of Allah is a balanced obligation that does not impose hardship; rather, Islam is characterized by ease and flexibility in its rulings. The verse grounds Muslim identity in the heritage of Prophet Abraham, establishing continuity with previous prophets while emphasizing the universal mission of the Muslim community to witness the truth before all of humanity. The call to establish prayer, give alms, and rely upon Allah serves as the practical manifestation of sincere devotion, revealing that genuine struggle is not merely internal conviction but finds expression through concrete actions and unwavering trust in God's protection and aid.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. Indeed, the believers have succeeded.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true success and prosperity are achieved through faith and belief in Allah. The word 'aflaha' (succeeded/prospered) denotes not merely worldly gain but spiritual triumph and ultimate felicity, suggesting that genuine success is measured by one's closeness to Allah and adherence to His guidance rather than by material wealth or temporal power. The verse affirms that faith is the foundational criterion for human success in both this life and the hereafter.

translation: Those who are during their prayers humble/submissive (in heart)
interpretation: This verse describes a key quality of the truly faithful believers - that they are present and emotionally engaged during their prayers, experiencing genuine awe and reverence before Allah rather than performing prayer as an empty ritual. The concept of khushu' (خشوع) emphasizes an inward spiritual state of humility, concentration, and focused devotion that should accompany the physical acts of prayer, indicating that true worship requires both body and soul to be present before the Divine.

translation: And those who turn away from idle talk
interpretation: This verse describes a characteristic of the righteous believers who intentionally avoid and disregard vain, frivolous, and meaningless speech. Their deliberate aversion to idle talk reflects spiritual maturity and wisdom, as they consciously choose to engage only in speech that has value and purpose. This quality demonstrates their commitment to purifying their conduct and protecting their faith from distractions that would diminish their spiritual standing and relationship with Allah.

translation: And those who are dutiful in giving zakat (obligatory alms)
interpretation: This verse describes one of the characteristics of the righteous believers - their consistent practice of zakat as a religious obligation and spiritual commitment. The phrase emphasizes that true piety is demonstrated through concrete action and regular fulfillment of this pillar of Islam, reflecting a heart that is conscious of God and responsive to the needs of the poor and vulnerable in society.

translation: And those who guard their private parts
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the virtue of chastity and self-restraint in matters of sexual conduct. It refers to believers who maintain moral discipline by protecting themselves from unlawful sexual relations and preserving their honor. The guarding of one's private parts represents a broader commitment to purity, modesty, and adherence to Islamic moral boundaries, reflecting the importance Islam places on regulating desires within the framework of divine law.

translation: Except with their wives or those whom their right hands possess, for indeed they are not blamed
interpretation: This verse addresses the exceptions to the prohibition against sexual relations outside of marriage. It permits intimate relations with one's spouse and with those in one's possession (captives or servants), establishing that within these specific contexts, believers are not culpable or blameworthy. The verse distinguishes between lawful and unlawful relationships by defining the legitimate channels through which such relations are permissible according to Islamic law, thereby framing the boundaries of moral responsibility and accountability.

translation: So whoever seeks beyond that, then those are the transgressors.
interpretation: This verse refers to those who transgress the boundaries set by Allah, particularly in matters of sexual relations and marriage. The phrase 'beyond that' refers to relationships outside the lawful bonds of marriage and what is permissible. The verse conveys that anyone who seeks to go beyond Allah's prescribed limits in this matter is considered one of the 'transgressors' (العادون), indicating that such behavior is a violation of divine law and a departure from the righteous path. This demonstrates that boundaries exist for human welfare and spiritual guidance, and exceeding them constitutes a serious transgression.

translation: And those who are guardians of their trusts and their covenants
interpretation: This verse describes a characteristic of the righteous believers - their meticulous preservation and fulfillment of both financial trusts placed in their care and the covenants they have made. The term 'راعون' (guardians/keepers) implies not merely passive holding but active, conscientious stewardship and protection of obligations. This reflects the Islamic principle that trustworthiness and covenant-keeping are fundamental pillars of moral character and accountability before Allah, with the believers understanding that these responsibilities will be questioned on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And those who are constant in their prayers (or: those who guard their prayers)
interpretation: This verse describes one of the characteristics of the righteous believers - their unwavering commitment and diligence in performing the daily prescribed prayers. The term 'يحافظون' (yahfizun) emphasizes not merely performing prayers, but actively protecting, preserving, and maintaining them with consistency and dedication. This suggests that true faith is demonstrated through concrete actions and disciplined practice, not merely in belief alone. The verse implies that those who consider prayer important enough to guard and preserve it, despite life's distractions and challenges, are among those worthy of God's favor and reward.

translation: Those are the inheritors
interpretation: This phrase refers to those who will inherit paradise and its blessings, emphasizing that the righteous and faithful believers are the true heirs of God's favor and reward in the afterlife, as their deeds and commitment to faith make them worthy recipients of divine grace and eternal blessing.

translation: Those who inherit Paradise - they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the eternal nature of Paradise as the ultimate reward for the righteous. The use of 'inherit' (yarithun) conveys that Paradise is not merely granted temporarily but is a rightful, permanent possession for believers, suggesting they have earned it through their deeds and faith. The phrase 'abide therein forever' (khâlidûn) underscores the permanence and endless duration of this bliss, establishing a fundamental Islamic concept that the reward for righteousness in the Hereafter is eternal and unchanging, in contrast to the temporary and transient nature of worldly life.

translation: And We have certainly created mankind from an extract of clay.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the humble origins of humanity, establishing that despite any intellectual or spiritual development humans may achieve, they are fundamentally created from base material - clay. This serves as a reminder of human humility before God and the insignificance of human pride, as all humans share this common material origin regardless of status or achievement. It underscores the equality of human nature and the need for spiritual consciousness as the distinction that elevates humans beyond their physical composition.

translation: Then We made him a sperm-drop in a secure resting place
interpretation: This verse describes the stage of human creation following the initial creation of Adam from clay. It emphasizes that after the initial formation, human beings develop from a microscopic sperm-drop placed in the protected environment of the womb. The phrase 'secure resting place' (قرار مكين) signifies the safety and stability of the womb as a sanctuary for the developing human, highlighting divine wisdom in designing a protected space for the delicate beginning of human life. This demonstrates the gradual and deliberate nature of divine creation, progressing from elemental matter to life stages, reflecting God's perfect knowledge and careful planning in bringing human beings into existence.

translation: Then We created the sperm-drop into a clinging form (alaqah), and We created the clinging form into a lump (mudghah), and We created the lump into bones, and We clothed the bones with flesh. Then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the magnificent stages of human embryonic development as evidence of Allah's creative power and wisdom. The progression from the simplest form (nutfah) through increasingly complex stages demonstrates that creation is not instantaneous but carefully orchestrated according to divine design. The phrase 'produced him as another creation' (ansha'ahu khalqan akhara) refers to the infusion of the soul (ruh), which represents a qualitative leap in the creation of the human being—from a merely physical development to the emergence of consciousness, awareness, and the capacity for moral and spiritual life. This transition from the material to the spiritual underscores the unique status of humans among creation, and the concluding affirmation 'blessed is Allah, the best of creators' calls the listener to recognize and submit to this perfect divine artistry as a source of gratitude and worship.

translation: Then indeed, after that, you will surely die.
interpretation: This verse reminds humanity of the inevitability of death as a divine decree that applies to all living beings without exception. It emphasizes that regardless of one's earthly accomplishments, status, or possessions, death is an inescapable reality that will come to pass. The verse serves as a sobering call to believers to recognize their mortality and the temporary nature of this worldly life, thereby encouraging them to prepare for the Hereafter and direct their focus toward eternal matters rather than being consumed by worldly pursuits.

translation: Then on the Day of Resurrection, you will be raised up.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the certainty of resurrection and divine accountability on the Day of Judgment. It serves as a reminder that despite the temporal nature of worldly life, all humans will be resurrected and brought before God for judgment of their deeds. The use of the emphatic particle 'ثم' (then) and the address to humanity collectively underscores the universality and inevitability of this event, which is foundational to Islamic belief and serves to motivate righteous conduct in this life.

translation: And We have created above you seven heavens, and We were never unmindful of (Our) creation.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes both the majesty of creation and Allah's constant vigilance over His creation. The reference to 'seven heavens' reflects the Qur'anic cosmology and serves to illustrate the vastness and complexity of the created universe. The second part reasserts that despite this immense creation, Allah remains fully aware and attentive to all that occurs within it, rejecting any notion of divine negligence or indifference toward the created beings.

translation: And We sent down from the sky water in measured amount, and We settled it in the earth. And indeed, We are capable of taking it away.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty and control over the vital resources upon which human survival depends. By mentioning both the provision of water in precise measure and the implicit threat of its withdrawal, Allah reminds humanity of their complete dependence on His will and the temporary nature of all blessings. The statement is both a reassurance of God's wisdom in sustenance and a warning against ingratitude and heedlessness, as humanity cannot secure or preserve these essential provisions without divine permission.

translation: So We produced for you thereby gardens of date-palms and grapevines in which you have abundant fruits, and from them you eat.
interpretation: This verse illustrates God's providential care and the chain of causality He established in creation, where water—sent from the heavens—becomes the means through which He brings forth luxurious gardens and diverse sustenance for human nourishment. It emphasizes human dependence on divine provision and the bounty God has made accessible to mankind through the natural world, demonstrating His mercy and the purposefulness of His creation in sustaining human life.

translation: And a tree that springs forth from Mount Sinai, producing oil and a condiment for those who eat.
interpretation: This verse refers to the olive tree growing on Mount Sinai, which Allah has blessed as a source of both nourishment and light. The mention of oil and condiment emphasizes the tree's dual utility and abundance of blessing - serving both as a nutritious food and as a clarifying substance. By specifically identifying Mount Sinai, a place sanctified by revelation, Allah draws attention to the sacred nature of His creation and the exceptional bounty He has granted in that blessed land, encouraging reflection on the signs of Divine provision and wisdom evident in nature.

translation: And indeed, in the cattle there is a lesson for you. We give you drink from what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the Divine wisdom and generosity embedded within creation, demonstrating that Allah has deliberately designed livestock as a source of sustenance and multiple benefits for humanity. The mention of drinking from what is in their bellies—referring to milk—highlights how Allah's provision comes in unexpected forms, inviting reflection on the complexity and purposefulness of creation as evidence of God's care and the proper function of creation in serving human needs. This serves as an invitation to recognize divine signs and to be grateful for the multifaceted blessings provided through animal husbandry.

translation: And upon it and upon the ships you are carried.
interpretation: This verse speaks to Allah's provision of means of transportation and sustenance for humanity. The 'it' refers to the earth, which carries and supports all living creatures. The mention of ships alongside the earth emphasizes Allah's creation of diverse modes of conveyance - both the land that sustains us and the vessels that allow us to traverse the seas. This is meant to inspire gratitude and recognition of Allah's mercy in providing humanity with the physical means necessary for survival, travel, and commerce. The verse underscores human dependence upon Allah's creation and His wisdom in designing the world for human benefit.

translation: And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he said, 'O my people, worship Allah. You have no deity other than Him. Will you not fear Him?'
interpretation: This verse establishes Noah as the first messenger sent by Allah to guide humanity toward monotheism. His message emphasizes the fundamental principle of tawhid (divine oneness) and the rejection of polytheism. The phrase 'what deity have you other than Him' serves as a rational proof against idolatry, while the rhetorical question 'will you not fear Him?' appeals to the conscience and self-interest of the people, urging them to recognize Allah's power and their accountability before Him. This demonstrates the classic methodology of the prophets: combining clear intellectual argument with an emotional and spiritual appeal to piety and God-consciousness.

translation: So the chiefs who disbelieved from among his people said, 'This is nothing but a human like you who wishes to gain superiority over you. And if Allah had willed, He would have sent down angels. We have not heard of this among our forefathers.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the arrogance and resistance of the disbelieving elite who rejected the message through their reliance on ancestral tradition and their refusal to accept that Allah chooses humans as messengers. Their claim that Allah would have sent angels instead demonstrates their attempt to set conditions for accepting divine guidance, reflecting a fundamental rejection of Allah's wisdom in choosing His messengers and a stubborn adherence to the status quo that preserves their worldly power and influence.

translation: He is not but a man possessed by madness, so wait with him for a while.
interpretation: This verse reflects the mockery and dismissal of the disbelievers toward the Prophet Muhammad. Rather than engaging with his message on its merits, they attribute his prophetic claims to mental illness or possession by jinn, which was a common accusation against prophets in Arabian society. The phrase 'wait with him for a while' suggests their arrogant confidence that time will prove him wrong, revealing their blindness to the truth and their reliance on ridicule as a defense against faith. The verse illustrates how those who reject divine guidance often resort to attacking the messenger's character rather than contemplating the message itself.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, help me against what they deny.'
interpretation: This verse reflects a plea from a messenger of Allah (likely Nuh, Hud, or another prophet) calling upon God for divine assistance against the disbelief and rejection of his people. The supplication demonstrates the prophet's complete reliance on Allah's power rather than his own strength, acknowledging that overcoming the denial of truth requires God's intervention. It illustrates the spiritual principle that when facing sustained rejection and mockery from those who deny the divine message, the faithful should turn to Allah for support, recognizing that their ultimate victory comes not through worldly means but through divine aid.

translation: So We revealed to him: 'Construct the ark under Our Eyes and Our guidance. Then, when Our command comes and the oven overflows, take aboard it of every creature two mates, and your family except those against whom the Word has already gone forth among them. And do not speak to Me on behalf of those who have done wrong; they shall surely be drowned.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's direct guidance and protection of Noah in his mission to build the ark, establishing that divine will and human obedience work in concert. The command to take paired creatures represents the preservation of creation through God's providence, while the exception regarding those against whom the decree had already been issued demonstrates that God's justice is predetermined and not subject to intercession, thereby teaching that mercy and justice operate within God's eternal knowledge, and that no plea can change what has been divinely ordained.

translation: So when you have settled, you and those with you, in the ship, say: 'All praise is due to Allah, who has saved us from the people who are oppressors.'
interpretation: This verse teaches the believer to recognize and acknowledge Allah's blessings through gratitude at moments of deliverance and safety. The command to say praise (al-hamd) upon boarding the ship and being secured with one's companions emphasizes that recognizing divine salvation from oppression is an essential spiritual practice. It demonstrates that believers should maintain consciousness of Allah's protection and mercy in concrete circumstances, transforming a physical journey into a spiritual acknowledgment of dependence on Allah and His deliverance from wrongdoing and tyranny.

translation: And say: 'My Lord, let me descend with a blessed descent, and You are the best of those who bring down [to destinations].'
interpretation: This verse teaches the believer to seek Allah's guidance and blessing in all matters of life, acknowledging that all beneficial outcomes and safe arrivals—whether physical, spiritual, or metaphorical—come only through Allah's will and grace. The supplication emphasizes both humility before Allah and trust in His superior wisdom, as the phrase 'You are the best of those who bring down' affirms that no one can provide true blessing and safe passage except Allah. The use of 'blessed descent' suggests seeking not merely material arrival but a descent into circumstances, knowledge, or states of being that are spiritually and practically beneficial.

translation: Indeed, in that are signs, and indeed We are being tested.
interpretation: This verse reflects the human condition of trial and examination through worldly experiences. The 'signs' (آيات) refer to divine evidence and guidance manifest in creation and circumstances, while the speaker acknowledges that both believers and all people are constantly tested by Allah through various trials and hardships. The verse teaches that recognizing these signs requires understanding that life itself is a period of testing, where one's response to both blessing and difficulty reveals one's true faith and character. This perspective transforms difficulties from mere misfortunes into opportunities for spiritual growth and demonstration of devotion.

translation: Then We produced after them another generation
interpretation: This verse refers to Allah's creation of successive generations of people after previous ones had passed away. It emphasizes the continuous cycle of human creation and replacement throughout history, illustrating Allah's power to create new peoples and civilizations, and implicitly suggesting the cyclical nature of human civilization and the testing of each generation with divine guidance and choice.

translation: So We sent among them a messenger from themselves, [saying], 'Worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not fear Him?'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine principle of sending prophets from within the communities they address, making the message relatable and comprehensible to them. The command to worship only Allah and reject all false deities, coupled with the rhetorical question 'Will you not fear Him?', serves as both a call to monotheism and a warning that rejecting this message demonstrates a lack of God-consciousness and fear of divine punishment. The verse highlights humanity's responsibility to recognize and respond to the signs sent through messengers who share their language, nature, and cultural context.

translation: And the notables of his people who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter—and We had given them ease in worldly life—said, 'This is nothing but a man like you. He eats from what you eat from and drinks from what you drink.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates how material prosperity and worldly comfort can blind people to truth and lead them to reject divine guidance. The disbelievers' argument that the Prophet is merely human like themselves reveals their spiritual blindness—they use the Prophet's humanity as grounds for rejection rather than recognizing that prophethood is compatible with human nature. Their affluence in worldly life has hardened their hearts, making them incapable of recognizing the signs of truth, as they are preoccupied with and attached to material gains rather than spiritual realities. The verse suggests that luxury and comfort can become obstacles to faith when they distract the soul from contemplating the divine message.

translation: And if you obey a human being like yourselves, then indeed you will be losers.
interpretation: This verse warns against blindly following human leaders or ideologies instead of guidance from Allah. The phrase 'a human being like yourselves' emphasizes the fundamental equality and fallibility of all humans, highlighting that no mortal possesses infallibility or the right to be obeyed unconditionally in matters of faith and morality. The consequence of such obedience—being losers—points to spiritual and moral ruin that results from substituting human judgment for divine guidance. The verse serves as a reminder that true salvation and success come only through adherence to Allah's revelation, not through allegiance to human authorities or popular opinion.

translation: Does He promise you that when you die and become dust and bones, you will indeed be brought forth?
interpretation: This verse presents the rhetorical question posed by disbelievers who find it absurd and impossible that Allah would resurrect humans after they have completely decomposed into dust and bones. The verse emphasizes the seeming impossibility of resurrection according to human rational understanding, highlighting the disbelievers' denial and mockery of the Day of Judgment. It serves to portray their arrogance in rejecting divine power and their inability to comprehend that Allah's ability transcends natural physical laws. The verse implicitly affirms that despite their doubt, resurrection is indeed a reality and a promise from Allah.

translation: Never, never will [this] come to pass that which you are promised.
interpretation: This verse expresses divine dismissal of the false promises made by the disbelievers to one another regarding their security from punishment. The repetition of 'hihāt' (never) emphasizes the absolute certainty and inevitability of judgment, conveying that their empty assurances and false hopes of escaping divine accountability are impossible delusions that will not materialize.

translation: It is naught but our life in this world; we die and we live, and we shall not be resurrected.
interpretation: This verse represents the argument of those who deny the Afterlife and divine resurrection, reflecting their materialist worldview that life is limited to this temporal existence with its cycles of death and birth. The verse serves as a rhetorical statement of disbelief that emphasizes the stubbornness of those who reject Allah's message regarding accountability in the Hereafter, demonstrating how some people construct their entire belief system around the rejection of divine truth and divine justice beyond this world.

translation: He is nothing but a man who has fabricated a lie against Allah, and we are not believers in him.
interpretation: This verse conveys the rejection and denial of the disbelievers toward the Prophet's message, viewing his claims as mere human invention rather than divine revelation. The phrase 'fabricated a lie against Allah' emphasizes their accusation that he falsely attributed his words to God, and their refusal to believe represents their arrogant dismissal of the truth and their hardened hearts against guidance.

translation: He said: 'My Lord, help me against what they deny.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the supplication of a messenger (likely Noah) calling upon Allah for divine assistance against those who reject and deny his message. The plea demonstrates the reliance of the prophets on Allah's support when facing opposition, emphasizing that ultimate victory and vindication come through divine intervention rather than human effort. The verse teaches that believers should turn to Allah in times of trial and rejection, trusting in His power to grant assistance and establish truth over falsehood.

translation: He said: 'Soon they will become regretful.'
interpretation: This statement reflects the consequence of rejecting divine guidance and choosing falsehood. The speaker (Salih, the Prophet) is declaring with certainty that those who persist in their arrogance and denial will inevitably experience regret and remorse when they face the reality of their choices, either in this life through punishment or in the afterlife when they confront the truth they rejected. This emphasizes the principle that rebellion against God's message leads to inevitable sorrow and loss.

translation: So the blast seized them in justice, and We made them [like] scattered debris. So away with the people who have wronged!
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of divine justice whereby those who persistently deny the signs of God and transgress His limits are overcome by His punishment - described here as a overwhelming blast. The transformation of the wrongdoers into 'scattered debris' (غثاء) symbolizes their complete annihilation and humiliation, reflecting how their former power and status become utterly insignificant. The concluding phrase expresses both God's absolute rejection of such people and a reminder to believers that those who persist in wrongdoing will ultimately find no refuge from divine retribution, serving as a warning against the path of arrogance and transgression.

translation: Then after them We brought forth other generations
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the cyclical nature of human history and divine providence. Allah replaced successive generations with new ones, indicating that no people or civilization is permanent or indispensable. This serves as a reminder of human transience and the inevitability of change, while underscoring that each generation is accountable for its own deeds and will face the consequences of accepting or rejecting divine guidance. The succession of generations demonstrates Allah's continued involvement in human affairs and His plan unfolding through time.

translation: No nation can advance its term, nor can they delay it.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of Allah over all matters of life and death. The appointed time of death for each individual and nation is predetermined by Allah alone, and neither humans nor nations have any ability to change, hasten, or postpone their destined hour. This serves to remind believers of their powerlessness over fate and to cultivate trust in divine wisdom, while encouraging them to focus on obedience to Allah rather than futile attempts to control their lifespan.

translation: Then We sent Our messengers in succession. Every time a messenger came to a community, they denied him. So We made some follow others, and We made them stories. So away with a people who do not believe.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the pattern of divine testing throughout history, emphasizing that the rejection of God's messengers is a recurring human failing that carries inevitable consequences. The phrase 'in succession' (تترى) denotes the continuous sending of prophets across time and nations, while 'We made them stories' (جعلناهم أحاديث) suggests that these nations became cautionary tales and historical examples for later generations. The final curse 'away with a people who do not believe' (فبعدا لقوم لا يؤمنون) conveys God's complete rejection of those who persistently deny truth despite repeated clear signs, establishing the principle that disbelief leads to destruction and erasure from God's mercy.

translation: Then We sent Moses and his brother Aaron with Our signs and clear authority.
interpretation: This verse establishes the divine mission of Moses and Aaron as messengers equipped with miracles (signs) and manifest proof (clear authority) to guide the people. The phrase 'clear authority' (sulṭān mubīn) indicates that their message came with undeniable evidence and the power to demonstrate the truth of their mission, suggesting that messengers are sent not merely with words but with substantive proof that distinguishes truth from falsehood and grants them legitimate standing to call people to Allah's way.

translation: To Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they were arrogant and were a people of great might.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the rejection of divine guidance by those who possess worldly power and status. The arrogance of Pharaoh and his establishment stemmed from their confidence in their material strength and elevated position, which blinded them to the truth. Their 'greatness' in earthly terms became an obstacle to their submission to Allah, demonstrating how wealth, authority, and social prominence can lead hearts away from faith rather than toward it. The verse emphasizes that true elevation comes not from worldly dominion but from obedience to the divine message.

translation: They said, 'Should we believe in two men like ourselves, whose people are subservient to us?'
interpretation: This verse reflects the arrogance and pride of the disbelievers who rejected the message of the two messengers (traditionally understood as Moses and Aaron, or in another context, two messengers sent to a community) based on their social status and earthly power. The disbelievers' dismissal reveals how worldly dominance and material superiority blind people to spiritual truth—they assume that prophethood must come from those already elevated in rank, and they use their control over others' submission as evidence of their own superiority and the messengers' inferiority, thereby committing the error of conflating political power with divine guidance.

translation: So they denied both of them, and thus they became among the destroyed.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the consequence of rejecting the message of the prophets. When people deny the truth brought by messengers from Allah, they incur divine punishment and destruction. The verse emphasizes that rejecting prophetic guidance is not merely a matter of disbelief, but rather a deliberate act of resistance that inevitably leads to ruin and perdition. It serves as a warning to those who turn away from divine truth and choose to remain in denial.

translation: And indeed, We gave Moses the Scripture, that perhaps they might be guided.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that divine guidance through revealed scripture is a mercy from Allah to humanity. The Torah was given to Moses as a comprehensive guide containing laws, wisdom, and ethical principles to help the Israelites find the straight path. The phrase 'that perhaps they might be guided' (لعلهم يهتدون) suggests that while Allah provides the means and opportunity for guidance through revelation, the actual acceptance and following of this guidance depends on human choice and will. The verse underscores the responsibility of those who receive divine revelation to heed it and act upon it, as the gift of scripture is meaningless without human receptivity and commitment to following its teachings.

translation: And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign, and We gave them shelter on a high ground with a spring of water flowing through it.
interpretation: This verse highlights the miraculous nature of Jesus and Mary by designating them as 'ayah' (a sign) for humanity - not merely as historical figures but as signs pointing to divine power and wisdom. The provision of refuge on elevated ground with water represents God's protection and sustenance for the righteous, symbolizing both physical safety and spiritual security. The specificity of the locale - a high, peaceful place with fresh water - suggests that God's care extends to the practical needs of His chosen ones, while the miraculous nature of their circumstances serves as evidence of divine intervention in human history.

translation: O Messengers, eat from the good things and do righteous deeds. Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the prophets and messengers are permitted to enjoy the lawful provisions of Allah while maintaining their commitment to righteous conduct. The command to 'eat from the good things' legitimizes the use of halal sustenance, addressing a misconception that righteousness requires self-deprivation. By coupling this permission with the command to perform righteous deeds, Allah teaches that spiritual elevation is achieved through the balance of enjoying lawful blessings while maintaining moral integrity. The concluding affirmation 'Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do' serves as both encouragement and accountability, reminding the messengers that Allah is fully aware of their intentions and actions, thus discouraging hypocrisy or the pursuit of worldly pleasures at the expense of their divine mission.

translation: And verily, this your religion is one religion, and I am your Lord, so fear Me.
interpretation: This verse establishes the fundamental unity of faith and purpose across all believers regardless of their circumstances. Allah emphasizes that despite apparent differences in laws, practices, or time periods, the core religion of monotheism and submission to the divine is singular and unified. The command to fear Allah serves as the binding principle that should unite the community in consciousness of accountability before Him, making Taqwa (God-consciousness) the essential requirement that transcends all other considerations and calls believers to prioritize obedience to God above all worldly concerns.

translation: So they divided their religion among themselves into sects, each group rejoicing in what they had.
interpretation: This verse describes how people fragmented their faith and created divisions among themselves based on their own desires and preferences, with each faction becoming attached to their particular position. The term 'zubur' (scraps or pieces) emphasizes the fractured and scattered nature of their unity, suggesting that such sectarianism represents a deviation from the cohesive guidance that religion should provide. The phrase 'each group rejoicing in what they had' indicates the spiritual danger of preferring one's own interpretation or tradition over seeking truth, as this contentment with division prevents genuine understanding and unity.

translation: So leave them in their delusion until a time
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet to cease attempting to convince those who persist in their denial and ignorance. The word 'غمرة' (ghimrah) refers to being immersed in delusion, heedlessness, or confusion. The instruction to leave them 'until a time' indicates that Allah has set a appointed term for them - a time of reckoning when they will face the consequences of their rejection. This reflects the principle that divine guidance cannot be forced upon those who willfully reject truth, and that patience in the face of stubborn denial is part of the Prophet's mission. The verse conveys that Allah's justice will ultimately prevail at the destined hour, making continued attempts to convince the obstinate unnecessary.

translation: Do they think that what We extend to them in wealth and children
interpretation: This verse introduces a cautionary statement about those who mistake material abundance for divine favor or as a sign of righteousness. The phrase uses a rhetorical question to challenge the assumption that worldly prosperity is necessarily evidence of Allah's approval or blessing, setting up the context for what follows regarding how such abundance may actually be a trial or test rather than an unmixed good.

translation: We hasten unto them with good things, but they perceive not.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine mercy and provision that Allah extends to those who believe, allowing them to advance in righteous deeds and good works. However, many people fail to recognize this divine facilitation and hastening of blessings in their lives, remaining heedless of how Allah smooths the path for those sincere in their faith. The phrase emphasizes both the reality of divine grace working in believers' favor and humanity's common failure to acknowledge or appreciate these blessings, serving as a reminder to cultivate awareness of God's subtle assistance in our spiritual journey.

translation: Indeed, those who are in fear of their Lord are apprehensive.
interpretation: This verse describes the true believers as those who possess a profound and reverent fear of Allah, characterized by constant awareness of His presence and accountability before Him. This fear is not born of terror or despair, but rather stems from deep consciousness (taqwa) that motivates them toward righteousness and obedience. The apprehension mentioned here reflects a spiritual vigilance and humility in their relationship with their Creator, where they continually strive to avoid displeasing Him and remain conscious of His majesty and perfect justice.

translation: And those who believe in the signs (verses) of their Lord
interpretation: This verse describes the believers as those who have faith in and accept the divine signs of Allah - encompassing both the Qur'anic verses and the natural signs manifested in creation. Their belief demonstrates sincere acknowledgment of God's guidance and their openness to receiving and following His message, distinguishing them as people of genuine conviction and spiritual awareness.

translation: And those who do not associate partners with their Lord
interpretation: This verse describes believers who maintain the fundamental Islamic principle of tawhid (monotheism) by refusing to ascribe partners or equals to Allah in worship, attributes, or lordship. They recognize Allah's absolute uniqueness and oneness, which is the cornerstone of Islamic faith and the basis for righteous action.

translation: And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful, that indeed to their Lord they are returning.
interpretation: This verse describes the sincere believers who give charity and fulfill their obligations, yet remain in a state of conscious fear and awe before God, continuously aware that they must account for their deeds on the Day of Judgment. Their giving is not accompanied by arrogance or self-satisfaction, but rather by humble concern about whether their deeds are acceptable to God, which is the mark of true consciousness of the Divine.

translation: Those are the ones who hasten toward good deeds, and they are foremost in doing them.
interpretation: This verse describes those who are truly righteous as being characterized by eagerness and swiftness in pursuing good works, not merely participating in them but actively competing to be first in their performance. The phrase 'they are foremost in doing them' (وهم لها سابقون) suggests a spiritual zeal and commitment that drives them to excel in virtue, indicating that true faith is not passive but manifests through proactive engagement in righteousness and an inner motivation to lead in good deeds.

translation: And We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity. And with Us is a record that speaks the truth, and they will not be wronged.
interpretation: This verse establishes the divine principle of mercy and justice in the assignment of religious and moral obligations. Allah does not impose tasks beyond human capability, acknowledging the legitimate limits of human nature and circumstance. The reference to a record that speaks truth emphasizes that God's perfect knowledge ensures accurate accounting on the Day of Judgment, guaranteeing that no person will face injustice or be held accountable for burdens beyond their capacity, thereby providing assurance that divine judgment is both merciful and absolutely just.

translation: Rather, their hearts are in ignorance concerning this, and for them are deeds other than this that they are doing.
interpretation: This verse describes those who remain heedless and unmindful of the divine message, emphasizing that their preoccupation with worldly pursuits and deeds keeps them distracted and prevents them from comprehending the truth. The 'غمرة' (ghimrah - ignorance or heedlessness) represents a state of being submerged or engrossed in confusion, suggesting that spiritual blindness is not merely passive but actively maintained through their engagement in actions that divert them from reflection and understanding of God's signs.

translation: Until when We seized their affluent ones with punishment, suddenly they cried out in distress.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine principle of divine retribution wherein those who were complacent in their wealth and luxury (al-mutrafun) become the first to experience God's punishment when it arrives. The word 'yajArun' (they cried out) emphasizes their sudden distress and desperate appeals after living in heedlessness. The verse demonstrates that material abundance and comfort in this life do not exempt one from accountability, and those who misuse their prosperity in transgression will face consequences when divine punishment comes, leading to their desperate pleas that will go unanswered—a reflection on the futility of calling for help once the decree of God has been executed.

translation: Do not cry out today; indeed, you are not to be helped by Us.
interpretation: This verse represents Allah's response to the inhabitants of Hell on the Day of Judgment, warning them that their pleas and desperate cries for relief will be futile and unheeded. It emphasizes the finality and irrevocability of their fate - that no rescue or divine assistance will come to them once they enter the punishment of Hell, serving as a stark reminder of the consequences of rejecting Allah's guidance in the worldly life and the absolute justice of Divine judgment.

translation: Indeed, My verses were being recited to you, but you were turning back on your heels, retreating (in rejection).
interpretation: This verse criticizes those who, despite hearing the clear signs and guidance of Allah, stubbornly rejected them and turned away from the truth, retreating backwards in denial and resistance rather than advancing toward faith and understanding. The imagery of turning on one's heels emphasizes the deliberate nature of their rejection and their refusal to progress spiritually despite having been presented with unmistakable evidence.

translation: Being arrogant about it, you forsake it by night
interpretation: This verse refers to the people's arrogant rejection and abandonment of the Qur'an during the night hours, suggesting their deliberate disregard and turning away from divine guidance out of pride and haughtiness, choosing ignorance over submission to God's message.

translation: Have they not pondered over the Word, or has there come to them something that did not come to their forefathers of old?
interpretation: This verse challenges the disbelievers to reflect deeply upon the Qur'an's message and its coherence. The rhetorical question presents two possibilities for their rejection: either they have neglected to contemplate the Qur'an's meanings and proofs, or they are using the excuse that this is a novel message without precedent. The verse implies that if they would only ponder the message carefully, they would recognize its truth and consistency, as it affirms the same fundamental teachings that their ancestors received. Thus, their disbelief stems not from any defect in the message itself, but from their own failure to think critically and their stubborn adherence to ancestral traditions.

translation: Or do they not recognize their Messenger, so they deny him?
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers' rejection of the Prophet Muhammad despite clear signs of his prophethood. The rhetorical question structure emphasizes the irrationality of their denial—they either fail to acknowledge who he truly is, or they recognize him yet choose to reject him out of obstinacy and pride. This reflects a fundamental spiritual blindness where people either lack knowledge of the truth or deliberately turn away from it despite understanding it.

translation: Or do they say, 'He is possessed by madness'? Rather, he has come to them with the truth, but most of them hate the truth.
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers' rejection of the Prophet Muhammad by attributing false motives to his message. Despite the clarity and justice of the truth he brings, their aversion to it—rooted in pride, material interest, and spiritual blindness—causes them to resort to baseless accusations rather than accept the message. The verse reveals that rejection of divine truth often stems not from intellectual uncertainty but from a willful resistance born of hatred and unwillingness to submit, demonstrating that the problem lies within the hearts of the rejecters, not in the message itself.

translation: And if the truth were to follow their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is within them would have been ruined. But We have given them their reminder, yet they turn away from their reminder.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the absolute governance of divine truth and justice over creation. The hypothetical scenario emphasizes that God's laws and divine order are immutable and not subject to human whims; were reality to conform to people's desires rather than divine truth, it would lead to universal corruption and chaos. The verse then pivots to establish that God has already provided humanity with guidance through revelation (the Qur'an as their reminder), yet despite this mercy, people deliberately reject and turn away from it. This reflects the tragedy of human choice—that knowledge and guidance are available, but willful aversion to truth is a matter of human responsibility and free decision.

translation: Or do you ask them for a reward? But the reward of your Lord is better, and He is the Best of Providers.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad, reminding him not to burden himself with concerns about compensation from people for his preaching mission. The verse emphasizes that Allah's provision and reward are superior to any earthly compensation that people might offer, and that reliance should be placed entirely upon Allah, the ultimate source of sustenance and blessing for all creation.

translation: And indeed, you are calling them to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the Prophet Muhammad's mission to guide people toward the path of monotheism and obedience to Allah. The "straight path" (sirat al-mustaqim) refers to the way of Islam and righteousness, which is unwavering and leads directly to Allah's pleasure. The verse underscores that the Prophet's sole function is to convey the message and invite people to this divinely guided way, though the acceptance of this call ultimately remains in Allah's hands. It affirms that the message of Islam provides clear moral and spiritual guidance that stands in stark contrast to deviation and falsehood.

translation: And indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the [straight] Path.
interpretation: This verse indicates that disbelief in the Hereafter is fundamentally incompatible with following the straight path. Those who reject accountability in the next life lose their moral compass and guidance in this world, as belief in the Hereafter is essential for maintaining righteous conduct and spiritual direction. The verse suggests that denial of divine judgment leads inevitably to spiritual waywardness and deviation from truth.

translation: And if We showed them mercy and removed the harm that is upon them, they would persist in their transgression, wandering blindly.
interpretation: This verse illustrates a profound principle about divine wisdom: mere material relief or removal of hardship does not necessarily lead to spiritual reform or gratitude when a person's heart is sealed in arrogance and rebellion. Allah is emphasizing that the root problem of these people is not their external circumstances but their spiritual condition—their heedlessness and deliberate transgression. This teaches that true guidance requires an internal willingness to turn to God, and that external comfort without this willingness only reinforces stubbornness in wrongdoing.

translation: And indeed, We seized them with punishment, but they did not humble themselves to their Lord, nor did they beseech Him.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the spiritual hardness and arrogance of those who, despite experiencing divine punishment and suffering, refuse to turn to Allah with humility and sincere supplication. Their refusal to submit and entreat to their Lord demonstrates a profound rejection of the message and a closing of their hearts to guidance, showing that mere suffering without spiritual openness cannot alone lead to repentance and reform.

translation: Until when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment, immediately they are in it in despair.
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment when God's punishment befalls those who persist in disbelief and wrongdoing. The metaphor of opening a gate represents the sudden, inevitable arrival of divine retribution that comes after a period of respite. The immediate transition from the opening of this gate to their despair illustrates the shock and hopelessness that overcomes them when they finally face the reality of consequences they denied or delayed. This serves as a warning that God's punishment, once decreed, comes swiftly and overwhelmingly, leaving no room for escape or regret, emphasizing the certainty of divine justice for those who reject God's signs.

translation: And it is He who created for you hearing, sight, and hearts. Little do you give thanks.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine gift of the faculties necessary for human perception and cognition—hearing, sight, and intellect (represented by hearts). The phrase 'little do you give thanks' is a lament about human ingratitude, suggesting that despite being endowed with these precious means to understand God's creation and recognize His signs, people rarely acknowledge this generosity through gratitude and obedience. The verse implicitly calls believers to recognize these blessings as divine gifts deserving thankfulness and to use these faculties to contemplate God's wisdom rather than in frivolous pursuits.

translation: And He is the One who created you upon the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.
interpretation: This verse establishes the fundamental Islamic doctrine of divine creation and resurrection. It emphasizes Allah's absolute sovereignty over human existence - from the initial creation of mankind on earth to their inevitable return to Him on the Day of Judgment. The verse reminds believers that earthly life is temporary and purposeful, with accountability awaiting all people before their Creator. It serves as a foundation for understanding human responsibility and moral obligation within the broader cosmic order under divine governance.

translation: And He is the One who gives life and causes death, and to Him belongs the alternation of night and day. Will you not then use reason?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute power and control over all existence, highlighting how the cycles of life and death, and the alternating pattern of day and night, are tangible manifestations of divine sovereignty that should prompt human reflection and rational thought. The rhetorical question at the end serves as an exhortation to recognize these signs as evidence of God's wisdom and authority, and to respond with intellectual engagement rather than heedlessness.

translation: Rather, they said the same as what the former people said.
interpretation: This verse highlights the stubbornness and resistance of the disbelievers who, despite receiving the Qur'an and clear signs from Allah, simply repeated the false claims and rejections of their predecessors. Rather than engaging with the new revelation on its merits, they defaulted to the tired objections and dismissals of those who came before them, demonstrating a spiritual stagnation and unwillingness to genuinely examine the truth being presented to them. This reflects the human tendency to conform to ancestral traditions without critical thought.

translation: They said, 'When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised up again?'
interpretation: This verse captures the disbelievers' rhetorical rejection of the resurrection, expressing their perception that death is the absolute end of existence. Their incredulity stems from the apparent impossibility of reconstituting human bodies from their decomposed remains, revealing how they prioritize material evidence over divine revelation. The verse illustrates how those who deny the afterlife construct their objection not merely as a question but as a challenge to God's power, treating the physical decomposition of the body as proof that restoration is impossible, thereby highlighting the fundamental spiritual blindness that prevents them from accepting what goes beyond sensory perception.

translation: We and our fathers have been promised this before. This is nothing but the tales of the former peoples.
interpretation: The disbelievers are responding to the message of the Hereafter with skepticism and dismissal, claiming that the warnings of resurrection and divine judgment are merely repetitions of ancient myths and folklore. By attributing these teachings to their ancestors' stories rather than divine truth, they are suggesting that the Qur'an's message is not a new revelation but merely recycled legends, thereby justifying their rejection of the Prophet's call to belief and accountability.

translation: Say, 'To whom belongs the earth and all those upon it, if you know?'
interpretation: This verse challenges the polytheists' understanding of reality by asking them to identify who truly possesses dominion over the earth and its inhabitants. Through this rhetorical question, Allah is directing the Prophet to make the pagans recognize that despite their claims of partnership with Allah through idolatry, they cannot deny that ultimate ownership and sovereignty belong to Allah alone, thereby exposing the logical inconsistency of their associating partners with Him.

translation: They will say, 'It is from Allah.' Say, 'Then will you not remember?'
interpretation: This verse expresses the reality that even those who associate partners with Allah will ultimately acknowledge that blessings and creation originate from Allah alone, yet they fail to act upon this knowledge by abandoning shirk and turning to sincere worship. The command to ask 'will you not remember?' serves as a rhetorical rebuke, calling them to reflect upon the contradiction between their verbal admission of Allah's sovereignty and their practical denial through polytheism, thereby urging them toward genuine remembrance and recognition of Allah's oneness.

translation: Say: 'Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?'
interpretation: This verse challenges the listener to recognize through reason that only Allah could be the Lord of the seven heavens and the Mighty Throne, thereby affirming His absolute sovereignty and power over all creation. The rhetorical question format compels the audience to arrive at the inevitable conclusion that no one else could possess such dominion, making it a powerful argument for monotheism rooted in logical necessity rather than mere assertion.

translation: They will say: 'To Allah.' Say: 'Will you not then fear (Him)?'
interpretation: This verse exposes the hypocrisy of those who claim belief in Allah's lordship while their actions contradict their confession. By asking 'will you not then fear (Him)?', the Qur'an is highlighting that mere verbal acknowledgment of Allah's sovereignty is hollow without corresponding piety and obedience. The question serves as a rhetorical rebuke, emphasizing that true recognition of Allah's dominion must necessarily lead to taqwa (fear and awareness of Allah), which manifests in conscious restraint from disobedience and commitment to His commands.

translation: Say: 'Who has in His Hand the dominion of all things, and He protects but is not protected against, if you only knew?'
interpretation: This verse challenges the polytheists to recognize Allah's absolute sovereignty and power over all creation. The phrase 'dominion of all things' refers to Allah's complete control and ownership of the entire universe. 'He protects but is not protected against' emphasizes that only Allah can grant protection and security to His creation, while no one can harm or threaten Him. The verse is a rhetorical question meant to awaken the listeners to the logical conclusion that if Allah alone possesses such ultimate authority and power, then He alone deserves worship and obedience, making any association of partners with Him in worship utterly irrational.

translation: They will say, 'It is from Allah.' Say, 'Then how is it that you are being bewitched?'
interpretation: This verse addresses those who attribute something they claim is good or miraculous to Allah while simultaneously engaging in forbidden practices or false beliefs. The Prophet is commanded to expose the logical contradiction in their stance: if they truly acknowledge Allah's authority and wisdom, they cannot justify their use of sorcery and deceptive practices, which contradicts divine guidance. The rhetorical question challenges them to recognize the inconsistency between their words and their actions, serving as a form of intellectual refutation that forces them to confront their hypocrisy.

translation: Rather, We have brought them the truth, and indeed they are liars.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's clarity in revelation against those who deny it. Despite receiving clear divine guidance, the disbelievers persist in falsehood and rejection. The verse underscores the culpability of those who reject truth not due to lack of clarity, but due to their own willful denial and obstinacy. It serves as both a statement of fact about their condition and an implicit warning about the consequences of choosing falsehood over manifest truth.

translation: Allah has not taken any son, nor is there with Him any deity. If there were, each deity would have taken what it created, and some of them would have overcome others. Exalted is Allah above what they describe.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the logical impossibility and absurdity of polytheism by presenting a rational argument: if multiple gods existed, each would independently control their creations and vie for supremacy, resulting in cosmic chaos and conflict. The verse refutes idolatry by showing that such a scenario would be incompatible with the order and unity observable in creation, thereby establishing that true divinity requires absolute oneness and unchallenged sovereignty.

translation: Knower of the unseen and the seen; exalted then is He above what they associate [with Him]
interpretation: This verse establishes Allah's absolute knowledge of all that is hidden from human perception (the unseen realm of divine secrets, the future, and the inner realities) and all that is apparent and manifest (the visible creation and affairs of this world). The verse concludes by emphasizing Allah's transcendence above the polytheistic associations made with Him—whether through idolatry or attributing partners to His divinity. The juxtaposition of these divine attributes with the refutation of shirk demonstrates that only a Being with such comprehensive knowledge and supreme otherness can legitimately claim sole worship and obedience, thereby condemning the logical incoherence and unworthiness of polytheistic beliefs.

translation: Say: 'O my Lord! If You show me what they are promised...'
interpretation: This verse expresses the Prophet's willingness to submit to Allah's judgment and divine wisdom. The statement begins a conditional plea where the Prophet acknowledges that the fulfillment of promises lies solely in Allah's hands, and he is ready to accept whatever divine decree comes to pass regarding the threatened punishment of the deniers, demonstrating complete trust in Allah's timing and ultimate justice.

translation: My Lord, so do not place me among the wrongdoing people
interpretation: This supplication expresses the servant's profound concern about the consequences of wrongdoing and their sincere plea to God for protection from being counted among the unjust. The speaker recognizes that injustice is a grave spiritual condition that distances one from God's mercy, and seeks divine protection by requesting not to be grouped with those who commit oppression or transgress God's boundaries. This reflects the understanding that one's spiritual state and moral character are ultimately determined by God's will, and that seeking His aid against wickedness is the path to righteousness.

translation: And indeed, We are able to show you what We have promised them.
interpretation: This verse assures the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) of Allah's absolute power and capability to fulfill His promises regarding the punishment and consequences that await those who disbelieve and reject the message. It emphasizes divine omnipotence and serves as a source of consolation and certainty for the Prophet, affirming that despite opposition and disbelief from the people, Allah will inevitably demonstrate the reality of His warnings either in this world or the hereafter.

translation: Repel evil with that which is better. We are most knowing of what they describe.
interpretation: This verse instructs believers to respond to harmful behavior and insults with virtue and moral excellence rather than retaliation in kind. It teaches that the superior response to wrongdoing is to counter it with good character, patience, and kindness. The phrase 'We are most knowing of what they describe' affirms that Allah is fully aware of the accusations and evil descriptions the disbelievers attribute to the believers, and this awareness should provide comfort that divine justice will ultimately prevail, encouraging believers to maintain their moral superiority rather than engage in verbal or physical retaliation.

translation: And say: 'My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the whispers of the devils.'
interpretation: This verse instructs the believer to seek divine protection from the satanic suggestions and temptations that lead towards evil and sin. The phrase 'hamzat al-shayatin' (whispers of the devils) refers to the intrusive thoughts and insinuations that devils plant in the hearts of humans to divert them from righteousness. By teaching this supplication, the Qur'an acknowledges human vulnerability to spiritual harm and emphasizes that true security and protection come only through conscious reliance upon Allah's power and authority. This demonstrates the Islamic principle that while humans have moral agency and responsibility, ultimate protection and guidance are divine gifts that must be actively sought through sincere supplication.

translation: And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, from their presence.
interpretation: This phrase expresses a profound prayer for protection from the harmful influence and proximity of those who reject the message of faith. The speaker (traditionally understood as Prophet Solomon in its Quranic context) seeks divine refuge specifically from being brought into close association with disbelievers or those who oppose God's command, recognizing that such proximity could represent a trial or test to one's faith and steadfastness. The invocation emphasizes complete dependence upon God's protective power against spiritual and social contamination from those whose presence poses a threat to one's religious integrity.

translation: Until when death comes to one of them, he says: 'My Lord, send me back,"'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the profound regret and desperate plea of those who neglected their faith during their worldly life. When death arrives and the soul realizes the reality of the afterlife, it seeks a second chance to return and perform righteous deeds, but this request is denied because the opportunity for action has ended. The verse emphasizes that true repentance and reform must occur during one's lifetime, and that the moment of death marks an irreversible threshold where no amount of regret can change one's fate.

translation: Perhaps I may do righteous deeds in what I have left behind. No! It is merely a word he is saying. And before them is a barrier until the day they are resurrected.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the futility of worldly regret at the moment of death. The soul, upon departing, falsely hopes to return to perform good deeds, but this is merely an empty utterance with no reality or fulfillment. The barrier (barzakh) separates the deceased from the living world, making all worldly aspirations and intentions void. This teaches that the time for action is exclusively in this life, and death marks an absolute and irreversible severance from all opportunity to do good works. The dead cannot return, cannot act, and cannot change their state—only the living possess this precious ability.

translation: So when the Horn is blown, there will be no kinship between them that day, nor will they ask one another.
interpretation: This verse describes the ultimate dissolution of worldly bonds and relationships on the Day of Judgment. When the Trumpet is sounded to signal the resurrection, all familial ties and social connections that defined people's identities in this life will cease to have any significance. The phrase "they will not ask one another" indicates a state of complete detachment and preoccupation with one's own fate, where people will be so consumed with their personal reckoning before Allah that they will have neither concern for nor interest in their former loved ones. This underscores the complete separation of souls in the afterlife and the individual nature of accountability before Allah, emphasizing that no worldly relationship can provide intercession or comfort in that pivotal moment.

translation: So those whose scales are heavy - those are the ones who will be successful.
interpretation: This verse refers to the weighing of deeds on the Day of Judgment, where those whose good deeds outweigh their sins will achieve eternal success and enter Paradise. The 'heavy scales' symbolize a preponderance of righteous actions and obedience to Allah, indicating that true success in the hereafter depends on the weight and substance of one's deeds rather than their quantity alone.

translation: And those whose scales are light - those are the ones who have lost themselves, in Hell abiding eternally.
interpretation: This verse describes the final judgment when deeds are weighed. Those whose good deeds are insufficient (whose scales are light) are those who have squandered their souls by failing to prepare for the Hereafter, and they will consequently face eternal punishment in Hell. The phrase 'lost themselves' emphasizes that they have forfeited their spiritual essence and eternal salvation through their negligence or transgression during their worldly life.

translation: The Fire will sear their faces, and they therein will have grim facial expressions (grimacing).
interpretation: This verse depicts the agonizing punishment of the disbelievers in Hell, where the intense heat of the Fire will burn and disfigure their faces, causing them to contort their features in pain and distress. The description emphasizes both the physical torment and the loss of dignity that results from rejecting faith, as their faces—symbols of human identity and honor—become marred by divine punishment. This serves as a powerful warning about the severe consequences of disbelief.

translation: Were not My verses recited to you, and you used to deny them?
interpretation: This verse expresses God's reproach on the Day of Judgment to those who disbelieved, highlighting that they had received clear signs and the revelation of God's verses, yet they chose to reject and deny them despite having full knowledge and access to the truth. It emphasizes the accountability of those who turn away from divine guidance that has been clearly presented to them, and underscores that their rejection was not due to ignorance but to willful denial and turning away from the truth.

translation: They said, 'Our Lord, our wretchedness has overcome us, and we were a people astray,'
interpretation: This verse reveals the confession of those who will be held accountable in the afterlife, acknowledging their own spiritual failure and moral decline. Their admission that 'wretchedness' (misery/iniquity) overwhelmed them signifies their acceptance of personal responsibility for their state of misguidance, rather than blaming external circumstances. The phrase 'we were a people astray' indicates they recognize that their deviance was collective and habitual, suggesting that without divine guidance and their own earnest effort to seek it, humans are prone to profound spiritual loss. This represents a moment of reckoning where denial is abandoned and the reality of their choices becomes undeniable.

translation: Our Lord, bring us out of this. If we return [to evil], then indeed we will be wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse expresses a sincere supplication from those who recognize their sins and seek divine deliverance from a state of transgression. The speaker acknowledges personal responsibility for wrongdoing by pledging that returning to such evil would constitute injustice against themselves, thereby demonstrating genuine repentance and a commitment to reform. The conditional statement ('if we return') reveals both humility before God and a resolve to avoid repeating past mistakes, making this a prayer for spiritual transformation rather than mere escape from hardship.

translation: He said, 'Get out into it (the Fire), and do not speak to Me.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the divine judgment upon those who rejected God's message and persisted in disbelief. The command to 'get out into it' signifies the entry into hellfire as punishment, while 'do not speak to Me' emphasizes the severing of all communication and mercy from God, indicating a permanent state of separation and abandonment. This conveys that those who turn away from God's guidance in this life will face a condition where they can no longer appeal to God's mercy or intercede, highlighting the ultimate consequence of rejecting divine revelation and the finality of God's justice on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Indeed, a group from among My servants used to say, 'Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the characteristics of sincere believers who combine their faith with humility and supplication. They do not presume themselves to be free from sin or weakness, but rather acknowledge their need for divine forgiveness and mercy. Their statement "and You are the best of the merciful" reflects their recognition that true mercy and compassion belong solely to Allah, expressing both their conviction in His divine attributes and their trust that He will respond to their sincere plea. This verse teaches that faith must be paired with repentance and seeking forgiveness, recognizing one's dependence on Allah's grace rather than relying on one's own deeds alone.

translation: So you took them in mockery, until they made you forget My remembrance, and you used to laugh at them.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the spiritual danger of ridiculing believers and the divine message. When people engage in mocking the faithful, they become gradually desensitized to the call of God, eventually losing their connection to His remembrance entirely.
