interpretation: This verse expresses profound regret over a relationship that led one away from righteousness and toward destruction. It reflects the bitter realization that choosing the wrong companions and confidants can be spiritually fatal, illustrating how close associations with those who disbelieve or disobey Allah can drag a person into misguidance despite one's own initial beliefs, and serving as a stern warning about the critical importance of selecting one's companions wisely in matters of faith and moral conduct.

translation: Indeed, he led me astray from the remembrance after it had come to me. And ever has Satan been to man a deserter.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the fundamental human struggle against Satan's influence and the danger of negligence regarding divine guidance. The speaker acknowledges that Satan succeeded in making him forget the Qur'an and the remembrance of Allah despite having received it, emphasizing Satan's role as a malevolent force that abandons humans in times of need, leaving them to face the consequences of their deviation alone. The verse serves as a warning about the ease with which one can fall away from the right path if they do not actively maintain their connection to Allah's message and remain vigilant against Satan's whispers.

translation: And the Messenger said, 'O my Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as [something to be] abandoned.'
interpretation: This verse (25:30) expresses the Prophet Muhammad's deep distress and complaint to Allah about his people's rejection and abandonment of the Qur'an—not merely in terms of disbelief, but in their neglect of its guidance, reflection upon it, and living by its teachings. The phrase 'mahjooran' (abandoned) conveys a sense of active disregard and forsaking rather than mere ignorance. This lament illustrates the emotional burden the Prophet carried in his mission, highlighting the profound suffering of seeing the divine message, which he was commanded to deliver, rejected and neglected by those he sought to guide. It serves as a reminder of the responsibility incumbent upon believers to honor, study, and implement the Qur'an in their lives, and the gravity of abandoning or neglecting divine guidance.

translation: And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals. And sufficient is your Lord as a guide and helper.
interpretation: This verse indicates that opposition to prophets from wrongdoers and criminals is an established pattern throughout human history, not a unique occurrence. The second part assures the Prophet Muhammad that Allah alone is sufficient as his guide and supporter against all enemies, emphasizing divine protection and guidance as the ultimate source of strength for those who follow the path of the prophets.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, 'Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?' Thus [it is], so that We may strengthen your heart thereby, and We have recited it to you in slow, measured rhythmic tones.
interpretation: This verse addresses the wisdom behind the gradual revelation of the Qur'an over twenty-three years rather than all at once. The disbelievers' objection reflects their superficial understanding, but Allah reveals that this measured, piecemeal revelation served the profound purpose of establishing the Prophet's heart in conviction and providing him strength through repeated reinforcement and reflection. The deliberate, measured recitation allows for deeper comprehension, memorization, and spiritual attachment to the message, demonstrating that gradual revelation is not a deficiency but rather a pedagogical mercy tailored to human psychological and spiritual capacity.

translation: And they do not come to you with any example except that We bring you the truth and a better explanation.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the superiority of the Qur'an's guidance over the objections and arguments raised by disbelievers. Whenever they present a parable, comparison, or rhetorical challenge to dispute the message of the Prophet Muhammad, Allah assures him that He will provide a decisive response that is both truthful and more eloquent, clearer, and more convincing than their arguments. This reflects Allah's promise to support His messenger with clarity and wisdom in refuting falsehoods and establishing the truth.

translation: Those who are gathered upon their faces into Hell - those are in the worst place and most astray in [their] way.
interpretation: This verse describes the humiliating and disgraceful manner in which the disbelievers will be gathered on the Day of Judgment, dragged on their faces toward Hell. The phrase 'gathered upon their faces' signifies both the physical degradation and the spiritual wretchedness of their state, emphasizing that they have not only chosen the wrong path in life but have become so spiritually inverted that they cannot even walk upright toward their destination. This condition represents the ultimate consequence of turning away from divine guidance - they lose both their dignity in this world and the correct path (sabil) in the next, making their position the most miserable and their deviation the most complete.

translation: And indeed, We gave Moses the Scripture, and We made with him his brother Aaron as a minister (or assistant).
interpretation: This verse establishes the principle that spiritual and prophetic guidance is often strengthened through collaborative leadership and support. By pairing Moses with Aaron as his minister, Allah demonstrates that even the greatest messengers benefit from trusted companions who share their mission. This reflects the importance of mutual counsel, shared responsibility in conveying divine truth, and emotional support in bearing the burden of prophecy. The selection of Aaron—Moses' own brother—emphasizes that the best helpers are those bound by familial ties and shared commitment to God's cause.

translation: So We said: Go to the people who denied Our signs. Then We destroyed them with utter destruction.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine principle of accountability and justice - that those who persistently reject God's signs and warnings through His messengers are ultimately held responsible for their rejection. The verse emphasizes that rejection of divine guidance is not a matter treated lightly by God, but rather invokes a powerful divine response of complete annihilation, serving as both a punishment for the transgression and a warning to subsequent generations about the consequences of turning away from God's truth.

translation: And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them and made them a sign for mankind. And We have prepared for the wrongdoers a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates that those who persistently reject God's messengers face severe divine punishment, and their destruction becomes a warning and lesson for subsequent generations. The drowning of Noah's people exemplifies how rejection of truth leads to inevitable consequences, while the mention of prepared punishment for the wrongdoers emphasizes that defiance of God's guidance carries both immediate worldly consequences and eternal punishment in the Hereafter.

translation: And [We destroyed] 'Ad and Thamud and the people of the Rass, and many generations between them.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the pattern of divine justice throughout history by naming specific destroyed peoples ('Ad, Thamud, and the people of the Rass) and indicating that countless other communities were similarly punished between these events. The phrase 'generations between that many' serves to highlight both God's patience in giving multiple nations extended opportunities to repent, and His ultimate inevitability in punishing those who persist in disbelief and transgression. It demonstrates that destruction is not arbitrary but a consistent consequence of rejecting God's messages across different times and peoples.

translation: And for each We have presented parables, and each We have utterly destroyed.
interpretation: This verse reflects the pattern throughout history where Allah has sent messengers with clear signs and examples to guide nations, yet those who rejected them faced complete destruction. The 'parables' (amthal) refer to the lessons and proofs provided through previous messengers, while 'utterly destroyed' (tabarna) describes the inevitable fate of those who turned away from guidance. The verse emphasizes the divine justice in the cycle of warning, rejection, and destruction that has repeated throughout human history, serving as a warning to the community being addressed about the consequences of disbelief and the certainty of punishment for those who persist in rejecting Allah's message.

translation: And indeed, they passed by a city upon which had been rained upon with a rain of evil. Did they not see it? Rather, they were not expecting resurrection.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the consequence of divine punishment and how those who reject God's signs remain spiritually blind and indifferent. The city rained upon with evil punishment (referring to the people of Lot) serves as a clear warning visible to all who pass by, yet the disbelievers refuse to contemplate or learn from it. Their failure to recognize this sign is ultimately rooted in their denial of the afterlife and resurrection—without belief in divine accountability in the Hereafter, they lack the spiritual motivation to heed warnings and turn to God. The verse emphasizes that disbelief in resurrection breeds a recklessness and hardness of heart that prevents reflection upon God's judgment in this world.

translation: And when they see you, they take you not except in mockery, saying: 'Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the arrogant rejection and ridicule that the polytheists of Mecca directed towards the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) despite the clarity of his message. Their dismissive mockery reveals the hardness of their hearts and their refusal to acknowledge the truth, demonstrating how those who are spiritually blind and materially proud often respond to divine guidance with contempt rather than reflection. The rhetorical question they pose shows their inability to accept that someone of humble background could be chosen by Allah as His messenger, exposing how their own prejudices and worldly criteria blindly reject what contradicts their expectations.

translation: He had almost led us astray from our gods, had we not remained steadfast upon them. And they will soon know, when they see the punishment, who is more astray from the path.
interpretation: This verse reflects the arrogant defiance of the disbelievers in response to the Prophet's preaching of monotheism. Their statement reveals how they perceived the call to abandon idolatry as a threat to their inherited beliefs and identity. The phrase 'had we not remained steadfast' shows their false confidence in their own resolve, while the concluding warning 'they will soon know...when they see the punishment' emphasizes that their certainty is misplaced—divine punishment will ultimately expose the falsehood of their path and the truth of the monotheistic message they rejected. The verse underscores how human stubbornness and attachment to ancestral practices can blind people to truth, despite clear warnings.

translation: Have you seen the one who has taken his desire as his god? Then will you be a guardian over him?
interpretation: This verse highlights the spiritual blindness of those who surrender themselves entirely to their worldly desires and passions, treating them as their ultimate authority rather than submitting to Allah's guidance. The rhetorical question directed to the Prophet conveys that it is not his responsibility to forcibly guide those who have chosen to worship their own desires, as true guidance can only come to those who genuinely seek it and open their hearts to divine truth. This underscores the limits of human responsibility in matters of faith and the ultimate autonomy of individual choice.

translation: Or do you think that most of them hear or understand? They are not but like livestock. Rather, they are more astray in way.
interpretation: This verse critiques those who reject faith by comparing their spiritual condition to that of animals. Despite possessing the faculties of hearing and intellect, those who turn away from God's signs use these abilities only for worldly pursuits and material concerns, never applying them to understand divine truth. The comparison suggests that while animals follow their instincts naturally, these people deliberately misuse their reason, making them spiritually worse off—more lost and further from the path of guidance than creatures who have no capacity for understanding God's message.

translation: Have you not considered your Lord, how He extends the shadow? And if He had willed, He would have made it stationary. Then We made the sun upon it a guide.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates Allah's perfect control over creation and invites reflection on His power and wisdom. The extension of shadow throughout the day as the sun moves is presented as a sign of divine mastery - Allah could have frozen the shadow in place, but instead He made it dynamic and changeable. The sun serves as a guide that marks the passage of time and regulates human life and activity. This is a call to recognize the subtle yet constant signs of Allah's sovereignty in the natural world that we experience daily, encouraging the observer to move beyond mere passive existence toward active awareness and gratitude for these divine signs.

translation: Then We seized him to Us with an easy seizure.
interpretation: This verse describes the death of Yahya (John the Baptist) in a gentle and merciful manner. The phrase "easy seizure" (قبضا يسيرا) emphasizes that Allah took his life without suffering or hardship, as a sign of His mercy and honor toward this righteous servant. It suggests that his death was swift and painless, reflecting Allah's compassion for His beloved prophets and the believers who serve Him faithfully.

translation: And it is He who made the night a garment for you and sleep a rest, and made the day a rising up.
interpretation: This verse illustrates Allah's perfect design for human well-being through the natural rhythm of day and night. The night is described as a 'garment' (clothing) to emphasize how it covers and conceals, providing comfort and refuge from activity, while sleep is a 'rest' that restores the body and soul. The day is described as 'nushur' (rising, resurrection, spreading) to convey renewal of life, activity, and the unfolding of daily pursuits. The verse points to Allah's wisdom in creating complementary cycles that sustain human life—rest and activity, darkness and light—demonstrating Divine care for human nature and the fitrah (natural disposition) with which humans are created.

translation: And it is He who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy, and We send down from the sky pure water.
interpretation: This verse illustrates Allah's merciful and benevolent provision for creation. The winds that precede rain serve as messengers of hope, announcing the arrival of beneficial moisture and fertility to parched lands and weary people. By describing water as 'pure' (tahur), the verse emphasizes both its physical cleanliness and its spiritual significance as a purifying element. Together, the wind and rain represent a coordinated divine system of provision that sustains life, demonstrates Allah's careful planning for His creation's needs, and exemplifies how seemingly ordinary natural phenomena are actually manifestations of divine compassion and order working in perfect harmony.

translation: That with it We may give life to a dead land, and give drink thereof to cattle and many people whom We have created.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine wisdom in creating rain as a means of sustenance and revival. The interpretation emphasizes that Allah demonstrates His power and provision through the cycle of water bringing life to barren earth, which then sustains both animals and humans. It reflects the principle that God's creation serves interconnected purposes - the revival of land benefits both livestock and people - and highlights human dependence on divine provision, teaching recognition of God's merciful arrangement of the natural world for all His creation.

translation: And We have certainly varied it [the Qur'an] among them so that they may remember, but most people refuse to be anything except deniers of gratitude.
interpretation: This verse reflects upon human nature and the divine strategy in revelation. Despite Allah's intentional repetition and variation of themes throughout the Qur'an—presented in different contexts and with different emphases to facilitate understanding and remembrance—most people nonetheless turn away in ingratitude and disbelief. The verse emphasizes that the burden of rejecting the message does not lie with the clarity or sufficiency of the divine signs, but rather with the inherent human inclination toward obstinacy and thanklessness. This reveals a fundamental truth about spiritual responsibility: the failure to believe and remember is rooted in human choice and the hardening of hearts, not in any deficiency of the divine message itself.

translation: And if We had willed, We would have sent a warner in every town/village.
interpretation: This verse reflects Allah's supreme wisdom and sovereignty in choosing the method and recipients of divine guidance. Rather than sending a messenger to every community simultaneously, Allah exercised His will to send messengers strategically, distributing them according to His divine plan. This demonstrates that Allah's choice of which communities receive direct warning is deliberate and purposeful. The conditional statement "if We had willed" emphasizes that the distribution of prophets and messengers was not obligatory upon Allah, but rather an expression of His infinite wisdom. It suggests that Allah's way of guiding humanity through selective prophethood is part of a greater divine scheme that tests human reason and moral capacity to recognize and respond to signs of truth.

translation: So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with it (the Qur'an) a great striving.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet to maintain unwavering commitment to the message of the Qur'an despite opposition from those who reject it. The 'great striving' refers to spiritual and intellectual struggle through the Qur'an itself—using its truth, wisdom, and clarity to counter falsehood and misconceptions—rather than relying on force. It emphasizes that the primary weapon against disbelief is the transformative power of the divine word, and that steadfastness in preaching the message constitutes the greatest form of resistance against those who deny it.

translation: And it is He who has released the two seas, this one fresh and sweet, and this one salty and bitter, and He has made between them a barrier and a forbidden partition.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates Allah's absolute power and wisdom in maintaining the natural order of creation. The barrier between the fresh and salt waters, despite their proximity and constant interaction, serves as a sign of Allah's precise control over the universe. This separation is both physical and divinely ordained, illustrating that nothing occurs except by Allah's will. The juxtaposition of these waters—each distinct in taste and properties—reminds humanity of the careful balance Allah maintains in creation and His ability to preserve differences and boundaries despite forces that would naturally mix them, symbolizing how Allah sustains the world through divine wisdom rather than random chance.

translation: And it is He who created from water a human being and made him (related by) lineage and marriage alliance. And your Lord is ever Capable.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine wisdom in creating human beings from water and establishing among them bonds of kinship and marital relationships. These bonds form the foundation of human society and social order. By mentioning that He is all-Capable, the verse emphasizes that creating these complex social structures and maintaining the intricate web of human relationships is well within Allah's infinite power, and serves as a profound sign of His wisdom in organizing creation.

translation: And they worship besides Allah that which neither benefits them nor harms them. And the disbeliever was, against his Lord, an ally [to Satan].
interpretation: This verse condemns the futility and irrationality of idolatry. The disbelievers direct their devotion toward false deities that are powerless to grant good or prevent harm, yet they persist in this worship while turning away from Allah, the only true source of benefit and protection. The phrase 'the disbeliever was against his Lord an ally' suggests that in rejecting Allah's guidance, the disbeliever aligns himself with Satan's cause, making himself an assistant to those who work against the divine truth. The verse emphasizes that idolatry is not merely a theological error but represents an act of enmity toward Allah through the adoption of falsehood and the abandonment of genuine beneficial knowledge and obedience.

translation: And We did not send you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner.
interpretation: This verse establishes the fundamental purpose of the Prophet Muhammad's mission: to convey two complementary messages to humanity. The 'bringer of good tidings' (mubashshir) represents the promise of reward, mercy, and salvation for those who believe and obey, while the 'warner' (nadhir) represents the warning of punishment for those who reject and disobey. Together, these roles encompass the complete call to faith—combining hope and fear as motivational forces to guide people toward God's path. The verse emphasizes that the Prophet's role was exclusively to deliver this message with clarity, while the acceptance or rejection of the message ultimately rests with the people themselves.

translation: Say: 'I do not ask you for any reward for this, except that whoever wishes may take a path towards his Lord.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the Prophet's selfless mission, highlighting that he seeks no material compensation for delivering God's message. The conditional phrase 'except that whoever wishes' indicates that the only benefit the Prophet seeks is the spiritual guidance of those who choose to turn towards God. This establishes that true belief and righteous action are matters of sincere choice and free will, not coerced nor motivated by worldly incentives from the messenger.

translation: And rely upon the Living One who does not die, and exalt Him with His praise. And sufficient is He, of the sins of His servants, All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse teaches that true reliance (tawakkul) must be placed in Allah alone, the Eternal Living God who will never perish, unlike all other created beings. The command to glorify Him with praise (tasbih) is not merely an act of worship but an expression of recognition of His sovereignty and an essential component of spiritual trust. The final clause reveals that Allah's complete knowledge of the hidden sins and secrets of His servants - even those concealed from others - serves as a merciful reminder that He is perfectly aware of all circumstances and needs, making Him the only worthy recipient of our trust and dependence in all matters.

translation: The One who created the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne. The Most Merciful - so ask about Him one who is knowledgeable.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that all knowledge about Allah's attributes and actions should be sought from those who possess true understanding of His divine nature. By connecting the mention of Allah's creative power and sovereignty to the instruction to inquire from the knowledgeable, the Qur'an teaches that recognizing Allah's majesty as Creator naturally leads one to seek wisdom from those who comprehend His attributes, and that proper understanding of the divine must come through reliable sources of knowledge rather than speculation or ignorance.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Prostrate to the Most Merciful,' they say, 'What is the Most Merciful? Should we prostrate to what you command us?' And it increases them in aversion.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the arrogance and spiritual heedlessness of those who reject faith. Their question 'What is the Most Merciful?' expresses not genuine inquiry but defiant denial and mockery of God's names. Their refusal to prostrate represents their rejection of submission to divine authority, instead demanding rational justification on their own terms as if they can dictate the conditions of obedience. The verse teaches that opposition to divine guidance does not stem from intellectual confusion but from a willful hardness of heart—their rejection actually deepens their aversion to truth rather than bringing them closer to understanding.

translation: Blessed is He who has placed in the sky constellations and placed therein a lamp (the sun) and an illuminating moon.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's majesty and wisdom demonstrated through the creation of celestial bodies. The mention of 'blessed' at the outset establishes that recognizing and reflecting upon these created signs is itself an act of worship and glorification. The deliberate placement of stars, sun, and moon serves both practical purposes for humanity—such as timekeeping and navigation—and spiritual purposes, inviting contemplation of the Creator's power and precision. The description of the moon as 'illuminating' despite being a reflected light suggests that even secondary or derivative sources of illumination possess value and fulfill their designated role, reflecting a divine order where everything has its appointed place and function in the cosmos.

translation: And He is the One who made the night and the day in succession for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful.
interpretation: This verse indicates that Allah has ordained the alternation of night and day as a means and opportunity for human spiritual reflection and gratitude. The succession of these two states serves as a continuous reminder of God's power and wisdom, providing occasions for those who seek remembrance (dhikr) of Allah and those inclined toward gratitude to exercise these virtues. The verse emphasizes that recognition of divine blessings and acknowledgment of God's sovereignty are not merely abstract concepts but are facilitated through the tangible, observable patterns of creation that recur constantly in human experience.

translation: And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth humbly, and when the ignorant address them, they say 'Peace.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the spiritual nobility of those who are truly devoted to God. Their humility in demeanor—manifested in their humble gait—reflects an inner state of consciousness aware of their servitude before God and the insignificance of earthly pride. More profoundly, their response to provocation with 'Peace' (salam) demonstrates that their spiritual development has transcended the ego's natural impulse to defend itself or retaliate. This gracious restraint is not weakness but rather the strength of one whose identity is rooted in God rather than in the validation or aggression of others. By responding to ignorance with peace, they break the cycle of escalation and reflect the attributes of God's mercy, thereby embodying the very servitude they profess.

translation: And those who spend the night before their Lord in prostration and standing (in prayer)
interpretation: This verse describes the characteristic of devoted believers who dedicate their nights to worship Allah through prayer, combining both states of humility (prostration/sujud) and alertness (standing/qiyam). The verse emphasizes that true devotion involves both physical acts of worship and continuous remembrance of Allah, suggesting that such believers have transcended mere daytime obligations and willingly sacrifice their rest for spiritual communion with their Lord. This dedication reflects a heart that prioritizes the divine connection above worldly comfort and sleep.

translation: And those who say, 'Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell. Indeed, its punishment is ever a permanent affliction,'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the desperate urgency with which believers should seek refuge from Hell's torment. The word 'gharama' (permanent affliction) conveys not merely temporary suffering but an inescapable, clinging consequence that clings to the soul. The verse teaches that genuine fear of Hell combined with sincere supplication to Allah is an essential characteristic of the righteous, reflecting awareness of accountability and humility before divine justice. Such prayer demonstrates both recognition of human vulnerability and trust in Allah's mercy as the only refuge.

translation: Indeed, it (the Fire) is an evil place of settlement and abode.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the severe punishment and absolute wretchedness of Hell as an eternal dwelling place, highlighting both its physical torment and spiritual desolation. The use of two terms—'mustaqarr' (settlement/resting place) and 'maqam' (station/abode)—reinforces that Hell is not temporary but permanent, and leaves no refuge or comfort. The verse serves as a powerful warning to dissuade believers from actions that lead to Hell, stressing that those who end up there will find nothing but misery and despair in their final destination.

translation: And those who, when they spend, do not spend excessively and do not stint, but maintain between that a balance.
interpretation: This verse describes the character of the righteous believers by highlighting their balanced approach to wealth and spending. The verse teaches that true piety lies in the middle path between two extremes: excessive spending (israf) that wastes resources and denies oneself necessities, and stinginess or deprivation (iqtaar) that causes hardship and prevents meeting genuine needs and obligations. This moderation represents wisdom in financial matters, reflecting trust in Allah's provision while exercising responsible stewardship of the resources He has granted, and demonstrates that virtue is found in following a measured, just course in all material dealings.

translation: And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity, and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except in right, and do not commit adultery; and whoever does that will meet a punishment.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the severity of three major sins—associating partners with Allah, unlawful killing, and adultery—by listing them together as grave transgressions that carry divine punishment. The placement of these sins alongside the consequence of facing torment underscores that they represent fundamental violations of the covenant between humanity and God, requiring conscious avoidance and repentance.

translation: The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein in disgrace.
interpretation: This verse refers to those who commit grave sins, particularly shirk (associating partners with Allah) or rejecting faith after knowledge. The doubling of punishment reflects that such individuals face consequences not only for their original transgression but also for their deliberate rejection of truth and warning. The emphasis on humiliation (mihanan) indicates that their punishment encompasses both physical torment and the psychological shame of being exposed before all of creation, permanently stripped of dignity. This underscores the severity with which Allah regards willful disobedience and the compounding nature of sin when it involves conscious rejection of divine guidance.

translation: Except for those who repent and believe and do righteous deeds - for those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse teaches that sincere repentance coupled with faith and righteous action is a transformative path that does not merely erase sins, but converts them into virtues. The replacement of evil deeds with good ones suggests that the regret and struggle against past wrongdoing becomes itself a source of spiritual elevation and moral rectification, demonstrating that Allah's mercy encompasses complete transformation for the truly repentant believer.

translation: And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, then indeed he turns to Allah in repentance, a good return.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that true repentance is not merely an expression of regret, but must be accompanied by righteous action as evidence of sincere transformation. The phrase 'good return' (matāba) suggests that Allah accepts and welcomes back those who genuinely turn to Him through both reformed intentions and reformed conduct, offering them a path of redemption and restored relationship with their Creator.

translation: And those who do not bear witness to falsehood, and when they pass by frivolity, they pass by with dignity
interpretation: This verse describes the moral character of believers who actively avoid participating in or endorsing falsehood and vain speech. Rather than merely abstaining passively, they conduct themselves with noble dignity and honor when encountering such things, demonstrating that true faith manifests not just in what one rejects, but in the gracious and dignified manner in which one conducts oneself in relation to the world's temptations and frivolities.

translation: And those who, when reminded of the verses of their Lord, do not fall upon them deaf and blind.
interpretation: This verse describes the quality of the believers—they remain receptive and responsive to Allah's signs and guidance. The phrase 'do not fall deaf and blind' is a figure of speech indicating they do not stubbornly reject or ignore the divine revelation through willful ignorance. Rather, they maintain spiritual awareness and intellectual openness, allowing the verses to penetrate their hearts and influence their understanding. This contrasts with those who deliberately turn away from divine guidance despite being reminded of it, suggesting that true faith requires conscious, active engagement with Allah's message rather than passive indifference or deliberate heedlessness.

translation: And those who say, 'Our Lord, grant us from our wives and our offspring the comfort of our eyes, and make us leaders of the pious,'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the character of righteous believers who extend their supplications beyond personal salvation to include their families and their spiritual role in society. By asking for their loved ones to be sources of joy and seeking to become exemplars of piety for others, they demonstrate that true faith encompasses both private devotion and public moral responsibility, recognizing that their righteousness has an obligation toward guiding others to God.

translation: Those are the ones who will be recompensed with the highest abode (al-Ghurfah) because they were patient, and they will be greeted therein with greetings and peace.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the reward structure of Paradise, where steadfastness and patience in faith become the currency of eternal honor. The 'highest abode' represents not merely a place but a station of proximity and honor in the Divine presence, while the continual greetings and peace signify the complete absence of conflict and the abundance of spiritual tranquility—suggesting that virtue in this world establishes one's spiritual rank in the next, and that the reward is not merely material but rooted in the establishment of perfect peace and recognition before all creation.

translation: Abiding therein eternally. Excellent it is as an abode and a place of settlement.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the permanence and excellence of Paradise as an eternal dwelling place for the believers. The word 'خالدين' (abiding/remaining) stresses the everlasting nature of their residence, while the subsequent description highlights that Paradise is not merely a temporary reward but the most beautiful and perfect place to dwell, combining both comfort (مستقرا) and stability (ومقاما), suggesting that believers will find complete contentment, security, and fulfillment in their eternal home with no cause for concern about loss or transience.

translation: Say: 'My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication. But you have denied (the truth), so a punishment will necessarily befall you.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that human worthiness in the sight of Allah is contingent upon sincere supplication and obedience to His revelation. The denial of Allah's message severs the relationship between humanity and their Creator, making divine punishment an inevitable consequence. The verse teaches that those who reject faith and refuse to call upon Allah for guidance have forfeited His mercy, and thus suffering becomes their due course. It conveys that worship and invocation are not merely acts of ritual, but expressions of dependency on Allah that acknowledge His absolute authority and sustain the bond between the servant and the Lord.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Ta-Seen-Meem.
interpretation: These are among the Quranic initials (al-huruf al-muqatta'at) whose precise meaning is known only to Allah, serving to emphasize the miraculous nature of the Qur'an and drawing attention to its divine origin, as these letters challenge the Arabs to produce something similar despite their mastery of language.

translation: Those are the verses of the clear Book.
interpretation: This phrase introduces and affirms the divine verses that follow, emphasizing that the Qur'an is a clarified and manifest scripture whose signs are luminous and unambiguous, serving as clear guidance for those who seek understanding and truth.

translation: Perhaps you are destroying yourself with grief because they do not believe.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad's emotional distress over the disbelief of his people, reminding him not to exhaust himself with sorrow over their rejection of the message. It emphasizes that the Prophet's responsibility is to convey the message clearly, while belief ultimately rests with Allah's will, not with the Prophet's efforts or emotional investment. This teaches the fundamental principle that a messenger cannot force people to believe, and excessive grief over rejection contradicts trust in Allah's divine plan and wisdom.

translation: If We willed, We could send down to them from the sky a sign, so their necks would remain bent in submission to it.
interpretation: This verse illustrates that God has the power to compel human submission through miraculous signs from the heavens, which would make people's resistance impossible and their submission inevitable. However, the verse suggests that God does not choose this path, implying that true faith and moral choice require human free will and voluntary submission rather than coercion, and that the absence of such overwhelming miracles tests humanity's capacity to believe based on the signs already provided and on their own reasoning and moral conscience.

translation: And there comes to them no reminder from the Most Merciful except that they turn away from it.
interpretation: This verse describes the hardened stance of those who persistently reject divine guidance. Despite receiving reminders from Allah through revelation and messengers, their response is consistent avoidance and turning away. The use of 'no reminder' combined with 'except that they turn away' emphasizes the comprehensiveness and inevitability of their rejection—it is not a matter of missing or misunderstanding the message, but rather an active, habitual choice to ignore it. This reflects the spiritual reality of those whose hearts have been sealed by their own continuous disbelief and obstinacy.

translation: So they have denied, and soon there will come to them the news of what they used to mock.
interpretation: This verse warns the deniers that their rejection and mockery of the truth will inevitably result in their confrontation with the consequences of their disbelief. The phrase 'news of what they used to mock' refers to the actual manifestation or arrival of the punishment and reality of what they ridiculed, emphasizing that divine justice is certain and inescapable, and that their arrogance in dismissing the message will be met with undeniable proof of its truth when they witness its consequences.

translation: Have they not observed the earth - how much We have produced therein of every noble pair (of plants)?
interpretation: This verse invites reflection upon the diversity and abundance of vegetation on earth as a sign of God's creative power and providence. The phrase 'every noble pair' refers to different types of plants that reproduce in pairs (male and female characteristics), each fulfilling its ordained purpose. The verse functions as an appeal to human reason and observation of the natural world, suggesting that such organized abundance and variety could only come from a wise Creator, and should inspire recognition of God's majesty and gratitude for His provisions.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.
interpretation: This verse highlights the contrast between the clarity of divine signs and human rejection of truth. Despite Allah presenting unmistakable evidence of His power and wisdom, the majority of people turn away due to stubbornness, heedlessness, or deliberate denial. The verse emphasizes that faith is not merely a matter of intellectual recognition of signs, but requires sincere hearts willing to submit to God's guidance. The pattern reflects how evidence alone cannot compel belief—only those whom Allah wills to believe will truly accept the truth, while others remain in denial regardless of the clarity of the signs presented to them.

translation: And indeed, your Lord, He is the Mighty, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse affirms that despite God's absolute power and might to punish wrongdoing, He is simultaneously characterized by mercy and compassion. The pairing of these two divine attributes (العزيز - the Mighty and الرحيم - the Merciful) conveys that God's justice is tempered with grace, and that His strength is exercised with clemency toward His creation. This balance reassures believers that while God is all-powerful and cannot be overcome, His justice is always accompanied by mercy for those who turn to Him.

translation: And when your Lord called Moses, saying: Come to the people who are wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse marks the beginning of Moses' divine commission, where Allah addresses him directly with a command to go to Pharaoh's people. The designation of them as 'the wrongdoers' (al-zalimeen) establishes the moral and spiritual condition of those Moses is being sent to, setting up the context for his prophetic mission of calling them to justice and monotheism. This direct address emphasizes the solemnity and importance of the task being assigned to Moses and the gravity of the people's transgression.

translation: The people of Pharaoh. Do they not fear?
interpretation: This verse expresses divine exasperation at the persistent disobedience and ingratitude of Pharaoh's people despite witnessing clear signs and miracles. The rhetorical question 'Do they not fear?' challenges their lack of God-consciousness and moral accountability, highlighting how the human capacity for denial and heedlessness can persist even in the face of overwhelming evidence. The verse serves as a moral indictment of those who choose worldly attachments and the influence of corrupt leadership over submission to God.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, indeed I fear that they will deny me.'
interpretation: This verse expresses the prophet's deep anxiety about his message's reception. The speaker acknowledges human nature's resistance to divine guidance and demonstrates reliance on God through supplication. The fear expressed here is not a lack of faith in God's power, but rather a realistic awareness of the burden of prophethood—that conveying God's message to those inclined toward disbelief is an immense responsibility that requires divine assistance to bear.

translation: And my chest is straitened and my tongue does not speak fluently, so send to Aaron
interpretation: This verse reflects the human experience of anxiety and self-doubt when facing a momentous task. Prophet Moses is expressing his genuine fear and inadequacy before being sent to confront Pharaoh, teaching us that even the greatest prophets experienced vulnerability and legitimate concern about their abilities. His request for Aaron's support demonstrates the wisdom of seeking help from those better suited for certain roles, and establishes that acknowledging our limitations and seeking assistance is not a sign of weakness but of prudent judgment and reliance on divine provision of means.

translation: And they have against me a crime (or grudge), so I fear that they will kill me.
interpretation: This verse reflects the speaker's awareness of past wrongs or crimes they have committed against others, which has created enmity and a threat to their life. The interpretation emphasizes the natural human consequence of wrongdoing—that evil deeds create lasting grievances that endanger the perpetrator, and this fear is a form of divine justice where one reaps the consequences of their own actions. The verse illustrates the principle that those who wrong others should rightfully fear retribution, and this fear serves as a deterrent against committing further injustices.

translation: He said, "No, go forth with Our signs. Indeed, We are with you, listening."
interpretation: This verse demonstrates Allah's confirmation and encouragement to His messengers (Moses and Aaron) despite Pharaoh's rejection. The phrase "No" is a rejection of Pharaoh's excuses and objections, while "go forth with Our signs" emphasizes that the messengers should proceed with confidence in their divine mission. The statement "Indeed, We are with you, listening" conveys Allah's intimate presence and support—He is aware of all that transpires, hears every word spoken, and will vindicate His messengers. This assurance serves to strengthen the faith of the messengers and remind them that they are never truly alone in their struggle against tyranny, as Allah's omniscience and divine assistance accompanies them throughout their mission.

translation: So they came to Pharaoh and said, 'Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the moment when Moses and Aaron approach Pharaoh with their divine mission. The phrase 'messengers of the Lord of the worlds' emphasizes that their authority and message come from God alone, not from any earthly power, establishing the fundamental contrast between divine truth and earthly tyranny. By identifying themselves as messengers of the Lord of all creation rather than merely as individuals making claims, they are asserting the universal and absolute nature of their mission, which transcends Pharaoh's limited earthly dominion.

translation: That you send with us the Children of Israel
interpretation: This phrase reflects the plea of Moses to Pharaoh to release the Israelites from bondage, emphasizing the divine command to liberate an oppressed people so they may worship Allah freely and establish their own community. The repetition of requests throughout the Qur'an illustrates both the persistence of prophetic mission and the resistance of those in power to justice and divine guidance.

translation: She said, 'Did we not raise you among us as a child? And you remained with us for years of your life.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the power of gratitude as a tool for moral persuasion. Pharaoh's wife appeals to Moses' sense of obligation and emotional connection to the household that nurtured him, attempting to soften his resolve against her husband through reminding him of past kindness. Her words reveal how human bonds and personal history can be weaponized in argument, yet the verse implicitly teaches that true loyalty must ultimately transcend personal debt when it conflicts with divine truth and justice.

translation: And you did that deed of yours which you did, while you were of the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse refers to Moses' killing of the Coptic man in Egypt before his prophethood, addressing a moment when he acted out of rage and personal judgment without divine guidance. The phrase 'while you were of the disbelievers' does not mean Moses was a disbeliever in God's existence, but rather that he was unaware of divine wisdom and acting without submission to God's plan, highlighting the spiritual immaturity of his youth before receiving revelation and the importance of patience and reliance upon Allah's guidance rather than human impulse.

translation: He said, 'I did it while I was among those who were astray.'
interpretation: This statement reflects the speaker's acknowledgment of their action and admission that they committed it during a state of spiritual blindness and ignorance, taking responsibility for their deed while also recognizing that they were not yet guided or conscious of the gravity of their transgression at that moment.

translation: So I fled from you when I feared you, and my Lord granted me wisdom and made me one of the messengers.
interpretation: This verse reflects Moses' acknowledgment of his flight from Egypt after killing the Egyptian. The verse emphasizes that divine protection and guidance followed his righteous action taken in fear of persecution. By stating that God granted him wisdom and appointed him as a messenger after this incident, the Qur'an teaches that sincere believers who flee oppression and wrongdoing, even when fearful, will be elevated by God and given greater responsibility and insight into divine truth. The verse demonstrates that apparent retreat from injustice is actually a means through which God prepares His prophets for their greater mission.

translation: And this is a favor you mention upon me - that you have enslaved the Children of Israel
interpretation: This verse captures Pharaoh's twisted perception of his own power and authority. He is sarcastically or delusionally crediting Moses with reminding him of what he considers his greatest achievement - the enslavement of the Israelites. The phrase highlights how despotic rulers distort reality, viewing oppression and domination as accomplishments worthy of pride rather than recognizing them as moral evils. It demonstrates the spiritual blindness and arrogance that comes from unchecked power, where the enslaver views his dominion over others not as a crime but as something to be celebrated.

translation: Pharaoh said, 'And what is the Lord of the worlds?'
interpretation: Pharaoh's question reflects his arrogant rejection and dismissal of God's existence and authority. By asking 'what is the Lord of the worlds' with contempt, he denies God's reality and power, revealing his spiritual blindness and his determination to maintain his position of absolute authority by refusing to acknowledge a power greater than himself. His question is not a genuine inquiry but an expression of defiance and disbelief.

translation: He said: 'Lord of the heavens and the earth and all that is between them, if you are certain (in faith).'
interpretation: This verse represents a profound affirmation of monotheistic belief, where the speaker (typically understood to be Abraham in Qur'anic context) invokes the majesty and completeness of God's dominion over all creation as the foundation of certainty in faith. By invoking God as the Lord of the heavens, earth, and everything between them—encompassing all existence—the verse emphasizes that true faith (yaqin) must be grounded in recognition of God's absolute sovereignty and power over the entire cosmos, suggesting that certainty in belief requires acknowledging the all-encompassing nature of God's dominion rather than relying on incomplete knowledge or partial conviction.

translation: He said to those around him, 'Do you not listen?'
interpretation: This verse captures a moment of exhortation or remonstrance, where the speaker addresses his immediate circle with urgency, calling them to pay attention to what he is communicating. The rhetorical question format ('ala tatasmiunun) emphasizes the importance and gravity of the message, suggesting that those addressed have been inattentive or negligent in listening. The speaker seeks to awaken their awareness and draw them into active engagement with what is being conveyed, implying that what follows is significant and demands their full attention.

translation: Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers said.
interpretation: This phrase establishes the absolute authority and continuity of God's lordship across all generations. By invoking both the Lord of the present audience and their ancestors, the verse emphasizes the timeless nature of God's sovereignty and His unwavering guidance throughout human history, reminding believers that they are part of an unbroken chain of monotheistic faith that extends back to the earliest generations of humanity.

translation: He said, 'Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the accusation made by the disbelievers against the Prophet Muhammad, attributing his message to madness rather than accepting it as divine revelation. This interpretation demonstrates how those who reject God's signs resort to dismissing the messenger's sanity as a means to avoid confronting the truth of the message itself, representing a common psychological defense mechanism against cognitive dissonance when faced with a call that challenges one's beliefs and way of life.

translation: He said, 'Lord of the East and the West and all that is between them, if only you would use reason.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute dominion over all creation and the spatial dimensions of existence, serving as a rhetorical assertion meant to awaken the intellect of those who hear it. By invoking Allah's sovereignty over the entire cosmos, the speaker appeals to reason itself as the faculty by which humans should recognize and acknowledge Divine oneness, suggesting that rational reflection on the vastness and order of creation naturally leads to belief in one Creator. The phrase 'if only you would use reason' is not a question but an exhortation, expressing the speaker's wish that the listeners would employ their God-given intellect to perceive the obvious truth of monotheism.

translation: He said, 'If you take a god other than Me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned.'
interpretation: This verse represents Allah's statement to humanity, emphasizing His absolute oneness and the severe consequences of associating partners with Him. The threat of imprisonment is not merely physical confinement but represents spiritual and existential punishment—a warning that those who reject monotheism and worship other than Allah will be trapped in deprivation, darkness, and separation from divine grace. The verse underscores the fundamental Islamic principle of Tawhid (monotheism) as the ultimate standard by which divine reward and punishment are measured.

translation: He said, 'But if I bring you a clear sign?'
interpretation: This verse represents Musa (Moses) offering to provide clear evidence or proof to Pharaoh, appealing to Pharaoh's sense of reason and the possibility of recognizing divine truth through unmistakable signs. It demonstrates Musa's strategy of attempting to convince Pharaoh through logical persuasion and observable miracles, rather than through compulsion, highlighting the principle that belief should be based on evidence that the intellect can perceive and verify.

translation: He said, 'Bring it if you are of the truthful ones.'
interpretation: This verse represents a challenge or demand for proof. When someone claims to possess truth or knowledge, they are being asked to demonstrate or substantiate their claim with concrete evidence. The phrase emphasizes that truthfulness must be backed by action and proof, not merely by assertion, highlighting the principle that claims require validation and that truth should be verifiable rather than simply professed.

translation: So he cast down his staff, and thereupon it became a serpent, manifest.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the first miraculous sign given to Moses by Allah to establish his credibility as a messenger. The transformation of an ordinary staff into a living serpent was designed to demonstrate Divine power and serve as proof of Moses's prophethood to both Pharaoh and the people of Egypt. The word 'manifest' (mubeen) emphasizes the clarity and undeniability of the miracle, allowing no room for doubt about its supernatural nature.

translation: And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white for all those who looked upon it.
interpretation: This verse refers to one of the miracles given to Prophet Moses, where when he drew his hand from his bosom, it became radiant white—a sign of divine power and proof of his prophethood. The whiteness was not from disease or leprosy, but rather a luminous brightness visible to all observers, serving as a manifest sign to convince Pharaoh and his people of Moses's divine mission. This miracle represents God's intervention to support His messenger and authenticate his claim, demonstrating that extraordinary phenomena can occur through God's will to establish faith and guide people toward the truth.

translation: He said to the assembly around him: 'Indeed, this is a learned sorcerer.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the arrogant dismissal of a message of truth by those in power who resort to character assassination rather than genuine engagement with the message. By labeling the messenger as a 'learned sorcerer,' the speaker attempts to discredit him through linguistic manipulation and social prejudice, revealing how those threatened by truth often respond with accusation and ridicule rather than rational debate.

translation: He wants to drive you out of your land by his magic. So what do you command?
interpretation: This verse reflects the Egyptians' fear and conspiracy against Prophet Moses, viewing his miracles as magic and expressing their anxiety about losing their land and power. Their question to Pharaoh reveals how desperation and prejudice can cause people to misinterpret divine signs, choosing instead to follow their leader's false narrative rather than acknowledging the truth before them.

translation: They said, 'Give him and his brother respite, and send in the cities gatherers (to collect people).'
interpretation: This verse reflects Pharaoh's arrogant response to Moses and Aaron's call to monotheism. Rather than heeding their message, Pharaoh's officials attempt to delay and dismiss them while organizing a systematic campaign to gather support and suppress their preaching. The verse demonstrates how those in power often respond to divine guidance with procrastination and coordinated resistance, seeking to consolidate their authority through collective action rather than genuine reflection on the truth presented to them.

translation: They come to you with every eloquent magician/deceiver
interpretation: This verse describes how the disbelievers persistently brought forth their most skilled and learned opponents to argue against the Prophet Muhammad, seeking to undermine his message through sophisticated rhetoric and clever argumentation. The verse emphasizes the relentless and organized nature of their opposition, as they continuously produced their most articulate and knowledgeable speakers, yet their efforts were ultimately futile against the truth of the Qur'an. This reflects the pattern of human resistance to divine guidance through intellectual arrogance and the deployment of rhetorical skill in service of falsehood.

translation: So the magicians were gathered at an appointed time on a known day.
interpretation: This verse describes Pharaoh's deliberate assembly of the most skilled magicians in Egypt at a predetermined time to confront Moses. The emphasis on 'known day' and 'appointed time' suggests Pharaoh's strategic planning and confidence in his magicians' ability to overcome the miraculous signs of Moses, reflecting the worldly preparation and coordination of those who rely on deception and false powers rather than truth.

translation: And it will be said to the people: 'Are you gathered together?'
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene from the Day of Judgment when all of humanity will be assembled before Allah. The rhetorical question serves to make the people aware of their complete gathering and the reality of the resurrection, emphasizing the certainty and inevitability of this divine gathering on the Day of Reckoning. It is designed to awaken consciousness of accountability and the gravity of standing before Allah with all of mankind.

translation: Perhaps we may follow the magicians if they are the ones who prevail.
interpretation: This verse reveals the conditional and opportunistic faith of those who witnessed Pharaoh's initial confidence. Their statement demonstrates how some people base their belief and allegiance not on truth and conviction, but on perceived power and worldly success. It exposes the weakness of human judgment when guided by material circumstances rather than spiritual discernment, serving as a warning against conforming beliefs to the majority or the powerful merely for security or advantage.

translation: So when the sorcerers came, they said to Pharaoh, 'Will there be a reward for us if we are the ones who prevail?'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the mercenary nature of those who oppose truth - the sorcerers approached the conflict with Moses not out of principle or loyalty, but with their eyes fixed on material compensation. Their immediate demand for a reward reveals that they had no conviction in Pharaoh's cause and viewed the confrontation as a transaction rather than a matter of righteousness, exposing how those who fight against divine truth are often motivated purely by worldly gain and personal interest rather than genuine belief.

translation: He said: 'Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near [to Allah].'
interpretation: This verse represents Allah's promise to His righteous servants of elevated status and proximity to Him in the afterlife. The affirmation 'yes' indicates Allah's confirmation of a preceding request or hope, and 'those brought near' (al-muqarrabun) refers to those closest to Allah's mercy and favor - the highest rank among the honored ones in Paradise. This reflects the Qur'anic theme that sincere devotion and obedience to Allah result not merely in entry to Paradise, but in a special nearness and intimacy with their Lord.

translation: Moses said to them, 'Cast down what you are going to cast.'
interpretation: This verse reflects Moses's confidence in Allah's power and his challenge to the magicians of Pharaoh. By telling them to cast their ropes and staffs first, Moses demonstrates his unwavering faith that the miracle Allah will perform through his staff will be greater than any magic they can produce. This statement also serves as a psychological assertion of authority, placing the burden on the magicians to act first while he awaits Allah's command, thereby establishing the superiority of divine truth over human deception.

translation: So they cast down their ropes and their staffs and said, 'By the might of Pharaoh, indeed we are the victorious ones.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the arrogance and false confidence of the magicians who relied on their perceived power and Pharaoh's authority rather than on truth. Their boastful declaration of victory before the challenge even began reveals the spiritual blindness that accompanies reliance on worldly power and status over divine guidance. Their confident assertion serves as a prelude to their humiliating defeat, teaching that false confidence rooted in material means and secular authority is ultimately futile against the truth of Allah.

translation: So Moses cast down his staff, and thereupon it swallowed up all that they had fabricated.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the miraculous power given to Moses as a sign from Allah, demonstrating his superiority over the magicians of Pharaoh's court. The staff consuming their false illusions symbolizes the triumph of divine truth over human deception and artifice. It emphasizes that genuine divine miracles are qualitatively different from and overwhelm mere human tricks, establishing Moses's credibility as a messenger and shaking the foundation of the magicians' claims to supernatural power.

translation: So the magicians fell down in prostration
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment when the magicians, after witnessing the miracle of Moses' staff becoming a snake, immediately recognized the truth of his message and submitted to Allah in prostration. Their swift surrender demonstrates that sincere recognition of divine truth compels the soul toward submission, transcending ego and professional pride. The act of prostration symbolizes the magicians' complete submission to Allah's authority and their acknowledgment that what they witnessed was beyond human capability, representing a transformation from arrogance to humility before divine power.

translation: They said: 'We have believed in the Lord of all worlds'
interpretation: This statement represents a declaration of faith and submission to Allah as the sole Lord and Creator of all creation. The phrase emphasizes the universality of God's dominion and authority over everything that exists, and the speakers' acknowledgment of His unique lordship without partners. This affirmation signifies their acceptance of monotheistic faith and their rejection of polytheism.

translation: Lord of Moses and Aaron
interpretation: This phrase refers to Allah as the sustainer and master of both Moses and Aaron, emphasizing His supreme authority over these two prophets who were chosen to lead the Children of Israel. It affirms the monotheistic relationship between Allah and His messengers, establishing that despite their elevated status as prophets, Moses and Aaron were servants entirely dependent upon Allah's will and guidance.

translation: He said, 'Have you believed in him before I gave you permission? Indeed, he is your greatest [one] who taught you magic. So you will soon know. I will surely cut off your hands and feet from opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you all.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates Pharaoh's response to his magicians' conversion to belief in Allah after witnessing Moses' miracle. The interpretation highlights how tyrannical rulers respond to those who reject their authority in favor of divine truth: through threats, punishment, and attempts to intimidate believers into submission. Pharaoh's emphasis on 'your greatest' and his question about permission before belief reveals his expectation of absolute obedience and control over his people's faith, and his severe punishment threats reflect the desperation of those whose power is threatened by the truth of monotheism.

translation: They said, 'There is no harm. Indeed, we will be returned to our Lord.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the steadfast faith and resignation to divine will of the believers in the face of trials. The phrase 'no harm' indicates that whatever loss or suffering they experience in this worldly life is inconsequential compared to their ultimate return to Allah and the eternal life to come. It demonstrates a perspective where earthly afflictions are viewed as temporary and insignificant when weighed against accountability before God and the promise of the Hereafter. The speakers prioritize their relationship with Allah over material concerns, showing that true believers measure harm and benefit by standards of faith rather than worldly loss alone.

translation: Indeed, we hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins because we were among the first believers.
interpretation: This verse expresses the believers' humble aspiration for divine forgiveness based on their virtue of being among the first to embrace faith. It teaches that early acceptance of God's message and sincere belief are grounds for seeking His mercy, while emphasizing the believers' awareness of their own shortcomings and their reliance on God's compassion rather than presumption of forgiveness. The verse illustrates the balance between recognizing one's spiritual merit and maintaining humility before God's ultimate judgment.

translation: And We revealed to Moses, 'Travel by night with My servants. Indeed, you will be pursued.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's direct communication with His prophets and reflects divine protection and foresight. God commands Moses to depart secretly at night, indicating that while the believers are in danger from Pharaoh's forces, they are not abandoned—God provides both the instruction and the assurance of knowledge about future events. The command carries both urgency and assurance, teaching that divine guidance often comes precisely when circumstances seem most dire, and that obedience to God's specific instructions at critical moments is the path to salvation.

translation: So Pharaoh sent among the cities those who would gather/conscript (people).
interpretation: This verse demonstrates Pharaoh's characteristic response to crises—to rely on governmental authority and coercion rather than justice or understanding. By sending out gatherers throughout the cities, Pharaoh attempts to assert control and mobilize resources through force, reflecting his pride and reliance on earthly power. This reveals how tyrannical rulers respond to challenges by expanding their oppressive machinery, and it sets the stage for the consequences that inevitably follow such resistance to truth. The verse illustrates the theme that power and authority divorced from righteousness lead to futile and ultimately self-destructive actions.

translation: Indeed, these are but a small group [of people].
interpretation: This verse reflects the perspective of the disbelievers who arrogantly dismissed the believers as insignificant in number and power. The word 'shirdhima' (شرذمة) carries connotations of a small, contemptible, or scattered group. This dismissal of the believers as numerically insignificant is presented to show the pride and delusion of those who trust in their material strength and numbers while failing to recognize the true power that comes from faith in Allah. The verse serves as a reminder that worldly assessments of significance based on numbers and wealth are superficial, and that what matters is the strength of conviction and adherence to divine guidance.

translation: And indeed, they are certainly a source of anger to us
interpretation: This phrase expresses the emotional response of frustration and provocation felt toward a group of people. The use of 'lغائظون' (source of anger/provocation) conveys not merely displeasure but a deliberate and intentional irritation, suggesting that the actions or presence of these people are designed to or inherently serve to test one's patience and resolve. The emphatic construction with 'إنهم' and the emphatic 'ل' reinforces the certainty of this aggravating effect, indicating that this provocation is unavoidable and real, often used to emphasize the severity of a challenge or trial one must endure with steadfastness.

translation: And indeed, we are all cautious/vigilant against it.
interpretation: This verse expresses collective vigilance and readiness to guard against something previously mentioned in context (typically falsehood, harm, or divine punishment). It emphasizes the shared responsibility and awareness among a group to protect themselves through cautious observation and preparedness, reflecting the Islamic principle that believers should maintain spiritual and practical vigilance against spiritual and worldly dangers.

translation: So We brought them out from gardens and springs of water
interpretation: This verse refers to Allah's removal of the disbelieving people from the blessings and comforts of their earthly possessions and fertile lands as a consequence of their rejection of the signs and ingratitude, demonstrating that worldly abundance and material prosperity are conditional blessings that can be withdrawn by Allah as a form of punishment for those who turn away from His guidance.

translation: And treasures and a noble position
interpretation: This phrase refers to the spiritual and material blessings that accompany prophethood and divine favor. The 'treasures' symbolize the abundance of blessings and knowledge from God, while the 'noble position' represents the elevated status and honor granted by Allah to His chosen servants, particularly prophets. Together, these blessings reflect the comprehensive nature of divine grace which encompasses both material provisions and elevated spiritual rank among creation.

translation: Thus We caused the Children of Israel to inherit it.
interpretation: This verse refers to Allah's granting of the promised land to the Israelites as their inheritance, fulfilling His covenant with their forefathers. The word 'thus' connects it to preceding divine judgments and miracles, indicating that the inheritance was part of Allah's established pattern of delivering believers and establishing them in positions of strength and authority as a consequence of faith and obedience.

translation: So they pursued them at sunrise.
interpretation: This phrase describes how the pursuing force followed their targets in the direction of the sunrise, indicating a specific direction and timing of pursuit. The term 'mushrikin' (at sunrise) emphasizes that the pursuit began at dawn, suggesting urgency and immediacy in their chase. This detail illustrates the swiftness of the action and may also symbolize clarity and visibility - pursuing in daylight rather than darkness, which could represent the clarity of purpose or inevitability of the pursuers' actions.

translation: So when the two groups saw each other, the companions of Moses said, 'Indeed, we will be overtaken.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the moment of crisis when the Israelites, fleeing Pharaoh's army, suddenly see their pursuers approaching. The disciples of Moses express fear and despair, believing they are about to be caught. This demonstrates how humans naturally succumb to fear when facing seemingly impossible circumstances, and it sets the stage for the divine rescue that follows, teaching that apparent hopelessness is often the prelude to God's intervention and salvation for the believers.

translation: He said, 'No! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me.'
interpretation: This verse expresses unwavering trust in divine guidance despite external pressure or danger. The speaker affirms that reliance on God's presence and protection is superior to yielding to worldly threats, demonstrating that true safety and direction come from maintaining faith in God rather than from material circumstances or human opposition.

translation: So We inspired to Moses, 'Strike the sea with your staff.' And it split, and each portion became like a great mountain.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the direct divine revelation and empowerment granted to Moses, highlighting that miracles are not acts of independent power but occur through obedience to Allah's command. The splitting of the sea into towering masses illustrates the absolute sovereignty of Allah over natural laws and the complete submission of creation to His will, while simultaneously serving as a test of faith for the believers following Moses—those who trust in divine guidance will be delivered, while those who resist will face consequences.

translation: And We brought near the others afterward
interpretation: This verse refers to God's power to bring groups of people near or close, emphasizing His sovereignty over time and sequence. The phrase suggests that God controls the order and proximity of events and people according to His will, indicating that those who come later are still within God's knowledge and control, just as those who came before. It underscores the reality that all creation is subject to God's command regardless of temporal position.

translation: And We saved Musa and all those with him
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's decisive intervention to deliver Prophet Musa and his followers from the pursuit of Pharaoh and his army. The phrase 'all those with him' (ajmaʿin) stresses the completeness of God's protection, extending salvation not just to the prophet but collectively to his entire community. This demonstrates God's attribute as the Savior (al-Munqidh) who responds to the sincere supplication of His oppressed servants and fulfills His promise to grant victory to the believers over their enemies through His perfect planning and almighty power.

translation: Then We drowned the others
interpretation: This verse refers to Allah's destruction of Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea after they pursued the Children of Israel. The 'others' refers to those who rejected Allah's signs and refused to believe in His message through Moses. This demonstrates Allah's power over His enemies and His fulfillment of His promise to protect His believers, while showing that persistent disbelief and arrogance against God's messengers leads to inevitable destruction.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign, and most of them were not believers.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that despite the clear evidence and miraculous signs presented by Allah, the majority of people turn away from belief due to their hardness of heart and preexisting disbelief. It reflects the recurring theme in the Qur'an that signs and miracles alone do not compel belief—faith requires both intellectual recognition of the evidence and a willing heart open to divine guidance. The verse serves as a sobering reminder that observable proof does not guarantee acceptance, as human beings possess free will and may choose denial even in the face of undeniable truth.

translation: And indeed, your Lord - He is the Mighty, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse establishes the dual nature of Allah's divine attributes, emphasizing that true power (might) and true compassion (mercy) coexist in His nature without contradiction. The affirmation 'indeed' (wa-inn) stresses certainty, reminding the believer that these are not merely aspirational qualities but defining characteristics of the Lord.
