This demonstrates that persistent injustice ultimately seals one's ability to respond or object to divine judgment.

translation: Have they not seen that We have made the night for them to rest therein, and the day for seeing? Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.
interpretation: This verse highlights the divine wisdom in creating the alternating cycles of night and day, where each serves a specific purpose ordained by Allah. The night provides rest and tranquility for living creatures after their daytime exertions, while the day provides light for productive activity and vision. The verse suggests that recognizing this purposeful design of creation is an act of divine guidance that awakens believers to appreciate Allah's careful provision for human needs and the interconnectedness of creation. This appreciation of natural design serves as evidence of Allah's existence and benevolence for those whose hearts are open to faith.

translation: And [warn of] the Day when the trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified except whom Allah wills. And all will come to Him in humility.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the certainty and universality of the Day of Judgment, where the sound of the trumpet will strike terror into all creation, yet Allah's sovereignty remains absolute - His will determines who may be spared from that fear. The final phrase stresses the inevitable submission of all beings to Allah's judgment, highlighting both the awesome power of that Day and the humbling reality that all creatures must ultimately return to their Creator for accountability.

translation: And you will see the mountains, thinking them fixed in place, while they pass by like the passing of clouds. Such is the work of Allah, who has perfected all things. Indeed, He is Aware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the transient and illusory nature of the material world, particularly what appears most solid and permanent—the mountains. Just as mountains appear static to our perception but are actually in constant motion relative to cosmic reality, all worldly phenomena lack ultimate stability and permanence. The verse emphasizes that this perfect creative design of a seemingly stable yet inherently dynamic universe demonstrates Allah's complete mastery and craftsmanship. The final statement reinforces that Allah's perfect knowledge encompasses all human actions, serving as a reminder of divine omniscience and accountability, suggesting that the illusion of worldly permanence should not distract from awareness of Allah's watchfulness over our deeds.

translation: Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it, and they will be secure from the terror of that Day.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the profound reward and protection that awaits those who perform righteous deeds. The phrase 'better than it' indicates that the reward for good actions exceeds the deed itself in value and benefit, both in this world and the next. The promise of being 'secure from the terror of that Day' (the Day of Judgment) connects righteous conduct to spiritual salvation and divine protection, conveying that ethical behavior and good works serve as a shield against the fear and anguish that will afflict others on the Day of Reckoning. This verse encourages believers by showing that virtue is not only virtuous in itself but also carries concrete, eternal consequences of safety and elevated status before God.

translation: And whoever comes with an evil deed will be cast down on their faces into the Fire. Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the principle of divine justice and accountability, showing that evil deeds inevitably lead to punishment in the Hereafter. The rhetorical question at the end underscores that there is no recompense except according to one's actions—no one receives more or less than what they have earned through their deeds, establishing the perfect fairness of Allah's judgment where consequences are precisely proportionate to one's moral choices in life.

translation: I am only commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred, and to whom belongs all things; and I am commanded to be of those who submit [to Him].
interpretation: This verse expresses the Prophet Muhammad's personal commitment to monotheism and submission to Allah, emphasizing that his mission is to worship Allah alone as the sole sustainer and sovereign of Mecca and all creation. The statement reflects the exclusivity of divine worship and the obligation to surrender one's will entirely to God's command, establishing the foundation of Islamic faith as complete devotion and obedience to the One God without association of partners.

translation: And that I recite the Qur'an. So whoever is guided is only guided for himself, and whoever goes astray, then say: 'I am only of those who warn.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the messenger's role as a communicator and warner rather than a compeller of belief. The guidance or misguidance of people ultimately rests with themselves—the messenger's responsibility is limited to clear transmission of the message, and he bears no burden for those who reject it. This establishes the principle of human free will and accountability before God, while absolving the prophet of responsibility for forcing people to believe.

translation: And say, 'All praise is due to Allah. He will show you His signs, and you will recognize them. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Allah will manifest His signs and proofs to humanity in due time, allowing them to recognize His truth and power, while simultaneously reminding the believers that Allah's omniscience encompasses all human actions, leaving nothing hidden from His knowledge—thus serving as both a promise of divine guidance and a warning against heedlessness in conduct.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Ta. Se. Meem.
interpretation: These are the isolated letters (Muqatta'at) that appear at the beginning of Surah Al-Qasas. Like other Quranic surahs that begin with such letters, their exact meaning remains one of the unseen matters known only to Allah and His Messenger. Classical scholars have offered various interpretations—some viewing them as divine signs affirming the Qur'an's miraculous nature despite being composed of the same letters of the Arabic alphabet used by all humans, others as abbreviations for divine attributes or names. The primary interpretive significance lies in recognizing them as a means to draw attention and demonstrate the inimitable nature of the Qur'an, establishing that even when challenged to produce something similar, the opponents could not, despite possessing mastery of these very letters themselves.

translation: These are the verses of the clear Book.
interpretation: This phrase emphasizes the clarity and luminosity of the Qur'an as divine scripture, affirming that its verses are manifest and evident signs that serve as guidance for humanity, free from ambiguity in their purpose of directing believers toward truth and righteousness.

translation: We recite to you the news of Moses and Pharaoh in truth for a people who believe.
interpretation: This verse establishes the Divine methodology of communicating historical narratives through revelation. By specifying that the account is conveyed 'with truth' (bil-haqq), it emphasizes the authenticity and reliability of the Quranic narrative as opposed to corrupted or invented versions. The phrase 'for a people who believe' indicates that the primary benefit of these stories is for those who accept the message and reflect upon it with faith, suggesting that spiritual receptiveness is necessary to extract guidance and wisdom from historical examples.

translation: Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a group among them—slaughtering their sons and keeping alive their women. Indeed, he was among the corruptors.
interpretation: This verse illustrates how tyrannical rulers maintain power through systematic oppression and the exploitation of social divisions. Pharaoh's strategy of fragmenting society into competing groups and targeting specific populations for subjugation reveals the destructive nature of despotism. The deliberate persecution—particularly the killing of male children and subjugation of women—demonstrates how authoritarian power corrupts not merely through individual injustice, but through institutionalized exploitation that fractures the social fabric. The description of Pharaoh as 'among the corruptors' emphasizes that such systematic oppression and social fragmentation constitute the gravest form of corruption (fasād), undermining the very foundations of human dignity and social order.

translation: And We wish to bestow favor upon those who were oppressed in the land, and make them leaders, and make them the inheritors.
interpretation: This verse expresses Allah's divine will and promise to elevate those who have been subjugated and powerless, transforming their condition from weakness to authority and inheritance of the earth. It conveys the principle of divine justice whereby the oppressed will ultimately receive vindication, leadership roles, and the rewards of the land, signifying a fundamental reversal of worldly hierarchies based on God's plan for human history and moral recompense.

translation: And We will establish them in the land, and We will show Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers from them (the believers) that which they were fearing.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine principle that those who have faith and patience will ultimately prevail against tyranny. Despite the believers' apparent weakness and subjugation under Pharaoh's rule, God promises not only their survival but their establishment of power and authority in the land. The revelation of what Pharaoh and his chiefs feared—the rise and strength of the believers—demonstrates that God's plan transcends human power structures, and oppressors will witness the fulfillment of their own anxieties. This conveys assurance to the oppressed that divine justice operates beyond immediate circumstances, and that those who trust in God will see vindication through God's sovereign will.

translation: And We revealed to the mother of Moses, saying: 'Suckle him, but when you fear for him, cast him into the river, and do not fear and do not grieve. Indeed, We will return him to you and make him one of the Messengers.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine protection and predestination of prophets despite apparent danger. Allah's revelation to Moses' mother demonstrates that the ultimate safeguard of His chosen servants transcends human vulnerability and parental fear. By commanding her to release her child into the river, Allah teaches that trust in divine providence supersedes natural instinct, and that those destined for prophethood are preserved by Allah's will even when placed in circumstances that would ordinarily appear catastrophic. The verse emphasizes that divine knowledge encompasses all events beforehand, and that believers should abandon anxiety when they place their trust completely in Allah's plan.

translation: Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, [and he was] to become for them an enemy and a source of grief. Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were [all] wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse reveals the divine irony and providential wisdom in which Allah places the means of one's destruction within one's own hands. Pharaoh, in adopting and raising Moses, unwittingly nurtures the very instrument of his downfall—the prophet who would challenge his authority, expose his falsehood, and lead his people to liberation. The phrase 'to become for them an enemy and a source of grief' emphasizes that despite their material power and control, they remain blind to how their own choices serve divine purposes against them. This teaches that wrongdoing inevitably generates the conditions for its own undoing, and that Allah's plan operates through the very actions of those who oppose His truth, making their resistance futile.

translation: And Pharaoh's wife said: 'A comfort to the eyes for me and for you. Do not slay him; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son.' And they did not know.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine providence at work through the heart of Pharaoh's wife, who becomes an instrument of God's plan to save Moses and prepare him for his future mission. Her instinctive mercy toward the infant Moses, motivated by maternal compassion and hope for future benefit, represents how God works through the natural human emotions and desires of His creation to fulfill His greater purposes, even when those involved remain unaware of the profound consequences of their actions.

translation: And the heart of Moses' mother became empty (of all else). Indeed, she was about to disclose him had We not strengthened her heart so that she would be of the believers.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the profound spiritual transformation that occurs through faith and divine support. The emptying of the mother's heart signifies her complete focus and anxiety regarding her son's safety. Yet rather than succumbing to despair or revealing her secret, Allah fortified her heart with certainty and trust. The verse demonstrates that true believers are given inner strength by Allah that enables them to endure trials with composure and wisdom, transforming their natural human weakness into steadfast resolve. Her restraint itself becomes evidence of her faith, showing that believing in Allah's protection grants the heart resilience beyond what the soul naturally possesses.

translation: And she said to her sister, 'Follow him.' So she watched him from a distance while they did not perceive.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the wisdom and prudence of Musa's sister in her role as guardian of her infant brother. Her instruction to follow the Pharaoh's wife represents her trust in divine providence and her readiness to act when an opportunity arose to reunite the family. By remaining vigilant from a distance while remaining unnoticed, she exemplified both caution and maternal instinct, demonstrating that Allah guides believers to fulfill His purposes through their conscious efforts and attentiveness to unfolding circumstances.

translation: And We forbade for him (the infant Moses) nursing mothers before, so she (his sister) said: 'Shall I direct you to a household that will care for him for you and they will be sincere to him?'
interpretation: This verse illustrates divine providence in the story of Prophet Moses. Allah prevented the baby Moses from accepting any nursing mother, creating a crisis that prompted his sister to intervene with a solution. The sister's offer to find a suitable household—which would be his biological mother—demonstrates how Allah orchestrates circumstances to fulfill His purposes. The phrase 'they will be sincere to him' emphasizes the trustworthiness and good intentions required for those entrusted with a child's welfare, and shows how the sister's wisdom and quick thinking became an instrument of Allah's plan to reunite mother and child while keeping Moses safely within Pharaoh's palace.

translation: So We restored him to his mother so that her eyes would be comforted and she would not grieve, and so that she would know that the promise of Allah is true; but most of them do not know.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the principle that Allah's promises to His believing servants are not merely abstract assurances but manifested in concrete, observable realities. The return of Musa to his mother exemplifies how Divine providence works according to His word—what He promises comes to pass. The recognition of this truth serves as a criterion distinguishing between those who perceive the signs of Allah's faithfulness and those who remain heedless despite witnessing them. The closing phrase highlights that recognition of Allah's truth requires intellectual and spiritual awareness, which remains absent in most people due to their resistance or indifference to signs of Divine reality.

translation: And when he reached his full strength and maturity, We gave him wisdom and knowledge. And thus do We reward those who do good.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of divine providence and reward for righteousness. As a person develops physically and intellectually to full maturity, Allah grants wisdom and discernment to those who utilize their faculties in service of truth and goodness. The verse teaches that spiritual and intellectual development is not automatic but contingent upon virtuous conduct, and that Allah's bestowal of understanding and insight is reserved for those who demonstrate moral excellence. This principle applies universally to all believers who strive to live righteously.

translation: And he entered the city at a time when its people were unaware, and he found in it two men fighting - one from his faction and one from his enemy. So the one from his faction called upon him for help against the one from his enemy, and Moses struck him with his fist and killed him. He said, 'This is of the work of Satan. Indeed, he is an enemy, clearly misleading.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates a critical moment in Moses' early life where he acts impulsively in defense of an Israelite being wronged by an Egyptian, resulting in the Egyptian's death. The interpretation reveals the danger of allowing emotional reaction to override deliberation and wisdom. Moses' immediate acknowledgment that this action stems from Satan's work demonstrates his conscience and understanding that even righteous causes do not justify unlawful killing. The verse serves as a spiritual lesson about how the Devil exploits our passion for justice to lead us into sin, showing that true guidance requires restraint, patience, and adherence to divine law rather than reactive violence, regardless of the justness of the underlying cause.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, so forgive me.' And He forgave him. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the path to Allah's forgiveness through sincere repentance and acknowledgment of one's sin. When a servant genuinely recognizes their wrongdoing and turns to Allah with humility and contrition, Allah's mercy extends to them immediately, demonstrating that His attribute of forgiveness and compassion is always available to those who seek it with sincerity, regardless of the gravity of their transgression.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, because You have favored me, I will never be a helper to the criminals.'
interpretation: This verse reflects a covenant of righteousness wherein the speaker, having been blessed by God with knowledge and understanding, commits himself to refusing complicity with wrongdoing. The statement reveals that true gratitude for divine blessings manifests not merely in passive piety but in active refusal to support or assist those who transgress God's laws, demonstrating that genuine faith requires moral courage and principled separation from sin.

translation: So he became in the city fearful, watching cautiously. Then behold, the one who had sought his help the day before was crying out to him for aid. Moses said to him: 'Indeed, you are clearly misguided.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates Moses's frustration with the Israelite man who had attacked him the previous day, despite Moses having helped him against an Egyptian. By calling him 'clearly misguided' (غوي مبين), Moses points to the man's lack of understanding and ingratitude—he fails to recognize that seeking help through violence only perpetuates conflict rather than resolving it. The verse highlights how some people, driven by their nature or circumstances, cannot escape cycles of aggression even when offered assistance, reflecting a commentary on those who persist in wrongdoing despite available guidance.

translation: So when he resolved to seize the one who was an enemy to both of them, Moses said, "Do you want to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday? You only want to be a tyrant in the land, and you do not want to be of those who set things right."
interpretation: This verse illustrates how the Coptic man falsely accuses Moses of tyranny and murder based on a single act of defending an Israelite, demonstrating how people often misinterpret righteous action through the lens of their own assumptions and prejudices, and how those who are quick to condemn may themselves be guilty of the very crimes they allege against others.

translation: And there came a man from the farthest end of the city, running. He said: 'O Moses, indeed the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you, so depart. Indeed, I am to you of the sincere advisors.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine protection of the righteous through the intervention of believers from unexpected quarters. Despite living in a society hostile to Moses, this man risks his safety to warn him, demonstrating that God provides means of deliverance through the faith and compassion of believers, even in the midst of opposition. The man's willingness to help, despite the danger, emphasizes that sincere advice and loyalty to the truth transcend worldly interests and social pressures.

translation: So he left from there in fear, awaiting. He said, "My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people."
interpretation: This verse depicts Moses fleeing Egypt after killing the Egyptian taskmaster, characterized by both physical fear and spiritual reliance on God. His prayer reveals that despite his anxiety about immediate danger, he recognizes that true salvation comes only through divine intervention, establishing a pattern of submission to God even in moments of personal vulnerability and uncertainty about the future.

translation: And when he set out towards Midian, he said, 'Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right path.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the spiritual disposition of Prophet Moses after his flight from Egypt - despite his uncertainty about the future and his vulnerable situation as a fugitive, he places his trust entirely in God's guidance rather than relying on his own judgment or earthly knowledge. His statement reflects the attitude of a believer who, facing an unknown journey, submits his affairs to Divine will and seeks divine guidance, demonstrating that true reliance on God emerges most powerfully in moments of personal difficulty and displacement.

translation: And when he arrived at the water of Madyan, he found upon it a community of people watering [their flocks]. And he found besides them two women holding back [their flocks]. He said, 'What is the matter with you?' They said, 'We do not water until the shepherds depart, and our father is an old man.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the qualities of patience, responsibility, and proper conduct that characterized Prophet Musa. The two women represent those who face hardship and social disadvantage yet maintain their dignity and propriety by waiting their turn rather than forcing themselves into the crowd. Their explanation reveals both filial duty toward their elderly father and a quiet acceptance of their difficult circumstances. The passage establishes these women as embodiments of virtue and integrity, setting the stage for Musa's recognition of worthy character and his subsequent assistance. It demonstrates that moral excellence is not dependent on social position or ease of circumstance, but rather on one's choices in the face of adversity.

translation: So he watered [the flock] for them, then he turned back to the shade and said, 'My Lord, indeed I am in need of whatever good You send down to me.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the virtue of combining righteous action with humble reliance upon Allah. Moses' watering of the flocks for the two women demonstrates kindness and service without expectation of reward, yet immediately after fulfilling this good deed, he turns to Allah in supplication, acknowledging his complete dependence on divine provision. This teaches that true servants of Allah maintain humility and recognize that all blessings ultimately come from Him alone, and that doing good works does not diminish one's need to seek Allah's mercy and sustenance with sincere devotion.

translation: Then one of them came to him, walking with shyness. She said, 'Indeed, my father invites you so that he may reward you for having drawn water for us.' So when he came to him and told him the story, he said, 'Do not fear. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people.'
interpretation: This passage illustrates the divine providence and justice that protects the righteous. Musa's refuge with Shu'ayb represents how Allah provides sanctuary for those who flee oppression and injustice. The modest approach of the young woman and her father's invitation to reward Musa demonstrates how virtuous conduct and good deeds attract blessing and protection. The reassurance 'do not fear' signifies that Allah's protection extends to those who uphold justice and reject tyranny, establishing a contrast between the just society Musa enters and the oppressive Pharaonic regime he escaped.

translation: One of them said, 'O my father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and the trustworthy.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the virtue of recognizing and appreciating quality character and capability in others. The daughter's recommendation of Musa (Moses) based on his strength and trustworthiness demonstrates that sound judgment in selecting workers or companions should be grounded in observable moral and practical qualities rather than appearance, social status, or mere familiarity. It reflects the Islamic principle that true worth comes from one's integrity and competence, not external factors.

translation: He said, 'Indeed, I wish to wed to you one of my two daughters on the condition that you work for me for eight years; and if you complete ten, it will be of your own kindness. I do not wish to make things difficult for you. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the righteous.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates a wise and merciful approach to employment negotiations. The offer reflects an understanding of fair exchange: the employer provides marriage (dignity and family status) as part of the compensation for labor, while requesting service in return. By stipulating eight years as the requirement but opening the possibility of ten, the speaker demonstrates generosity and flexibility—the extra two years become a gift from the worker rather than an obligation. The closing declaration of righteousness is significant: true justice in dealings is a manifestation of piety and fear of Allah, suggesting that honest business conduct and fair treatment of others are integral to one's spiritual character and relationship with God.

translation: He said, 'That is settled between you and me. Whichever of the two periods I fulfill, there will be no wrong upon me, and Allah is witness over what we say.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the principle of contractual honesty and fair dealing in agreements. The speaker (Moses) agrees to the terms proposed by his employer without complaint, acknowledging that fulfilling either agreed-upon period of service is binding and just. By invoking Allah as witness to their words, the verse emphasizes that all dealings between people are ultimately observed by the Divine, establishing accountability before God as the foundation of trustworthy transactions. This teaches that contracts made in good faith are sacred, and that invoking God's witnessing of agreements ensures integrity in human relations.

translation: So when Musa had completed the term and was traveling with his family, he perceived a fire from the direction of the mountain. He said to his family, 'Wait here; I have noticed a fire. Perhaps I can bring you from it some information or a burning brand so that you may warm yourselves.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates how Allah guides His servants through seemingly ordinary circumstances. Musa's discovery of the fire was divinely orchestrated to lead him to his ultimate purpose—receiving the divine mission. The act of Musa seeking to help his family by bringing them warmth demonstrates noble character and compassion, which made him a worthy recipient of prophethood. His willingness to investigate the unusual fire, rather than ignore it, reflects the attentiveness and duty that characterized him as Allah's chosen messenger. This encounter marks the threshold moment where Musa transitions from an ordinary traveler into the bearer of divine revelation.

translation: So when he reached it, he was called from the right side of the valley in the blessed spot from the tree: 'O Moses, indeed I am Allah, the Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse demonstrates the divine selection and honor bestowed upon Moses, as Allah's call to him came from a sacred, blessed location—the right side of the valley and specifically from a tree. The specification of these particular details emphasizes the solemnity and authenticity of the divine encounter, establishing that Moses was not a recipient of empty claims or delusions, but rather the chosen messenger directly addressed by the Lord of all creation. The revelation of Allah's identity and lordship at this specific moment marks the definitive beginning of Moses' prophetic mission and his direct communion with the Divine.

translation: And cast down your staff. Then when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned in flight and did not look back. O Moses, do not be afraid. Indeed, you are of the secure ones.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the psychology of fear and the power of faith in overcoming it. Pharaoh's immediate flight upon witnessing the miraculous transformation of the staff into a serpent demonstrates how the human soul, despite its outward pride and authority, is vulnerable to signs that challenge its rationality. God's reassurance to Moses that he is "of the secure ones" is not merely a comfort, but an affirmation of the spiritual protection granted to those who stand firmly upon God's truth. The command "do not be afraid" elevates Moses beyond the natural human reaction to danger, positioning him as one whose mission is divinely protected, thereby establishing that true security comes not from physical power or worldly position, but from alignment with God's purpose.

translation: Put your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without disease. And draw your wing close to yourself from fear. So these two are signs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs. Indeed, they were a transgressing people.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the miraculous signs given to Moses—the luminous hand and the shielding wing—were not arbitrary acts of magic, but divinely ordained proofs (burhan) designed specifically for Pharaoh and his nobles. The reference to Pharaoh and his people being 'fasiqin' (transgressors) indicates that despite witnessing these clear evidences of God's power, they rejected them due to their inherent disobedience and arrogance. The verse thus highlights the tragedy of those who encounter undeniable truth yet refuse to submit, demonstrating that miraculous signs alone cannot compel belief when hearts are sealed in rebellion against God.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, indeed I have killed one of them, so I fear that they will kill me.'
interpretation: This verse expresses Moses' anxiety and his need for divine protection after he unintentionally killed an Egyptian. Rather than pride or justification, Moses turns to Allah with vulnerability and fear, demonstrating that even prophets experience human emotion and depend upon God's mercy and guidance in moments of peril. His confession of the act and his fear reveal his consciousness of wrongdoing and his reliance on God's will for his survival and safe passage.

translation: And my brother Aaron is more eloquent in speech than me, so send him with me as a helper to confirm me. Indeed, I fear that they will deny me.
interpretation: This verse illustrates that seeking assistance from those more capable in specific skills is not a weakness but a wise and strategic approach to important tasks. Moses acknowledges his brother's superior eloquence and requests his support not out of self-doubt about his divine mission, but out of practical recognition that effective communication requires matching the audience's capacity to understand. This teaches that relying on the complementary strengths of others strengthens one's ability to convey truth and serves the ultimate goal of delivering the message, while also demonstrating humility and tactical wisdom in the face of potential rejection.

translation: He said: We shall strengthen your arm with your brother, and We shall give you both authority, so they shall not reach you. By Our signs, you and those who follow you will be the victorious ones.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates Allah's promise of support to those who undertake His mission with sincerity and unity. The strengthening of Moses and Aaron through their brotherhood symbolizes how unity of purpose and mutual support among believers creates a formidable force against opposition. The phrase 'by Our signs' indicates that victory comes through adherence to Allah's guidance and clear proofs, not through material might alone. The assurance that 'you and those who follow you will be victorious' establishes the principle that those who remain steadfast in faith and follow divine guidance are guaranteed ultimate success, regardless of the worldly power of their enemies.

translation: So when Moses came to them with Our clear signs, they said, 'This is nothing but fabricated sorcery, and we have not heard of this among our forefathers.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the psychological phenomenon of rejection that occurs when people encounter truth that contradicts their inherited beliefs and cultural traditions. The Egyptians' denial of Moses' miracles as mere sorcery reveals how individuals often dismiss evidence that challenges their worldview, taking refuge in claims of precedent and ancestral authority. Their insistence that they never heard such claims before serves as a defense mechanism against cognitive dissonance, demonstrating that disbelief frequently stems not from logical incapacity but from emotional and social resistance to abandoning established norms and the status quo.

translation: And Moses said, 'My Lord is most knowing of who comes with guidance from Him and who will have the best end in the Hereafter. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper.'
interpretation: Moses affirms his trust in Allah's perfect knowledge and judgment, asserting that only Allah truly knows who possesses divine guidance and whose ultimate destination is eternal success. This reflects the principle that worldly success or apparent advantage does not determine one's true standing with Allah, and that those who commit injustice and reject truth will inevitably fail in their ultimate outcome, regardless of their temporary gains or influence.

translation: And Pharaoh said, 'O nobles, I know not of any god for you other than myself. So kindle for me, O Haman, [a fire] upon the clay, and make for me a tower that I might climb up to the god of Moses. And indeed, I think he is among the liars.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates Pharaoh's arrogance and spiritual blindness - his declaration of self-divinity reveals not merely political tyranny but a fundamental rejection of monotheism rooted in ego and denial of the divine reality beyond himself. His absurd plan to build a tower to ascend to God, construed as proof of Moses' deception, demonstrates how the human soul ensnared by pride becomes incapable of perceiving truth; his suspicion that Moses lies paradoxically reflects his own condition as one who is profoundly deceived by his own delusions of power and grandeur, making him a cautionary example of how absolute authority without faith corrupts the conscience entirely.

translation: And he was arrogant, he and his soldiers on earth, without right, and they thought that they would not be returned to Us.
interpretation: This verse illustrates how arrogance and tyranny cause one to become heedless of divine accountability. The phrase 'without right' emphasizes that their pride was baseless and unjustified, yet their arrogance blinded them to the reality of divine power and the inevitability of returning to God for judgment. This demonstrates the spiritual consequence of haughtiness—it severs one's awareness of God's omnipotence and the ultimate reckoning that awaits all creatures.

translation: So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea. So see how was the end of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine principle of retribution for oppression and transgression. The drowning of Pharaoh and his army serves as a concrete manifestation of God's justice, demonstrating that no amount of worldly power or defiance against the divine message can shield the wrongdoers from divine punishment. The command to 'see' invites reflection on this historical outcome as a warning and lesson for those who witness injustice or are tempted toward similar arrogance and denial of truth.

translation: And We made them leaders who call to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection, they will not be helped.
interpretation: This verse describes the consequence of those who turned away from divine guidance: their persistent rejection and deviation from the truth becomes so ingrained that they become leaders in misguidance, actively drawing others toward punishment and damnation. The verse emphasizes their utter abandonment on the Day of Judgment, when neither their influence nor their followers will avail them, and no one will come to their aid—a profound expression of divine justice where those who led others astray will face complete isolation and helplessness in the afterlife.

translation: And We followed them in this worldly life with a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised.
interpretation: This verse indicates the comprehensive punishment that encompasses both the temporal and eternal realms for those who reject the divine message. The curse in this life manifests through divine estrangement, degradation in hearts, and the corruption of their deeds, while the description 'despised' on the Day of Resurrection emphasizes their utterly contemptible status before God and creation, stripped of all honor and dignity—a fate reserved for those who persisted in rejecting God's guidance.

translation: And indeed, We gave Moses the Scripture after We had destroyed the former generations, as clear proofs for the people and a guidance and mercy, so that perhaps they would remember.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the Torah was given to Moses as a divine gift not only to guide his own people but also as a warning and reminder to all humanity. The phrase 'after We had destroyed the former generations' suggests that the giving of the Scripture was a merciful opportunity granted to subsequent generations to learn from the fate of their predecessors and avoid similar transgressions. The three descriptors—'clear proofs,' 'guidance,' and 'mercy'—highlight the comprehensive nature of divine revelation as evidence of God's existence and will, a path to righteousness, and an expression of God's compassion. The concluding phrase 'so that perhaps they would remember' indicates that while God provides the means for salvation and remembrance, human acceptance and adherence to the message remains contingent upon individual choice and reflection.

translation: And you were not at the western side when We decreed the matter to Moses, nor were you among those who witnessed [it].
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad, emphasizing that he was not present during the revelation to Moses at Mount Sinai, establishing that his knowledge of these events comes from divine revelation rather than personal observation. This serves to authenticate the Qur'an's account of past prophets and affirms that the Qur'an is indeed a revelation from God, as it provides knowledge of unseen matters that the Prophet could not have known through ordinary means. The verse underscores the continuity of divine revelation across different prophets while clarifying the distinct nature of each prophetic mission.

translation: But We created generations, and long ages passed over them. And you were not dwelling among the people of Madyan to recite Our signs to them, but We were the ones sending [messengers].
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad, emphasizing that he was not physically present during the time of the people of Madyan (Midian) to preach to them, yet he has been entrusted with the message of God just as other messengers were sent to their respective peoples. The verse serves to remind the Prophet that each nation received guidance through messengers sent to them in their own time, establishing the principle of divine justice and the continuity of God's guidance throughout human history. It also implicitly validates the authenticity of the Prophet's mission by showing that this pattern of sending messengers has been God's consistent methodology.

translation: And you were not at the side of the Mount when We called (Musa), but (it is) a mercy from your Lord that you warn a people to whom no warner has come before you, that they may remember.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine source of the Prophet's mission through a contrast: he did not witness the events at Mount Tur, yet he has been given knowledge of them and a message to convey. The phrase 'mercy from your Lord' indicates that the Prophet's appointment as a messenger to warn his people is purely an act of God's grace and compassion, not something earned or achieved through his own effort. The purpose is to warn a community that has been deprived of divine guidance, awakening them to remembrance and consciousness of God's truth.

translation: And had it not been that a disaster would strike them for what their hands have sent forth, and they would say: 'Our Lord, why did You not send us a messenger so that we might have followed Your signs and been among the believers?'
interpretation: This verse explains that Allah's wisdom in sending messengers is to establish proof against mankind, so that they cannot use ignorance or the absence of divine guidance as an excuse on the Day of Judgment. The verse emphasizes that if Allah were to punish people without having sent them a messenger first, they would have legitimate grounds to protest and claim they were deprived of the means to know the truth. Thus, the sending of messengers is an act of divine mercy and justice, ensuring that people are warned and given the opportunity to believe before they face consequences for their rejection of truth.

translation: So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, 'Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?' Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before? They said, 'Two magicians supporting each other,' and they said, 'Indeed, we are disbelievers in all of it.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the pattern of human obstinacy and rejection of divine signs—that those who reject the truth will constantly move the goalposts of their objections, demanding new miracles even as they deny the validity of previous ones. Their cry for Moses-like miracles while simultaneously denying what Moses was given reveals that their real problem is not lack of evidence but a hardened heart resistant to belief. The accusation that both Moses and Muhammad were magicians collaborating together exposes the incoherence and bad faith of their rejection, showing that their disbelief stems from preexisting bias rather than rational evaluation of the signs presented to them.

translation: Say, 'Then bring a Scripture from Allah that is more guiding than these two, and follow it if you are truthful.'
interpretation: This verse challenges the disbelievers to produce a divine revelation superior to the Qur'an and the Torah if they claim to possess truth and guidance. The challenge is rhetorical and conclusive, as it is impossible for anyone to produce a book equal to or better than Allah's revelation, thereby establishing the superiority and divine origin of the Qur'an as the final and most complete guidance for humanity.

translation: If they do not respond to you, then know that they follow only their desires. And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: This verse teaches that when people reject the divine message despite its clarity, their refusal stems not from intellectual deficiency but from their deliberate choice to follow their base desires and passions over truth. The verse establishes a causal relationship between abandoning divine guidance and being led astray—the greatest form of misguidance is when someone knowingly chooses their whims over God's direction. Allah's non-guidance of the unjust is not arbitrary but a consequence of their own choice to turn away; they have sealed their hearts through their own rebellious actions.

translation: And indeed, We have conveyed to them the word [of guidance] so that perhaps they might remember.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Allah has made His message clearly accessible and repeated it in multiple ways to humanity through His prophets and scriptures, giving people ample opportunity to reflect, comprehend, and take heed. The phrase 'perhaps they might remember' suggests that while the message is delivered with clarity and completeness, its acceptance ultimately depends on human choice and willingness to pay attention—Allah has fulfilled His responsibility in communicating guidance, and the onus now lies on people to respond to it with mindfulness and contemplation rather than negligence.

translation: Those to whom We gave the Scripture before it - they believe in it.
interpretation: This verse refers to the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) who possessed the Torah and Gospel before the Qur'an was revealed. They recognize and affirm the truth of the Qur'an because it aligns with and confirms the divine guidance contained in their own scriptures. Their belief serves as a testimony to the authenticity and divine origin of the Qur'an, as those most knowledgeable about previous revelation acknowledge its consistency with what they already possess.

translation: And when it is recited to them, they say: 'We believe in it. Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed, we were Muslims before it.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the state of those who possessed prior knowledge from the Torah and Gospel, who recognized the Qur'an as a confirmation of what they already knew to be God's truth. Their declaration reflects an immediate recognition of divine guidance rather than conversion, emphasizing that true faith in God's message is not merely belief upon hearing, but a continuation and affirmation of submission to God that preceded the Qur'an itself. The verse highlights the distinction between those whose hearts are open to God's signs and those whose understanding is already rooted in authentic monotheism.

translation: Those are the ones who will be given their reward twice because of their patience, and they repel evil with good, and from what We have provided them, they spend.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of multiplied divine reward for those who combine steadfast patience in faith with active virtue. The 'reward twice' signifies both the spiritual elevation gained through endurance and the ultimate recompense in the Hereafter. The phrase 'repel evil with good' teaches that the believer's response to harm should not be retaliation but rather moral excellence, transforming conflict through virtue into a means of spiritual refinement. The concluding mention of spending from divine provision establishes that true patience is inseparable from generosity and charitable action, making patience not merely a passive endurance but an active engagement in righteousness that encompasses ethical behavior, moral character, and social responsibility.

translation: And when they hear ill speech, they turn away from it and say, 'For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. Peace be upon you; we do not seek out the ignorant.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the moral conduct of believers who encounter vulgar or sinful talk: they neither participate in it nor respond with hostility. Instead, they gracefully disengage, affirm that each person bears responsibility for their own actions, extend a courteous greeting of peace, and make a conscious choice to avoid association with those who engage in foolishness. The verse emphasizes that true piety involves not merely avoiding sin oneself, but also maintaining ethical boundaries in social interaction and refusing to be drawn into disputes with those of poor character.

translation: Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills. And He is most knowing of those who are guided.
interpretation: This verse teaches that guidance is ultimately in Allah's hands alone, not in the power of any human being, even the Prophet. It humbles the Prophet and all believers by clarifying that sincere love and desire for someone's guidance cannot override Allah's will. The verse emphasizes that Allah's knowledge of who truly deserves and will benefit from guidance is perfect and comprehensive, establishing that divine wisdom supersedes human intention and effort in matters of faith and guidance.

translation: And they said: 'If we follow the guidance with you, we shall be snatched away from our land.' Have We not established for them a sanctuary (of security) to which are brought fruits of all things as sustenance from Us? Yet most of them do not know.
interpretation: The verse exposes the hypocrisy of the disbelievers' excuses for rejecting faith. Their claim that following guidance will cause them to lose their homeland and livelihood is shown to be unfounded, since God has already granted them Mecca as a secure sanctuary where all the fruits of the earth are brought to them. Their reluctance stems not from practical concern but from ignorance and willful rejection of God's provision and blessings, revealing that their resistance to the message is rooted in denial of God's sustenance and care rather than in any real danger to their security.

translation: And how many a town have We destroyed that reveled in its comfortable living! And those are their dwellings, which have not been inhabited after them except for a few. And it is We who are the inheritors.
interpretation: This verse warns of the consequences of arrogance and complacency born from material abundance. When people become intoxicated with luxury and prosperity, they often abandon gratitude and moral responsibility, leading to their downfall. The destruction is not arbitrary punishment but the natural result of spiritual corruption that accompanies excessive indulgence. The desolation of their cities and Allah's inheritance of the earth serve as perpetual reminders that all worldly possessions are temporary, and true power belongs only to the Divine. The lesson extends to all peoples and generations, cautioning against the spiritual dangers inherent in unlimited material comfort divorced from faith and righteousness.

translation: And your Lord would not destroy the cities until He sends to their mother a messenger reciting to them Our verses. And We were not destroying the cities except while their people were wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse establishes a fundamental principle of divine justice: that Allah does not punish a people with destruction unless He has first sent them a messenger to warn them and convey His message. The 'mother' of cities refers to the main or central city. This teaches that destruction is a consequence of willful rejection and transgression after clear guidance has been provided, making the punishment just and removing any excuse. It reflects Allah's mercy in giving people the opportunity to repent before any severe punishment, and emphasizes that wrongdoing and rejection of divine guidance are the necessary preconditions for such destruction.

translation: And whatever you have been given is only enjoyment of worldly life and its adornment. And whatever is with Allah is better and more lasting. Then will you not use reason?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the ephemeral nature of material possessions and worldly acquisitions, characterizing them as temporary adornments and fleeting enjoyments. The verse contrasts the transient nature of dunya (the worldly life) with the eternal nature of what Allah possesses, inviting the listener to reflect upon the permanence of the hereafter and divine rewards as opposed to the perishable nature of material wealth and status. The concluding rhetorical question serves as a call to intellectual awakening, urging believers to employ their rational faculties to recognize this fundamental truth about the relative values of worldly and divine blessings, and to prioritize their actions and aspirations accordingly.

translation: Is then he to whom We have promised a good promise, which he will meet, like him to whom We have given the enjoyment of the life of this world, and then on the Day of Resurrection he will be among those brought forward (to punishment)?
interpretation: This verse contrasts two categories of people: those whom Allah has promised a good promise (Paradise) and who will certainly attain it, versus those given worldly pleasures and enjoyment in this life only to be brought for punishment on the Day of Judgment. The rhetorical question emphasizes that these two conditions are not comparable—the faithful believer with certainty of reward is in no way equal to the person distracted by temporary worldly gains who will face divine punishment. This teaches that true success lies not in material wealth and fleeting earthly pleasures, but in faith and righteousness that guarantee eternal reward.

translation: And on the Day when He will call to them and say, 'Where are My partners whom you used to claim?'
interpretation: This verse depicts the Day of Judgment when Allah will confront the polytheists with a rhetorical question designed to expose the falsity of their beliefs. By asking them to produce their supposed partners with Allah, Allah demonstrates that these false deities—whether idols, angels, jinn, or other beings—never existed as divine entities, thereby establishing the absolute unity of God and the futility of all forms of shirk (associating partners with Allah). The question serves as both a moment of reckoning and a final vindication of Allah's oneness.

translation: Those against whom the word has been passed will say: 'Our Lord, these are the ones we led astray. We led them astray as we ourselves were led astray. We dissociate ourselves before You. It was not us they were worshipping.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the ultimate excuse and blame-shifting of those who misled others away from God's path. On the Day of Judgment, those condemned to punishment will attempt to evade responsibility by claiming they merely followed the same path as their followers, thereby denying culpability. They will attempt to distance themselves from God by claiming they bear no responsibility for their followers' worship, suggesting their influence was not the primary cause of misguidance. The verse exposes the hollow and desperate nature of such excuses, as each person will ultimately be held accountable for their own choices and their deliberate efforts to lead others astray, regardless of their attempts at disavowal.

translation: And it will be said, 'Call upon those you associated with Allah as partners.' So they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them. And they will see the punishment. If only they had been guided.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the ultimate futility of polytheism on the Day of Judgment when the disbelievers desperately appeal to their false deities for salvation, only to discover that these imagined partners cannot help them in any way. The divine wisdom in this confrontation is to expose the complete powerlessness of idolatry and vindicate monotheism, while the plea 'if only they had been guided' emphasizes that the disbelievers had the opportunity in this life to recognize the truth but chose rejection and obstinacy instead.

translation: And [remember] the Day when He will call to them and say, 'What did you answer the messengers?'
interpretation: This verse describes a scene from the Day of Judgment where Allah addresses those who were called to faith, asking them to account for their response to the messengers sent to them. The question serves as a powerful reminder that humanity's reception and treatment of Allah's messengers is a matter of utmost significance, and believers will be held accountable for whether they heeded or rejected the divine guidance delivered through them. This establishes that accepting the message of the prophets is not merely a worldly concern but a fundamental matter upon which the eternal fate of souls depends.

translation: So the news became obscured to them that day, and they will not ask one another.
interpretation: This verse describes the state of disbelief and confusion that will overcome the deniers on the Day of Judgment when confronted with the reality of divine punishment. The phrase 'news became obscured' signifies that the realities which were previously hidden from them are now made manifest in a way that overwhelms their cognition, rendering them incapable of rational discourse or questioning among themselves. Their silence and inability to question reflects their complete loss of understanding and their resignation to their fate, as all arguments and pretenses are stripped away in the face of absolute truth. This illustrates the consequence of rejecting divine guidance in this world—a total severance from understanding and communication in the next.

translation: As for those who repented and believed and did righteous deeds, perhaps they will be among the successful ones.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that true success and salvation in the sight of Allah are contingent upon three essential actions: sincere repentance from wrongdoing, genuine faith in Allah and His message, and consistent performance of righteous deeds. The use of 'perhaps' (عسى) indicates that while these conditions create the pathway to success, ultimate success remains within Allah's will and judgment, encouraging humility and continuous striving rather than presumption of guaranteed reward. The verse affirms that those who fulfill these three criteria have genuine hope of achieving felicity in both this life and the hereafter.

translation: And your Lord creates what He wills and chooses. They have no choice. Exalted is Allah and high above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes divine omnipotence and absolute authority: Allah alone possesses the power to create and select according to His wisdom, while creatures have no capacity to choose or determine the course of creation. The prohibition against associating partners with Allah (shirk) is grounded in this fundamental principle—since Allah's creative and selective will is supreme and unconstrained, no other being deserves worship or can possess the authority attributed to Allah by those who commit shirk. The verse thus establishes tawhid (monotheism) as the logical consequence of recognizing Allah's sole dominion over creation.

translation: And your Lord knows what their hearts conceal and what they declare
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute and comprehensive knowledge of both the hidden intentions and secret thoughts within human hearts as well as their outward statements and actions. It conveys the concept that nothing is hidden from Allah—neither private thoughts nor public declarations—establishing that accountability before Allah extends beyond mere external behavior to include the inner states of human beings, which serves as a moral reminder that one cannot deceive Allah regardless of the disparity between inner conviction and outer expression.

translation: And He is Allah - there is no deity except Him. To Him belongs [all] praise in the first [life] and the last [life]. And to Him belongs [all] decision, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute oneness of Allah and His complete sovereignty over all existence. The phrase 'to Him belongs all praise in the first and the last' signifies that Allah alone deserves gratitude and recognition throughout time - both in this worldly life and in the Hereafter. The statement 'to Him belongs all decision' affirms that ultimate authority and judgment rest exclusively with Allah, making clear that no creature possesses any genuine power or authority apart from what Allah grants. The final phrase 'to Him you will be returned' reminds believers of their ultimate accountability before Allah, emphasizing that all affairs ultimately belong to Him and all souls will return to face His judgment.

translation: Say, 'Have you considered: if Allah made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, which deity other than Allah could bring you light? Then will you not listen?'
interpretation: This verse employs a rhetorical challenge to awaken human consciousness about Divine power and dependency. By presenting an impossible scenario—eternal night—the Qur'an emphasizes that the alternation of day and night is not a natural given but a deliberate Divine blessing that demonstrates Allah's sole authority over the cosmic order. The question 'which deity other than Allah could bring you light?' serves to dismantle the logical foundation of polytheism by showing that no conceived deity possesses the power to alter fundamental natural laws. The final appeal 'will you not listen?' is a call to rational reflection, suggesting that recognizing this manifest sign should lead people to embrace monotheism and abandon idolatry, as only reason and listening to clear evidence can guide humanity toward the truth.

translation: Say: 'Have you considered if Allah made the day eternal for you until the Day of Judgment, which god other than Allah could bring you a night in which you rest? Do you not see?'
interpretation: This verse appeals to human reason by directing attention to the divine mercy and wisdom evident in the alternation of day and night. The rhetorical question challenges the listener to recognize that the provision of rest through darkness is a fundamental necessity for human survival and well-being that only Allah can provide. By framing the question as a logical impossibility—that no other god could replace this essential function—the verse aims to awaken the listener's consciousness to Allah's sole authority and to the futility of associating partners with Him. It underscores that the natural world's perfect design and the cycle of rest and activity are signs of Allah's unique power and care for His creation.

translation: And of His mercy, He has made for you the night and the day, so that you may rest in it and so that you may seek from His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the alternation of night and day is a manifestation of Allah's mercy tailored to human needs and nature. The night provides rest and tranquility for the weary body, while the day provides the opportunity to work and seek sustenance through lawful means. The verse concludes with the condition 'perhaps you will be grateful,' indicating that recognizing these two blessings and acting upon them with gratitude—by resting when appropriate and working righteously—is the ultimate purpose behind their creation, highlighting the intrinsic connection between divine mercy and human gratitude.

translation: And [on] the Day He will call to them and say, 'Where are My 'partners' whom you used to claim?'
interpretation: This verse depicts the scene on the Day of Judgment when Allah will confront those who associated partners with Him during their worldly life. By asking 'Where are My partners?', Allah is exposing the falsehood and reality of their shirk (polytheism), forcing them to confront the emptiness of their claims. The verse emphasizes that all the idols, false deities, and entities they worshipped will be absent and unable to help them, thereby demonstrating the ultimate futility of polytheism and the inevitable vindication of Allah's absolute oneness.

translation: And We will extract from every nation a witness, then We will say, 'Produce your proof.' Then they will know that the truth belongs to Allah, and lost to them will be that which they used to invent.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine principle of accountability on the Day of Judgment, where Allah will call forth a representative witness from each community to testify against their people. The verse emphasizes that when confronted with the demand to present evidence for their false claims and idolatrous practices, the disbelievers will be forced to acknowledge the absolute truth of Allah's oneness. Their fabrications and invented falsehoods will vanish, revealing the stark reality that all authority, judgment, and truth belong solely to Allah. This conveys the futility of human innovation in religious matters that contradicts divine guidance, and the inevitable exposure of falsehood before the truth on the Day of Reckoning.

translation: Indeed, Qarun was from the people of Moses, but he rebelled against them. And We gave him of treasures, such that their keys would burden a company of strong men. When his people said to him: 'Do not exult. Indeed, Allah does not love those who exult.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the spiritual danger of excessive wealth and pride when disconnected from gratitude and humility before God. Qarun's rebellion despite witnessing Moses's message demonstrates that material abundance, when it becomes a source of arrogance rather than a means of charity and service, corrupts the soul and distances one from divine favor. The people's warning to him reveals that true consciousness of God requires restraint and humility, not the joyful display of one's blessings, for exultation in wealth is a form of ingratitude that Allah abhors.

translation: But seek, by means of what Allah has given you, the home of the Hereafter; and forget not your share of this world. And be good to others as Allah has been good to you. And seek not to spread corruption in the earth. Indeed, Allah does not love those who spread corruption.
interpretation: This verse establishes a balanced approach to life by directing believers to pursue eternal reward through righteous use of their worldly blessings, while maintaining legitimate engagement with the material world. It emphasizes that spiritual devotion and worldly prosperity are not contradictory; rather, one must use resources received from Allah to secure the Hereafter, fulfill reasonable needs in life, treat others with the same kindness Allah has shown them, and refrain from causing harm or corruption. The instruction reflects the Islamic principle of moderation (wasatiyyah) and personal accountability, warning that pursuing material gains through destructive means or neglecting ethical responsibility incurs divine displeasure.

translation: He said, 'I have only been given this because of knowledge I possess.' Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him of the generations those who were stronger than him in power and greater in accumulation? And the criminals will not be asked about their sins.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the spiritual blindness of arrogance and material success. Qarun's attribution of his wealth solely to his own knowledge, without acknowledging Allah's bestowal, represents the delusion that worldly power and riches are the result of personal merit alone. The verse serves as a warning that such pride is futile—those far mightier and wealthier than him were destroyed before him, yet he remained heedless of this lesson from history. The final phrase suggests that on the Day of Judgment, these arrogant criminals will face their reckoning without excuse, as their very arrogance prevents them from recognizing their need to account for their deeds.

translation: So he went forth to his people in his splendor and adornment. Those who desired the worldly life said, 'Oh, would that we had the like of what Qarun has been given! Indeed, he is a possessor of great fortune.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the spiritual danger of worldly wealth and the blindness it can cause in those who lack spiritual insight. The envious response of the people reveals how material abundance can become an object of desire that distracts from higher purposes, demonstrating that true success is not measured by outward display and possessions, but by one's relationship with the Divine. The verse subtly condemns the acquisitiveness and covetousness of those who measure worth solely by material wealth.

translation: And those who were given knowledge said, 'Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for those who believe and do righteous deeds. And none attains it except the patient.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that true knowledge leads to wisdom and virtue in speech. Those possessed of genuine understanding recognize that the temporary pleasures and vanities of this world pale in comparison to the eternal reward from Allah, which is reserved exclusively for the believers who combine faith with righteous action and maintain steadfastness through trials. The virtue of patience is presented as an essential condition for achieving Allah's ultimate reward, suggesting that perseverance in faith and obedience is not merely recommended but necessary for spiritual success.

translation: So We caused the earth to swallow him and his dwelling. Then he had no company to help him against Allah, nor was he among those who could save themselves.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of divine justice and the consequences of arrogance and ingratitude. The destruction of Qarun (Korah) and his mansion symbolizes how material wealth and worldly power provide no protection against God's punishment when accompanied by pride and disobedience. The verse emphasizes that no worldly possessions, companions, or resources can avail against God's judgment, and that true power lies only with the Divine, while human strength and support are ultimately powerless in the face of God's will.

translation: And those who yesterday wished to be in his place began to say, 'Woe to us! Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it. If not that Allah had favored us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us. Woe! Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the transformative effect of witnessing divine punishment and loss of worldly wealth. Those who envied the rich man's prosperity now recognize that wealth is not a measure of favor with Allah, and they acknowledge their dependence on His mercy. The verse teaches that material fortune is contingent on Allah's will alone, not on human merit, and that the absence of punishment in this life should inspire gratitude rather than arrogance. The concluding statement emphasizes that those who reject this truth and remain ungrateful for Allah's blessings cannot achieve true success.

translation: That is the home of the Hereafter which We assign to those who do not desire dominance on earth, nor corruption. And the good outcome is for the righteous.
interpretation: This verse illustrates that eternal paradise is reserved for those characterized by humility and righteousness - those who neither seek to oppress others through arrogance and superiority on earth, nor spread moral decay and destruction. The verse connects this noble character to ultimate success, teaching that true victory and honor belong to those who fear Allah and restrain themselves from worldly ambitions rooted in ego, showing that genuine greatness lies in spiritual restraint rather than earthly domination.

translation: Whoever comes with a good deed will have something better than it, and whoever comes with an evil deed - those who did evil deeds will not be recompensed except for what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse establishes the principle of divine justice and reward in the afterlife: good deeds are rewarded with something superior to the deed itself, reflecting God's generosity and bounty, while evil deeds receive equal recompense, reflecting the principle of proportionate justice. The asymmetry between reward and punishment teaches that God's mercy exceeds His justice, as the righteous receive more than they deserve while the wrongdoers receive exactly what they deserve.

translation: Indeed, He who has ordained upon you the Qur'an will restore you to a place of return. Say, 'My Lord is most knowing of who has brought guidance and who is in clear error.'
interpretation: This verse reassures the Prophet Muhammad that Allah, who revealed the Qur'an to him, will ultimately vindicate him and bring him to a place of final judgment and return (the Day of Resurrection). The Prophet is instructed to affirm that knowledge of who truly follows guidance and who remains in manifest error belongs exclusively to Allah, thus placing the burden of judgment with the Divine rather than with human opinion or the rejection of disbelievers, and establishing that success and vindication rest ultimately in Allah's hands alone.

translation: And you did not expect that the Book would be given to you except as a mercy from your Lord. So do not be a supporter of the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse reminds the Prophet Muhammad that receiving the Qur'an was purely an act of divine grace and mercy, not something he deserved or anticipated. The second part serves as a consequent warning: precisely because this revelation is a mercy from Allah, he must not align himself with or assist those who reject it. The verse emphasizes that accepting divine guidance obligates one to maintain moral boundaries and not compromise with those who deny the truth, as doing so would contradict the very mercy that was bestowed.

translation: And let them not avert you from the signs of Allah after they have been revealed to you. And call to your Lord, and be not among those who associate partners with Allah.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet Muhammad to remain steadfast in conveying Allah's message despite opposition and pressure from those who reject faith. It emphasizes the primary obligation of preaching monotheism and warns against compromising with polytheism or being swayed by the disbelievers' attempts to distract him from his divine mission. The verse underscores that true obedience lies in unwavering commitment to Allah's guidance and resisting the temptation to accommodate shirk (associating partners with Allah) in any form.

translation: And do not invoke with Allah another deity. There is no deity except Him. Everything will perish except His Face. To Him belongs all judgment, and to Him you will be returned.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute uniqueness and sovereignty of Allah by warning against associating partners with Him in worship, establishing that monotheism is the foundation of faith. The statement that 'everything will perish except His Face' conveys that all creation is perishable and dependent, while only Allah's eternal essence endures, thereby highlighting His transcendence and the vanity of relying on anything other than Him. The concluding affirmation that judgment belongs to Him alone and that all creation returns to Him reinforces His ultimate authority and the inevitable accountability before Him on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Alif, Lam, Meem
interpretation: These are among the mysterious letters (Huruf al-Muqatta'at) that appear at the beginning of certain Qur'anic chapters. While their exact meaning has been debated by scholars throughout Islamic history, they serve as a rhetorical device to arrest the listener's attention and emphasize the miraculous nature of the Qur'an—challenging those who doubted its divine origin to produce something similar despite understanding the Arabic alphabet and its letters. They may also represent a divine seal affirming the authenticity of the message that follows.

translation: Do people think they will be left alone because they say 'We believe,' without being tested?
interpretation: This verse establishes the principle that mere verbal profession of faith is insufficient without facing trials and tests that purify and strengthen one's faith. The verse challenges the assumption that believing Muslims will escape tribulation, conveying that adversity and hardship are divinely ordained as a means of distinguishing sincere believers from those whose faith is superficial or conditional. Through such trials, God separates the truthful from the hypocrites and refines the faith of the sincere.

translation: And We have already tested those before them. So Allah will surely make clear those who are truthful, and He will surely make clear the liars.
interpretation: This verse conveys that trials and afflictions are a divine mechanism through which Allah distinguishes between the sincere believers and those who are deceptive or insincere in their faith. The testing is not arbitrary punishment but rather a means of revealing the true nature and commitment of people—those who endure trials with steadfastness demonstrate their truthfulness, while those who falter or abandon their faith under hardship reveal themselves as false claimants. This principle applies across generations, establishing that tribulation serves as a clarifying filter in the human experience of faith.

translation: Or do those who do evil deeds think that they can outrun Us? How evil is what they judge!
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the inevitability of divine justice and the futility of attempting to escape God's reckoning. The verse rejects the false assumption that wrongdoers can evade divine accountability through speed or cunning. The phrase 'yasbiqu-na' (to outrun Us) conveys that no evildoer can escape God's grasp or hasten ahead of His justice. The concluding phrase 'sa'a ma yahkumun' (how evil is their judgment) criticizes the faulty reasoning and judgment of those who harbor such delusions, indicating that their belief in being able to escape divine consequences reflects a fundamentally flawed understanding of God's power and the nature of accountability in the afterlife.
