Their disbelief stems not from intellectual deficiency but from spiritual blindness rooted in their attachment to worldly comforts and social status. The verse highlights how material prosperity can become a barrier to faith, as those accustomed to their elevated position perceive the divine message as a threat to their existing order and privileges rather than as guidance for salvation.

translation: And they said, 'We are greater in wealth and children, and we will not be punished.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the arrogance and false sense of security that the disbelievers possessed, believing that their material prosperity and numerous offspring would protect them from divine punishment. Their statement reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of God's justice—they equated worldly abundance with divine favor and imagined themselves immune to accountability, when in reality material possessions have no bearing on one's fate in the Hereafter. This attitude exemplifies how wealth can blind people to spiritual truths and lead them to reject God's warnings.

translation: Say: 'Indeed, my Lord expands the provision for whom He wills and restricts it. But most of the people do not know.'
interpretation: This verse teaches that divine provision is distributed according to God's wisdom and will, not according to human expectations or merit. The apparent inequality in worldly sustenance is a test of faith, reminding believers that what they perceive as restriction may contain hidden blessings, and what seems abundant may be a trial. Most people fail to recognize that all sustenance ultimately comes from God and that true wealth lies in gratitude and spiritual richness rather than material accumulation.

translation: And your wealth and your children are not the things that will bring you closer to Us in rank, except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds. For those, there will be a multiplied reward for what they did, and they will be secure in the upper chambers.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that material possessions and offspring, which people often pursue as measures of success and sources of pride, hold no intrinsic value in God's sight. The true criterion for elevation in God's favor is faith combined with righteous action. The promise of a doubled reward and eternal security in Paradise is God's affirmation that spiritual achievement and moral conduct are the only lasting sources of honor and proximity to Him, thereby redirecting human values from worldly accumulation to spiritual devotion and ethical living.

translation: And those who strive against Our signs to prevent them - those will be brought into the punishment.
interpretation: This verse warns those who actively oppose and resist God's signs and revelations, attempting to obstruct their message or render them ineffective. The phrase 'معاجزين' (mu'ajizin) implies they seek to neutralize or counteract the divine signs. The verse conveys that such deliberate opposition and obstruction of God's message will inevitably lead to severe punishment, emphasizing that resistance to divine truth carries serious consequences in the afterlife.

translation: Say, 'Indeed, my Lord extends provision for whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it. And He is the best of providers.'
interpretation: This verse teaches that sustenance comes entirely from Allah's divine wisdom and will - He expands provision for some and restricts it for others according to His knowledge of what is best for each person. The assurance that whatever is spent in obedience to Allah will be replaced emphasizes that generosity and charitable spending should not be feared, as Allah guarantees compensation and is the most merciful provider. This addresses human anxiety about scarcity and encourages trust in divine providence.

translation: And [mention] the Day when He will gather them all together; then He will say to the angels, 'Did these [people] used to worship you?'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine humiliation and exposure of false worship on the Day of Judgment. Allah will publicly confront the polytheists before the angels, asking the angels whether they ever claimed or desired to be worshipped. This serves multiple purposes: it demonstrates the absurdity and futility of idolatry by having the accused 'gods' themselves deny any role in encouraging such worship, it vindicates the angels from complicity in shirk, and it sets the stage for the polytheists to face the full weight of their sin with no excuse or defense.

translation: They said, 'Exalted are You! You are our protector, not them.' Rather, they worshipped the jinn—most of them believed in them.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the irony and contradiction inherent in shirk (polytheism). The disbelievers invoke Allah and acknowledge His supremacy by declaring His transcendence (tasbih), yet in practice they do not limit their worship and devotion to Him alone. Instead, they direct their religious devotion and trust to the jinn, treating them as intermediaries and objects of faith. The contradiction between their verbal affirmation of Allah's superiority and their actual worship of created beings reveals the self-deception and internal inconsistency of polytheism—they confess the truth with their tongues while their hearts and actions are bound to false objects of devotion. This demonstrates how idolatry and false belief systems persistently conflict with and undermine the natural recognition of divine oneness that humans possess.

translation: So today you will not be able to help one another, nor will one of you be able to harm another. And We will say to those who wronged: 'Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the complete severance of all worldly bonds and mutual dependencies on the Day of Judgment, highlighting the absolute isolation each soul will experience before Allah. The statement to the wrongdoers that they will taste the very punishment they denied serves as a poignant reminder that the consequences of rejecting divine truth are not abstract or escapable, but tangible and inescapable realities that the deniers themselves will directly experience, making their previous rejection and mockery of these truths now manifest in their own suffering.

translation: And when Our clear verses are recited to them, they say, 'This is nothing but a man who wishes to turn you away from that which your fathers worshipped.' And they say, 'This is nothing but a fabricated falsehood.' And those who disbelieve say of the truth when it comes to them, 'This is nothing but obvious magic.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the multi-layered nature of disbelief and the various tactics used by those who reject the divine message. Rather than engaging with the substance of the truth presented through clear signs, the deniers resort to rhetorical deflections: attributing the Prophet's motivation to personal ambition, dismissing the revelation as fabrication, and reframing it as sorcery. This reveals that rejection often stems not from intellectual deficiency but from a willful turning away—rooted in the desire to preserve inherited traditions and resist the challenge to their worldviews. The progression from one excuse to another shows how denial lacks a coherent foundation, relying instead on whatever objection might temporarily suffice to dismiss the message.

translation: And We did not give them any scriptures to study, nor did We send to them any warner before you.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the unique position of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) as the first and primary messenger sent to the Arabs, highlighting that they were left without divine guidance or written revelation until his mission. It underscores the magnitude of the favor of sending the Qur'an and the Prophet to them, as they had been deprived of previous scriptures and messengers, thereby making their responsibility to accept and follow the message even greater.

translation: And those before them denied [the truth], and they did not attain [even] a tenth of what We had given them. But they denied My messengers, so how [terrible] was My reproach.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the pattern of rejection and ingratitude that persists across generations. Those who came before the addressees rejected God's truth despite being blessed with material abundance—yet they did not even reach one-tenth of the blessings given to the current generation. The verse emphasizes that their rejection of God's messengers was not due to deprivation but to willful denial and ingratitude for divine blessings. The rhetorical question at the end serves as a solemn warning about the terrible consequences of denying God's signs and messengers, inviting the current generation to reflect on the fate of their predecessors and avoid the same path of rejection.

translation: Say, 'I only advise you of one thing: that you stand for Allah, individually and in pairs, and then reflect. There is no madness in your companion. He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the fundamental principle of sincere devotion to Allah through mindful reflection and self-examination. The command to 'stand for Allah' individually and in pairs suggests that believers should engage in deliberate contemplation both in solitude and in consultation with others, using reason and reflection to understand the truth of the message. By defending the Prophet's sanity and clarifying his role as a warner, the verse invites people to approach his message with intellectual honesty rather than dismissal, urging them to recognize that accepting the message is not a matter of emotional impulse but of rational consideration of the serious consequences of rejecting divine guidance.

translation: Say: 'Whatever reward I have asked of you is for yourselves. My reward is only from Allah, and He is a Witness over all things.'
interpretation: The Prophet is instructed to clarify that any benefit from his message belongs to the people themselves, not to him. He seeks no material compensation from them, making clear that his motivation is purely divine, not personal gain. This establishes his credibility and removes any suspicion that he preaches for worldly benefit. By affirming that Allah alone is his true rewarder and witness to all deeds, he emphasizes the accountability before God that transcends human judgment, reinforcing the message's divine origin and the Prophet's sincerity in his mission.

translation: Say: 'Indeed, my Lord casts (or hurls) the truth - He is the Knower of the unseen.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that God's truth is forcefully and definitively established, and that this truth emanates from One who possesses complete knowledge of all hidden matters, whether past, present, or future. The metaphor of 'casting' or 'hurling' conveys the power and certainty with which divine truth is sent down, penetrating falsehood and establishing itself with irresistible force. The verse reassures the Prophet that he should confidently proclaim God's message, for it comes from an all-knowing source beyond human comprehension, and no hidden reality or secret agenda of those who reject it can escape God's knowledge.

translation: Say: 'The truth has come, and falsehood neither originates nor returns.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the definitive victory and permanence of truth over falsehood. The phrase 'neither originates nor returns' suggests that falsehood cannot create anything genuinely new or lasting, nor can it restore what truth has replaced. It conveys the idea that truth is self-sustaining and self-renewing, while falsehood is inherently sterile and temporary. The verse serves as a proclamation of divine truth's inevitable triumph, encouraging the Prophet and believers to be confident in their message despite opposition, as falsehood ultimately has no power to establish itself or perpetuate itself against divine truth.

translation: Say, 'If I have gone astray, then I go astray only to my own detriment. And if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, Ever-Near.'
interpretation: This verse establishes the accountability of the Prophet Muhammad and by extension all humanity for their choices, while emphasizing complete dependence on divine guidance. The asymmetry in responsibility—where misguidance is attributed to oneself alone while guidance comes entirely from God—illustrates that humans bear the consequences of rejecting truth, yet true guidance is exclusively a gift from Allah, not a human achievement. The closing affirmation of God's attributes reminds us that Divine guidance is not distant but intimately aware of and responsive to the sincere seeker.

translation: And if you could see when they are terrified, there will be no escape, and they are seized from a place near (at hand).
interpretation: This verse depicts the swift and inescapable punishment of the wrongdoers on the Day of Judgment. The phrase 'from a place near' suggests that divine punishment encompasses them from all directions and proximity, emphasizing that neither flight nor distance can save them from the consequences of their deeds. The proximity of the punishment underscores the absolute power and omnipresence of God's justice, leaving no refuge or means of escape for those who rejected faith.

translation: And they said, 'We believe in it,' but how can they attain it from a place so distant?
interpretation: This verse refers to those who rejected the message when it was presented to them during their lifetime, but then hoped to believe after death or in the Hereafter when the reality of the Deen becomes manifest. The 'distant place' symbolizes their removal from the opportunity to accept faith when it mattered—in the worldly life. The verse illustrates the futility of delayed belief and emphasizes that genuine faith must be embraced during one's lifetime when the choice is available. It serves as a warning that belief becomes impossible or unaccepted once one has rejected it in the world of obligation and trial.

translation: And they had disbelieved in it before, and they cast conjecture from a place far away.
interpretation: This verse describes the stubbornness and blindness of the disbelievers who reject the signs of Allah despite their clarity. They not only deny the truth when it is presented to them, but they also engage in baseless speculation and unfounded accusations from a distance, lacking any real knowledge or direct experience. The phrase 'from a place far away' suggests their detachment from the truth and the irrationality of their opposition—they speak without proper understanding, merely following conjecture and hearsay rather than evidence, which characterizes the nature of disbelief as being rooted in ignorance and stubborn denial rather than rational deliberation.

translation: And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire, as was done to their likes before. Indeed, they were in doubt, suspicious.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of divine justice whereby those who persistently reject truth and live in doubt are separated from their desires and good outcomes, just as their predecessors faced the same consequence. The phrase 'a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire' signifies that their own rejection and suspicion create a veil preventing them from attaining spiritual fulfillment and closeness to Allah. The reference to 'their likes before' emphasizes that this is a consistent pattern throughout history—denial of truth inevitably leads to deprivation—and the mention of their 'suspicious doubt' identifies the root cause of their condition: they refused to accept the signs with certainty, thereby sealing themselves off from guidance and blessing.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. All praise is due to Allah, the Creator of the heavens and the earth, who made the angels as messengers with wings—two, three, and four. He adds to creation what He wills. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse establishes Allah's absolute power and creative mastery by highlighting His creation of the heavens, earth, and angels. The mention of angels with varying numbers of wings (two, three, and four) demonstrates the diversity and precision of Allah's creation, while the statement that 'He adds to creation what He wills' emphasizes His limitless creative authority beyond what we can perceive or enumerate. The verse concludes by affirming that this power is boundless, as Allah is capable of all things, establishing the foundation for human submission and recognition of divine sovereignty.

translation: Whatever mercy Allah opens for the people, there is no one who can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, there is no one who can release it after Him. And He is the Mighty, the Wise.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of Allah over all provisions and blessings. It conveys that Allah alone has complete control over the distribution of mercy and sustenance to His creation, and no force in the universe can counteract His will. The verse teaches believers that their dependence should be entirely upon Allah, as all doors of blessing are in His hands alone, making it futile to seek help from anyone else or to rely on worldly means as the ultimate source of provision. The attributes of Might and Wisdom at the end underscore that His control is exercised with perfect power and divine wisdom.

translation: O mankind! Remember the favor of Allah upon you. Is there any creator other than Allah who provides for you from the sky and the earth? There is no deity except Him. So how are you turning away?
interpretation: This verse is a call to humanity to reflect upon and acknowledge Allah's blessings and their complete dependence on Him for sustenance, using the existence of provision from the heavens and earth as evidence of His unique creative and sustaining power. The verse serves to rebuke those who, despite witnessing these clear signs of Allah's oneness and provision, turn away from monotheism and associate partners with Him, highlighting the irrationality of ingratitude and polytheism in the face of undeniable divine favor.

translation: And if they deny you, then messengers before you were indeed denied. And to Allah are returned all matters.
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by reminding him that rejection by people is not unprecedented in the prophetic tradition, nor is it a reflection of the truth or falsity of the message. Rather, it is a pattern throughout history that messengers have faced denial. The verse also establishes that despite human rejection, ultimate judgment and justice rest with Allah alone, who will determine the final outcome of all affairs. This serves to strengthen the Prophet's resolve by contextualizing his struggle within the broader divine plan.

translation: O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true. So let not the worldly life delude you, and let not the deceiver delude you concerning Allah.
interpretation: This verse warns humanity against two forms of deception that lead people away from accountability before Allah: the allure and distraction of worldly pursuits that make people heedless of the afterlife, and the whispers of Shaytan (the deceiver) who causes people to doubt or become complacent regarding Allah's judgment. The verse establishes that Allah's promise of the Day of Judgment is absolute truth, and therefore people must not allow temporary worldly concerns or satanic temptation to obscure this reality and cause them to neglect their spiritual obligations and preparation for the afterlife.

translation: Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his party to become inhabitants of the blaze.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the necessity of recognizing Satan as a sworn adversary whose sole purpose is to lead mankind toward destruction and punishment. By characterizing Satan's call as extending only to 'his party' (those who accept his whisperings), the Qur'an illustrates that Satan's influence is not forced upon humanity but rather operates through persuasion of those who align themselves with his goals. The command to 'take him as an enemy' calls for conscious vigilance and active resistance against Satan's temptations, implying that believers must deliberately maintain awareness of his enmity and reject his suggestions, thereby distinguishing themselves from those who become his followers destined for hellfire.

translation: Those who disbelieve - for them is a severe punishment. And those who believe and do righteous deeds - for them is forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: This verse establishes the fundamental principle of divine justice in the Hereafter: accountability is determined by one's faith and actions. The contrast between the two groups emphasizes that disbelief and righteous deeds are not morally equivalent - those who reject God's message face consequences proportional to their choice, while those who combine sincere belief with virtuous conduct receive God's mercy and boundless recompense. The verse thus motivates believers to maintain both inner conviction and outward obedience, as salvation requires the integration of faith (belief in God) with practical righteousness (good deeds).

translation: Is he, then, to whom the evil of his deed has been made fair-seeming, so that he considers it good, [like one who is rightly guided]? For God lets go astray whom He wills, and guides whom He wills. So let not your soul waste away in grief over them. Verily, God is All-Knowing of what they do.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet's emotional burden regarding those who reject faith despite clear guidance. The passage explains that some people become so enslaved to their desires that they perceive evil as good—a spiritual blindness that results from their persistent rejection of truth. The verse establishes that divine guidance and misguidance operate according to God's wisdom and the people's own choices and conditions of heart. The instruction to the Prophet not to grieve excessively teaches that while believers must convey the message with sincere concern, ultimate responsibility for people's choices rests with God alone. This brings solace to the Prophet by reminding him that his duty is to communicate clearly, and that God's knowledge encompasses all hidden intentions and actions—nothing escapes His awareness or wisdom.

translation: And Allah is the one who sent the winds, so they stir up clouds, and We drove it to a dead land, and We revived the earth with it after its death. Thus is the resurrection.
interpretation: This verse uses the natural phenomenon of rain reviving dead land as a metaphor for divine resurrection and the bringing back to life on the Day of Judgment. Just as Allah demonstrates His power to restore lifeless earth through wind and rain, He similarly possesses the absolute power to resurrect all creation after death, establishing a logical connection between observable natural signs and the unseen reality of the Hereafter.

translation: Whoever desires honor - to Allah belongs all honor. To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deeds raise it. But those who plot evils for them is a severe punishment, and the plotting of those will perish.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true honor and dignity come exclusively from Allah and cannot be obtained through worldly means or corrupt ambitions. It teaches that the path to elevation with Allah consists of pure speech combined with righteous actions, which together create a synergy of spiritual ascendancy. The second part serves as a warning that those who substitute honest means with evil schemes and deception will find their efforts ultimately destroyed and themselves punished, illustrating the divine principle that corruption and schemes against truth are inherently self-defeating and deserve divine retribution.

translation: And Allah created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then He made you pairs. And no female conceives nor does she give birth except by His knowledge. And no one is granted long life nor is his life shortened except in a Record. Indeed, that for Allah is easy.
interpretation: This verse establishes Allah's complete sovereignty over creation and all aspects of human life - from origin to reproduction to the span of years. The progression from dust to sperm-drop to pairs illustrates the stages of creation, while the emphasis on conception, birth, and lifespan occurring only by Allah's knowledge (علمه) demonstrates that nothing in existence happens outside His awareness and decree. The concluding statement that 'this is easy for Allah' emphasizes that managing and controlling all these matters requires no effort for the Divine, highlighting the absolute power and effortless nature of Allah's dominion over creation and time itself.

translation: And the two seas are not alike. This is fresh, palatable to drink, and that is salty and bitter. And from each you eat fresh meat and extract ornaments which you wear. And you see the ships therein plowing through it, that you might seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine wisdom in creating two distinct bodies of water with opposite characteristics—one fresh and drinkable, the other salty and undrinkable—as evidence of God's perfect design and providence. The distinction between these two seas serves as a metaphor for how God has arranged the natural world with careful differentiation and purpose, providing sustenance through fish and pearls, enabling commerce through ships, and inviting human reflection on divine bounty as a catalyst for gratitude. The verse emphasizes that recognition of these divinely created differences and the benefits derived from them should inspire thankfulness to the Creator.

translation: He merges the night into the day and merges the day into the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion. And those whom you invoke other than Him do not possess even the thin membrane of a date pit.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute sovereignty and the futility of polytheism by contrasting the precise, ordered system of celestial mechanics—where day and night transition, sun and moon orbit in perfect measure—with the complete powerlessness of idols. The metaphor of the date pit's membrane (the thinnest, most worthless thing) illustrates that the idols possess not even the most insignificant fraction of power, underscoring the irrationality of devoting worship to beings who lack dominion over creation, let alone themselves.

translation: If you call upon them, they will not hear your call, and even if they heard, they could not respond to you. And on the Day of Resurrection, they will deny your association of them with Allah. And none can inform you like the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the futility and spiritual bankruptcy of associating partners with Allah in worship. The idols and false gods that polytheists invoke cannot perceive, hear, or respond to their pleas—highlighting the absurdity of directing worship toward lifeless entities incapable of agency or compassion. Furthermore, on the Day of Judgment, these false deities will themselves renounce any connection to those who worshipped them, leaving their adherents completely abandoned. The final clause asserts that only Allah, who is all-knowing and all-seeing, possesses true knowledge of reality and can provide authoritative guidance about the consequences of shirk (associating partners with God), making polytheism not merely ineffective but fundamentally delusional.

translation: O mankind, you are the poor in need of Allah, and Allah - He is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute dependence of all creation upon Allah, establishing that human poverty and need (faqr) before Allah is not merely a material condition but a fundamental existential reality. Regardless of worldly wealth or power, every soul stands in complete need of Allah's sustenance, guidance, and mercy. In contrast, Allah possesses perfect self-sufficiency and needs nothing from creation, while being worthy of all praise. The verse thus corrects any false sense of self-reliance or arrogance in humans by reminding them of their inherent weakness and servitude before their Creator.

translation: If He wills, He can take you away and bring a new creation
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute power and sovereignty over creation. It conveys that human existence is entirely dependent on God's will - just as He created humanity initially, He has the power to remove them entirely and replace them with an entirely new creation. This serves as a reminder of human insignificance before Divine might and is intended to humble those who might be arrogant or disobedient, emphasizing that our very existence and continuation are contingent upon God's permission and will alone.

translation: And that is not difficult for Allah.
interpretation: This phrase emphasizes Allah's absolute power and capability to accomplish anything. It conveys that what may seem impossible or difficult to human beings is trivial and effortless for Allah, reinforcing the concept of divine omnipotence and removing any doubt about His ability to fulfill His promises, resurrect the dead, or bring about any event He wills.

translation: No soul shall bear the burden of another. And if a heavily laden soul calls (another) to carry its load, nothing of it shall be carried, even if they are relatives. You can only warn those who fear their Lord in the unseen and establish prayer. And whoever purifies himself, purifies himself for his own benefit. And to Allah is the final return.
interpretation: This verse establishes the fundamental Islamic principle of individual accountability before God, emphasizing that each person bears sole responsibility for their own deeds and cannot transfer their sins or spiritual burden to others, regardless of kinship. The passage further clarifies that the Prophet's role is to warn only those whose hearts are receptive—those who possess God-consciousness and actively practice righteousness—while spiritual purification undertaken by anyone is ultimately a personal spiritual investment from which they themselves benefit, with all souls ultimately returning to God for judgment based on their individual record of deeds.

translation: And the blind and the sighted are not equal
interpretation: This verse uses the physical contrast between blindness and sight as a metaphor for the difference between spiritual ignorance and knowledge, particularly regarding belief in God and His revelation. It illustrates that those who reject faith and guidance are like the blind in their spiritual perception, while those who accept and follow divine guidance are like those with sight. The verse emphasizes that the states of believers and disbelievers are fundamentally incomparable in terms of their understanding, guidance, and closeness to truth.

translation: And not the darknesses and not the light
interpretation: This verse reflects God's transcendence beyond physical categories and human perceptions. The darknesses and light represent all observable, measurable phenomena and contrasts in the created world. By negating both, the Qur'an emphasizes that God is beyond such dualities and limitations, signifying His absolute uniqueness and that nothing in creation can be compared to Him. He is neither dependent on nor contained within the physical laws and visual categories that humans use to understand reality.

translation: And not the shade, nor the heat
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment when the righteous will be protected from the scorching heat of the sun while the disbelievers will be left without shelter or shade. It emphasizes that on that Day, neither the comfort of shade nor any relief from the intense heat will be available to those who rejected the truth, illustrating the stark contrast between the fate of the believers and the disbelievers in the Hereafter.

translation: And not equal are the living and the dead. Indeed, Allah hears whom He wills, and you cannot make hear those in the graves.
interpretation: This verse establishes a fundamental distinction between those who are spiritually alive through faith and receptiveness to guidance, and those who are spiritually dead through rejection and heedlessness. The reference to graves symbolizes spiritual death and the impossibility of revival for those whose hearts have been sealed. The verse teaches that hearing Allah's message is ultimately a matter of divine will and grace, not merely human effort—one cannot compel others to accept guidance no matter how much one communicates, as the capacity to truly hear and understand is a gift from Allah that He grants to whom He wills.

translation: You are nothing but a warner.
interpretation: This verse establishes the Prophet Muhammad's primary role and limitation: he is sent as a messenger to warn people of the consequences of disbelief and to convey God's message, but he is not responsible for their acceptance of faith. His duty is to deliver the message clearly and persistently, while belief or disbelief remains the choice of each individual. This underscores the principle that prophets are communicators of divine truth, not compellers of hearts, and teaches that the Prophet should not feel burdened by those who reject his message, as guidance is ultimately from God alone.

translation: Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of good tidings and a warner. And there is no nation but that a warner has passed through it.
interpretation: This verse establishes that prophethood is a continuous divine pattern throughout human history. The mention of sending the Prophet Muhammad with both good tidings (bashir) and warning (nadhir) reflects the dual nature of prophetic mission—to encourage righteousness and to caution against disobedience. The second part affirms that this pattern of divine guidance through warners is not unique to the Prophet's time but represents an eternal divine principle, meaning Allah has always sent messengers to every community to ensure no people are without guidance. This underscores both the universality of prophetic responsibility and the accountability of all peoples for receiving or rejecting divine messages.

translation: And if they deny you, then those before them also denied. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, the scriptures, and the enlightening book.
interpretation: This verse provides historical and theological consolation to the Prophet Muhammad by reminding him that the rejection he faces is not unique or unexpected. The pattern of rejecting messengers is a recurring theme throughout human history, as documented in previous scriptures. The reference to 'clear proofs,' 'scriptures,' and 'the enlightening book' emphasizes that messengers were not sent without adequate evidence and divine guidance. This interpretation suggests that Allah's message has always been accompanied by sufficient signs and written revelation to guide those willing to believe, and that rejection is a consequence of human choice rather than a deficiency in the message itself. The verse thus serves to strengthen the Prophet's resolve by contextualizing contemporary disbelief within a universal historical pattern ordained by Allah.

translation: Then We seized those who disbelieved. So how was My rejection (of them)?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's power to punish those who reject His signs and deny His oneness. The rhetorical question 'How was My rejection of them?' is meant to highlight the severity and completeness of Allah's punishment, inviting reflection on the consequences of disbelief and rejection of divine guidance. It serves as a warning to believers about the inevitable consequences of turning away from Allah's message.

translation: Have you not seen that Allah has sent down water from the sky, and with it We have brought forth fruits of various colors? And from the mountains are streaks of white and red, varying in their colors, and [some] extremely black.
interpretation: This verse invites reflection upon the divine signs in creation, demonstrating Allah's power and wisdom through the multiplicity and variation visible in nature. The mention of water as the source of life and fertility, the diverse fruits it produces, and the varied colors of mountains all serve as evidence of Allah's intentional design and creative mastery. The verse uses sensory observation as a means to guide human consciousness toward recognition of divine agency and the futility of denying such manifest signs.

translation: And among mankind and animals and livestock, there are creatures of different colors likewise. Indeed, only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Mighty and Forgiving.
interpretation: The verse establishes a hierarchy of understanding and spiritual awareness: just as Allah demonstrates His creative power through the visible diversity of His creation, He expects His servants to recognize His majesty through knowledge ('ilm). True fear of Allah (khashyah) is not a blind or emotional response, but rather a consequence of genuine knowledge and understanding of His attributes, power, and wisdom. Those who possess such knowledge—encompassing both rational understanding and spiritual insight—are the ones who develop genuine reverence for Allah. The verse indicates that fear of Allah is proportional to one's comprehension of divine truths, suggesting that ignorance and understanding represent different spiritual states.

translation: Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah and establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly, hope for a trade that will never fail.
interpretation: This verse describes the characteristics of the truly faithful believers and illustrates that their obedience to Allah—through reciting His Book, establishing prayer, and giving charity both privately and publicly—is motivated by sincere hope in Allah's eternal reward. Their actions constitute a spiritual investment with Allah that yields returns far exceeding any worldly gain, as their transaction is guaranteed never to diminish or be lost, emphasizing the absolute trustworthiness and permanence of Allah's promises to those who are sincere in their devotion.

translation: So that He may give them their wages in full and increase them from His bounty. Indeed, He is Forgiving and Appreciative.
interpretation: This verse illustrates Allah's divine justice and generosity toward those who do righteous deeds. The phrase 'give them their wages in full' signifies that no good deed goes unrewarded, emphasizing the certainty of divine recompense. The additional phrase 'and increase them from His bounty' reveals that Allah's reward transcends mere equivalence—He grants abundantly beyond what is deserved. The concluding attributes 'Forgiving and Appreciative' establish a profound theological principle: Allah overlooks human shortcomings and deficiencies (Ghafur) while simultaneously recognizing and rewarding even the smallest acts of obedience and faith (Shakur). Together, these names convey that the Divine mercy encompasses both clemency for sins and magnanimous recognition of virtue, creating an incentive for believers to trust in Allah's generosity and strive toward righteousness.

translation: And what We have revealed to you of the Book is the truth, confirming what came before it. Indeed, Allah is ever Watchful and All-Seeing over His servants.
interpretation: This verse establishes the divine authentication of the Qur'an by affirming its truth and its role as a confirmation of previous scriptures, while simultaneously emphasizing that Allah's perfect knowledge and vigilant oversight of His servants encompasses both their faith in this revelation and their actions in response to it. The verse connects epistemological certainty about revelation with the practical consequence of divine accountability, suggesting that accepting the truth of the Qur'an must be paired with awareness that one's deeds and beliefs are never hidden from Allah's perfect knowledge.

translation: Then We granted the Book as inheritance to those whom We chose from among Our servants. So among them is one who wrongs himself, among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who races ahead in good deeds by the permission of Allah. That is the great bounty.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the diversity of human response to divine guidance despite receiving the same revelation. The three categories of inheritors of the Book represent the reality that divine knowledge and scripture are received differently by people based on their choices and efforts: some use it harmfully against themselves through disobedience, some maintain balance in faith and practice, and some excel in virtue and obedience. This classification emphasizes personal responsibility and free will within the framework of divine grace, demonstrating that the inheritance of sacred knowledge creates differentiated outcomes determined ultimately by human choice and divine will working in concert.

translation: Gardens of Eden - they will enter them, wherein they will be adorned with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their garments therein will be silk.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the material pleasures and beautification that await the righteous in Paradise, signifying not mere worldly indulgence but rather the fulfillment of human dignity and the manifestation of honor and esteem in the divine presence. The mention of gold, pearls, and silk represents a state of complete well-being where even the adornments and clothing reflect purity and refinement, emphasizing that heavenly reward transcends earthly luxury through its spiritual perfection and permanence.

translation: And they will say: 'All praise is due to Allah, who has removed from us [all] sorrow. Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the gratitude of the inhabitants of Paradise as they reflect on their deliverance from worldly suffering and spiritual distress. The phrase 'Forgiving' (Ghafur) refers to Allah's pardoning of their sins that could have prevented their salvation, while 'Appreciative' (Shakur) indicates that Allah rewards the believers abundantly for their small deeds and remembrance of Him. The verse emphasizes that divine mercy is not merely the erasure of harm, but an active appreciation and magnification of human effort, suggesting that Allah's grace multiplies the value of righteous deeds beyond what they objectively merit.

translation: He who has made us settle in the House of Permanence out of His grace - no fatigue shall touch us therein, nor shall weariness touch us therein.
interpretation: This verse reflects the believer's grateful recognition of Divine grace in granting them residence in Paradise. The repetition of the phrase 'shall not touch us' emphasizes complete immunity from all forms of suffering - both nصب (physical fatigue) and لغوب (weariness and exhaustion). The verse teaches that Paradise is a state of perfect comfort and rest, distinguished by the absolute absence of any hardship or suffering that characterizes earthly life. The emphasis on Divine grace (من فضله) indicates that this blessing is entirely undeserved and dependent on Allah's mercy rather than human merit, instilling humility in the believer's heart.

translation: And those who disbelieve, for them is the fire of Hell. They will not be allowed to die therein so they may be relieved, nor will the punishment thereof be lightened for them. Thus do We recompense every ingrate.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the eternal and unrelenting nature of the punishment for those who reject faith, establishing that disbelief in God and ingratitude toward His blessings result in unending torment without respite or possibility of annihilation as an escape from suffering. The denial of both death as relief and any diminishment of punishment underscores the consequence of choosing persistent ingratitude and rejection of divine truth.

translation: And they will cry out therein, saying: 'Our Lord, remove us from this; we will do righteous deeds other than what we used to do.' Did We not give you a lifespan long enough for whoever wished to take heed to take heed, and did not the warner come to you? So taste [the punishment], for the wrongdoers have no helper.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the accountability of those who denied the message during their lifetime. Their plea for a second chance in the afterlife is rejected through a rhetorical question pointing to the sufficient respite Allah gave them in this world to reflect and reform. The mention of the warner coming to them stresses that they had been provided with clear guidance and opportunity for repentance, making their rejection inexcusable. The verse teaches that the window for repentance is in this life alone, and delaying reform until after one enters Hell demonstrates the futility of regret when the time for action has passed. It serves as a warning to believers to seize the opportunity of this life for obedience while they still can.

translation: Indeed, Allah is the Knower of the unseen of the heavens and the earth. Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the hearts (of people).
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute and comprehensive knowledge that extends beyond the realm of human perception. While humans are limited to observing the manifest world, Allah's knowledge encompasses all hidden matters in creation, including the innermost thoughts and intentions within human hearts. This establishes that no thought, feeling, or secret intention can remain hidden from Allah, which serves as a foundation for accountability on the Day of Judgment and reinforces the importance of sincerity in faith and actions, as external deeds are meaningless without genuine intention (niyyah).

translation: He is the One who made you successors on the earth. So whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief. And their disbelief does not increase the disbelievers except in hatred with their Lord. And their disbelief does not increase them except in loss.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes personal accountability for one's choice to reject faith: each person bears the consequence of their own disbelief, and that disbelief simultaneously increases both God's hatred toward them and their own spiritual ruin. The repetition of the phrase about disbelief increasing loss underscores the compounding nature of rejection—that turning away from truth creates both a severing of the relationship with God and a progressive deterioration of one's condition in this life and the next.

translation: Say, 'Have you considered your partners whom you invoke besides Allah? Show me what they have created from the earth, or do they have a share in the heavens? Or have We given them a book so they are upon clear evidence from it?' Rather, the wrongdoers do not promise one another except delusion.
interpretation: This verse challenges the logical fallacy of polytheism by demanding empirical evidence for the divine status of idols and false deities. The rhetorical questions establish that these supposed partners with Allah possess none of the attributes of divinity—they create nothing, control no portion of the cosmos, and possess no revealed guidance. The final statement reveals that the mutual assurances between those who associate partners with Allah are baseless deceptions, illustrating how false religious beliefs are perpetuated through empty promises rather than any substantive foundation, thereby exposing the irrational nature of shirk (associating partners with Allah).

translation: Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth, lest they cease to exist. And if they were to cease, none could hold them [in place] after Him. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute power and control over the universe's continued existence. The cosmos remains in perfect order only through Allah's constant preservation and divine will. The mention of Allah being forbearing and forgiving at the verse's end suggests that despite humanity's weakness and dependence on His maintenance of creation, Allah continues to sustain all things with mercy rather than destruction, demonstrating His clemency toward His creation even as they remain entirely dependent on His preservation.

translation: And they swore by Allah their strongest oaths that if a warner came to them, they would be more guided than any of the nations. But when a warner came to them, it only increased them in aversion.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the contradiction between human arrogance and actual spiritual readiness. The people's confident oath that they would follow guidance if it came reveals their self-deception—they believed themselves capable of recognizing and accepting truth when presented. However, when the Prophet Muhammad came as the promised warner, instead of accepting his message, they turned away with greater hostility. The verse exposes how those who lack sincere commitment to truth often confuse theoretical willingness with actual receptiveness, and how pride and stubbornness can transform a messenger's arrival into an occasion for increased rejection rather than reform.

translation: Out of arrogance in the earth and evil plotting. But evil plotting does not encompass except its own people. So do they await except the way of the former peoples? For you will never find in the way of Allah any change, and you will never find in the way of Allah any alteration.
interpretation: This verse establishes the divine law that arrogance and evil deception inevitably return upon those who perpetrate them, and that Allah's established patterns of dealing with wrongdoers are immutable and unchangeable. The believer is being assured that the same principles that destroyed previous nations will apply to the arrogant disbelievers of every age, emphasizing the certainty and constancy of divine justice throughout history.

translation: Have they not traveled through the land and observed how was the end of those before them? And they were stronger than them in power. And there is nothing that could escape Allah in the heavens or on the earth. Indeed, He is ever Knowing and Powerful.
interpretation: This verse calls humanity to reflect upon the historical consequences that befell previous civilizations who were materially stronger and more powerful, yet were destroyed due to their disobedience and rejection of God's signs. The verse emphasizes that no one can evade God's knowledge or escape His power, serving as a warning that material strength and superiority offer no protection against divine justice, and that the same fate awaits those who follow the path of those before them in denial and transgression.

translation: And if Allah were to punish the people for what they have earned, He would not leave upon it any creature. But He defers them to a specified term. So when their term comes, then indeed Allah is ever Seeing of His servants.
interpretation: This verse demonstrates Allah's mercy and forbearance toward humanity despite their continuous wrongdoing. The hyperbolic imagery of not leaving a single living creature on earth emphasizes the severity of human sins and how they deserve immediate punishment. However, Allah's choice to postpone accountability to an appointed time reveals His wisdom in granting respite, allowing people opportunity for repentance and reform. The final clause about Allah being watchful of His servants serves as a reminder that this deferment is not out of heedlessness but out of deliberate divine knowledge and ultimate justice—Allah sees all and will settle accounts when their appointed time arrives.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Ya-Seen.
interpretation: This verse represents the opening invocation (Basmala) followed by the mysterious letter "Ya-Seen" (Ys), which is one of the abbreviated letters (Huruf Muqatta'at) that appear at the beginning of certain chapters of the Qur'an. These mysterious letters serve as a reminder of the inimitable nature of the Qur'an and its divine origin, challenging those who claim they can produce something similar to acknowledge that despite knowing all the letters of the Arabic language, they cannot replicate the Qur'an's eloquence and wisdom, thereby establishing the absolute proof of the Qur'an's divine authorship.

translation: By the Qur'an, full of wisdom
interpretation: This is an oath sworn by Allah upon the Qur'an itself, emphasizing its divine nature and perfect wisdom. The swearing by the Qur'an indicates its supreme importance and serves to draw attention to a consequential statement that follows. The attribute 'al-hakeem' (the wise) underscores that every word, command, and guidance within the Qur'an contains profound divine wisdom that surpasses human understanding, demonstrating that the Qur'an is not merely a book of laws but a complete system of guidance rooted in infinite divine knowledge.

translation: Indeed, you are of the messengers
interpretation: This verse affirms the prophetic status of Muhammad (peace be upon him), declaring with certainty that he belongs to the lineage of God's messengers. The use of 'inna' (إن) adds emphasis and conviction to this statement, reflecting divine affirmation of his mission and authority as a messenger chosen by God to convey revelation to humanity.

translation: Upon a straight path
interpretation: This phrase, which appears in Surah Al-Fatihah (1:6), refers to the guided path of monotheism, righteousness, and obedience to Allah. The 'straight path' (al-sirat al-mustaqim) represents the way of truth that leads to salvation and divine favor, in contrast to the ways of those who have gone astray or incurred Allah's wrath. It signifies the necessity of seeking divine guidance and adherence to the teachings of Islam throughout one's life.

translation: The revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful
interpretation: This phrase emphasizes that the Qur'an is a divine revelation sent down from Allah, who possesses absolute power and might (Al-'Aziz) and encompasses all mercy (Ar-Rahman). The designation of these two divine attributes at the outset of revelation establishes that divine guidance combines both justice and compassion—the strength to enforce truth and the mercy to guide humanity toward it. This frames the entire revelation as coming from a source of ultimate authority that is simultaneously infinitely merciful, assuring believers that the Qur'an's guidance, though demanding, is fundamentally an act of divine compassion.

translation: To warn a people whose fathers were not warned, so they are heedless.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine purpose of revelation as a mercy to those who have had no prior guidance. The focus is on warning those in spiritual darkness who lack the benefit of their ancestors' instruction. Their heedlessness is both a result of this deprivation and a manifestation of their turning away from the signs of Allah. The verse underscores that the Messenger's task is to awaken the conscience of people who have inherited ignorance rather than knowledge, making the responsibility of the message even more crucial for their salvation.

translation: The word has already been fulfilled against most of them, for they will not believe.
interpretation: This verse conveys the divine decree that disbelief has become the established fate of the majority, reflecting the Qur'anic principle that those who persistently reject truth and close their hearts to guidance have crossed a point beyond which their transformation becomes unlikely. It emphasizes the consequences of rejecting divine signs - not as arbitrary punishment, but as a natural result of one's own choices and the hardening of the heart that follows sustained rejection of truth.

translation: Indeed, We have placed upon their necks shackles that reach to their chins, so their heads are forced upward.
interpretation: This verse depicts the spiritual and metaphorical bondage of those who reject faith and divine guidance. The shackles reaching to the chin and forcing the head upward symbolize the constraints and distortions of their nature caused by their disbelief—they are imprisoned in their own denial, unable to see or accept the truth. The imagery conveys that their stubborn rejection of God's signs has become a self-imposed prison that prevents them from achieving spiritual freedom and understanding, representing the inevitable psychological and spiritual consequences of turning away from divine guidance.

translation: And We have placed before them a barrier and behind them a barrier, and We have covered them, so they do not see.
interpretation: This verse describes the spiritual blindness and deafness that befalls those who persistently reject the truth after it has been made clear to them. The 'barriers' represent the multiple obstacles and impediments that prevent them from perceiving and understanding the signs of Allah, both in terms of past warnings and future consequences. The covering (ghashiyyah) symbolizes how Allah seals their hearts, minds, and senses as a natural consequence of their own choice to turn away from guidance. This is a punishment that corresponds to their actions—they chose not to see, so Allah grants them their wish by removing the ability to perceive truth from their hearts.

translation: And it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them - they will not believe.
interpretation: This verse describes the spiritual state of those whose hearts have been sealed by Allah due to their persistent rejection of truth and guidance. Their disbelief is not due to a lack of clarity in the message or insufficient warning from the Prophet, but rather stems from their own willful turning away and hardened hearts. The verse emphasizes that when people consistently reject divine signs and guidance, they reach a condition where external warnings become ineffective, as their choice to disbelieve has become firmly established in their nature. This conveys the principle that guidance and faith ultimately depend on divine will and human receptivity, not merely on the repetition of warnings.

translation: You can only warn those who follow the Reminder and fear the Most Merciful unseen. So give them good tidings of forgiveness and a generous reward.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the Prophet's warning and message are effective only for those who are already inclined toward faith—those who follow divine guidance and maintain fear of Allah even when unseen. The verse emphasizes that sincere belief stems from an internal consciousness of God's presence and majesty. The good news of forgiveness and generous reward is specifically for these believers, indicating that receptiveness to divine warning is itself a sign of Allah's grace upon the believer, and those who respond to the reminder with reverence will ultimately receive Allah's mercy and honor.

translation: Indeed, We give life to the dead and We record what they have sent forward and their traces. And all things We have enumerated in a Clear Record.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes divine omniscience and accountability, asserting that God preserves a complete record of all human actions—both the deeds performed and their lasting consequences—in an eternal, manifest register. It establishes that nothing escapes God's knowledge or documentation, and serves as a powerful reminder that all actions will be accounted for on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And strike for them an example of the people of the city, when the messengers came to it.
interpretation: This verse introduces a parable that illustrates the consequences of rejecting divine guidance. Allah commands the Prophet to present the story of a city whose inhabitants rejected the messengers sent to them as a cautionary example for the disbelievers of Mecca. The parable serves to demonstrate that rejection of God's messengers is not unprecedented and has always led to dire consequences, thereby warning the Prophet's contemporaries about the gravity of their own denial and the inevitable punishment that follows such rejection.

translation: When We sent to them two [messengers], they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third. They said, 'Indeed, we are messengers sent to you.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine pattern of sending messengers with increasing emphasis and support. When the initial message was rejected, God reinforced His message by sending an additional messenger, demonstrating that rejection of truth necessitates stronger evidence and renewed calls to guidance. The multiplication of messengers serves as both a mercy to the people and a means of removing all excuses for disbelief, establishing that God's message is undeniable and demands serious consideration.

translation: They said: 'You are nothing but human beings like us, and the Most Merciful has not sent down anything. You are only lying.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the arrogant dismissal of the disbelievers toward the prophets and their message. By claiming the prophets are merely ordinary humans like themselves, the disbelievers use a reductionist argument to reject divine revelation, implying that extraordinary claims require no extraordinary evidence and that human messengers lack credibility. Their assertion that God has sent down nothing reflects their refusal to acknowledge the signs and revelations presented to them, attributing the message itself to human fabrication rather than divine origin. This represents the fundamental denial of prophecy rooted in pride and the refusal to submit to guidance from those they consider their equals.

translation: They said, 'Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the messengers' confidence in their divine commission despite facing rejection from their people. By appealing to God's knowledge as their ultimate witness and source of authority, they anchor their credibility not in human persuasion or signs, but in the divine truth of their mission, suggesting that true conviction comes from trusting in God's knowledge and plan rather than seeking worldly validation or immediate acceptance from the audience.

translation: And upon us is nothing except the clear conveyance.
interpretation: This verse establishes the fundamental responsibility of the Prophet and believers as messengers: to clearly and plainly communicate the divine message to humanity. The verse defines the boundary of human duty—to deliver the message faithfully and unambiguously—while freeing the messenger from responsibility for whether people accept or reject it. The emphasis on 'clear conveyance' (البلاغ المبين) underscores that the message must be presented in an unmistakable, comprehensible manner, free from obscurity or ambiguity. This principle liberates the messenger from the burden of controlling people's hearts or forcing acceptance, shifting accountability to those who receive the message while ensuring the messenger has fulfilled their sacred trust.

translation: They said, 'We see an ill omen in you. If you do not desist, we will surely stone you, and there will befall you from us a painful punishment.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates how people attribute their misfortunes to the messengers and believers, blaming them for perceived bad luck or calamity. The disbelievers' threat of violence reveals their hardened hearts and resort to intimidation when confronted with the message of truth. Their accusation of causing misfortune (tatayyarna) through superstitious belief demonstrates the psychological mechanism by which people reject divine guidance—they externalize their own spiritual confusion onto the bearers of the message rather than examining their own resistance to truth. The verse highlights the eternal pattern of persecution faced by those who call to monotheism, emphasizing that such opposition stems from arrogance and spiritual blindness rather than rational objection.

translation: They said, 'Your fate-bird is with you. Is it because you reminded us? Rather, you are a transgressive people.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the stubbornness and rejection of disbelievers who attribute their misfortunes to bad omens (the 'fate-bird' - a pre-Islamic Arab practice) rather than accepting divine guidance. By blaming the messengers for bringing bad luck through their reminders of God's oneness, they reveal their resistance to truth and their tendency to exceed bounds in wrongdoing and denial of God's signs. The phrase emphasizes that disbelief itself, not the messenger's call, is what leads to their downfall.

translation: And there came from the farthest end of the city a man running. He said, 'O my people, follow the messengers.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the power of individual conviction and courage in facing collective blindness. The man's urgency (expressed through 'running') and his isolation (coming alone from the city's periphery) underscore the difficulty of standing against the prevailing disbelief of one's community. His direct appeal to follow the messengers represents the fundamental Islamic principle that salvation and truth come through obedience to God's prophets, and it emphasizes that sincere guidance often comes from unexpected sources and individuals willing to risk their social standing for truth.

translation: Follow those who do not ask you for any reward and who are rightly guided.
interpretation: This verse instructs believers to follow and emulate those righteous individuals—such as the prophets and their truthful followers—who sincerely convey the divine message without seeking worldly compensation, material gain, or personal benefit. The phrase 'and they are rightly guided' emphasizes that such selfless devotion to truth is itself a sign and confirmation of their spiritual rectitude and alignment with God's guidance, making them reliable exemplars of faith.

translation: And why should I not worship the One who created me, and to Him you will be returned?
interpretation: This verse expresses the fundamental obligation of servitude to Allah based on the primordial relationship between Creator and creation. The questioner (Prophet Ibrahim) emphasizes that worship is a logical consequence of being created by Allah, as the Creator alone deserves worship and obedience. The reminder that all souls return to Him reinforces that ultimate accountability lies with Allah alone, making His worship not merely a choice but an inescapable reality that should govern human conduct during their earthly existence.

translation: Should I take gods other than Him? If the Most Merciful intends for me harm, their intercession will not avail me at all, nor will they save me.
interpretation: This verse expresses the futility of relying on false deities or intermediaries. The rhetorical question conveys the speaker's rejection of polytheism, emphasizing that when facing divine decree or punishment from Allah, no false god or intercessor can help. The verse underscores the monotheistic principle that only Allah possesses the power to benefit or harm, and that genuine protection and salvation come only from God alone, making the worship of anything besides Him logically irrational and spiritually worthless.

translation: Indeed, I would then be in clear error.
interpretation: This verse expresses the speaker's recognition that accepting false claims about God would constitute manifest deviation from truth. It reflects a principle of consciousness and accountability - the awareness that rejecting divine guidance constitutes a state of obvious misguidance. The phrase emphasizes the clarity and obviousness of such error, not merely a minor mistake but a fundamental departure from what is evidently right. This demonstrates the human capacity to recognize and acknowledge the severity of spiritual deviation when confronted with divine truth.

translation: Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.
interpretation: This verse expresses the speaker's declaration of faith and a call for others to heed their words based on that faith. The phrase suggests that believing in God grants authority and credibility to one's message, making it incumbent upon others to listen and obey. It emphasizes the connection between sincere belief and the moral obligation it creates for others to pay attention to divinely-guided counsel.

translation: It was said, 'Enter Paradise.' He said, 'I wish my people knew'
interpretation: This verse depicts a righteous believer's response upon entering Paradise, expressing his deep compassion and concern for his people who remained behind. Rather than being consumed with personal joy at his own salvation, his first thought is a wish that his people could witness his reward and understand the truth he tried to convey to them, reflecting the characteristic mercy and sincere desire for guidance that marks the believers who devoted themselves to calling others to the right path.

translation: Because my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored ones
interpretation: This verse reflects the speaker's gratitude and recognition of divine grace, emphasizing that honor and status in the sight of God are not achieved through human effort alone but are ultimately granted by God's forgiveness and mercy. The verse teaches that true honor comes not from worldly position or self-achievement, but from God's favor and acceptance, and that the grateful acknowledgment of this divine gift is the proper response to such blessing.

translation: And We did not send down upon his people after him any soldiers from the sky, nor were We ever going to send them down.
interpretation: This verse clarifies that after a messenger departs (referring to a specific prophet in context), Allah does not employ supernatural military intervention through heavenly forces to punish that people. Instead, accountability for those who reject the message comes through natural consequences, and ultimate judgment belongs to Allah alone in the afterlife. This teaches that divine punishment is not arbitrary or automatically swift, and that rejection of divine signs carries consequences determined by Allah's wisdom rather than immediate supernatural retribution.

translation: It was but a single cry, and thereupon they were extinguished.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the sudden and absolute nature of divine punishment upon the disbelieving people. The 'single cry' (صيحة) represents the overwhelming force of God's judgment that comes instantaneously, leaving no room for escape or resistance. The phrase 'they were extinguished' (خامدون) conveys not merely death but complete annihilation and silence, emphasizing the totality of their destruction and the powerlessness of humanity against God's will. This serves as a reminder of God's supreme power and the inevitable consequence of rejecting His message.

translation: O the regret upon the servants! There comes not to them any messenger except that they mock him.
interpretation: This verse expresses Allah's sorrow and lamentation over the persistent pattern of human rejection and ridicule of His messengers throughout history. It reveals the tragedy of human nature—that despite Allah sending guidance through His chosen messengers, people's typical response is mockery and derision rather than acceptance. The phrase 'ya hasrata' (O the regret) emphasizes the deep sorrow over this repeated cycle of rejection, highlighting the loss and missed opportunity for humanity when they turn away from divine guidance out of arrogance and contempt. The verse demonstrates that this pattern of mockery was not unique to one people or time, but a recurring phenomenon that characterizes human resistance to truth.

translation: Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, to which they will not return?
interpretation: This verse serves as evidence and warning to the people of Prophet Muhammad's time by pointing them to the historical destruction of previous nations and peoples who rejected divine guidance. The rhetorical question emphasizes the irreversible nature of divine punishment - those destroyed generations are permanently gone and will never return - as a reminder that the same fate awaits those who persist in disbelief and disobedience. The verse aims to awaken the awareness and conscience of the audience to take heed from the lessons of history before it is too late.

translation: And indeed, all of them - together - will be brought before Us.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the certainty of the Day of Judgment when all creation will be gathered and presented before Allah for divine accountability. The phrase 'all of them together' (كل...جميع) stresses the universality and simultaneity of this event, leaving no one behind, which serves to reinforce the inescapability of divine judgment and the absolute sovereignty of Allah over all beings.

translation: And a sign for them is the dead earth. We revived it and brought forth from it grain, so from it they eat.
interpretation: This verse presents the resurrection of the earth as a miraculous sign demonstrating Allah's power and provision. The barren, lifeless land coming back to life through rain and producing sustenance serves as a metaphor and tangible proof of Allah's ability to resurrect human beings after death, just as He revives the dead earth. The grain that sustains human life exemplifies how divine mercy operates through natural processes, inviting believers to reflect on their dependence upon Allah and to connect observable phenomena in creation with the greater reality of the afterlife and divine judgment.

translation: And We placed therein gardens of date-palms and grapevines, and We caused springs to gush forth therein
interpretation: This verse illustrates Allah's creative power and generosity in transforming barren land into fertile, life-sustaining spaces through divine intervention. The abundance of gardens and flowing springs represents both the physical provision of sustenance and a metaphor for spiritual nourishment, demonstrating how Allah's blessings flow abundantly for those who receive them when they turn towards Him.

translation: So they may eat from its fruit and [benefit from] what their hands have made. Then will they not be grateful?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine provision of sustenance through both natural resources created by Allah and the fruits of human labor, serving as a profound reminder that all blessings—whether from creation or effort—ultimately originate from Allah's grace and therefore demand gratitude and recognition of His generosity rather than arrogance about one's own accomplishments.

translation: Exalted is He who created all pairs from what the earth produces, from themselves, and from that which they do not know
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine transcendence and power by highlighting Allah's creation of complementary pairs throughout existence. The phrase 'all pairs' encompasses the biological reproduction found in plants, humans, and animals. The final clause 'that which they do not know' suggests the vast hidden dimensions of creation beyond human comprehension, reminding humanity of the limits of their knowledge and the infinite wisdom of the Creator in organizing all of existence through complementary dualities.

translation: And a sign for them is the night. We strip from it the day, and thereupon they are in darkness.
interpretation: This verse presents the alternation between night and day as a sign (ayah) of God's power and design for humanity. The stripping away of daylight from the night demonstrates God's continuous creation and control over celestial bodies, serving as evidence of divine wisdom. The resulting darkness is not merely a physical phenomenon but symbolizes the human condition of spiritual blindness and dependence on God's guidance, reminding people that just as they are helpless in the darkness of night, they are ultimately dependent on divine illumination for spiritual understanding and direction.

translation: And the sun runs its course to an appointed term for it. That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the precise cosmic order established by Allah, emphasizing that even the sun, with all its immense power, moves according to a predetermined path and duration. The phrase 'appointed term' (mustaqarr) refers to the sun's ultimate destiny—whether understood as its daily trajectory, its yearly cycle, or eventually its end—demonstrating that all celestial bodies operate under divine law. By attributing this cosmic governance to 'the Mighty, the All-Knowing,' the verse underscores that only Allah possesses both the power to create and sustain such a vast system, and the complete knowledge to determine its precise operations, thereby inviting reflection on divine omnipotence and perfect wisdom underlying the universe's function.

translation: And the moon - We have ordained for it phases/stages, until it returns like the old crescent/branch of a date palm.
interpretation: This verse describes the wisdom of Allah in establishing the lunar cycle, where the moon progresses through distinct phases each month until it returns to its crescent shape at the beginning of the new lunar month. The comparison to an old, curved date palm branch emphasizes the worn, thin crescent appearance of the new moon, illustrating the cyclical nature of creation and demonstrating Allah's perfect ordering of the heavens. This serves as a sign of Allah's power and providence in maintaining the regular patterns that govern time and seasons for mankind.

translation: It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor for the night to outstrip the day. Each swims in an orbit.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine order and precision governing the celestial bodies, emphasizing that each heavenly body follows a predetermined path and cannot exceed or violate its assigned boundaries. The imagery of swimming (yabahun) in orbits conveys the idea of celestial bodies moving in harmonious, continuous motion according to God's established laws, reflecting the perfect regularity and balance of creation and serving as a sign of God's wisdom and omnipotence.

translation: And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship (the Ark).
interpretation: This verse presents the preservation of Noah's progeny through the Ark as a divine sign of God's power and mercy.
