interpretation: This verse describes the state of those who commit crimes and transgress against Allah's commands as being trapped in a dual condition of spiritual darkness and torment. 'ضلال' (misguidance) refers to their moral and spiritual blindness that prevents them from recognizing truth, while 'سعر' (suffering/blazing fire) alludes to the consequences of their actions both in this life through psychological distress and in the afterlife through punishment. The verse emphasizes that criminality and transgression are not merely external acts but reflect and produce an internal state of deprivation from guidance and righteousness, with inevitable suffering as their consequence.

translation: The Day when they will be dragged over their faces into the Fire, [it will be said], 'Taste the touch of Saqar.'
interpretation: This verse vividly depicts the punishment of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, emphasizing the humiliation and torment that awaits them in Hell. The graphic imagery of being dragged on their faces symbolizes utter degradation and the reversal of their worldly pride, while 'taste the touch of Saqar' (Hellfire) is an ironic command that conveys both the reality of their punishment and the mockery of their former denials of the Hereafter, serving as a stern warning about the consequences of rejecting Allah's signs.

translation: Indeed, all things We have created with measure (proportion and decree).
interpretation: This verse expresses the Islamic principle of divine qadar (predestination and divine measure), establishing that Allah's creation is neither haphazard nor excessive, but follows a precise divine plan where everything exists in perfect proportion and is decreed according to Allah's infinite wisdom. It conveys both the theological concept of divine predetermination and the observable reality that all creation follows laws and measures established by the Creator.

translation: And Our command is not but one, like the twinkling of an eye.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute power and sovereignty of Allah over all creation. His command and will are executed instantly and effortlessly, without any delay or difficulty. The comparison to the twinkling of an eye illustrates the immense swiftness and perfection of Divine action - just as the eye blinks in an instant, Allah's decree is fulfilled immediately when He wills something to be. This conveys that all the complex operations of the universe occur with such rapidity and precision that they demonstrate the unified, singular nature of Allah's absolute control, where there is no separation between His will and its manifestation.

translation: And indeed, We destroyed your similar ones before. So is there anyone who will take heed?
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine warning to those who follow the same path of disbelief and arrogance as the destroyed nations before them. By reminding them of the fate of their predecessors who rejected God's messengers and messages, Allah calls humanity to reflect on the consequences of rejection and to learn from history. The phrase 'is there anyone who will take heed' is an appeal to the faculty of reason and memory, inviting the listeners to exercise wisdom and change their course before meeting the same destruction.

translation: And everything they did is recorded in the records.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine recording of all human actions and deeds. The 'records' (al-zubur) refers to the preserved writings or scriptures where Allah has recorded every action of the people, signifying that nothing is hidden from Allah's knowledge and all deeds will be brought forth as evidence on the Day of Judgment. This serves as a reminder of divine accountability and the certainty of consequences for all actions.

translation: And every small and great thing is inscribed/recorded
interpretation: This verse refers to the divine recording of all deeds and actions, both insignificant and significant. It emphasizes that nothing escapes God's knowledge or documentation—every human action, whether seemingly trivial or momentous, is meticulously recorded and will be accounted for on the Day of Judgment. This conveys the concept of divine omniscience and accountability, reminding believers that their conduct is continuously observed and preserved by God.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and rivers.
interpretation: This verse describes the reward of those who practice piety and fear Allah (the righteous) in the Hereafter. The mention of gardens and rivers symbolizes a state of paradise characterized by beauty, abundance, and eternal peace. The emphasis on 'indeed' (inna) at the beginning establishes a strong affirmation of this divine promise, serving as both encouragement for believers to maintain taqwa (piety) and reassurance of Allah's justice in rewarding the faithful. The dual imagery of gardens and rivers represents both material and spiritual contentment in the afterlife.

translation: In a seat of honor near a Mighty King
interpretation: This verse describes the ultimate reward and elevated status that the righteous will attain in Paradise - being seated in a place of truth and honor in the presence of Allah, the All-Powerful King. It signifies the closeness to Allah's mercy and the dignity bestowed upon those who have pleased Him, emphasizing that their faithful deeds have earned them an exalted position in the eternal realm.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. The Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse establishes that Allah is characterized by mercy and compassion as His defining attributes. The repetition of 'al-Rahman' (The Most Merciful) emphasizes that mercy is the foundational quality through which Allah relates to His creation, suggesting that all of Allah's actions and dealings with humanity are rooted in and motivated by His infinite mercy, compassion, and clemency.

translation: The knowledge of the Qur'an
interpretation: This phrase refers to the deep understanding and comprehension of the Qur'an's meanings, principles, and guidance. It emphasizes that true knowledge is not merely memorization of verses, but rather a profound grasp of the Qur'an's wisdom, legal rulings, spiritual teachings, and how to apply them in one's life, which is a lifelong pursuit requiring sincere devotion, reflection, and guidance from Allah.

translation: He created mankind
interpretation: This phrase refers to Allah's act of creating humanity, emphasizing the Divine origin of human existence. It underscores the fundamental relationship between Creator and creation, establishing that all human beings owe their existence to Allah's will and design, which forms the foundation for understanding human responsibility and purpose in Islamic theology.

translation: He taught him eloquent speech / He taught him clear expression
interpretation: This phrase refers to Allah's bestowal of the ability to communicate clearly and eloquently. It emphasizes that clear communication and the ability to express oneself well are divine gifts from Allah, not merely human acquisitions. This underscores the importance of language and articulate expression as essential tools for conveying truth and wisdom, and suggests that the faculty of clear speech is a profound blessing that enables one to guide others and fulfill one's role in society.

translation: The sun and the moon [move] by calculation
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the precise, mathematical order inherent in creation, where the celestial bodies follow predictable, predetermined courses governed by divine law. It reflects the Qur'anic teaching that the universe operates according to established divine principles rather than chaos, and serves as evidence of Allah's perfect knowledge and wisdom in maintaining cosmic harmony. The verse invites reflection on the signs of divine orderliness visible in nature as a path to recognizing the Creator's ultimate authority and mastery over all things.

translation: And the stars and the trees prostrate themselves.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the universal submission of all creation to Allah's will. The stars and trees, despite their apparent lack of consciousness, are depicted as fulfilling their ordained purpose and glorifying their Creator through their existence and function. This conveys that all of creation, whether animate or inanimate, visible or invisible, submits to divine law and divine will, and this submission is a form of prostration. For humans, this serves as a reminder that we too are part of this cosmic order and should willingly submit to Allah just as all of creation does naturally.

translation: And the sky He raised high, and He established the balance.
interpretation: This verse refers to Allah's creation of the heavens at a great height, making it a sign of His power and majesty. The 'balance' (al-mizan) refers to justice and equilibrium in the universe - both the physical laws that govern creation and the moral and social justice that Allah has ordained for humanity. Together, these clauses convey that Allah's creation demonstrates both His power through the vastness of the sky and His wisdom through the perfect balance and order He has established in all things.

translation: Do not transgress in the balance/scale
interpretation: This verse warns against dishonesty and fraud in commerce and measurement. It emphasizes the moral imperative to conduct fair transactions and not cheat others by using false weights or measures. Beyond commercial dealings, it serves as a broader reminder to maintain justice and integrity in all affairs, as the 'balance' symbolizes equity and fairness in human interactions and dealings with one another.

translation: And establish weight with justice and do not diminish the scale
interpretation: This verse commands believers to conduct their commercial and material transactions with perfect honesty and fairness, using accurate measurements and avoiding any form of fraud or deception. The emphasis on establishing weight 'with justice' suggests that fairness in commerce is not merely a practical concern but a moral and religious obligation rooted in divine justice, reflecting the principle that truthfulness and integrity in dealings are fundamental to a righteous society and individual conscience.

translation: And the earth - He placed it for all creatures/mankind
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Allah created the earth as a dwelling place and means of sustenance for all living beings, highlighting the divine purpose behind creation and humanity's stewardship responsibility toward the natural world and its resources.

translation: Therein is fruit and palm trees with sheaths (or enclosed fruit clusters).
interpretation: This verse describes the bounties of Paradise, emphasizing the abundance and perfection of its provisions. The mention of fruit represents general sustenance and nourishment, while the specific reference to palm trees with their sheaths (al-akimam) - which are the protective coverings that safeguard the dates as they grow and ripen - symbolizes how the blessings of Paradise are both generous and perfectly preserved. The detail about sheaths suggests that the fruits in Paradise are protected from decay and spoilage, representing the eternal and incorruptible nature of divine blessings, unlike the perishable fruits of this world. This conveys that Paradise is a place of complete satisfaction where one lacks nothing and where all provisions are superior and everlasting.

translation: And the grain with its stalks and herbage
interpretation: This verse describes Allah's creation of vegetation in its various forms - both the staple crops (grain with stalks) and the aromatic plants (herbage). The verse emphasizes the diversity and bounty of Allah's creation, demonstrating His power and providence in sustaining life through the provision of plants that serve both practical and aesthetic purposes for humanity and other creatures.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surah Al-Rahman, serves as a rhetorical challenge to both jinn and humankind, compelling them to contemplate the countless blessings and mercies they have received from Allah. The repetition emphasizes the absurdity and ingratitude of denying or rejecting the truth of Allah's existence and oneness when confronted with overwhelming evidence of His provision, creation, and compassion. It is designed to awaken consciousness and provoke reflection on whether any rational being could reasonably reject such manifest favors.

translation: He created man from sounding clay like pottery
interpretation: This verse describes the origin of humanity using vivid imagery that emphasizes both the material composition and the transformation involved in human creation. The 'sounding clay' (صلصال) refers to clay that makes a sound when struck, suggesting the brittleness and fragility of human nature. The comparison to pottery indicates that just as clay is molded and hardened by fire to become pottery, so too does the human form undergo a process of shaping and refinement. This interpretation underscores the humility of human origin from earthly materials, reminding humanity of their dependence on Allah and their inherent weakness and need for divine guidance, while paradoxically highlighting the miraculous transformation of simple matter into the complex, living being that is humanity.

translation: And He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire.
interpretation: This verse establishes the nature of jinn as beings created from fire without smoke, distinguishing them from humans who were created from clay. The term 'mārij' (smokeless flame) emphasizes the pure, intense nature of their creation, suggesting that jinn possess a different essence and composition than humans, which explains their distinct nature, capabilities, and their existence in a realm partially hidden from human perception. This fundamental difference in creation accounts for their different behavioral patterns and their ability to move between the unseen and seen worlds.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse is an address to the jinn and mankind, challenging them to acknowledge the countless blessings and signs they have been given from Allah. By posing this rhetorical question, the Qur'an emphasizes the irrationality and ingratitude of denying divine favor, as it invites reflection on the abundance of mercies one experiences - from life itself to sustenance, guidance, and intellect - making any denial unreasonable and unjustifiable.

translation: Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests
interpretation: This phrase emphasizes Allah's absolute sovereignty over all directions and the entire creation. The mention of 'two easts' and 'two wests' refers to the two points where the sun rises and sets during the summer and winter solstices, signifying Allah's dominion over all of space, time, and the celestial movements that regulate human life and seasons. It conveys that there is no place or moment beyond Allah's control or knowledge, establishing His transcendence and the comprehensive nature of His lordship over all existence.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse presents a rhetorical question aimed at jinn and humans, emphasizing the absurdity of denying Allah's blessings. The repetition of this refrain throughout Surah Ar-Rahman serves to awaken consciousness and conscience, highlighting that despite the countless favors and mercies bestowed by Allah upon creation, there persists an inexplicable tendency to deny, disbelieve, and turn away from the truth. The verse challenges the listener's intellect and heart to recognize ingratitude as not merely a sin of omission but an active rejection of evident reality.

translation: He has let loose the two seas, meeting [one another]
interpretation: This verse refers to God's creative power in allowing two bodies of water with different properties to flow together while maintaining their distinct characteristics. The interpretation emphasizes God's control over the natural world and the miraculous phenomenon of how water bodies can coexist in close proximity without losing their individual properties—symbolizing divine wisdom in maintaining order and distinction within creation, and serving as a sign of God's ability to manage contrasting elements in perfect balance.

translation: Between them is a barrier they do not transgress
interpretation: This verse depicts the divine wisdom in maintaining the boundary between fresh and salt water, signifying how Allah has established natural laws and boundaries in creation that prevent chaos and disorder. The barrier represents the divinely ordained separation that allows each element to maintain its distinct nature and purpose, teaching that God's creation operates according to perfect wisdom and proportion, with boundaries serving as a means of sustaining cosmic and material harmony.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, serves as a rhetorical challenge to both humans and jinn, compelling them to reflect on the countless blessings and mercies they receive from Allah. The verse's repetitive structure functions as a powerful reminder that denying or failing to acknowledge divine grace is not merely ungrateful but logically indefensible, since the favors are undeniable and self-evident. By framing the question this way, the Qur'an confronts listeners with the absurdity of ingratitude and encourages conscious recognition and gratitude for creation, sustenance, guidance, and all forms of divine provision.

translation: From them comes forth pearls and coral
interpretation: This verse, referring to the two bodies of water (salt and fresh water) mentioned previously, describes how pearls and coral are extracted from the seas as divine treasures. The verse illustrates God's provision and the wealth hidden within His creation, emphasizing that valuable and beautiful things emerge naturally from the meeting point of different waters. This serves as a sign of Divine provision and the hidden benefits God has placed in nature for mankind to discover and utilize, demonstrating the sophistication and purposefulness of God's creation.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, poses a rhetorical question that challenges humanity and jinn to recognize the countless blessings and mercies (ayat/favors) that God has bestowed upon them. The question is not asked expecting a logical answer, but rather serves as a profound reminder of divine grace and an implicit reprimand against ingratitude and denial. By repeatedly asking this question after each enumeration of God's blessings—from creating humans from clay, providing nourishment, establishing the heavens, and setting cosmic order—the verse emphasizes the irrationality and audacity of rejecting God's signs when the evidence of His benevolence is so overwhelming and undeniable. It is a call to consciousness and accountability.

translation: And to Him belong the ships constructed [and moving] in the sea like mountains.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's complete ownership and dominion over all creation, specifically highlighting the magnificent ships that traverse the oceans. By describing ships as being 'like mountains,' the Qur'an draws attention to their impressive size and grandeur as a testament to human ingenuity and craftsmanship granted by Allah. The verse serves to remind believers of Allah's infinite power and control over all moving vessels and maritime endeavors, encouraging gratitude for the blessings of transportation and commerce that facilitate human life and livelihood.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, serves as a rhetorical challenge that awakens human consciousness to the countless blessings bestowed by Allah upon mankind and the jinn. By using the dual form 'you both,' it addresses both humans and jinn, emphasizing that despite the overwhelming abundance of divine favors—sustenance, life, faculties, guidance, and mercy—there is a tendency to deny or take for granted these blessings through ingratitude, disobedience, and heedlessness. The verse functions as a powerful call to reflection and accountability, questioning the logical absurdity of denying the Creator's generosity when those very denials are made possible only through the use of the blessings themselves. It is ultimately an exhortation to gratitude and recognition of divine majesty.

translation: Everyone upon it will perish.
interpretation: This verse affirms the inevitable reality of death and the transient nature of all creation on Earth. It conveys that all living beings, regardless of their status, power, or importance in this world, are mortal and will eventually cease to exist. This serves as a humbling reminder of human mortality and the impermanence of worldly life, encouraging people to focus on their eternal purpose and accountability before God rather than becoming attached to temporary worldly pursuits and possessions.

translation: And there remains the Face of your Lord, the Possessor of Majesty and Generosity
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the eternal and immutable nature of Allah's divine attributes and presence. While all worldly things are transient and subject to decay, Allah's essence and attributes—characterized by supreme majesty and honor—endure forever. The verse teaches that unlike the fleeting nature of creation, divine reality is permanent and unchanging, serving as a reminder that ultimate permanence belongs only to Allah and that all human concerns and attachments to material existence are temporary in comparison to the eternal divine reality.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a rhetorical challenge to the jinn and mankind, reminding them of Allah's countless blessings and mercies while implicitly condemning their ingratitude and denial of these favors. The repetition of this verse throughout Surah Ar-Rahman emphasizes that denying or being ungrateful for Allah's blessings is irrational and inexcusable, as no reasonable person could logically reject the clear signs of divine favor evident in creation.

translation: Those who are in the heavens and on the earth ask Him. Every day He is in a state of affairs.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's supreme dominion and constant engagement with creation. The phrase 'every day He is in a state of affairs' indicates that Allah is perpetually occupied with managing and sustaining His creation—answering supplications, fulfilling needs, and orchestrating the affairs of the universe. The repetition of 'every day' stresses the continuous and eternal nature of Allah's administrative power, demonstrating that His work of creation and sustenance never ceases or diminishes, and that all creatures depend upon His active providence at every moment.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated 31 times throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, serves as a rhetorical challenge to humanity and jinn, emphasizing the absurdity of denying God's blessings. Despite the countless favors—life, sustenance, intellect, guidance, mercy—that God bestows upon creation, people still turn away and reject His signs. The verse's repetition amplifies the rebuke, highlighting the unreasonableness of ingratitude and disbelief in the face of overwhelming divine bounty, and implicitly warns of the consequences of such denial.

translation: We will turn our attention to you, O two heavy ones (jinn and mankind)
interpretation: This verse suggests that Allah will address and hold accountable both the jinn and mankind together on the Day of Judgment, emphasizing that both creation bears responsibility for their deeds in this world and neither can escape the divine reckoning, highlighting the impartiality of divine justice.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, serves as a rhetorical question challenging the jinn and humankind to recognize the countless blessings bestowed upon them by Allah. The question is not seeking an answer but rather functioning as a powerful reminder that denying or being ungrateful for divine favors is irrational and indefensible, since every blessing in existence—life, intellect, sustenance, guidance—originates from God's mercy. The repetition emphasizes the absurdity of disbelief in the face of overwhelming evidence of divine benevolence.

translation: O company of jinn and mankind, if you are able to penetrate beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then penetrate! You will not penetrate except with authority (power/permission).
interpretation: This verse illustrates the absolute supremacy of Allah's dominion and the limitations of all creation. The challenge presented to both jinn and mankind to escape the bounds of the heavens and earth if they can is rhetorical, emphasizing that no creature, regardless of their nature or capabilities, can evade Allah's control or jurisdiction. The phrase 'except with authority' signifies that any ability or power that created beings possess comes solely from Allah and remains under His complete sovereignty. The verse serves to humble both jinn and humans before Allah's infinite might and to demonstrate that ultimate authority belongs to Him alone.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse addresses both jinn and humans, reminding them of Allah's countless blessings and mercies upon them, and questions how they can possibly deny or reject these obvious signs of divine favor. The repetition of this phrase throughout Surah Ar-Rahman emphasizes the irrationality of ingratitude and the importance of recognizing and acknowledging God's continuous bounties as the foundation of faith and obedience.

translation: He will send upon both of you a flame of fire and melted brass, and you will not be able to defend yourselves.
interpretation: This verse describes the severe punishment that will befall those who persist in disbelief and transgression in the Hereafter, emphasizing their complete helplessness and inability to resist or escape from God's punishment. The imagery of fire and molten brass represents the intensity and overwhelming nature of divine retribution, conveying that those who reject God's signs will find themselves utterly defenseless with no means of salvation or protection.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse employs direct rhetorical questioning to challenge the addressees (the jinns and humans) to recognize the absurdity of their denial of divine blessings. The repetition of this phrase throughout Surah Al-Rahman emphasizes that every observable phenomenon in creation—life, sustenance, beauty, and guidance—constitutes clear evidence of God's favors and mercy. The verse's fundamental interpretation centers on exposing the illogicality and ingratitude inherent in denying what is self-evident, thereby calling for intellectual honesty and acknowledgment of divine benevolence as a prerequisite for faith and righteous conduct.

translation: So when the sky is split open and becomes like a rose colored with oil/paint
interpretation: This verse describes the dramatic rupturing of the heavens on the Day of Judgment, depicting it transformed into something soft, pliable, and luminous like a rose petaled flower or colored oil. The imagery conveys the complete transformation and destruction of the existing cosmic order, emphasizing the awesome power of Allah and the utter devastation of creation at the appointed hour. The comparison to something as delicate as a rose paradoxically highlights the vulnerability and impermanence of the seemingly solid and eternal sky, underscoring that only Allah's will is truly eternal and immutable.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse addresses both humans and jinn, questioning them about their denial of the numerous blessings and signs of God's mercy and provision. The rhetorical question emphasizes the irrationality and ingratitude of rejecting God's favors despite their obvious abundance in creation, sustenance, and guidance. It serves as a powerful reminder that denial of God's blessings is not only ungrateful but also illogical, as these favors are undeniable manifestations of divine care and power.

translation: So on that Day, no human will be asked about his sin, nor will any jinn be asked about his sin.
interpretation: This verse describes a specific moment on the Day of Judgment when Allah will not inquire about the sins of humanity or the jinn, suggesting that the reckoning has already been completed and the decision regarding their fate is already determined, or that they will be too preoccupied with their own overwhelming circumstances to be questioned, indicating a state of complete helplessness and despair when excuses and explanations become irrelevant.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse challenges humans and jinn to recognize and acknowledge the countless blessings and mercies that Allah has bestowed upon them, implying that denying or being ungrateful for these divine favors is irrational and a fundamental act of rebellion against the Creator. The repetition of this refrain throughout Surah Ar-Rahman serves to emphasize the absurdity and ingratitude of rejecting divine truth after witnessing such abundant evidence of Allah's mercy and provision.

translation: The criminals will be known by their marks, so they will be seized by their forelocks and their feet.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the wicked will be identifiable by distinctive signs of their guilt and disgrace on the Day of Judgment, and thus will be humiliated and overpowered by the angels, being dragged by their forelocks and feet—a depiction of complete subjugation and loss of dignity before divine justice.

translation: Then which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the ingratitude and irrationality of denying God's blessings by posing a rhetorical question that challenges the listener to acknowledge which specific favor they could possibly deny. The question format serves to awaken conscience and self-reflection, suggesting that all blessings from God are evidently undeniable, making their denial absurd and indefensible. By repetition throughout Surah ar-Rahman, this verse reinforces that rejecting God's grace despite overwhelming evidence of His generosity is the height of foolishness and moral blindness.

translation: This is Hell, which the criminals deny.
interpretation: This verse presents Hell as a concrete reality that will confront the deniers on the Day of Judgment. The criminals' prior rejection of Hell's existence will make no difference when they face it directly. The verse emphasizes that denial of God's punishment does not negate its reality, serving as a warning that disbelief in divine consequences will not prevent their occurrence.

translation: They will circulate between it and between boiling water
interpretation: This verse describes the punishment of the inhabitants of Hell, who will be eternally tormented by being driven back and forth between the intense heat of the fire and scalding water. The repetitive cycle of this torment emphasizes the relentlessness and hopelessness of their suffering, as they are given no respite or escape from their agony, symbolizing the permanent and complete nature of divine punishment for those who reject Allah's signs.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, poses a powerful rhetorical question that serves as a call to reflection and gratitude. The verse challenges both humans and jinn (the two addressed parties) to recognize the countless blessings and favors they have been granted from Allah, and to examine whether they can truthfully deny or reject any of them. The repeated nature of this refrain emphasizes the absurdity of ingratitude and the irrationality of rejecting divine blessings. It functions as a reminder of human accountability, inviting introspection about whether we truly appreciate and acknowledge the divine favors we experience daily, from the fundamental gifts of existence and sustenance to spiritual guidance, and implicitly warns against the sin of denying or being ungrateful for Allah's signs and blessings.

translation: And for those who feared the standing before their Lord, there are two gardens.
interpretation: This verse describes the reward for those who possess the consciousness and fear of standing before Allah in the Hereafter. The mention of two gardens signifies an abundance of blessings and rewards for those who maintain God-consciousness and piety. The reference to 'fearing the standing before the Lord' indicates that true righteousness stems from the awareness that one will ultimately be held accountable before Allah, making it a fundamental motivation for moral and spiritual conduct in this life.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse is addressed to the jinn and mankind, emphasizing the rhetorical rebuke of those who deny or ignore the countless blessings and signs of Allah despite their obvious manifestation. The verse serves as a powerful reminder of human and jinn ingratitude and denial of divine grace, highlighting that there is no legitimate basis for rejecting Allah's favors since they are evident and indisputable. The repeated nature of this verse throughout Surah Ar-Rahman drives home the central message that denying divine blessings is illogical and indefensible, regardless of how one might attempt to rationalize such denial.

translation: Two gardens with branches/lush vegetation
interpretation: This phrase refers to two gardens characterized by their abundant greenery and verdant branches, emphasizing their beauty, fertility, and flourishing state. The word 'afnan' (branches) is used metaphorically to convey the richness and luxuriance of the gardens in Paradise, suggesting divine abundance and the reward of beauty that awaits the righteous.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, serves as a rhetorical challenge to both humans and jinn, compelling them to reflect on the countless blessings they receive from Allah. By juxtaposing the enumeration of divine favors with the accusation of denial, the verse emphasizes the ingratitude and irrationality of rejecting Allah's signs and bounties. It is a powerful call to gratitude and acknowledgment of divine benevolence, while simultaneously highlighting the inexcusability of those who turn away from truth despite the overwhelming evidence of God's mercy manifest in creation.

translation: In them are two springs flowing.
interpretation: This verse refers to the gardens of Paradise, emphasizing the abundance and beauty of running water as one of the greatest blessings and signs of Divine grace. The flowing springs symbolize eternal sustenance, life, and refreshment, representing the perpetual provision and comfort that awaits the righteous in the afterlife. The mention of two springs specifically suggests completeness and richness of blessing in Paradise.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, serves as a rhetorical challenge to humanity and jinn, emphasizing the boundless blessings bestowed upon them by Allah. The question is not meant to elicit a logical answer but rather to awaken consciousness and gratitude, forcing the listener to recognize the absurdity and ingratitude of denying or rejecting the signs and mercies of the Creator. By repeating this refrain, the Qur'an aims to penetrate the hardened hearts of those who turn away from divine guidance despite being surrounded by countless proofs of Allah's existence and benevolence.

translation: In both of them (are) of every fruit two kinds
interpretation: This verse refers to the fruits of Paradise, indicating that in the two gardens of Paradise, there exists a variety and abundance of fruits in complementary pairs or varieties. The mention of 'two kinds' (zowjaan) suggests a divine design of abundance and diversity in Paradise, where believers will enjoy fruits of different types and qualities, emphasizing the richness and completeness of the reward awaiting the righteous in the afterlife.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, is a rhetorical challenge directed at both humanity and the jinn, emphasizing the absurdity and ingratitude of denying Allah's countless blessings and favors. By posing this question after describing various divine blessings, the verse serves to awaken the conscience and provoke reflection on the irrationality of rejecting the signs of Allah's mercy and power when all evidence of His providence surrounds us. The repetition reinforces the message that denial of divine favors is not merely a spiritual failing but a logical contradiction—how can one reasonably deny what is abundantly evident?

translation: Reclining upon couches whose inner linings are of silk, and the fruits of the two gardens are brought near (easy to reach).
interpretation: This verse depicts the ease and luxury of Paradise, where the righteous will recline comfortably on couches adorned with silk, symbolizing ultimate comfort and rest from worldly hardship. The proximity of the garden's fruits emphasizes divine provision and the absence of toil—the inhabitants need only reach out to enjoy the blessings prepared for them, representing God's perfect fulfillment of all desires for those who believe and do righteous deeds.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, serves as a powerful rhetorical question challenging the addressees (often understood as jinn and humans, or the various creation itself) to reflect on their refusal to acknowledge and be grateful for God's countless blessings and provisions. The repetition emphasizes the irrationality of denying divine favors that are evident everywhere, calling for recognition of God's generosity and a response of gratitude rather than ingratitude.

translation: In them are chaste women, restraining their glances, whom neither man nor jinn has touched before them.
interpretation: This verse describes the pure and virtuous wives promised to the righteous in Paradise. The phrase 'restraining their glances' signifies their modesty and dignity, while the statement that they have not been touched before emphasizes their absolute purity and being reserved exclusively for their believing husbands. This conveys the perfection and beauty of Paradise where relationships are unblemished and eternal, contrasting with the transient and imperfect nature of worldly relations. The mention of both men and jinn establishes the completeness of their chastity across all creation.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, serves as a rhetorical challenge to both jinn and humans, inviting them to reflect on the countless blessings they have received from Allah. By asking this rhetorical question after enumerating divine favors, the verse emphasizes the ingratitude and irrationality of denying Allah's bounties and His existence, highlighting that such denial is contrary to reason and evidence, and should provoke the conscience of the listener to acknowledge and be grateful for these blessings.

translation: As if they were pearls and coral
interpretation: This verse describes the beauty and luminosity of the inhabitants of Paradise, particularly women, using the metaphor of precious gems. The comparison to pearls (pearls being white and lustrous) and coral (being red and vibrant) suggests an otherworldly radiance and beauty that transcends earthly description. The 'as if' construction indicates that while no earthly comparison can truly capture their magnificence, these precious substances offer the closest approximation to convey their radiant and pristine nature to the human mind.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful rhetorical challenge emphasizing human ingratitude and the futility of denying God's signs and blessings. By addressing both humans and jinn (as indicated by the dual form), the verse reminds the creation that they constantly benefit from divine favors—life, sustenance, intellect, beauty of creation—yet they turn away and reject the truth. The repetition of this refrain throughout Surah Ar-Rahman is designed to provoke deep reflection on the absurdity of denying what is evident and manifest, and to awaken the conscience to acknowledge dependence on the Divine.

translation: Is there any reward for goodness other than goodness?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the principle of divine reciprocity and moral beautification - that when one performs good deeds with pure intention and excellence (ihsan), Allah responds with goodness and grace in this world and the next. It suggests that virtue generates virtue, establishing that the natural and divine consequence of doing good is receiving good in return. The verse also implies that no material reward or external compensation is necessary or superior to the intrinsic reward of goodness itself, elevating moral action as its own purpose and recompense.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, is a rhetorical rebuke inviting reflection on the countless blessings and signs from Allah that both humans and jinn possess, yet often deny or overlook through ingratitude and heedlessness. The verse emphasizes personal accountability by directing the question to both recipients of divine grace, challenging them to recognize that denial of these manifest blessings is unreasonable and without justification.

translation: And besides these two, there are two other gardens.
interpretation: This verse refers to the existence of additional gardens in Paradise beyond the two previously mentioned. In Qur'anic descriptions of the afterlife, this passage emphasizes the abundant rewards and multiple levels of blessing that await the righteous in Paradise. The phrase suggests divine generosity and the multifaceted nature of celestial rewards, indicating that the blessings of Paradise extend far beyond what might be initially conceived, with different gardens representing different stations of honor and spiritual elevation for the believers.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, serves as a powerful rhetorical question that confronts both humans and jinn with the reality of God's countless blessings and mercies. The phrase challenges the listener to reflect on their ingratitude and denial, implying that to deny or reject God's favors is irrational and unjustifiable. By asking which favor could possibly be denied, the verse emphasizes the absurdity of disbelief and ingratitude when one is surrounded by evidence of divine generosity at every moment of existence.

translation: Both gardens are green and luxuriant
interpretation: This word describes the verdant, lush state of the two gardens mentioned in Surah Al-Rahman (55:64), emphasizing their vibrant greenery and abundant vegetation as a reward for the righteous. The term underscores the perpetual freshness and vitality of paradise, symbolizing eternal beauty and the flourishing life that awaits the believers in the Hereafter.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surah Ar-Rahman, serves as a rhetorical challenge to humanity and jinn, emphasizing the rhetorical futility and irrationality of denying Allah's blessings. By posing this question after listing divine favors, the verse confronts the listener with the absurdity of ingratitude, suggesting that given the overwhelming abundance of Allah's mercy and provision evident in creation, any denial or rejection of His existence or favor is logically indefensible and morally inexcusable.

translation: In both of them are two springs gushing forth
interpretation: This verse refers to the two gardens described in Surah Al-Rahman, emphasizing their abundance of fresh water from springs that continuously flow and gush forth. The dual form 'عينان' and 'نضاختان' conveys the idea that each garden contains two distinct springs, symbolizing divine generosity, sustenance, and the refreshing blessings awaiting the righteous in Paradise. The word 'نضاخ' specifically denotes a spring that flows abundantly and continuously, emphasizing the eternal and inexhaustible nature of these rewards.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse challenges humanity and the jinn to recognize the countless blessings and signs from Allah that surround them. It emphasizes accountability by posing a rhetorical question that exposes the irrationality of denying divine favors—whether health, sustenance, guidance, or existence itself—when these blessings are evident and undeniable. The repetition of this refrain throughout Surah ar-Rahman serves to provoke reflection on human ingratitude and to awaken consciousness of dependence upon the Divine.

translation: In both of them are fruits, palm trees, and pomegranates.
interpretation: This verse describes the abundance and diversity of sustenance in the two gardens of Paradise, emphasizing that they contain not just basic fruits but specifically palm trees and pomegranates—plants that represent both nourishment and beauty. The mention of these specific fruits illustrates how Paradise is characterized by variety, richness, and the fulfillment of all desires, suggesting that divine provision in the afterlife encompasses both what is physically sustaining and what brings delight to the senses and soul.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful rhetorical challenge to the addressees (the jinn and mankind in Surah Ar-Rahman), compelling them to recognize the futility and irrationality of denying God's countless blessings. The repetition of this refrain throughout the surah emphasizes that denial of divine grace is not merely sinful but fundamentally illogical—when faced with undeniable evidence of God's provision, protection, and mercy in every aspect of creation and existence, any rejection becomes indefensible and absurd. The dual address highlights the universal nature of this truth applicable to all conscious beings.

translation: In them are good qualities and beauty
interpretation: This phrase emphasizes that the women being referenced possess both inner virtue and outer beauty. The term 'khairat' (good qualities) refers to moral excellence, righteousness, and noble character, while 'hisan' (beauty) refers to physical attractiveness. The verse is affirming that true worth in women encompasses both spiritual/moral excellence and physical beauty, presenting these as complementary attributes rather than contradictory ones. This interpretation suggests that the Qur'an values the holistic excellence of women, recognizing that both inner virtue and outward beauty are legitimate and good aspects of human existence.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the accountability of the jinn and mankind for their ingratitude and denial of Allah's blessings. Despite the countless favors and signs that Allah has bestowed upon both creation, they persistently reject the truth and deny His grace, which represents a grave spiritual and moral failing that will have serious consequences on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Hoor (fair maidens) confined in tents
interpretation: This verse describes the pure and beautiful women of Paradise who are kept in a state of honor and virtue, protected within pavilions or tents. The concept of being 'confined' (maqsurah) emphasizes their dignity, chastity, and exclusive nature - they are preserved and honored in Paradise, not exposed or diminished. This reflects the idea that the greatest rewards in Paradise include companionship with virtuous and beautiful beings, emphasizing the elevated and protected status of these maidens in the divine reward.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the ingratitude and denial of mankind and jinn despite the countless blessings they receive from Allah. The rhetorical question is designed to make the listener reflect on the absurdity of denying obvious divine favors—favors so numerous and indisputable that to reject them is irrational. The verse serves as a profound call to gratitude and acknowledgment of Allah's benevolence, suggesting that denial of these blessings is not merely a matter of disagreement but a fundamental rejection of evident truth.

translation: No man has touched them before, nor any jinn
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the purity and chastity of the maidens of Paradise, describing them as untouched and preserved exclusively for the believers. The mention of both humans and jinn conveys the absolute nature of their virginity and separation from all creation, underscoring that these women are a unique divine gift reserved solely for the righteous inhabitants of Paradise, which serves to highlight the extraordinary and incomparable rewards awaiting the faithful.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse, repeated throughout Surah Al-Rahman, serves as a powerful rhetorical question challenging humanity and jinn to acknowledge the countless blessings bestowed upon them by Allah. Rather than merely listing divine favors, the verse functions as a call to spiritual consciousness and gratitude, implying that denying or being ungrateful for these blessings is irrational and unreasonable. The repeated refrain emphasizes that no matter how many favors are enumerated, rejection of them represents a fundamental disregard for divine mercy, and this refusal becomes increasingly unjustifiable as the catalog of blessings multiplies throughout the surah.

translation: Reclining upon green cushions and beautiful carpets of rich fabric
interpretation: This verse describes the physical comfort and luxury that the people of Paradise will experience, emphasizing the aesthetic beauty and material abundance of their environment. The green color symbolizes freshness, life, and vitality in Islamic tradition, while the fine furnishings represent the complete satisfaction of comfort and ease that believers will enjoy in the afterlife, free from the hardships and struggles of the worldly life.

translation: So which of the favors of your Lord do you both deny?
interpretation: This verse is addressing both jinn and mankind, challenging them to acknowledge and be grateful for God's countless blessings and bounties. The repetition of this refrain throughout Surah Ar-Rahman emphasizes that denying or being ungrateful for God's favors is illogical and inexcusable, as every blessing ultimately comes from Him. The verse serves as a rhetorical device to awaken human and jinn consciousness to the reality of divine favor and to condemn ingratitude and denial of God's signs as a fundamental error in judgment and morality.

translation: Blessed is the name of your Lord, the Possessor of Majesty and Honor
interpretation: This verse invokes a declaration of the sanctity and transcendence of Allah's names and attributes. The word 'Tabarak' (blessed) indicates that Allah's name is beyond all imperfection and is a source of all blessings and goodness. By attributing to Him 'Al-Jalal' (majesty) and 'Al-Ikram' (honor), the verse emphasizes that Allah alone possesses perfect power, grandeur, and dignity, worthy of all reverence and worship. This serves as both a statement of divine glory and an implicit call to the believers to recognize the supremacy of their Lord and to direct their devotion solely to Him.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. When the Event (the Day of Judgment) occurs,
interpretation: This verse opens Surah Al-Waqi'ah by invoking God's mercy and introducing the certainty of the Day of Judgment as an inevitable reality. The use of 'when' (idha) rather than 'if' emphasizes that this event is not a matter of possibility but absolute certainty that will definitely come to pass. The term 'Al-Waqi'ah' (the Event/Happening) is a name for the Day of Resurrection, and by addressing it as already certain to occur, the Qur'an is drawing attention to the absolute authority and knowledge of Allah over all affairs, compelling the believer to recognize their accountability and prepare accordingly.

translation: There is nothing false about its occurrence
interpretation: This verse refers to the certainty and inevitability of the Hour (Day of Judgment). Allah is emphasizing that when the Hour comes, it will definitely happen and there is nothing deceptive or untrue about its occurrence. This serves as a powerful reminder that the Day of Judgment is an absolute truth that will certainly come to pass, and believers should prepare themselves accordingly by living righteously and faithfully.

translation: It lowers some and raises others
interpretation: This phrase describes the ultimate justice and power of divine decree, emphasizing that Allah's will elevates whom He chooses and humbles whom He chooses, regardless of worldly status or ambition. It conveys that true honor and degradation come from Allah alone, not from human efforts or social position, and serves as a reminder of divine sovereignty over all affairs.

translation: When the earth is shaken with a terrible shaking
interpretation: This verse describes the violent trembling of the earth that will occur on the Day of Judgment, signifying the cosmic upheaval and dissolution of the natural world order when divine justice is about to be executed. The double mention of 'rajj' (shaking) emphasizes the severity and intensity of this cataclysmic event, serving as a vivid reminder to humanity of the reality of the afterlife and the accountability that awaits all souls.

translation: And the mountains were spread out as a carpet
interpretation: This verse describes how Allah spread out the mountains across the earth as if laying down a vast carpet, emphasizing the deliberate divine design and arrangement of the mountains to serve as a foundation for the earth and to provide stability for human habitation. The metaphor of a carpet conveys both the careful placement and the functional purpose of mountains in creating a habitable world for mankind.

translation: So it became scattered dust
interpretation: This phrase describes how the deeds of those who associate partners with Allah become utterly worthless and dispersed like particles of dust scattered in the wind. It illustrates the complete nullification and utter insignificance of the works of the disbelievers, emphasizing that their efforts in this life amount to nothing and will have no lasting value or reward on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And you were three kinds (of groups)
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment when humanity will be divided into three categories based on their deeds and spiritual state. The three groups are typically understood as: the foremost in good deeds (the companions of the right hand), those who are moderate in their faith, and those who denied the truth and strayed far from God's guidance (the companions of the left hand). This division emphasizes the fundamental differentiation that occurs in the afterlife based on one's choices and relationship with Allah during earthly life.

translation: Then the companions of the right - what are the companions of the right?
interpretation: This verse introduces and emphasizes the people of the right side on the Day of Judgment through rhetorical questioning, drawing attention to their blessed status and creating anticipation for the description of their ultimate reward that follows. The repetition of the phrase itself serves to heighten the listener's attention and convey the excellence and significance of this group among those who will be judged.

translation: And the companions of the left hand - what will be the companions of the left hand?
interpretation: This verse expresses the gravity and severity of the fate of those who are assigned to the left hand on the Day of Judgment. The repetition of the question 'what will be' emphasizes the terrible and indescribable nature of their punishment, creating a sense of awe and warning about the consequences of disbelief and disobedience to Allah.

translation: And the foremost, the foremost (ones).
interpretation: This verse refers to those who excel in faith and righteous deeds, specifically those who were among the first to embrace Islam and demonstrate precedence in submission to Allah. The repetition of 'al-sabiqun' (the foremost) emphasizes their unique and eminent status in the eyes of Allah, suggesting that they occupy the highest ranks among believers due to their swiftness in accepting the truth and their dedication to serving the religion.

translation: Those are the ones brought near (to Allah)
interpretation: This phrase refers to the righteous and faithful servants of Allah who have attained the highest stations of closeness to their Lord through their devotion, obedience, and spiritual excellence. They are distinguished by their special proximity to Allah's favor and mercy, representing the spiritual elite who have purified their hearts and souls and dedicated themselves completely to worshipping and obeying Allah.

translation: In the gardens of bliss
interpretation: This phrase describes the ultimate reward for the righteous believers in Paradise, emphasizing that it is a state of perfect pleasure and comfort where all desires are fulfilled and all suffering is eliminated. The repetition of this phrase throughout the Qur'an reinforces that the eternal gardens of Paradise represent the highest aspiration and goal of a believer's faith and righteous deeds.

translation: A group of the former peoples
interpretation: This phrase refers to a small company or group from the earlier generations of humanity, emphasizing the continuity of divine guidance and accountability across different eras. The word 'ثلة' (group) combined with 'الأولين' (the former ones) suggests that salvation and closeness to God were available to select righteous individuals throughout human history, not exclusively to any single generation, highlighting that righteousness and divine favor transcend temporal boundaries and are determined by sincere faith and righteous deeds rather than mere chronological placement in history.

translation: And few of the others
interpretation: This phrase refers to those who are few in number among the remaining people, emphasizing the scarcity or rarity of a particular quality or characteristic among most of humanity. The phrase suggests exclusivity and highlights that only a small proportion possess the attribute or quality being discussed in the broader context, serving as a reminder that spiritual insight, faithfulness, or righteousness is not widespread but rather limited to a select few.

translation: upon couches decorated [with gold]
interpretation: This phrase describes the luxurious furnishings of Paradise, emphasizing that the righteous will enjoy not merely basic comfort but refined and ornate surroundings. The word 'موضونة' (maḍūnah) suggests fine craftsmanship and careful arrangement, conveying that Divine reward includes aesthetic beauty and dignity, reflecting the honor and esteem granted to the blessed in the afterlife.

translation: Reclining upon it, facing one another
interpretation: This verse describes the posture and arrangement of the inhabitants of Paradise as they recline upon couches or thrones facing each other. The phrase emphasizes the comfort, leisure, and social companionship that characterizes the blessed state in Paradise, where people sit in dignified repose while engaging in pleasant conversation with one another. This conveys both physical ease and spiritual fulfillment through communal fellowship in the afterlife.

translation: There will circulate among them eternal youths
interpretation: This verse describes the attendants in Paradise who will serve the inhabitants of the Gardens. The term 'mukhallad' (eternal/immortal) indicates that these youths will not age or perish, remaining forever in their youthful state to serve the blessed. This imagery emphasizes the perfection and permanence of Paradise's delights, where all aspects of bliss, including the service provided, are eternal and unchanging, free from the decay and diminishment of the earthly world.

translation: With cups and pitchers and a cup from a flowing spring
interpretation: This verse describes the vessels and drinks that will be served to the inhabitants of Paradise, emphasizing the abundance and perfection of delights in the afterlife. The mention of cups, pitchers, and a special cup from a flowing spring symbolizes the variety, quality, and perpetual availability of pure drinks that surpass earthly beverages, serving as a metaphor for the comprehensive and superior nature of divine reward.

translation: They will not be turned away from it, nor will they be deprived of it.
interpretation: This verse describes the eternal nature of the blessings granted to the people of Paradise. The phrase indicates that the inhabitants of Paradise will continuously enjoy the fruits and drinks provided to them without interruption or exhaustion. The dual negations emphasize the permanence and abundance of these divine gifts, suggesting that unlike worldly pleasures which diminish or become unavailable, the delights of Paradise remain constant and inexhaustible throughout eternity, reflecting God's infinite mercy and the completeness of His reward for the righteous.

translation: And fruits from whatever they choose
interpretation: This verse describes one of the blessings and rewards available to the righteous in Paradise, emphasizing divine generosity and the fulfillment of desires. The phrase conveys that the inhabitants of Paradise will have access to an abundance of fruits, and notably they will have the freedom to select whatever they prefer, signifying complete satisfaction of their wishes without constraint or scarcity. This reflects the Qur'anic theme that Paradise transcends earthly limitations and provides unlimited provision tailored to the preferences of its inhabitants.

translation: And the flesh of fowl from whatever they desire
interpretation: This verse describes one of the delights available to the inhabitants of Paradise, emphasizing that the blessed will enjoy meat from birds according to their wishes. The phrase illustrates the concept of fulfillment of desires in Paradise - whatever the righteous soul wishes for will be readily available, reflecting the ultimate mercy and generosity of Allah toward those who pleased Him in the worldly life. The mention of specific foods is meant to convey the comprehensive nature of Paradise's rewards, going beyond mere physical sustenance to represent complete satisfaction and the removal of all deprivation.

translation: And fair maidens with wide, beautiful eyes
interpretation: This verse refers to one of the blessings promised to the righteous in Paradise, describing women of extraordinary beauty characterized by their striking eyes. The phrase emphasizes spiritual and physical beauty as a reward for the faithful, reflecting the Qur'anic theme that Paradise contains pleasures beyond earthly comprehension as recompense for those who lived righteously and maintained their faith.

translation: Like the likeness of pearls well-preserved/hidden
interpretation: This phrase describes the purity, beauty, and precious nature of something being compared to pearls that are carefully concealed and protected. The metaphor emphasizes the valuable, refined, and unblemished quality of what is being described, suggesting something of exceptional worth and luminosity that has been safeguarded from contamination or diminishment.

translation: A recompense for what they used to do
interpretation: This phrase emphasizes the principle of divine justice wherein people receive rewards or punishments that are proportionate and precisely matched to their deeds and actions in life. The use of 'jaza' (recompense) indicates an exact correspondence between one's conduct and the consequence one receives from Allah, reflecting the Qur'anic teaching that accountability before God is absolute and fair, with no action going unnoticed or unrewarded.

translation: They will not hear therein any vain discourse, nor any sin.
interpretation: This verse describes the spiritual environment of Paradise, emphasizing its purity and wholesomeness. The inhabitants of Paradise will be shielded from all forms of harmful or frivolous speech (laghw) and sinful talk (ta'thim), indicating that the discourse and communication in Paradise will be exclusively righteous, meaningful, and conducive to spiritual elevation. This reflects the Qur'anic theme that Paradise is a realm of absolute perfection where nothing base, corrupting, or spiritually damaging exists, and where the believers experience complete peace and harmony in their interactions with one another.

translation: Except a greeting of "Peace, Peace"
interpretation: This phrase refers to the exclusive dialogue that will occur between the inhabitants of Paradise and Hell on the Day of Judgment. The people of Paradise will greet the people of Hell with words of peace, acknowledging their separation and blessed state, while those in Hell will receive only this distant, merciful greeting rather than being addressed with words of harshness or reproach. It emphasizes Allah's justice and mercy even in the final judgment—the blessed do not mock or torment the damned with words, but offer only peaceful acknowledgment of the ultimate decree.

translation: And the companions of the right - what are the companions of the right?
interpretation: This rhetorical question from Surah Al-Waqi'ah draws attention to the blessed status of those who will be placed on the right hand on the Day of Judgment, emphasizing their excellence and desirability by expressing wonder at their exalted position, while simultaneously creating anticipation for the description of their reward that follows.

translation: In a lote-tree with thorns removed
interpretation: This phrase refers to the blessed tree in paradise that the Prophet Muhammad saw during his night journey (Isra'), characterized by its thorns being removed, symbolizing the perfection and purification of the heavenly realm where all impurities and harms have been eliminated. The removal of thorns emphasizes how paradise is a place of absolute comfort and safety, free from any pain or disturbance that exists in the earthly world.

translation: And fruit-laden date palms
interpretation: This phrase refers to the abundant, densely-clustered fruit of date palms in Paradise, symbolizing the richness and perfection of divine reward. The word 'munḍūd' (منضود) emphasizes that the fruit is tightly arranged and fully ripe, suggesting completeness and inexhaustible blessing. It serves as evidence of Allah's providential care and the incomparable beauty awaiting the righteous, evoking both physical abundance and the spiritual satisfaction of those in Paradise.

translation: And a shadow extended/stretched out
interpretation: This phrase describes the cooling shade provided to the people of Paradise, symbolizing comfort, rest, and protection from hardship. The extended shadow represents Allah's continuous provision of ease and mercy to the righteous, emphasizing the perpetual nature of divine blessing in the afterlife.

translation: And water poured forth
interpretation: This phrase refers to the abundant provision of water as a sign of God's mercy and sustenance. The imagery of 'poured forth' (muskūb) emphasizes the generous, flowing nature of divine provision, suggesting that God grants water abundantly and continuously to His creation. This reflects the Qur'anic theme of recognizing the blessings and signs of God's power in the natural world, specifically in the essential element of water that sustains all life.

translation: And abundant fruit
interpretation: This phrase refers to the blessings and provisions of Paradise, emphasizing the diversity and abundance of fruits that will be available to the righteous in the afterlife. The mention of 'many' or 'abundant' fruit highlights God's generous provision and the contrast between earthly scarcity and the unlimited bounty of Paradise, serving as a motivation for righteous conduct in this life.

translation: Neither cut off nor prevented/denied
interpretation: This phrase describes a state of continuous provision and uninterrupted sustenance, emphasizing that divine blessings flow without cessation or obstruction. It suggests the permanence and reliability of God's mercy and bounty, conveying that those favored by God experience an endless stream of benefits that cannot be severed or withheld.

translation: And cushions raised high
interpretation: This phrase describes the luxurious furnishings of Paradise, emphasizing both comfort and elevation. The raised cushions symbolize the elevated status and dignity of the inhabitants of Paradise, while also representing the layered pleasures and refined comforts that await the righteous. The mention of 'raising' suggests both literal elevation in terms of construction and metaphorical elevation in terms of honor and distinction granted to those in Paradise.

translation: Indeed, We created them a creation [of new origin/uniqueness]
interpretation: This verse refers to the creation of the women of Paradise with a unique and perfect creation distinct from the creation of the people of this world, emphasizing the special and elevated nature of their existence in the Hereafter as a divine gift and manifestation of Allah's perfect creative power.

translation: So We made them virgins (restored their virginity)
interpretation: This verse refers to the miraculous restoration of virginity to the wives of the Prophet in Paradise as a divine blessing and honor. It symbolizes purity, renewal, and the special status granted to the righteous in the afterlife, emphasizing that Paradise contains blessings beyond the comprehension of the earthly mind and that Allah's power extends to all aspects of existence.

translation: Companions of equal age
interpretation: This phrase describes souls or companions of matching maturity and age, often used in Islamic tradition to refer to the righteous companions in Paradise who are compatible with one another. The term emphasizes compatibility and suitability in companionship, suggesting that divine arrangement ensures harmony between those who dwell together in the afterlife.

translation: For the companions of the right hand
interpretation: This phrase refers to the righteous believers who will be placed on the right side on the Day of Judgment, a position of honor and distinction that signifies their acceptance by Allah and their entry into Paradise. The 'right hand' is a symbol of favor, blessing, and salvation in Islamic tradition, contrasting with those on the left who face punishment.

translation: A group of the earlier ones
interpretation: This phrase refers to a select number of righteous people from the generations that came before, emphasizing their elevated status and blessing. The term 'ثلة' (a group) suggests a distinct minority chosen for honor, often used in the Qur'an to describe those believers from earlier nations who will be among the closest to God and highest in rank on the Day of Judgment, highlighting the consistency of God's favor toward His righteous servants across all generations.

translation: And a group of others
interpretation: This phrase refers to an unspecified additional group of people whose exact identity or number is left deliberately vague, emphasizing that there are more beyond those already mentioned, which is typical in Qur'anic discourse to indicate completeness or to humble the listener by reminding them that Allah's knowledge encompasses what they do not fully know or enumerate.

translation: And the companions of the left - what are the companions of the left?
interpretation: This verse expresses divine emphasis and wonder at the fate of those destined for Hell, drawing attention to the magnitude and severity of their condition. The rhetorical repetition of the phrase serves to awaken the listener's consciousness about the gravity of transgression and the consequences of turning away from God's guidance, making the reality of divine justice unmistakably clear.

translation: In poison and boiling water
interpretation: This phrase refers to the severe and painful punishments of Hell, where the condemned will be subjected to both toxic substances (poison) and extremely hot liquids (boiling water). The mention of these two torments emphasizes the multifaceted nature of divine punishment—addressing both internal suffering through ingestion of harmful substances and external torment through extreme heat. Together, they symbolize the comprehensive and inescapable nature of hellish torment for those who rejected God's guidance, serving as a powerful warning about the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing.

translation: And shade from black smoke
interpretation: This phrase refers to the torment of Hell, where the shade is not cooling comfort but rather from the choking, suffocating black smoke that rises from the fire. The word 'yahamoom' (يحموم) specifically denotes thick, dark smoke, emphasizing that in Hell there is no relief or mercy - even what appears to be shelter becomes a source of additional suffering. This illustrates the complete reversal of comfort in the afterlife for those who reject God's signs.

translation: Neither cool nor hospitable/generous
interpretation: This phrase describes something that is neither refreshing nor pleasing - neither possessing a desirable quality nor demonstrating kindness or generosity. It can be understood as depicting a state of complete undesirability or lack of benefit, whether physical or moral. The pairing of opposites emphasizes total deprivation of positive qualities.

translation: Indeed, they were before that indulging in luxury and ease.
interpretation: This phrase describes a state of spiritual heedlessness that comes from material abundance and comfort. The verse suggests that their previous luxurious living made them complacent and inattentive to divine guidance, causing them to become distant from spiritual awareness and moral responsibility. Indulgence in worldly pleasures often leads to neglect of one's relationship with God and can become a barrier to recognizing truth and heeding warning signs.

translation: And they were persisting in the great sin/oath-breaking.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the stubbornness and willful persistence of people in committing grave transgressions. The emphasis on 'persisting' (يصرون) conveys not mere commission of sin, but a deliberate, repeated, and obstinate adherence to wrongdoing despite knowledge of its severity. This reflects the Qur'anic theme that those who knowingly and persistently violate their covenants with Allah or commit major sins demonstrate a hardening of the heart and resistance to divine guidance, which compounds their moral culpability. The 'great sin' suggests both the magnitude of the transgression and its consequences, serving as a warning about the spiritual danger of habitual disobedience.

translation: And they used to say, 'When we are dead and have become dust and bones, will we indeed be raised up?'
interpretation: This verse reflects the skepticism and disbelief of the polytheists regarding the resurrection and afterlife. Their doubt is rooted in a materialist perspective that sees death as final annihilation, unable to conceive how bodies reduced to dust and scattered bones could be restored and revived. The verse illustrates the human tendency to deny what contradicts observable physical reality, revealing how those who reject divine resurrection are trapped by their limited understanding of God's power and knowledge of the unseen realm.

translation: Or our first forefathers
interpretation: This phrase expresses the objection of those who reject the message of resurrection and the afterlife by appealing to the practices and beliefs of their ancestors, suggesting that if their forefathers did not believe in such matters, then they need not either. It reflects the tendency of people to justify their disbelief through ancestral tradition rather than through rational consideration of the truth, highlighting how cultural inertia and blind following of predecessors can prevent people from accepting divine guidance.

translation: Say: 'Indeed, the former peoples and the latter peoples...'
interpretation: This verse (Surah Al-Waqi'ah 56:49) begins a statement where the Prophet Muhammad is commanded to declare a truth about all of humanity across time - both those who lived before and those who will come after. The verse emphasizes the universality of the divine message and the accountability that applies to all human beings regardless of their era, establishing that no generation is exempt from God's judgment and the obligation to follow His guidance.

translation: We will indeed be gathered together on a Day appointed
interpretation: This verse affirms the Islamic belief in resurrection and the Day of Judgment, emphasizing that all people will be assembled at a predetermined time known only to Allah. It serves as a reminder of the certainty and inevitability of divine accountability, encouraging the faithful to prepare themselves through righteous deeds and moral conduct, as they will ultimately face judgment for their actions in this life.

translation: Then indeed, you are the misguided ones, the liars/deniers.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who reject the truth and willfully turn away from guidance, describing them with two condemning attributes: being astray from the right path and being deniers of divine signs.
