translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. O Prophet, why do you forbid yourself what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking to please your wives? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad's personal choice to abstain from something permissible (likely referring to honey or a particular concubine) in order to appease his wives, illustrating the tension between personal preferences and marital harmony. The verse teaches that while seeking to please one's family is understandable, one should not unnecessarily restrict oneself from what Allah has permitted, and reminds the Prophet that Allah's forgiveness and mercy extend even to such human inclinations toward compromise and self-denial for relational peace.

translation: Allah has prescribed for you the expiation of your oaths, and Allah is your protector, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse establishes that when Muslims break their oaths, they have been given a merciful way to atone rather than being left burdened with broken vows. The mention of Allah as their protector and His attributes of knowledge and wisdom suggests that this divine prescription is not a harsh punishment but a compassionate legal framework that balances accountability with mercy, recognizing human weakness while maintaining moral responsibility.

translation: And when the Prophet confided a matter to one of his wives, and when she disclosed it and Allah made it known to him, he acknowledged part of it and avoided part of it. And when he informed her of it, she said: 'Who told you this?' He said: 'The All-Knowing, the All-Aware has informed me.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine accountability that applies to all believers, including the Prophet himself, demonstrating that no one—not even the closest companions of the Prophet—can breach trust without divine knowledge and justice. The Prophet's response, attributing his knowledge to Allah's attributes as 'Al-'Aleem' (The All-Knowing) and 'Al-Khabeer' (The All-Aware), emphasizes that Allah's perfect knowledge and awareness encompass all hidden matters, and that truthfulness and trustworthiness are paramount values in Islamic ethics, even in intimate relationships. The incident serves as a moral lesson about the importance of confidentiality and the consequences of disclosure, while affirming that ultimately all deeds and breaches are known to Allah.

translation: If you two turn in repentance to Allah, then your hearts have already inclined [to it]. But if you support one another against him, then indeed Allah is his ally, and Gabriel and the righteous among the believers, and the angels, after that, are [also] supporters.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine protection afforded to the Prophet Muhammad and warns against opposing him. It demonstrates that those who align themselves against the Prophet face opposition not merely from believers, but from Allah, His angels (Gabriel being singled out), and the righteous community. The verse indicates that repentance is always available as a path back to obedience, suggesting that the hearts of those addressed are capable of inclination toward truth if they choose it. Fundamentally, it establishes the superiority of the Prophet's position through his connection to the divine order and the angelic realm, while simultaneously showing Allah's mercy by leaving the door open for repentance rather than immediate punishment.

translation: Perhaps his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you - submitting women, believing women, obedient women, repentant women, worshiping women, fasting women, previously married women and virgins.
interpretation: This verse reminds those who might be divorced that they should not despair, as Allah can replace them with women of superior spiritual qualities. The emphasis on the plural qualities - submission, faith, obedience, repentance, worship, and devotion - suggests that true value in marriage lies not in worldly status or appearance, but in a woman's righteousness and piety. The verse implicitly encourages women to cultivate these spiritual attributes, knowing that such qualities are what Allah values and what makes a person truly excellent and worthy of respect in His sight.

translation: O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones, over which are angels, harsh and severe; they do not disobey Allah in what He has commanded them but do what they are commanded.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the believer's personal responsibility to cultivate piety and righteousness not only within themselves but also to extend this spiritual guardianship to their families. The detailed description of Hellfire—fueled by people and stones, guarded by stern angels—serves as a powerful motivator for moral accountability. By first reforming oneself and then guiding one's household toward obedience to Allah, one creates a protective barrier against divine punishment. The verse teaches that spiritual protection is an active obligation requiring constant vigilance and the transmission of faith values to those under one's care, rather than passive acceptance of fate.

translation: O you who have disbelieved, make no excuses this Day. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who rejected faith and warns them that on the Day of Judgment, excuses and justifications will be neither accepted nor beneficial. The Divine judgment is based upon their actual deeds and intentions during their lifetime, not upon any explanations or apologies offered in the afterlife. It emphasizes the principle of absolute accountability before Allah, where one's actions alone determine one's fate, and there is no avenue for evasion or excuse once the time for accountability has arrived.

translation: O you who have believed, repent to Allah with sincere repentance. Perhaps your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, on the Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and those who have believed with him. Their light will proceed before them and to their right, while they say, 'Our Lord, perfect for us our light and forgive us. Indeed, You are over all things competent.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that sincere repentance (tawbah nusuh) is not merely a momentary regret but a comprehensive turning back to Allah with genuine commitment and transformation. The verse illustrates that true believers maintain constant connection with Allah through their deeds (represented by the light), and despite their imperfections, they humbly seek divine completion and forgiveness, recognizing that their ultimate success depends entirely on Allah's power and mercy. The light symbolizes righteous actions and faith that illuminate the path of believers in this life and the hereafter, demonstrating that sincere repentance combined with continued striving and humility is the pathway to salvation.

translation: O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them. And their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad's responsibility to firmly oppose those who reject faith and those who feign belief while harboring disbelief. The command to be 'harsh' (aghluẓ) reflects the necessity of resolute leadership in matters of faith and guidance, not through physical cruelty but through unwavering conviction and uncompromising moral stance. The mention of Hell as their destination serves as both a warning of divine justice and a reminder to the Prophet that the ultimate judgment and accountability rest with Allah, thereby placing the burden of persuasion and preaching upon him while absolving him of responsibility for who ultimately believes. This establishes the principle that spiritual struggle requires firmness in principles even when facing opposition.

translation: Allah presents an example of those who disbelieved: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. They were both under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them. So they [the righteous servants] availed them not at all against Allah, and it was said, 'Enter the Fire with those who are entering.'
interpretation: This verse teaches that proximity to righteousness and faith does not automatically guarantee salvation or protection; one's own choices and actions determine one's fate. The disbelief and betrayal of these wives demonstrate that no amount of association with the righteous—whether through kinship or proximity—can substitute for personal faith and obedience to Allah. This serves as a warning that family lineage and close relationships with the pious are ineffectual without genuine faith, and that accountability before Allah is individual and personal.

translation: And Allah presents an example for those who have believed: the wife of Pharaoh, when she said, 'My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds and save me from the wrongdoing people.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates that true faith transcends worldly status and power. Despite living in the palace of the mightiest ruler of her time, Pharaoh's wife demonstrated that genuine belief in Allah is characterized by a longing for the eternal rewards of Paradise over temporary worldly comfort, and a consciousness of spiritual danger from those who promote falsehood, regardless of their outward authority. Her example teaches believers that closeness to Allah matters infinitely more than proximity to earthly power, and that sincere faith compels one to seek salvation from the spiritual corruption of oppressive systems.

translation: And Mary, the daughter of Imran, who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her (through Our spirit), and she believed in the words of her Lord and His scriptures, and she was among the obedient.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Mary's exceptional virtue and faith as exemplary qualities for believers. Her guarding of her chastity is presented as a prerequisite for her selection as a vessel for a divine miracle, demonstrating that moral integrity and purity precede spiritual elevation. The phrase 'she believed in the words of her Lord and His scriptures' highlights that true honor comes not merely from physical purity but from intellectual and spiritual submission to divine truth. Her designation as 'among the obedient' (al-qanitin) signifies that her obedience was active and continuous rather than passive, making her a model of complete devotion where body, mind, and spirit are unified in submission to God's will.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. Blessed is He in whose hand is sovereignty, and He is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true power and dominion belong exclusively to Allah, and all authority derives from His divine hands. The phrase 'blessed is He' (tabaraka) conveys not only blessing but an affirmation of Allah's absolute perfection and sanctity. By asserting His competence over all things, the verse emphasizes that there is no limit to Allah's power and capability, inviting the believer to recognize the futility of relying on created beings and to place complete trust in Allah's governance of all affairs.

translation: He who created death and life that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed. And He is the Mighty, the Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the alternation between life and death—or the existence of both states in the universe—is not random or meaningless, but rather a deliberate trial from Allah. The test is not merely about belief, but specifically about the quality of one's actions. By attributing both 'might' and 'forgiveness' to Allah at the verse's conclusion, the Qur'an presents a balanced picture: while humans will be rigorously tested and judged for their deeds, Allah's forgiveness remains available to those who repent and improve themselves, thus motivating believers to strive for excellence while maintaining hope in divine mercy.

translation: He who created seven heavens in layers. You do not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any disproportion. So return your gaze—do you see any flaw?
interpretation: This verse invites the observer to recognize the perfect order and harmony in Allah's creation of the heavens, challenging them to find any defect or inconsistency. The command to 'return your gaze' repeatedly emphasizes the invitation to careful contemplation, suggesting that thoughtful reflection upon creation should lead one to acknowledge the flawlessness of Allah's design and, by extension, His absolute power and wisdom. The rhetorical question expects a negative answer, confirming that no imperfection exists in Allah's creative work.

translation: Then return your gaze twice. Your sight will return to you humbled and weary.
interpretation: This verse invites the observer to repeatedly examine the heavens with careful attention, implying that such contemplation of the creation will lead to a humbling recognition of one's own insignificance and weakness. The 'return' of the sight 'humbled and weary' suggests that true reflection on the vastness and perfection of divine creation inevitably produces a sense of human limitation and fatigue in the attempt to comprehend it, thereby drawing the observer closer to faith and awareness of Allah's absolute power.

translation: And We have indeed adorned the lowest heaven with lamps, and We have made them (as) missiles to drive away the devils, and We have prepared for them the punishment of the blazing fire.
interpretation: This verse illustrates Allah's complete sovereignty over creation and His knowledge of future events. The celestial bodies serve a dual purpose in the divine order: they provide beauty and illumination for the created universe, while simultaneously functioning as a means to repel the devils' attempts to eavesdrop on heavenly communications. This demonstrates that Allah's creation operates according to His perfect wisdom, where even the most visible elements of creation—the stars—serve purposes beyond human perception. The verse also establishes the certainty of divine punishment for those who rebel against Allah, preparing the believer's heart to recognize that justice and accountability are fundamental to the cosmic order.

translation: And for those who disbelieve in their Lord is the punishment of Hell; and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: This verse establishes the ultimate consequence of rejecting divine guidance and denying Allah's lordship. The emphasis on 'wretched is the destination' serves not merely as a statement of punishment, but as a warning of the absolute deprivation and hopelessness that results from turning away from truth, highlighting that Hell represents not an arbitrary punishment but the natural and inevitable outcome of conscious rejection of God.

translation: When they are cast into it, they hear from it a roaring sound while it boils.
interpretation: This verse describes the sensory experience of the inhabitants of Hell, emphasizing their awareness of its torment through both sound and sight. The 'roaring sound' (shahiq) and the boiling (tafur) serve as vivid reminders that Hell is not a state of unconsciousness or numbness, but rather conscious punishment. The mention of hearing and witnessing the hellfire's violent activity underscores that the damned remain fully aware of their suffering, making the punishment more severe through psychological awareness in addition to physical pain. This heightens the gravity of rejection and disobedience in this life.

translation: They almost burst with rage. Every time a group is cast into it, its keepers ask them, "Did there not come to you a warner?"
interpretation: This verse illustrates the intense emotional reaction of those in Hell to the arrival of new inhabitants, reflecting their anger at seeing others condemned to the same fate they suffer. The keepers' repeated questioning serves to establish the justice of their punishment by confirming that all had received divine warnings in the worldly life, highlighting the theme that no one will enter Hell without having been given the opportunity to know and obey God's message.

translation: They said: "Yes, indeed a warner came to us, but we denied him and said: 'Allah has not sent down anything. You are in great error.'"
interpretation: This verse illustrates the arrogance and obstinacy of the deniers when confronted with divine guidance. Despite acknowledging the arrival of a messenger (nذير), they consciously rejected the message and attributed falsehood to Allah by claiming He had revealed nothing, thereby condemning the messenger and believers as being in grave misguidance. Their response demonstrates how rejection of truth is often a deliberate choice rooted in pride and stubborn denial rather than genuine doubt or lack of evidence.

translation: And they said, 'If we had listened or reasoned, we would not have been among the inhabitants of the Fire.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the regret and self-awareness of the dwellers of Hell who acknowledge that their damnation was a consequence of their own choices—their refusal to listen to the message of truth and their rejection of rational reflection on the signs presented to them. The verse emphasizes personal responsibility and divine justice, showing that Hell's inhabitants cannot blame anyone but themselves, as they possessed the faculties of hearing and intellect but chose willfully to ignore both revelation and reason.

translation: So they admitted their sin. Then away with the companions of the Blaze!
interpretation: This verse illustrates the ultimate recognition of truth by those destined for Hell - they will openly confess and acknowledge their wrongdoing before their punishment. The phrase 'away with them' (سحقا) expresses divine condemnation and rejection, emphasizing that confession without acceptance in this life and without good deeds provides no refuge. The verse conveys that mere acknowledgment of sin in the Hereafter, after all opportunity for repentance has passed, is futile and leads only to ruin, serving as a stern warning about the necessity of sincere repentance and righteous action in this world.

translation: Indeed, those who fear their Lord in private will have forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the spiritual quality of fearing God when no one is watching. It highlights that true piety is demonstrated through one's hidden conduct and sincere devotion, not merely through outward display of religiosity. The promise of forgiveness and great reward affirms that God's mercy extends to those whose faith and obedience stem from genuine reverence rather than seeking worldly recognition or approval from others.

translation: And conceal your speech or publicize it; indeed, He is knowing of that within the breasts.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's complete and absolute knowledge of all human thoughts, intentions, and secrets of the heart, whether words are spoken aloud or kept hidden. It conveys the message that Allah's knowledge transcends the distinction between the public and private realms, serving as a reminder that one cannot hide anything from Allah, which should inspire consciousness of Him in all circumstances and encourage sincerity in intention regardless of who is listening.

translation: Does He not know who created? And He is the Most Subtle, the All-Aware.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Allah, as the Creator of all things, possesses complete and intimate knowledge of His creation. The attributes of Al-Lateef (The Subtle) and Al-Khabeer (The All-Aware) emphasize that His knowledge penetrates the innermost depths of creation—nothing escapes His notice, whether apparent or hidden. The rhetorical question functions as a powerful assertion that it would be inconceivable for the Creator to lack knowledge of what He has created, thereby refuting any doubt about Allah's omniscience and His perfect understanding of the intricate details of His creation.

translation: He is the one who made the earth subservient to you, so walk upon its paths and eat from His provision. And to Him is the resurrection.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's deliberate facilitation of human life on earth by rendering it manageable and accessible for human habitation and sustenance. The metaphor of the earth being 'made subservient' (dhulul) conveys that God has removed impediments to human movement and livelihood, inviting humanity to actively engage with the world through travel and consumption. The mention of walking on its paths and eating from God's provision establishes that human activity and enjoyment of earthly resources are part of God's intentional design. The final clause brings this back to divine sovereignty by reminding humans that despite their temporal engagement with the earth, their ultimate return and accountability are solely to God, thereby framing earthly life within the larger context of divine purpose and the afterlife.

translation: Have you become secure that He who is in the heaven will not cause the earth to sink with you, and suddenly it will sway?
interpretation: This verse warns against false security and complacency in faith. It emphasizes the omnipotence of Allah and His ability to punish those who turn away from Him, using the dramatic imagery of the earth opening up or trembling beneath them as a metaphor for sudden and catastrophic consequences of rejecting divine guidance. The rhetorical question challenges believers to remain vigilant and humbly conscious of their dependence on Allah's mercy, rather than assuming they are immune to divine judgment.

translation: Or do you feel secure that He who is in the heaven will not send upon you a storm of stones? Then you will know how [serious] is My warning.
interpretation: The verse emphasizes divine accountability by posing a rhetorical question that awakens human conscience to the reality of God's power and the certainty of consequences for negligence of His warnings. The phrase 'storm of stones' (hāṣib) is a metaphor for sudden, catastrophic punishment, and the concluding statement 'then you will know how serious is My warning' underscores that experience and reality will ultimately validate God's messengers and demonstrate the folly of rejecting divine guidance. This interpretation conveys the dual purpose of the warning: both as an invitation to reflection before punishment arrives, and as an assurance that history will vindicate God's messengers.

translation: And indeed, those before them denied, so how was My rejection?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the established pattern of divine justice throughout history: those who rejected God's messengers in the past faced severe consequences and punishment. The rhetorical question 'so how was My rejection?' conveys the certainty and severity of God's retribution against deniers, serving as a warning to the current disbelievers that they too will face inevitable consequences if they persist in denial, just as their predecessors did.

translation: Have they not observed the birds above them with wings outstretched and wings folded? Nothing holds them up except the Most Merciful. Indeed, He is seeing of all things.
interpretation: This verse invites reflection on the natural phenomenon of birds in flight as evidence of divine power and sustenance. The birds' ability to soar and maneuver in the sky—spreading and folding their wings—is presented as a manifest sign that only Allah's mercy and power maintain their existence and movement. The verse teaches that all creatures, despite their apparent independence and natural abilities, are ultimately sustained solely by God's will and care. The concluding statement that Allah is All-Seeing emphasizes His complete knowledge and oversight of creation, reinforcing that nothing escapes His awareness or exists outside His providential care.

translation: Or is there one who is an army for you that will help you other than the Most Merciful? The disbelievers are not in anything but delusion.
interpretation: This verse presents a rhetorical question emphasizing human vulnerability and dependence on Allah alone. By asking if anyone besides Allah can be an army or helper to humanity, the Qur'an removes any false reliance on earthly powers or material forces. The verse then characterizes disbelievers as living in delusion (ghurur) because they falsely imagine that worldly alliances, wealth, or military strength can protect them or substitute for divine protection. The interpretation underscores that true security and victory come only from Allah's mercy and protection, while those who reject this reality deceive themselves about their actual condition of weakness and needfulness before their Creator.

translation: Is it not He who provides for you, if He withholds His provision? Yet they persist in obstinacy and aversion.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute dependence of creation upon Allah's mercy and sustenance, while condemning the stubborn rejection and turning away from divine truth despite obvious signs of Allah's lordship. The rhetorical question highlights how those who deny Allah's oneness remain willfully heedless even when confronted with the manifest reality of their dependence on Him for their very livelihood, exposing the irrationality and arrogance that underlie their denial.

translation: Is one who walks fallen upon his face better guided, or one who walks upright upon a straight path?
interpretation: This verse presents a rhetorical question that contrasts two states of spiritual condition: those who follow falsehood and live in spiritual blindness (depicted as walking fallen on their face), versus those who follow the guidance of Allah and maintain moral uprightness (depicted as walking upright on the straight path). The rhetorical nature of the question expects an affirmative answer to the second part, making clear that true guidance is exclusive to those who follow Allah's revelation and maintain spiritual and moral rectitude, while those who reject guidance are in a state of spiritual degradation and confusion.

translation: Say, 'He is the One who created you and gave you hearing, sight, and hearts. How little you are grateful.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the fundamental gifts from Allah that enable human perception and cognition—hearing, sight, and intellect (hearts/minds)—and rebukes humanity for their ingratitude despite receiving these essential faculties that distinguish them and enable their survival and understanding of the world. The rhetorical reproach 'how little you are grateful' serves as a reminder that human thankfulness for these divine blessings is vastly disproportionate to their magnitude and necessity.

translation: Say, 'He is the One who created you upon the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes divine origin and ultimate accountability. The phrase 'scattered you upon the earth' (ذرأكم في الأرض) conveys that Allah is the sole creator and sustainer who dispersed mankind across the earth with different nations, languages, and stations. The complementary phrase 'to Him you will be gathered' points to the inevitable Day of Judgment, establishing that the same Creator who brought humanity into existence will reassemble all souls for divine reckoning. Together, these two principles—creation and resurrection—serve as foundational pillars of Islamic theology, reminding believers that their origin and destiny are both in Allah's hands, thereby negating any claims of independent power or self-sufficiency and underlining complete dependence on and submission to the Divine.

translation: And they say, 'When will this promise come to pass, if you are truthful?'
interpretation: This verse reflects the arrogant defiance of the disbelievers who mockingly challenge the believers regarding the divine promise of the Day of Judgment. Their demand for proof reflects their denial of the unseen and their attempt to discredit the message by questioning its timeline, while simultaneously revealing their spiritual blindness—for they are testing the messenger's sincerity by insisting on empirical evidence for metaphysical realities that lie beyond human perception. The verse illustrates how the disbelievers use skepticism as a tool to dismiss revelation rather than as a genuine pursuit of truth.

translation: Say: 'Knowledge is only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the limitation of human knowledge and the Prophet Muhammad's role as a messenger. By asserting that true knowledge belongs exclusively to Allah, the verse teaches humility in the face of divine wisdom and reminds believers that ultimate understanding of unseen matters rests solely with God. The Prophet's role is restricted to delivering the clear warning of monotheism and accountability, not to claiming knowledge of matters beyond his scope.

translation: So when they saw it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved became distressed, and it was said, 'This is that which you used to invoke.'
interpretation: The verse depicts the moment when the disbelievers witness the arrival of the Day of Judgment or divine punishment, causing their expressions to show despair and anguish. The statement 'This is that which you used to invoke' conveys the ironic and humbling realization that what they mocked, denied, or sarcastically called upon has now become their reality, transforming their arrogance into helplessness as they confront the consequences of their rejection of truth.

translation: Say, 'Have you considered: if Allah destroys me and those with me, or has mercy upon us, who will protect the disbelievers from a painful punishment?'
interpretation: This verse challenges the disbelievers to reflect on their vulnerability before Allah's power. The Prophet is instructed to pose a rhetorical question highlighting that regardless of what befalls the believers—whether destruction or divine mercy—the disbelievers have no refuge or protector against Allah's punishment. The verse emphasizes the futility of their opposition and the inevitability of Allah's justice, demonstrating that neither the believers' status nor their adversaries' power can change the course of divine retribution for those who reject faith.

translation: Say, 'He is the Most Merciful; we have believed in Him, and upon Him we have relied. And you will come to know who is in clear error.'
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet to declare belief in Allah's perfect mercy and absolute trustworthiness, establishing that those who truly understand mercy and place their reliance in the Most Merciful demonstrate wisdom and guidance, while the rejection of this reality and the refusal to rely upon Allah's providence is the clearest form of deviation—a spiritual misguidance that will become evident through its consequences in this life and the next.

translation: Say, 'Have you considered: if your water were to sink into the earth, who then would bring you flowing water?'
interpretation: This verse uses a hypothetical scenario of water disappearing into the depths of the earth to awaken human consciousness about their dependence on Allah for life's necessities. By posing this rhetorical question, the Qur'an directs attention to mankind's helplessness and utter need for divine sustenance, challenging people to recognize that despite their knowledge and capabilities, they cannot secure the basic requirements of life without Allah's provision and mercy.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Nun. By the pen and what they write.
interpretation: This verse is an oath (qasam) by which Allah swears by the pen and the act of writing, emphasizing the supreme importance of knowledge, literacy, and the written word in human civilization and divine guidance. The pen is highlighted as an instrument through which Allah's wisdom is recorded and transmitted across generations, establishing that the preservation and communication of knowledge through writing is a divinely honored means by which truth is conveyed to humanity and by which human deeds are recorded.

translation: You are not, by the grace of your Lord, mad or possessed.
interpretation: This verse defends Prophet Muhammad against the false accusations of his opponents who claimed he was mad, possessed, or mentally disturbed. The phrase 'by the grace of your Lord' emphasizes that the Prophet's sound judgment and clear mind are gifts from Allah, serving to vindicate his mission and authority. The verse affirms that the Prophet's message comes from divine inspiration, not from delusion or mental illness, thereby strengthening the believers' confidence in him and dismissing the slanders of the disbelievers.

translation: And indeed, for you is a reward that will never be cut off.
interpretation: This verse assures the Prophet Muhammad (and by extension, all believers who remain steadfast in their faith and obedience to God) that their compensation and recompense from Allah is eternal and inexhaustible, never to be withheld or diminished. It emphasizes that Allah's promise to reward those who serve Him faithfully is absolute and permanent, serving as encouragement to persevere in faith despite worldly hardships and trials.

translation: And indeed, you are of a great moral character
interpretation: This verse affirms the excellence of the Prophet Muhammad's moral conduct and character, which served as the practical embodiment of the Qur'anic teachings. The word 'khulq' (character/conduct) encompasses not merely outward behavior but the inner virtues that shape one's actions, including honesty, mercy, patience, and justice. By designating his character as 'azim' (great/mighty), the Qur'an elevates moral integrity as among the highest human qualities and presents the Prophet's exemplary conduct as the living manifestation of Islamic values, establishing him as the model for believers to emulate in their own spiritual and ethical development.

translation: So you will see, and they will see.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment when the truth of the Prophet's mission and the reality of God's punishment will become manifest to both the believers and the disbelievers. The seeing here is not merely physical sight but rather a comprehensive realization and understanding of the truth that was denied or hidden in this worldly life. The balanced structure emphasizes that all parties will witness the same reality, though their outcomes will differ based on their deeds in this life.

translation: Which of you is mad? / Which of you is possessed?
interpretation: This phrase expresses the speaker's rhetorical challenge and dismissal of those who follow falsehood or reject the truth. It implies that those being addressed are foolish or deluded for their beliefs or actions, using a question form that emphasizes the speaker's conviction that such behavior is irrational. The question is meant to provoke reflection on the absurdity of the opposing position rather than to genuinely seek an answer.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Allah's knowledge encompasses both those who reject His guidance and those who accept it. The message reassures believers that Allah does not judge based on outward appearances or claims, but has complete awareness of the true state of each person's heart and their sincere intentions. It also serves as a warning that no one can deceive Allah about their true spiritual condition, establishing that ultimate judgment belongs solely to Him who possesses perfect knowledge.

translation: So do not obey the deniers/those who reject the truth.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet Muhammad (and by extension, all believers) to remain steadfast in their conviction and not be swayed by those who reject the message of God. The emphasis is on maintaining integrity and not compromising the truth to please those who deny God's revelation, highlighting the importance of spiritual resilience in the face of opposition and mockery from disbelievers.

translation: They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise [as well].
interpretation: This verse describes how the disbelievers desired the Prophet to make concessions in his faith and principles, hoping that if he would yield on fundamental matters of belief and practice, they too would be willing to meet him halfway. The verse reflects the reality that the enemies of Islam sought to dilute the message through mutual compromise, but the Prophet was commanded to maintain the integrity of Islam without surrender to their demands, establishing that truth cannot be negotiated or softened to appease those opposed to it.

translation: And do not obey every lying, contemptible swearer
interpretation: This verse warns against following those who are characterized by constant false oaths and degrading behavior. The 'lying swearer' refers to someone who makes frequent oaths but lacks integrity and truthfulness. The instruction to avoid such people implies that one should not be swayed by their persuasive words or false assurances, as their character is fundamentally flawed and unreliable. This serves as a moral guideline to discern between trustworthy and untrustworthy individuals, emphasizing that piety and righteousness require careful judgment about whose influence we accept in our lives.

translation: A slanderer, going about with calumny
interpretation: This phrase describes a person of contemptible character who spreads malicious gossip and false accusations among people to create discord and harm. The verse emphasizes the spiritual danger of such behavior, marking it as one of the traits most despised by Allah. The use of these descriptive terms (hammaz and mashaa' bi-nameemi) conveys that this is not merely occasional slander, but a habitual, deliberate practice of the person's nature. This serves as a stern moral warning against engaging in character assassination and spreading false rumors, which destroys the bonds of community and society, and distances one from the path of righteousness.

translation: A preventer of good, transgressive and sinful
interpretation: This phrase describes a person characterized by three vices: preventing or withholding good from others, being transgressive in their bounds and limits, and committing sin. These attributes depict someone of deeply corrupt character who not only pursues wrong action themselves but actively obstructs others from doing good, embodying a comprehensive moral depravity that encompasses both personal wickedness and harm to society.

translation: A transgressor after that, and one who is illegitimate [or of doubtful lineage]
interpretation: This verse describes the spiritual and moral character of someone who rejects faith and persists in arrogance despite receiving clear signs. The term 'atl (عتل) refers to someone crude, obstinate, and rebellious against the truth, while 'zanim' (زنيم) suggests illegitimacy or baseness of character. Together, these descriptions emphasize that continued rejection of divine guidance leads to a degradation of one's moral nature, making the person not only spiritually estranged but also morally deficient and unworthy of noble status.

translation: That he possessed wealth and children
interpretation: This phrase refers to one who is blessed with material resources and offspring, highlighting the arrogance that sometimes accompanies worldly abundance. The context suggests that such blessings can lead a person to become heedless of God's guidance and to rely on their own power rather than submitting to divine will, demonstrating how material prosperity can become a spiritual trial if one forgets that all blessings are ultimately from Allah and create a false sense of self-sufficiency.

translation: When Our verses are recited to him, he says, 'Tales of the ancients.'
interpretation: This verse describes the arrogant rejection of God's signs by those whose hearts are sealed against faith. The dismissal of the Qur'an as mere legends or folklore from previous generations reflects a spiritual blindness and pride that prevents such a person from recognizing divine truth when it is presented to them. Their refusal to acknowledge the verses as revelation from God stems from stubbornness and a predetermined disbelief rather than intellectual doubt.

translation: We will brand him on the snout/muzzle
interpretation: This verse refers to Allah's promise to mark the false claimant to prophethood (specifically Musaylimah al-Kadhdhab) with a visible mark on his nose as a sign of disgrace and divine punishment, serving as a clear indication to the people of his falsehood and the consequences of rejecting the true message of Islam.

translation: Indeed, We have tested them just as We tested the companions of the garden, when they swore that they would surely harvest it in the morning.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle that trial and testing are universal experiences in the spiritual journey. The comparison between the contemporary community and the companions of the garden emphasizes that God's method of testing believers across time is consistent and purposeful. The mention of the gardeners' oath to harvest in the morning serves as a cautionary example that human certainty and plans, however firm they may seem, are subject to divine will and can be disrupted in ways we do not anticipate, thereby teaching humility and reliance upon God rather than placing absolute confidence in material possessions or future outcomes.

translation: And they do not make exceptions
interpretation: This phrase refers to those who speak with certainty about future matters without acknowledging that all outcomes ultimately depend on God's will. The phrase highlights the human tendency to make absolute statements about what will happen tomorrow without the qualification 'if God wills it' (insha'Allah), which reflects a lack of proper reliance on God and an overconfidence in human ability to determine the course of events. It emphasizes the importance of humility and the recognition of God's absolute sovereignty over all affairs.

translation: So a visitation from your Lord passed over it while they slept.
interpretation: This verse describes how Allah's punishment came upon the people of the garden while they were asleep and unaware. The 'visitation' (طائف) refers to a calamity or divine affliction that swiftly swept over their vineyard, destroying it completely. The verse emphasizes the sudden and inevitable nature of divine punishment for those who transgress, and how Allah's justice operates when people are negligent and fail to remember their Lord. It serves as a reminder that divine punishment can come unexpectedly when people become heedless and arrogant, thinking themselves secure from the consequences of their wrongdoing.

translation: So it became like the dark night of harvest (or like a harvested field)
interpretation: This phrase describes the sudden destruction of the garden as a divine punishment. The word 'صريم' (al-Sireem) refers to a barren, darkened, or harvested field - a state of complete devastation and loss. The verse illustrates how the arrogant owners who refused to set aside provisions for the poor were left with nothing overnight, their once-thriving garden rendered useless and darkened. This serves as a powerful reminder of divine justice and the consequences of neglecting the rights of others and showing ingratitude for blessings.

translation: Then they called out in the morning
interpretation: This phrase describes the regretful cry of the inhabitants of the garden mentioned in Surah Al-Qalam (68:20), who rushed to their plantation early in the morning to harvest it, only to find it had been destroyed during the night. Their calling out reflects their shock, grief, and realization of their sudden loss—a divine trial that tests the believers' patience and acceptance of Allah's will. The verse illustrates how worldly possessions are temporary and subject to sudden change, serving as a reminder to detach from material attachments and trust in divine providence.

translation: Go early to your field if you are determined (to harvest).
interpretation: This verse (from Surah Al-Kahf 19:22) illustrates the importance of diligence, punctuality, and determined action in pursuing one's livelihood and responsibilities. The command to go early emphasizes that success requires not merely intention but prompt and committed effort. The conditional phrase 'if you are determined' suggests that such early rising and commitment are the marks of those who are truly serious about their goals, teaching that sincere determination must be coupled with timely action rather than mere procrastination or wishful thinking.

translation: So they departed while they were whispering to one another
interpretation: This verse depicts a group of people secretly conversing in hushed tones as they leave, suggesting they are discussing something they wish to conceal or are cautious about revealing. The act of whispering indicates either guilt, conspiracy, or fear of being overheard, emphasizing the clandestine nature of their departure and the private nature of their discourse.

translation: That no poor person should enter it upon you today
interpretation: This verse reflects the owners' arrogant intention to exclude the poor and needy from benefiting from their garden's harvest, revealing how wealth can foster exclusivity and a lack of compassion. Their deliberate act of gatekeeping demonstrates how material possessions can corrupt the human heart and lead one to forget their social responsibilities toward the vulnerable members of society. The phrase 'today' emphasizes their immediate and firm resolve to implement this exclusionary practice.

translation: And they went forth in the morning while they were able/with strength
interpretation: This verse illustrates the human tendency to persist in wrongdoing despite clear signs of divine punishment. The phrase suggests that the people, after witnessing destruction, continued their sinful behavior with determination and capability, demonstrating hardened hearts that reject guidance. It emphasizes how repeated exposure to evidence of God's justice does not necessarily reform those who are spiritually blind, as they convince themselves of their power and ability to withstand consequences.

translation: So when they saw it, they said: 'Indeed, we are those who have gone astray.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the moment when people perceive a clear sign or truth that contradicts their previous beliefs or assumptions, causing them to suddenly recognize their former state of delusion or misguidance. The realization serves as a humbling acknowledgment that their prior convictions were based on error, suggesting that truth, when finally witnessed directly, has the power to shatter false certainties and awaken human consciousness to reality.

translation: Rather, we are deprived ones.
interpretation: This phrase expresses a sense of deprivation and exclusion, conveying the speaker's perception of being denied or cut off from something desirable. In Qur'anic context, such expressions of complaint often reflect a lack of faith or ingratitude toward divine provision, serving as a reminder that true deprivation lies in spiritual emptiness rather than material circumstances, while those who deny Allah's blessings are themselves the truly deprived despite any worldly possessions they may have.

translation: The wisest/most moderate among them said: 'Did I not tell you: Why do you not glorify (Allah)?'
interpretation: This verse presents a moment of reflection and rebuke among a group, where the most balanced or reasonable person among them addresses the others by reminding them of a prior warning he had given them. The phrase 'why do you not glorify' suggests that the group failed to acknowledge or praise God despite being cautioned beforehand. The speaker is highlighting their negligence in remembrance and worship, emphasizing that their predicament resulted from their failure to heed his earlier advice to engage in divine glorification and remembrance, thereby pointing to the spiritual responsibility each person bears to maintain consciousness of God.

translation: They said, 'Exalted is our Lord! Indeed, we were wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse captures a moment of recognition and repentance when the wrongdoers acknowledge their transgressions and submit to the majesty of their Lord. The statement reflects the inevitable realization that comes when one confronts the truth of Divine justice—that their wrongdoing was a violation of their covenant with God. This admission, whether it occurs in this life or hereafter, demonstrates that the human soul ultimately knows its Lord and the gravity of its disobedience, a fundamental aspect of human nature (fitrah) asserting itself when pretense and denial can no longer be sustained.

translation: So some of them turned upon others, blaming one another.
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene of mutual recrimination and blame among people in a state of distress or difficulty, illustrating how humans tend to shift responsibility and accuse one another when facing consequences or misfortune, rather than taking accountability for their own actions or seeking unified solutions.

translation: They said, 'O woe to us! Indeed, we were transgressors.'
interpretation: This verse captures the moment of anguished recognition when those who rejected truth confront the reality of their rebellion against Allah. The phrase 'ya waylana' (O woe to us) expresses profound remorse and despair at having crossed the boundaries set by Allah. The interpretation reveals that transgression (tughyan) is not merely a single act of disobedience, but a state of habitual rebellion and excess that characterized their lives. Their confession 'innana kunna tagheen' (we were transgressors) indicates a belated acknowledgment that they lived in defiance of divine guidance, choosing arrogance and excess over submission. This moment of clarity, though coming too late for redemption, demonstrates how the human soul ultimately recognizes its own wrongdoing when confronted with divine truth, signifying that the capacity for moral discernment remains even in those who persistently denied it during their earthly lives.

translation: Perhaps our Lord will replace it for us with something better than it. Indeed, we are turning to our Lord in hopeful desire.
interpretation: This verse expresses the believers' trust in divine providence and their acceptance of loss through patient submission to God's will. Rather than despairing over what has been taken away, the speaker demonstrates faith that God may grant them something superior, while simultaneously affirming their continued devotion and hopeful supplication directed solely toward their Lord. It teaches that true reliance on God transcends attachment to worldly possessions and involves maintaining hope in His wisdom and generosity.

translation: Thus is the punishment (in this life). And indeed, the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the disparity between worldly punishment and the eternal punishment of the Hereafter, suggesting that the immediate consequences believers witness in this life are minor compared to the ultimate divine justice that awaits those who reject truth. The conditional phrase 'if they only knew' indicates that ignorance or denial of this reality is what prevents people from changing their ways, implying that true knowledge of the Hereafter's severity would serve as a deterrent to wrongdoing.

translation: Indeed, for the righteous with their Lord are gardens of bliss.
interpretation: This verse assures believers of the certainty and reality of Paradise as a reward for piety and consciousness of God. The phrase 'with their Lord' emphasizes that this reward is not merely a distant or uncertain promise, but is established in divine knowledge and secured by God's guarantee. 'Gardens of bliss' describes not merely physical gardens, but a comprehensive state of ultimate contentment, pleasure, and spiritual fulfillment where all desires are satisfied and all pain is removed. The verse's opening with 'Indeed' conveys absolute certainty, encouraging the faithful to pursue righteousness knowing that their efforts are not in vain but lead to a reward both real and eternally lasting.

translation: Should We then make the Muslims like the criminals?
interpretation: This verse expresses the rhetorical rejection of equating the righteous believers with the wicked criminals, emphasizing that Allah does not treat the obedient and the disobedient in the same manner. It underscores the principle of divine justice and differentiation between those who follow the straight path and those who commit sins and transgression.

translation: What is wrong with you? How do you judge?
interpretation: This verse expresses divine rebuke and astonishment at the irrational or unjust judgments of people, particularly those who reject the truth despite clear evidence. It challenges the audience to reflect on the basis and validity of their decisions and beliefs, implying that their judgments contradict reason, justice, or divine guidance.

translation: Or do you have a scripture in which you study?
interpretation: This verse challenges the polytheists of Mecca by questioning whether they possess a revealed book or written authority that legitimizes their beliefs and practices. The rhetorical question implies that they lack any divine evidence or scripture to support their false doctrines of polytheism, suggesting that their idolatry is based merely on inherited custom and conjecture rather than on revealed truth. It highlights the contrast between their unfounded claims and the clear evidence of the Qur'an.

translation: Indeed, in it for you is that which you choose.
interpretation: This verse refers to the bounties and provisions contained within something previously mentioned in context (such as livestock, gardens, or the earth's resources). The phrase emphasizes Allah's generosity in providing choices and options for humanity, allowing them to select what suits their needs and desires from the abundance He has created. This demonstrates divine mercy in granting human free will and agency in selecting from permissible provisions, rather than imposing uniformity or scarcity.

translation: Or do you have oaths binding upon Us, extending to the Day of Judgment? Indeed, for you is whatever you judge.
interpretation: This verse challenges the disbelievers' presumption that they have secured binding covenants from Allah that guarantee them worldly benefits or protection until the Day of Judgment. The rhetorical question emphasizes that they possess no such guarantee, and whatever authority or judgment they exercise is only temporary and will be rendered meaningless on the Day of Resurrection. The verse serves as a reminder that only Allah's will is absolute and permanent, while all human power and authority are contingent and ephemeral.

translation: Ask them which of them will be responsible for that.
interpretation: This phrase, occurring in Surah Al-Qalam (68:41), challenges the polytheists by asking them to identify who among their claimed intercessors would guarantee or take responsibility for the claim that idols can intercede with Allah. The verse serves as a rhetorical question designed to expose the absurdity and groundlessness of their belief system by forcing them to confront the fact that no one can actually vouch for such false claims, thereby highlighting the weakness of polytheistic arguments and the necessity of monotheistic faith.

translation: Or do they have partners (with Allah)? Then let them bring their partners if they are truthful.
interpretation: This verse challenges the polytheists to produce evidence for their claimed partners to Allah by bringing them forth to demonstrate their divine attributes or powers. The verse uses logical challenge and rhetorical questioning to expose the inconsistency of associating partners with Allah, implying that such partners cannot exist or be produced, thereby demonstrating the falsity of polytheism and establishing the necessity of monotheism.

translation: The Day when the shin will be exposed and they will be called to prostrate, but they will not be able to.
interpretation: This verse describes an eschatological event where God will reveal His shin (a sign of His majesty and power), and the disbelievers will be called to prostrate before Him. However, they will be unable to do so due to their arrogance, pride, and their hardened hearts during their earthly lives. This reflects the irreversible nature of their rejection of faith; their physical and spiritual inability to submit represents the consequence of their willful denial in the world, emphasizing that belief and obedience must come willingly in this life when it is still possible.

translation: Their eyes humbled, humiliation overwhelming them, while they used to be invited to prostration when they were unharmed.
interpretation: This verse depicts the regretful state of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, contrasting their former rejection of faith when they enjoyed ease and prosperity with their present condition of utter shame and degradation. The reference to being 'invited to prostration when they were unharmed' highlights their willful refusal to obey God's command to worship during their worldly life when they had the capacity and opportunity to do so, making their current humiliation a just consequence of their deliberate turning away.

translation: So leave Me and those who deny this statement. We will draw them on gradually from where they do not know.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's patience with disbelievers and His method of punishment through gradual, imperceptible steps. Rather than immediate destruction, Allah allows the deniers to be led astray progressively through their own desires and choices, and they remain unaware of the consequences accumulating until they face the final reckoning. The verse conveys that Allah's way of dealing with those who reject the truth is to let them proceed in their delusion while they unknowingly advance toward their doom, teaching believers not to be troubled by the deniers' rejection, as Allah's justice operates according to His wisdom and timing.

translation: And I grant them respite; indeed, My plan is firm.
interpretation: This verse reflects God's measured patience with wrongdoers, allowing them time and provisions despite their disobedience. The phrase emphasizes that this apparent delay is not weakness but part of a deliberate divine strategy—God's plan is unshakeable and will ultimately prevail. The verse teaches that extended opportunity for repentance should not be mistaken for indifference; rather, it is a manifestation of divine wisdom working toward a certain and inevitable reckoning.

translation: Or do you ask them for a reward, so they are burdened by a debt?
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad, reassuring him that his preaching of the message does not depend on financial compensation from the people. The phrase suggests that even if the Prophet were to ask for payment, the people would not feel obligated or burdened by it, since his true purpose is to convey Allah's guidance freely. This reflects the selfless nature of prophetic mission and serves to remind the audience that the message of Islam is a mercy offered without material expectation, thereby distinguishing it from false prophets and charlatans who exploit people for wealth.

translation: Or do they have [access to] the unseen, so that they write [it down]?
interpretation: This verse challenges the disbelievers' claims to knowledge they do not possess, suggesting they speak with certainty about matters beyond human perception without any basis for their assertions. The rhetorical question implies that their arguments are baseless fabrications rather than grounded in genuine knowledge of the unseen, which is exclusively within God's domain.

translation: So be patient for the judgment of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the whale when he called out while he was in distress.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet Muhammad to maintain steadfast patience in his mission despite opposition and difficulties, using the example of Jonah (the companion of the whale) as a cautionary contrast. Jonah's impatience and despair when he cried out from within the whale's belly while stifled in anguish represents a failure to maintain composure and trust in God's plan. The verse teaches that patience and faith in divine wisdom during trials are essential spiritual virtues, and warns against abandoning this patience through complaint or loss of hope, no matter how dire one's circumstances may appear.

translation: Had not a grace from his Lord overtaken him, he would indeed have been cast upon the naked ground while he was blamed.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of divine mercy and intervention in human affairs. It emphasizes that salvation from disgrace and ruin depends entirely upon God's grace and intervention rather than upon human effort alone. The passage teaches humility by showing that without God's specific mercy (nعمة) reaching a person at the moment of crisis, one can be reduced to utter shame and degradation. It conveys that God's grace is not earned but is a gift that comes to those whom He wills, and that reliance on this mercy rather than self-sufficiency is the proper stance for the believer.

translation: So his Lord chose him and made him of the righteous ones
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine selection and purification of a chosen servant by Allah, emphasizing that righteousness is not merely an individual achievement but ultimately a grace granted by the Almighty who elevates and reforms the hearts of those He wills. The phrase conveys that true spiritual reformation comes through divine favor and acceptance, not through human effort alone.

translation: And indeed, those who have disbelieved almost make you slip with their eyes when they hear the Reminder, and they say, 'Indeed, he is mad.'
interpretation: The verse illustrates how the disbelievers' hostile gaze and their accusation of madness against the Prophet represent their desperate attempt to undermine his message through ridicule and intimidation. Their very reaction to hearing the Qur'an—attacking the messenger's character rather than engaging with the message itself—inadvertently confirms the power and effect of the revelation, while their baseless accusation of insanity becomes a demonstration of their own spiritual blindness and moral weakness in the face of truth.

translation: And it is not but a reminder for the worlds (or all creation)
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the universal and timeless nature of the Qur'an's message, asserting that it functions as an admonition and guidance applicable to all peoples and nations throughout time, not limited to a particular group or era. It underscores the Qur'an's role as a comprehensive message of remembrance from Allah meant to reach and benefit all of humanity and creation.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Al-Haqqah (The Inevitable Reality/The Sure Event).
interpretation: This verse invokes God's name and introduces the 69th chapter of the Qur'an, which focuses on the certainty and inevitability of the Day of Judgment. Al-Haqqah refers to a truth that cannot be denied or avoided—the ultimate reality of divine accountability and resurrection. The emphasis on Allah's mercy and compassion at the outset suggests that while judgment is certain, it is administered by a Lord of infinite compassion, establishing that divine justice and mercy are intertwined in the final reckoning.

translation: The Inevitable Reality (or The Inevitable Hour/The Overwhelming Calamity)
interpretation: This is the opening of Surah Al-Haqqah, where 'Al-Haqqah' refers to the Day of Judgment - the inevitable, undeniable reality that will surely come to pass. The verse introduces the theme of divine truth and accountability, emphasizing that the Day of Judgment is an absolute certainty that cannot be denied or escaped, serving as a warning to humanity about the consequences of their deeds and the need for righteousness and faith in preparation for that unavoidable day.

translation: And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?
interpretation: This rhetorical question emphasizes the awesome, incomprehensible nature of the Day of Judgment (Al-Haqqah), suggesting that the gravity and magnitude of this event are beyond human understanding. By asking this question, the Qur'an draws attention to the listener's limited knowledge and invites contemplation of the profound reality of the final day, creating a sense of awe and humility before the divine truth that defies complete human comprehension.

translation: Thamud and Aad denied the Striking Hour (the Day of Judgment).
interpretation: This verse illustrates the consequence of rejecting divine warnings: both ancient peoples, despite receiving clear messages from their respective prophets (Salih and Hud), refused to believe in the inevitability of God's judgment and accountability in the afterlife. Their denial of the inevitable Hour (al-Qari'ah) represents their fundamental rejection of God's truth, which ultimately led to their destruction as a punishment for their disbelief and arrogance.

translation: As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the transgression/tyranny
interpretation: This verse refers to the destruction of the Thamud people as a consequence of their own excessive transgression and arrogance. The use of 'the transgression' (al-taghiya) as the agent of their destruction suggests that their own moral corruption and defiance of divine guidance became the means of their annihilation, emphasizing that divine punishment comes as a natural consequence of persistent wrongdoing and rejection of the truth.

translation: As for 'Ad, they were destroyed by a furious, cold wind.
interpretation: This verse describes how the people of 'Ad were punished by Allah through a violent, harsh wind that devastated them. The specific emphasis on the wind being both 'sarsar' (cold/violent) and 'atiya' (raging/fierce) underscores the overwhelming and inescapable nature of Allah's punishment upon a people who rejected their prophet Hud. The destruction serves as a warning of the severe consequences for those who turn away from divine guidance.

translation: He sent upon them a wind of seven nights and eight days in succession, so you would see the people therein overturned, as if they were hollow trunks of date palms.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine punishment inflicted upon the people of 'Aad through a devastating windstorm that lasted for a continuous period of seven nights and eight days. The graphic imagery of the people being overturned and lying like hollowed-out date palm trunks emphasizes both the complete destruction of their bodies and the totality of their humiliation. The description serves to demonstrate that those who reject Allah's signs and arrogantly resist His messengers face inevitable and overwhelming destruction, making manifest the consequences of their disbelief and arrogance.

translation: So do you see for them any remnant?
interpretation: This verse reflects a rhetorical question emphasizing the complete and utter destruction of a people who rejected divine guidance. By asking if any trace or remainder exists of those who were destroyed for their disbelief, the verse conveys that God's punishment is absolute and leaves nothing behind—serving as a warning that those who turn away from God's signs will be erased from existence, with no legacy or continuation to remain. The question invites contemplation on the inevitable fate of those who persist in rejection.

translation: And Pharaoh came, and those before him, and the overturned cities with the sinful deed.
interpretation: This verse describes how Pharaoh and the corrupt societies before him, including the destroyed peoples of Sodom and Gomorrah (the overturned cities), all shared in committing grave sins and transgression against God's signs. The verse emphasizes the continuity of human rebellion against divine guidance across generations, showing that defiance of God's message is not unique to any one period but a recurring pattern among those who reject truth and persist in wrongdoing.

translation: So they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord, and He seized them with a seizing grip.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of divine justice and accountability: those who reject and disobey the messengers sent by God face inevitable punishment. The phrase 'seizing grip' (أخذة رابية) emphasizes the overwhelming and irresistible nature of God's punishment, suggesting that disobedience to divine guidance leads to inescapable consequences. This serves as a warning that rejection of truth and the messengers who convey it results in severe divine retribution.

translation: Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you in the sailing ship.
interpretation: This verse refers to the flood during Noah's time, emphasizing God's mercy and protection of the believers. It demonstrates the principle that God preserves the faithful through trials and punishments by providing them with means of salvation. The 'sailing ship' (the Ark) becomes a symbol of divine deliverance for those who heed God's message, while simultaneously illustrating the consequences of rejection and transgression for those who refuse to obey God's commands.

translation: We will make it (a lesson) for you so that ears that are conscious may retain it.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the purpose of divine revelation is to serve as a reminder (تذكرة) that awakens consciousness and mindfulness in those who listen with attentiveness. The phrase 'ears that are conscious' (أذن واعية) signifies that the acceptance and retention of guidance is not merely a passive hearing, but requires an active, receptive consciousness—indicating that understanding the Qur'an demands both intellectual engagement and spiritual awareness from the listener.

translation: So when the trumpet is blown with a single blast
interpretation: This verse describes the moment of the Day of Judgment when the Archangel Israfil will blow the trumpet (the Sûr) once, which will mark the end of the world and the resurrection of all creation. The phrase emphasizes the singular, instantaneous nature of this cosmic event - a single, decisive blast that will transform all existence. This interpretation underscores the absolute power and certainty of Allah's command over creation, and the inevitable reality of the Day of Judgment that awaits all humanity.

translation: And the earth and the mountains are carried and crushed with one crushing.
interpretation: This verse describes the catastrophic events of the Day of Judgment when the earth and mountains will be pulverized into dust, signifying the complete destruction of the physical world and the end of all material existence. The repetition of "crushing" (daka) emphasizes the totality and finality of this cosmic upheaval, conveying the absolute power of Allah and the inevitability of resurrection.

translation: And on that Day, the Event (the Hour) shall occur.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment, emphasizing its certainty and inevitability. The phrase 'the Event' (al-Waqiah) is a name for the Day of Resurrection, highlighting that it is an appointed, inevitable occurrence that will come upon humanity. The use of 'on that Day' stresses the specific, definite nature of this momentous occasion, reminding believers of the reality of the afterlife and the final reckoning that awaits all creation.

translation: And the sky will be split open, so on that day it will be weak/fragile.
interpretation: This verse describes an apocalyptic scene from the Day of Judgment where the heavens, which have been maintained by divine power, will lose their structural integrity and tear apart. The word 'wahiya' (weak/fragile) suggests that what was once solid and firm will become feeble and unable to maintain its form, signifying the complete dissolution of the physical order as we know it and marking a decisive moment in the cosmic transformation that occurs when Allah's will for the end of creation is executed.

translation: And the angels will be at its borders, and eight angels will be bearing the Throne of your Lord above them on that Day.
interpretation: This verse describes the divine majesty and power of Allah by depicting the Throne (Arsh) of the Lord being carried by eight angels on the Day of Judgment, emphasizing the incomprehensible scale of the cosmic order when the Day of Judgment arrives and the veils of the unseen are lifted. The specific mention of eight angels underscores the immense weight and significance of divine authority, suggesting that even this great number of powerful beings are necessary to bear what belongs only to Allah, thereby affirming His absolute supremacy and the vastness of His dominion over creation.

translation: On that Day you will be exposed; not a single thing about you will be hidden.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment when all souls will be brought before Allah for reckoning. The verse emphasizes the absolute exposure and transparency of all deeds, thoughts, and secrets that were hidden in this worldly life. No person will be able to conceal anything from Allah's knowledge or the witnessing of the angels and other observers. This serves as a powerful reminder of accountability and divine omniscience, encouraging believers to be conscious of their actions knowing that nothing escapes Allah's awareness and that all will eventually be revealed.

translation: As for he who is given his record in his right hand, he will say, 'Come, read my record!'
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the righteous on the Day of Judgment, depicting the joy and confidence of those whose deeds are recorded favorably. The person receiving their book in the right hand is a sign of honor and acceptance, and their eager invitation to others to read their record reflects their pride in their righteous deeds and their assurance of salvation. This contrasts with those who receive their record in their left hand or behind their backs, symbolizing shame and punishment.

translation: Indeed, I thought that I would surely meet my account (in the Hereafter).
interpretation: This verse reflects the speaker's awareness and consciousness of the certainty of facing divine accountability after death. The use of 'zannanu' (I thought/was certain) expresses a deep conviction that God's justice demands a reckoning for all deeds. This interpretation emphasizes the psychological and spiritual state of the believer who maintains constant awareness of divine judgment, which serves as a motivating force for righteous conduct and moral vigilance in this life.

translation: So he is in a pleasant life, content.
interpretation: This verse describes the blessed state of the righteous servant of Allah who receives His mercy and guidance. The phrase 'pleasant life' (عيشة راضية) signifies not merely material comfort, but a state of spiritual contentment and satisfaction that comes from living in obedience to Allah and recognizing His blessings. The word 'راضية' (radhiya - pleasant, satisfied) suggests that this contentment permeates both the internal spiritual condition and external circumstances, reflecting the inner peace that accompanies sincere faith and submission to Allah's will. This is the true measure of a good life in Islamic understanding - not worldly luxury alone, but the harmony between one's actions, conscience, and divine guidance.

translation: In a garden on high
interpretation: This phrase describes the elevated and exalted nature of Paradise, emphasizing that it is a place of supreme honor, dignity, and closeness to the Divine. The "high" or "elevated" garden signifies both the physical elevation and the spiritual superiority of Paradise as a realm beyond the material world, reserved for those who have achieved spiritual excellence and closeness to Allah.

translation: Its clusters are near/hanging down close
interpretation: This phrase describes the fruits of Paradise as being easily accessible and conveniently positioned for the inhabitants to pluck without difficulty or effort. It symbolizes the effortless abundance and comfort of Paradise, where everything desirable is within immediate reach, reflecting the perfect ease and satisfaction that awaits the righteous in the afterlife. The proximity of the fruits represents divine generosity made tangible and immediate, emphasizing that in Paradise there is no striving or hardship—only peaceful enjoyment of blessings.

translation: Eat and drink contentedly for what you sent forward in the bygone days
interpretation: This verse addresses the inhabitants of Paradise, reminding them that their present enjoyment and eternal reward are the direct result of the righteous deeds and good actions they performed during their lifetime in the world. The phrase 'what you sent forward' refers to the concept of sending ahead good deeds in advance of oneself toward the afterlife, establishing the principle of personal accountability and the direct connection between one's earthly conduct and eternal consequences. The verse emphasizes that pleasure and happiness in the hereafter are not arbitrary gifts but rather the natural and deserved outcome of one's own righteous efforts and obedience to Allah in the temporal world.

translation: But as for he who is given his record in his left hand, he will say, 'Oh, I wish I had not been given my record.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the regret and despair of those destined for punishment on the Day of Judgment, who receive their deeds written in their left hand - a sign of their condemnation. Their cry reflects the ultimate moment of realized consequences, when all denial and excuses become impossible, illustrating the absolute justice of divine reckoning where one's own deeds bear witness against oneself, and the profound desire to undo one's transgressions comes too late to change one's fate.

translation: And I did not know what my account (record of deeds) would be
interpretation: This phrase expresses the speaker's unawareness and lack of preparedness regarding the reckoning of their deeds on the Day of Judgment.
