The spring is characterized by its pleasant and easy flow, and it is among the delights prepared for the righteous believers in the afterlife. The naming and description of this spring emphasizes that Paradise contains pleasures beyond ordinary human experience, with even water itself being elevated to a state of perfect refinement and purity. This reflects the Qur'anic principle that the rewards of the faithful transcend earthly comprehension and expectation.

translation: And there circulate among them eternal youths. When you see them, you would think them scattered pearls.
interpretation: This verse describes the inhabitants of Paradise and emphasizes their eternal youthfulness and beauty. The comparison to scattered pearls conveys the brilliance, purity, and value of these eternal servants, suggesting that the blessed will be surrounded by an abundance of radiant beauty and perfect attendants throughout eternity, symbolizing the completeness and perfection of the Paradisiacal experience.

translation: And when you see there, you see blessings and a great kingdom
interpretation: This verse describes the magnificent reality of Paradise that awaits the believers. The repetition of 'when you see' emphasizes the certainty and clarity of witnessing these blessings, suggesting that what the faithful will perceive in the afterlife transcends worldly understanding. The combination of 'blessings' (ni'ama) and 'great kingdom' (mulk kabir) indicates that the joys of Paradise encompass both spiritual contentment and material abundance, representing the comprehensive fulfillment of all desires and the absolute majesty of Allah's creation that believers will experience.

translation: Upon them will be garments of fine green silk and brocade, and they will be adorned with bracelets of silver, and their Lord will give them to drink a pure beverage.
interpretation: This verse describes the material blessings and spiritual purification granted to the righteous in Paradise. The green silk and brocade symbolize beauty and honor, while the silver bracelets represent adornment and value. The pure drink bestowed by Allah directly emphasizes both the physical comfort of the inhabitants of Paradise and their spiritual sanctity, as the drink itself is described as 'tahur' (pure/purifying), suggesting that every aspect of their existence in Paradise—material and spiritual—has been perfected and cleansed by the grace of Allah.

translation: Indeed, this has been a reward for you, and your effort has been appreciated.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the principle of divine justice and recognition - that those who strive and exert effort in obedience to Allah will receive acknowledgment and reward from Him. The phrase 'your effort has been appreciated' emphasizes that Allah does not overlook the sincere striving of His servants, highlighting the divine mercy and justice that underlies the relationship between human effort and divine recompense. It encourages believers to understand that their struggles and endeavors in righteousness are not in vain, but are witnessed and valued by the Almighty.

translation: Indeed, We have sent down the Qur'an to you in stages.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's direct involvement in revealing the Qur'an to Prophet Muhammad, establishing the divine origin and authenticity of the text. The mention of gradual revelation (تنزيل - tanzīl) indicates that the Qur'an was revealed progressively over approximately 23 years in response to various situations and circumstances the Muslim community faced, which served pedagogical purposes by allowing believers to understand and gradually implement divine guidance while reinforcing the Qur'an's relevance to their lived experiences.

translation: So be patient for the judgment of your Lord, and do not obey among them any sinner or disbeliever.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the Prophet's need to remain steadfast in his mission despite opposition from those who reject faith or persist in sin. The instruction to avoid obedience to wrongdoers and disbelievers serves as guidance to maintain the integrity of the divine message and not compromise Islamic principles for the sake of those who refuse guidance. The patience prescribed is not passive resignation but active perseverance in conveying and upholding God's truth, trusting in God's ultimate judgment and wisdom even when facing hostility and resistance.

translation: And remember the name of your Lord in the morning and in the evening.
interpretation: This verse commands the servant to engage in the remembrance (dhikr) of Allah's name at the beginning and end of each day, emphasizing the importance of maintaining a continuous connection with the Divine throughout one's waking hours. The mention of these specific times—morning and evening—represents the transitions of the day and symbolizes the need for spiritual consciousness during all periods of life, while the focus on His name (not merely His attributes in general) underscores the importance of direct acknowledgment of Allah's identity and uniqueness.

translation: And from the night, prostrate to Him and glorify Him during a long night.
interpretation: This verse encourages the believer to dedicate a portion of the night for special worship, particularly prostration and remembrance of Allah. The 'long night' refers to extending one's devotion and spiritual practice during the quiet hours when distractions are minimal, signifying the importance of night prayers and midnight remembrance as a means of achieving closeness to Allah and strengthening one's faith through dedicated worship when the world sleeps.

translation: Indeed, these people love the immediate life and leave behind them a Day that is heavy.
interpretation: This verse condemns those who prioritize worldly pleasures and immediate gratification over preparation for the Day of Judgment. By describing the Day of Judgment as 'heavy' (thaqīl), the Qur'an emphasizes its gravity, weight, and fearsome nature, suggesting that those who neglect it in favor of fleeting worldly pursuits have made a grave miscalculation of what truly matters, ignoring the inevitable and consequential reckoning that awaits them.

translation: We have created them and strengthened their frames. And when We will, We can replace them with others like them, completely.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute power and sovereignty over creation. The phrase 'strengthened their frames' refers to the physical structure and constitution of human beings. The verse conveys that human existence and form are entirely contingent upon Allah's will, and while He has created and sustained humanity with strength and capability, this does not grant them permanence or independence. The threat that Allah can replace humanity with other beings serves as a reminder of human vulnerability and dependence, humbling mankind against pride or arrogance, and reinforcing that all existence is subject to divine will and can be exchanged at any moment.

translation: Indeed, this is a Reminder, so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the Qur'an serves as a means of guidance and remembrance, while establishing human free will in accepting or rejecting faith. The phrase 'take to his Lord a way' suggests that choosing to follow the Qur'an's teachings is not imposed but represents an active choice to draw closer to Allah through obedience and righteous conduct. The verse places responsibility on individuals to recognize the truth presented to them and consciously decide to pursue a path of submission to Allah.

translation: And you will not unless Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of Allah's will over all human actions and desires. It teaches that human free will operates only within the framework of Allah's divine will - whatever intentions people formulate or actions they attempt to undertake are ultimately subject to Allah's permission and decree. The mention of Allah being All-Knowing and All-Wise at the end reinforces that this divine will is not arbitrary but based on perfect knowledge and supreme wisdom, serving purposes beyond human comprehension. This establishes the Islamic concept of qadar (divine decree) and human responsibility, showing that while humans have choice, they are ultimately dependent upon Allah's will for the execution of their plans.

translation: He admits into His mercy whom He wills. And for the wrongdoers, He has prepared a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of Allah in His mercy - it is not earned through human merit alone but granted according to His divine will and wisdom. Simultaneously, it establishes the principle of divine justice: those who persist in wrongdoing (dhulm) and transgress against Allah's commands and the rights of others will inevitably face severe consequences. The verse balances hope in Allah's mercy with the reality of accountability, teaching that while we should strive for righteousness and hope for His mercy, we cannot be heedless of the consequences that await those who deliberately choose injustice and disobedience.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. By the winds sent forth in succession,
interpretation: This verse invokes Allah's names and begins Surah Al-Mursalat by invoking an oath through the winds (or winds bearing clouds), which are described as being sent in succession and gently. This oath structure emphasizes the certainty of the divine message that follows, as Allah swears by His creation to establish the truthfulness of the Resurrection and the Day of Judgment that the Surah goes on to discuss. The repetitive mention of "So which of the favors of your Lord do you deny?" throughout the Surah is presented as the inevitable consequence of these winds and other signs of Allah's power.

translation: By those that scatter with a scattering
interpretation: This verse uses the swiftly moving winds as an oath to emphasize the certainty of what follows. The repetition of the word from the same root ('aasifat, 'asfa) creates a rhythmic emphasis that underscores the divine power manifested in nature's forces. The oath structure indicates that what God is about to assert is absolutely inevitable and true, just as these natural phenomena are certain to occur.

translation: And those that spread spread widely
interpretation: This verse refers to the winds that spread and scatter things across the earth, as part of the signs of Allah's power and wisdom in creation. It emphasizes how Allah uses the winds as a means to disperse seeds, rain, and other provisions, demonstrating divine management of natural phenomena for the sustenance and benefit of creation.

translation: By those that separate with distinction
interpretation: This verse refers to the angels or divine forces that distinguish between truth and falsehood, good and evil, or the believers and the disbelievers. It emphasizes that God's creation possesses the ability to differentiate and separate matters according to divine wisdom, highlighting the fundamental role of discernment in the cosmic order and in distinguishing right from wrong.

translation: So those [angels] who cast [the message] as a reminder
interpretation: This verse refers to the angels appointed by Allah to deliver His message and reminder to humanity. It emphasizes the divine function of these celestial beings in transmitting revelation and guidance to mankind, highlighting that the delivery of God's word is not a random occurrence but an ordained responsibility entrusted to specific entities in the heavens.

translation: An excuse or a warning
interpretation: This phrase refers to the dual purpose of the Qur'an and the warnings of the Prophet: it serves as an excuse for those who reject the message (their claim of ignorance is removed), and as a warning to those who heed it. The revelation eliminates any legitimate grounds for disbelief, making rejection a deliberate and culpable act rather than an innocent one.

translation: Indeed, what you are promised is surely coming to pass.
interpretation: This verse affirms the certainty and inevitability of the Day of Judgment and all divine promises. The word 'إنما' (innama) emphasizes the exclusivity and definite nature of this promise, while 'واقع' (wāqi') means something that will definitely happen and cannot be avoided. The verse serves to assure believers and warn disbelievers that God's promises regarding the afterlife, reward, and punishment are not mere threats or possibilities, but absolute realities that will certainly occur.

translation: Then when the stars are extinguished/blotted out
interpretation: This verse describes a moment of cosmic upheaval during the Day of Judgment when the stars lose their light and visibility, signifying the collapse of the natural order and the end of the world as we know it. It emphasizes the absolute power of Allah to transform creation and serves as a reminder of the inevitability and magnitude of the final hour, calling believers to awareness of divine sovereignty and accountability.

translation: And when the heaven is split asunder
interpretation: This verse describes one of the signs of the Day of Judgment, emphasizing the complete upheaval and transformation of the natural order when the sky will be torn apart. It serves as a reminder of the certainty of the afterlife and the futility of rejecting divine truth, compelling believers to reflect on the transient nature of worldly existence and the inevitability of standing before God.

translation: And when the mountains are blown away/scattered
interpretation: This verse describes a scene from the Day of Judgment when the mountains, which appear to mankind as the most solid and immovable features of creation, will be completely destroyed and dispersed like dust. The use of 'nisfat' (blown away) emphasizes the violent and total nature of their destruction, serving as a powerful reminder of the absolute power of Allah and the inevitability of the resurrection. Mountains symbolize permanence and stability in human perception, yet even they cannot endure the cataclysm of the Last Day, reinforcing the insignificance of worldly attachments and the certainty of divine judgment.

translation: And when the messengers are appointed (to come forward)
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment when the messengers will be gathered and their time of witnessing and testifying against their peoples will arrive. The word 'أقتت' (uqqitat) means 'were appointed' or 'their time came,' suggesting that each messenger will have a specific moment to stand and give testimony about how they conveyed the message to their nations and how their people responded. This indicates the accountability and purpose of the messengers' mission will be fully realized and vindicated on the Day of Resurrection.

translation: For what Day have you postponed it?
interpretation: This rhetorical question is addressed to those who deny the Day of Judgment, emphasizing their futile attempt to postpone or reject belief in the resurrection. It conveys divine rebuke by questioning their audacity in delaying their reckoning with God and their willful disbelief in the appointed Day, highlighting the inevitability and certainty of Allah's judgment regardless of human denial.

translation: For the Day of Judgment/Decision
interpretation: This phrase refers to the inevitable Day of Judgment when Allah will make the final determination between believers and disbelievers, sorting and separating people based on their deeds. It emphasizes the certainty and finality of divine justice, serving as a reminder that all will be held accountable before Allah on that decisive day.

translation: And what can make you know what is the Day of Judgment?
interpretation: This rhetorical phrase emphasizes the absolute incomprehensibility and magnitude of the Day of Judgment to human understanding. By asking 'what can make you know,' the Qur'an conveys that the realities and terrors of that Day are beyond human capacity to fully grasp or perceive in this worldly life, thereby impressing upon the listener the gravity and inexpressible nature of the divine reckoning that awaits all creation.

translation: Woe, on that Day, to those who deny!
interpretation: This verse expresses severe condemnation of those who reject the signs of Allah and deny the truth of the Qur'an and the message of the Prophet. The word 'ويل' (wail/woe) conveys intense distress and punishment awaiting the deniers on the Day of Judgment, emphasizing the grave consequences of rejecting divine guidance and persistent disbelief throughout one's lifetime.

translation: Did We not destroy the former peoples?
interpretation: This rhetorical question emphasizes Allah's power and established pattern of divine justice throughout history. By referencing the destruction of previous civilizations that rejected their messengers, the Qur'an reminds the contemporary audience of Mecca that they are not exempt from this divine consequence if they persist in disbelief. The verse serves as a warning that stubbornness against Allah's guidance will inevitably lead to destruction, just as it did for those who came before.

translation: Then We will make the others follow after them
interpretation: This phrase refers to God's pattern of sending successive generations of people to follow those who came before, creating a continuous cycle of human experience and accountability. It emphasizes God's comprehensive and ongoing system of creation where each generation inherits the earth and must face the consequences of their own choices, rather than merely repeating the past without their own moral responsibility.

translation: Thus do We deal with the criminals
interpretation: This phrase illustrates the divine principle of justice whereby those who commit crimes and transgress against Allah's laws face inevitable consequences and punishment. The word 'thus' references the preceding punishment or judgment, emphasizing that such retribution is not arbitrary but a consistent and established pattern of how Allah handles wrongdoing. It serves as a warning to potential transgressors that criminal behavior will inevitably result in divine punishment, reinforcing the Quranic theme that justice is absolute and inescapable in Allah's system of moral accountability.

translation: Woe that Day to those who deny (the truth).
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the severe consequences and divine punishment awaiting those who reject the signs of Allah and deny the resurrection and the Day of Judgment. The word "woe" (ويل) conveys profound distress and ruin, indicating that deniers will face an inescapable and catastrophic fate on the Day of Resurrection when all their denial will be proven false and accountability becomes absolute.

translation: Did We not create you from despicable water?
interpretation: This verse reminds humanity of their humble origins - from a weak and insignificant substance - to instill humility and counteract arrogance. By emphasizing the lowly nature of human beginnings (semen), the verse serves as a powerful check against human pride and vanity, urging reflection on the contrast between our insignificant origins and our eventual standing before God on the Day of Judgment.

translation: So We placed him in a secure abode (in the womb)
interpretation: This verse refers to Allah's merciful placement of the human embryo in the protected environment of the womb, emphasizing divine providence in the early stages of human development. The 'secure abode' (qarar makīn) signifies both the physical safety and stability of the womb as a sanctuary for fetal growth, and metaphorically represents Allah's protection and favor upon human creation from its inception.

translation: to a predetermined measure
interpretation: This phrase emphasizes the divine determination and precise limitation of all things according to God's perfect knowledge. It conveys that everything in creation—whether sustenance, lifespan, or provision—has been measured and appointed by Allah according to His wisdom, and nothing exceeds the boundaries He has set. This instills in the believer a sense of trust in divine providence and acceptance of God's decree.

translation: Then We determined it, and excellent are We at determining.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's perfect wisdom and control in determining the course of creation, particularly in the context of human development and the stages of fetal growth. The phrase reflects the absolute sovereignty of Allah in orchestrating all affairs according to His divine will and infinite knowledge, highlighting that His determination is not merely mechanical but reflects His supreme capability and excellence in all matters He decrees.

translation: Woe, that Day, to those who deny.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the severe punishment and regret that will befall those who rejected the truth and denied the signs of Allah on the Day of Judgment. The repetition of 'woe' (ويل) at the beginning underscores the urgency and intensity of the suffering awaiting the deniers, highlighting that their rejection of divine truth will result in irreversible consequences in the afterlife.

translation: Have We not made the earth a container/receptacle?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's provision and care by highlighting how the earth serves as a comprehensive container that holds and sustains all life - encompassing the living and the dead, plants and animals, water and minerals. The rhetorical question (Alm) expects an affirmative answer, reminding humanity to recognize and be grateful for this fundamental divine blessing that makes life possible, while also implying that just as the earth embraces all creatures in life and gathers them in death, humans should embrace their role as stewards of creation.

translation: Alive and dead
interpretation: This phrase refers to the state of human beings in the afterlife, contrasting those who are alive in paradise (experiencing the rewards of their righteous deeds) with those who are dead in hellfire (experiencing the punishment of their sins). It underscores the reality of existence beyond this worldly life and the distinct consequences that await people based on their deeds and faith, emphasizing that death is not the end but a transition to a permanent state of either life or death in the hereafter.

translation: And We placed therein firm mountains towering high, and We gave you to drink sweet water.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's provision for humanity through the establishment of stable geographical features (mountains) that serve practical purposes such as preventing earthquakes and stabilizing the earth's crust, along with the provision of fresh water for drinking and sustenance. The imagery conveys divine care and the deliberate arrangement of creation to support human life and survival.

translation: Woe on that Day to the deniers.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the severe punishment and regret that will befall those who rejected the signs of Allah and disbelieved in His messages on the Day of Judgment. The word 'wail' (ويل) expresses profound calamity and destruction, indicating that the consequences of denial and disbelief are not merely temporary but will culminate in eternal torment. The phrase 'on that Day' specifically refers to the Day of Resurrection when all people will be held accountable for their choices, and those who persistently denied the truth will face the ultimate reckoning and despair.

translation: Depart to that which you used to deny.
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, commanding them to proceed toward the punishment they denied and mocked during their earthly life. It reflects the divine justice that those who rejected the truth regarding Hell and the afterlife will now face the reality of what they arrogantly dismissed, serving as a profound consequence of their denial and a manifestation of God's perfect justice where words and actions have inevitable accountability.

translation: Depart toward a shadow having three branches
interpretation: This verse describes the inhabitants of Hell being driven toward a specific punishment - a shadow with three branches that offers no coolness or relief, emphasizing their torment. The 'shadow' symbolizes the false protection or apparent refuge that ultimately provides no comfort, serving as a metaphor for the despair and hopelessness of the afterlife punishment, while the 'three branches' may represent the multiplicity or comprehensive nature of their suffering from different directions.

translation: No shade and it will not protect from the flames
interpretation: This phrase describes the utter helplessness and despair of the inhabitants of Hell, emphasizing that nothing in that realm can provide relief or escape from the torment of the fire. It conveys the absolute futility of seeking comfort or protection once one is in punishment, serving as a powerful warning about the consequences of disobedience and the inability to find any refuge from divine justice.

translation: Indeed, it throws sparks like great logs of wood (or like palaces/fortresses).
interpretation: This verse describes the intense and massive sparks being hurled from the blazing fire of Hellfire, comparing their size and intensity to great wooden logs or towering structures. The comparison emphasizes the immense scale and power of the punishment awaiting the disbelievers, illustrating how the consequences of rejecting faith are not trivial but catastrophically severe and overwhelming.

translation: As if they were yellow camels (or gold/empty vessels).
interpretation: This phrase from Surah Al-Fil (105:4) describes the attacking elephants and their riders, comparing them to yellow camels, suggesting their appearance seemed strange, foreign, or yellow in color to the onlookers, emphasizing the unfamiliar and terrifying nature of this unprecedented assault on the Ka'bah, which serves to highlight the miraculous intervention of Allah against this attack.

translation: Woe on that Day to those who deny (the truth)
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the severe punishment and anguish that will befall those who rejected the signs of Allah and denied the message of the prophets on the Day of Judgment. The word 'wail' (ويل) signifies extreme distress and calamity, underlining the grave consequences of disbelief and denial. This is a warning against rejection of divine guidance and a reminder of divine justice on the Last Day.

translation: This is a Day when they will not speak.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment when the disbelievers and sinners will be rendered mute and unable to defend themselves or make excuses before Allah. Their silence is a manifestation of their shame and the overwhelming nature of that divine reckoning, where all false narratives collapse and only the truth remains evident. This powerlessness to speak represents both a punishment for their denial and the absolute authority of Allah's judgment.

translation: And they will not be permitted to make excuses
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment when the disbelievers will be denied the opportunity to offer excuses for their rejection of faith and disobedience. Their excuses will be rejected and they will have no acceptable justification before Allah, emphasizing the finality of judgment and the accountability that cannot be evaded through false pretenses or explanations on that day.

translation: Woe, on that Day, to the deniers.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the severe punishment and regret awaiting those who rejected the truth and denied the signs of Allah on the Day of Judgment, expressing the gravity of their fate through the expression of lamentation and sorrow.

translation: This is the Day of Judgment; We have gathered you and the former peoples together.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the reality and inevitability of the Day of Judgment, when Allah will assemble all of humanity—both the contemporary generation being addressed and all previous nations—to face divine justice. It serves as a solemn reminder that no one escapes divine accountability, and that the gathering on the Day of Judgment is an absolute certainty decreed by Allah, transcending all temporal and generational boundaries.

translation: So if you have a scheme, then scheme (against me).
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Prophet Yusuf to his brothers, represents a challenge issued with complete confidence in Allah's protection. The Prophet is asserting his trust in Divine providence and inviting his brothers to do their worst if they believe they have the power to harm him. This demonstrates the state of tawakkul (reliance on Allah) where the believer, secure in faith, is unafraid of earthly schemes and plots. It serves as a powerful statement that those who place their trust in Allah need not fear the machinations of others, as no harm can come except by Allah's permission.

translation: Woe, on that Day, to those who deny (the truth).
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the severe punishment and regret that awaits those who reject the signs of Allah and deny the Day of Judgment on that inevitable day of reckoning. The word 'wail' (ويل) conveys profound grief and calamity, signifying that denial of God's truth is not merely an intellectual error but a grave transgression with dire eternal consequences. The verse serves as a powerful warning to those who stubbornly reject the message of the prophets, underscoring that their disbelief will result in irreversible loss and suffering when they face divine judgment.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in shade and springs [of water].
interpretation: This verse describes one of the rewards awaiting the pious believers in Paradise. The 'shade' represents protection and comfort from the heat and hardship, symbolizing divine mercy and relief from worldly suffering. The 'springs' signify abundant provision and refreshment, both physical and spiritual. Together, these blessings emphasize that those who maintain taqwa (fear and reverence of Allah) will experience complete comfort, ease, and satisfaction in the afterlife, protected from all discomfort and provided with all they need.

translation: And fruits from whatever they desire
interpretation: This phrase describes one of the blessings promised to the inhabitants of Paradise, indicating that they will have access to all varieties of fruits that they could possibly wish for or enjoy, without any limitation or restriction. It emphasizes the abundance and perfect satisfaction of desires in the afterlife, where every wish will be fulfilled according to their preferences.

translation: Eat and drink in pleasure for what you used to do
interpretation: This verse addresses the inhabitants of Paradise, indicating that their enjoyment and consumption of the blessings therein is a direct reward corresponding to their righteous deeds in the worldly life. The phrase 'in pleasure' (hani'an) emphasizes that their reward is guilt-free and pure, devoid of any anxiety or regret that characterized worldly sustenance. The connection between their actions and their reward demonstrates the principle of divine justice - that every deed receives its appropriate consequence in the afterlife.

translation: Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse establishes a divine principle that virtuous deeds and good conduct receive corresponding rewards from Allah. It emphasizes that goodness is not without consequence in the sight of God, serving as both an encouragement for believers to persist in righteous actions and a reassurance that their efforts are witnessed and will be justly recompensed. The phrase "thus do We reward" reflects God's consistent pattern of honoring excellence and virtue.

translation: Woe on that Day to those who deny (the truth).
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the severe punishment and regret that will befall the deniers of Allah's signs and the message of His prophets on the Day of Judgment. The word 'wil' (ويل) denotes destruction, ruin, and anguish, reflecting the ultimate consequence of obstinate rejection of divine guidance. The phrase 'on that Day' establishes the temporal reality of accountability in the afterlife, serving as a warning to those who persist in disbelief and rejection of truth despite clear evidence.

translation: Eat and enjoy yourselves a little; indeed, you are criminals.
interpretation: This verse represents the voice of those who deny the consequences of their actions and encourage others toward material indulgence despite knowing the moral wrong of their deeds. It reflects the attitude of those who, recognizing their criminal nature before God, nonetheless choose to pursue worldly pleasures briefly, implicitly acknowledging that this enjoyment is temporary and will be followed by divine punishment. The verse serves as a rebuke to such willful blindness and self-deception, highlighting how those immersed in sin may simultaneously be aware of their transgression yet persist in heedlessness.

translation: Woe that Day to those who deny (the truth).
interpretation: This verse expresses the severe punishment and regret that will befall those who rejected the signs of Allah and denied the message of the Prophet on the Day of Judgment. The word 'wail' (ويل) denotes extreme sorrow, ruin, and destruction, emphasizing that denial of truth is one of the gravest sins with the most consequential punishment in the afterlife. The phrase 'that Day' refers specifically to the Day of Judgment when all deceptions will be exposed and every person will face the consequences of their choices.

translation: And when it is said to them: 'Bow down (in prayer),' they do not bow down.
interpretation: This verse describes the defiance and stubborn rejection of disbelievers when called to obedience and worship. Their refusal to bow represents a fundamental rejection of submission to Allah's commands. The verse illustrates how some people resist spiritual guidance out of arrogance, pride, or disbelief, choosing instead to maintain their independence from divine law. This disobedience is not merely a physical refusal, but a rejection of the entire framework of Islamic submission that 'bowing' symbolizes - representing their unwillingness to humble themselves before Allah despite clear calls to faith and prayer.

translation: Woe that Day to those who deny (the Truth)
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the severe punishment and regret that awaits those who reject the message of truth and divine guidance on the Day of Judgment. The word 'Woe' (Wil) conveys intense suffering and despair, indicating that denial of truth is not merely an intellectual disagreement but a grave transgression with eternal consequences. The phrase 'that Day' anchors this warning to the specific moment of divine reckoning when all deceptions will be exposed and accounts will be settled, serving as a deterrent for those who knowingly turn away from the signs of God.

translation: Then in what statement after it will they believe?
interpretation: This verse questions the obstinacy of those who reject the Qur'an despite its clarity and eloquence. If they refuse to believe in the Qur'an—which is the greatest miracle and most perfect divine speech—what other message or evidence could possibly convince them? The rhetorical question emphasizes that rejection of the Qur'an reflects a fundamental hardness of heart and unwillingness to accept truth, rather than any deficiency in the evidence presented. It points to the futility of seeking alternative guidance when the clearest guidance has been rejected.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. About what do they ask one another?
interpretation: This verse opens Surah An-Naba and poses a rhetorical question that captures attention, inviting listeners to wonder about the nature and importance of the matter being discussed. The question serves to emphasize that what follows concerns something of profound significance—the Day of Judgment—which should be the subject of serious inquiry and reflection rather than casual dismissal, as the disbelievers of Makkah were treating it.

translation: Concerning the Great News
interpretation: This phrase refers to the message of the Qur'an itself and the revelation brought by Prophet Muhammad, which is considered the most significant and consequential news for humanity—particularly regarding the Day of Judgment, divine guidance, and salvation. The use of 'great' emphasizes the paramount importance and transformative nature of this divine message for believers' spiritual and eternal fate.

translation: Concerning which they are disputing
interpretation: This phrase refers to a matter of disagreement or dispute among people. It emphasizes that despite clear evidence or guidance, humans are prone to disagreement and division over matters of faith, truth, and divine signs. The verse highlights human nature's tendency toward discord and the persistent rejection of truth by those who choose skepticism over belief, illustrating the reality of doctrinal and theological disputes that arise even when divine guidance is presented.

translation: No! They will soon know.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the certainty of divine justice and accountability in the afterlife. The emphatic particle 'Kalla' (No!) rejects any denial or dismissal of God's power and judgment, while the future tense 'will soon know' conveys that disbelievers will inevitably discover the truth of God's warnings when they face the consequences of their deeds. It serves as a powerful reminder that those who reject God's signs cannot escape the reality of the Day of Judgment, no matter how they deny it in this life.

translation: Then nay, soon they will know.
interpretation: This verse conveys a warning of divine judgment and accountability. The phrase expresses God's promise that those who reject truth or engage in wrongdoing will eventually face consequences and recognize the reality of God's power and justice. It serves as both a deterrent against disbelief and a reassurance to the believers that their suffering and the deniers' rejection will not go unaddressed, as ultimate knowledge and understanding will come to all at the Day of Judgment.

translation: Did We not make the earth a bed (for you)?
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's provision and care for humanity by creating the earth as a comfortable and stable foundation for human existence. The metaphor of the earth as a 'bed' (mihad) conveys the idea that Allah has made the earth soft, receptive, and accommodating to human needs - suitable for dwelling, cultivation, and the fulfillment of life's necessities. It is an appeal to human gratitude and recognition of divine favor, prompting reflection on how Allah has deliberately designed the earth to sustain human life with ease and comfort.

translation: And the mountains as stakes/pegs
interpretation: This verse describes how Allah has created mountains to stabilize and anchor the earth, functioning as pegs or stakes that prevent the ground from shaking and shifting. The mountains serve as stabilizing forces that maintain the structural integrity of the earth, preventing excessive seismic movement and providing stability for the land and the creatures upon it. This reflects both the physical reality of mountain ranges' role in tectonic stability and their metaphorical function as anchors for creation's order.

translation: And We created you in pairs (or couples).
interpretation: This verse indicates the fundamental creative principle of duality and complementarity that Allah has established in human existence. The creation of humans in pairs—male and female—serves not only biological reproduction but represents a divine wisdom in establishing social bonds, mutual support, and the continuation of human civilization. It emphasizes that partnership and companionship are integral to the human condition and part of Allah's deliberate design for humanity.

translation: And We made your sleep a state of rest
interpretation: This verse highlights the divine wisdom in creating sleep as a restorative and rejuvenating state for human beings, emphasizing that sleep serves a vital biological and spiritual purpose—it is not merely the absence of wakefulness but rather a deliberate mercy from Allah that allows the body and mind to recover and renew, enabling humans to continue their earthly existence and worship.

translation: And We made the night as a covering/garment for you
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine purpose of night as a means of rest and comfort for humanity. Just as a garment envelops and protects the body, night envelops the earth, providing darkness and quietude that naturally incline people toward sleep and respite from the labors of the day. The metaphor of night as clothing emphasizes how intimately night is designed to meet human needs for rest and restoration, reflecting Allah's tender care in creating the cycles of day and night for human well-being.

translation: And We made the day for livelihood
interpretation: This verse indicates that Allah has designated the daylight hours as the time for human activity, work, and earning one's sustenance. The day, with its light and visibility, is a divine provision that enables people to conduct their affairs, pursue their occupations, and secure their livelihoods. This reflects the divine wisdom in creating the alternation of day and night as a framework for human life and productivity.

translation: And We built above you seven strong [heavens]
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the majesty and power of Allah's creation by describing the seven celestial spheres as 'strong' (shidad), highlighting their stability and permanence. The phrase 'above you' (fawqakum) indicates the vastness of creation that transcends human existence and understanding, serving to remind humanity of their smallness before the grandeur of the divine cosmos and to inspire awe and humility toward the Creator's infinite power and wisdom.

translation: And We made it a lamp that gives light
interpretation: This verse refers to the sun as a celestial body that provides illumination to the earth. The term 'siraj' (lamp) symbolizes the sun's role as a source of light and warmth essential for life, while 'wahhaj' (intensely bright or blazing) emphasizes the sun's tremendous power and brilliance. The verse reflects the Qur'an's method of describing natural phenomena in ways that guide humans to contemplate divine creation and recognize Allah's wisdom in establishing systems that sustain life and make the world habitable.

translation: And We sent down from the clouds water pouring down in torrents.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's power and mercy in providing abundant water through rain, which is essential for sustaining life on earth. The use of the word 'ثجاجا' (thajjajan) - meaning heavy, continuous pouring - conveys the generosity and abundance of Allah's provision, and serves as a sign of His complete control over nature and His constant care for His creation's survival and sustenance.

translation: That We may bring forth therewith grain and vegetation
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's power to create and sustain life through water, illustrating how divine provision flows from the most basic elements of nature. The mention of both grain and vegetation highlights the comprehensive bounty provided to humanity, demonstrating that sustenance depends entirely on Allah's will and the natural processes He has ordained. It invites reflection on the necessity of water for all life and the divine wisdom in creating this cycle of provision.

translation: And gardens full of thick vegetation
interpretation: This phrase describes the lush, densely planted gardens of Paradise as a reward for the believers. The word 'alfafa' (ألفافا) refers to dense, intertwined vegetation and greenery, emphasizing the abundance, beauty, and fullness of the gardens in Paradise. It conveys the idea of complete and perfect provision, where nothing is lacking or sparse, symbolizing the comprehensive blessing and completeness of divine reward.

translation: Indeed, the Day of Judgment has been appointed as a fixed time.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the certainty and predetermined nature of the Day of Judgment, indicating that Allah has established it as an immutable appointment that will inevitably occur. The use of 'miqa'ta' (appointed time) suggests both its definiteness and the completeness of Allah's knowledge and planning, serving as a reminder to humanity of their ultimate accountability and the absolute reliability of the Divine promise regarding the final reckoning.

translation: The Day when the Trumpet will be blown, and you will come forth in crowds.
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Resurrection when the angel Israfil will blow the horn, signaling the end of the world and the resurrection of all people. The phrase 'in crowds' (أفواجا) emphasizes that humanity will come forth in successive waves or groups, overwhelming in their numbers and movement. The verse conveys the overwhelming and catastrophic nature of the Day of Judgment, where the established order of existence is overturned and all souls are summoned to stand before their Creator for accountability.

translation: And the sky was opened, so it became gates.
interpretation: This verse describes the eschatological event of the Day of Judgment when the physical barriers of the sky will be torn asunder, symbolizing the collapse of the natural order and the complete exposure of all creation before God. The transformation of the sky into 'gates' signifies multiple openings through which Divine punishment and the angels will descend, emphasizing the inevitability and overwhelming nature of God's judgment that no creature can escape or hide from.

translation: And the mountains will be removed and will become a mirage.
interpretation: This verse depicts the Day of Judgment when the mountains, which appear eternal and immovable in this life, will be set in motion and transformed into dust, ultimately resembling a mirage—something that appears to exist but lacks substance. This represents the complete dissolution of the physical world as we know it, emphasizing the futility of relying on or taking pride in worldly structures and possessions that will vanish entirely when Allah brings about the end of creation.

translation: Indeed, Hell has been lying in wait (as a place of ambush).
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Hell is not a place of random punishment, but rather a carefully prepared consequence that awaits those who reject faith and divine guidance. The metaphor of 'ambush' (mirsad) suggests that Hell is positioned and destined as an inevitable result for the disbelievers, underlining the certainty of divine justice and the inescapable nature of accountability for one's deeds. It conveys that Hell stands ready as a predetermined station for those who persistently turn away from Allah's signs.

translation: For the transgressors will be a return (to punishment).
interpretation: This verse speaks of the inevitable consequence awaiting those who rebel against Allah's guidance and exceed all bounds in their disobedience. The 'return' (ma'ab) refers to their final destination and fate on the Day of Judgment, emphasizing that wrongdoing and tyranny do not go unanswered, and that justice ultimately prevails when wrongdoers are held accountable for their actions.

translation: Remaining therein for ages/epochs
interpretation: This phrase describes an eternal or extremely prolonged punishment, emphasizing the unending nature of the consequence. The word 'ahqab' (epochs/ages) is used to stress that the duration is incomprehensibly long, conveying the severity and permanence of divine punishment for those who reject faith. It underscores that this is not a temporary state but an everlasting condition that reflects the gravity of disbelief and its consequences.

translation: They will not taste therein any coolness nor any drink.
interpretation: This verse describes the deprivation of those in punishment, emphasizing the severity of their suffering by denying them the basic comforts and relief that human beings naturally seek - coolness to soothe their distress and drink to quench their thirst. The mention of these two fundamental needs highlights the completeness of their torment, where not even momentary respite or the simplest pleasures will be granted, underscoring the justice of divine punishment for those who rejected truth.

translation: Except boiling water and pus/discharge
interpretation: This verse describes the specific torments awaiting the disbelievers in Hell, emphasizing their complete deprivation of comfort or mercy. The mention of boiling water and pus represents not merely physical suffering, but the degradation and humiliation that accompanies punishment for those who rejected Allah's signs and turned away from His guidance. These gruesome substances symbolize the utter filth and corruption that defines the state of those who lived in spiritual corruption, now receiving an appropriate recompense that matches the nature of their rebellion against their Creator.

translation: A recompense, equivalent (to their deeds)
interpretation: This phrase emphasizes the precise and just nature of divine retribution, where the punishment or reward is exactly proportionate to one's actions. It reflects the Quranic principle of divine justice - that Allah neither oppresses nor favors anyone, but rather grants each soul a consequence that perfectly corresponds to what it has earned through its deeds.

translation: Indeed, they were not expecting any reckoning.
interpretation: This verse describes the state of those who denied the Hereafter and lived without accountability—they rejected the concept of divine judgment and consequences for their deeds. The verse conveys that their disbelief in the Day of Judgment allowed them to act without moral restraint, as they harbored no fear of standing before Allah to answer for their actions. This serves as a warning about the spiritual danger of denying accountability before God, which removes the strongest incentive for righteous conduct.

translation: And they denied Our signs, a denying most stubborn.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the willful rejection of divine guidance by those who persistently and defiantly deny the clear signs and proofs of Allah. The phrase 'kithaban' (denying most stubborn) emphasizes the deliberate and emphatic nature of their rejection, suggesting not mere disbelief but an active, intentional contradiction of obvious truth. This represents a spiritual state where hearts are sealed against guidance despite evidence, reflecting the consequences of repeated rejection of divine messages.

translation: And We have enumerated all things in a clear record
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute knowledge and meticulous accounting of all creation. Nothing escapes divine awareness—every deed, thought, and particle of existence is recorded in God's cosmic register. This establishes the theological foundation for divine justice on the Day of Judgment, assuring believers that their righteous acts are witnessed and will be requited, while warning wrongdoers that their deeds are similarly documented. The phrase conveys both comfort to the faithful and a sobering reminder of accountability before God's omniscience.

translation: So taste [the punishment]; for We will not increase you except in torment.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the consequence of disbelief and rejection of Allah's signs—that those who persist in denying the truth will experience increasing severity of punishment. The command to 'taste' serves as a vivid metaphor making them experience the full reality of their wrongdoing, while the statement 'We will not increase you except in torment' underscores that the only increase awaiting them is further and perpetual suffering, reflecting the justice of Allah upon those who willfully turn away from guidance.

translation: Indeed, for the righteous there is a place of success/victory.
interpretation: This verse affirms that those who practice piety and God-consciousness (taqwa) will achieve ultimate triumph and salvation. The 'mafaza' (place of success) refers to Paradise and the eternal reward awaiting the righteous in the Hereafter, emphasizing that true victory is not measured by worldly gains but by one's standing with God through conscious obedience and moral integrity.

translation: Gardens and grapevines
interpretation: This phrase refers to the material blessings and sustenance that Allah provides to His servants. Gardens represent cultivated land and vegetation that provide both nourishment and beauty, while grapevines specifically symbolize prosperity and abundance. The pairing of these two items emphasizes the variety and richness of divine provision, illustrating how Allah grants His creation not merely the basic necessities for survival, but also the fruits of cultivation and labor that enhance human life and are sources of both physical nourishment and aesthetic pleasure.

translation: And maidens of equal age
interpretation: This phrase describes the companions of paradise as young, full-breasted women of the same age, emphasizing the perfect beauty and desirability of the houris (celestial beings) promised to the believers in paradise. The term 'kawawib' (كواعب) specifically refers to young women with rounded breasts in the prime of youth, while 'atraba' means of equal age, suggesting uniformity and idealized perfection in their appearance and eternal youth.

translation: And a cup overflowing [with wine]
interpretation: This phrase describes a cup filled to the brim and running over, symbolizing abundant blessing and reward in Paradise. The word 'dihaq' (overflowing) emphasizes completeness and excess, indicating that the blessings granted to the righteous in the afterlife are not merely sufficient but lavishly abundant, reflecting the generosity and perfection of divine reward.

translation: They will not hear in it any vain talk, nor any falsehood.
interpretation: This verse describes the speech and discourse in Paradise, emphasizing that the environment is purified of all that is worthless, frivolous, or deceitful. The mention of both 'vain talk' (laghw) and 'falsehood' (kithab) indicates that Paradise is characterized by pure, truthful, and meaningful communication. This reflects the Quranic theme that Paradise is a realm of perfection where believers are freed from the corruptions and defilements of this worldly life, particularly the spiritual pollution caused by false speech and empty discourse. The negation establishes that only that which is good, true, and beneficial remains in the eternal abode.

translation: A reward from your Lord, a gift calculated [in measure]
interpretation: This verse describes the nature of the reward granted by Allah to His servants as a precise and generous gift. The phrase 'calculated in measure' emphasizes that while the reward is abundantly given, it is not arbitrary but rather carefully determined by Allah's perfect wisdom and justice. It reflects the divine principle that every good deed receives its appropriate recompense, neither diminished nor excessive, demonstrating both Allah's generosity and His meticulous accounting of human actions.

translation: Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, the Most Merciful. They cannot address Him.
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute sovereignty and dominion of Allah over all creation, emphasizing His transcendence and majesty through His title as the Most Merciful. The phrase 'they cannot address Him' conveys the impossibility of created beings speaking to or demanding audience with Allah without His permission, highlighting the vast distance between the Creator and His creation, and the proper etiquette of submission and humility that creatures must maintain before their Lord.

translation: The Day when the Spirit and the angels will stand in rows - they will not speak except for one to whom the Most Merciful has given permission, and he will speak what is right.
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Judgment when all creation will be arranged in perfect order and silence will prevail, emphasizing the absolute authority and sovereignty of Allah over all beings. No one will dare to speak on that Day except by His explicit permission, and only those permitted to speak will utter only truth and righteousness, signifying that on that ultimate Day, falsehood will have no place and only truth will be expressed, illustrating both the majesty of Allah's dominion and the final establishment of absolute justice.

translation: That is the Day of Truth. So whoever wills may take to his Lord a way of return.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the Day of Judgment is an absolute reality that will certainly occur. The phrase 'Day of Truth' underscores its inevitability and certainty. The conditional statement that follows conveys divine mercy and human responsibility: God presents humanity with the choice to turn back to Him through repentance and righteous action in this life. The word 'mab' (way of return) suggests that sincere repentance and obedience constitute the pathway to reconciliation with the Lord before that Day arrives. This interpretation highlights both the warning of accountability on the Last Day and the opportunity for redemption available to those who choose to return to God.

translation: Indeed, We have warned you of a punishment near - the Day when a man will see what his hands have sent forward, and the disbeliever will say, 'Oh, would that I were dust!'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the inevitability of divine judgment and the anguish of accountability on the Day of Resurrection. The 'punishment near' refers to the closeness of the Day of Judgment in terms of its certainty and the swift consequences that await. When disbelievers witness the reality of their deeds manifested before them, they will experience profound regret, wishing they had never existed at all. The mention of wishing to be dust conveys the deepest despair - a desire to be completely non-existent rather than face eternal punishment. This interpretation serves as a powerful warning to heed God's message in this worldly life, as the opportunity for repentance is limited and the judgment is assured.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. By the angels who tear out [souls] with violence,
interpretation: This is the opening of Surah An-Naziat, where Allah swears by the angels who forcefully extract the souls of the dying, establishing their reality and power as a prelude to affirming the certainty of the Day of Judgment and resurrection, emphasizing that just as these angels carry out their divine function with certainty, so too will all souls face accountability before Allah.

translation: By the ones that scatter with scattering
interpretation: This verse from Surah 'Abasa (80:31) refers to the winds or angels that spread and disperse things, serving as a divine oath to affirm the power and majesty of God's creation. The repetition of the word in its different forms (participle and verbal noun) emphasizes the vigorous, energetic nature of their activity. Some scholars interpret this as referring to the winds that scatter seeds and rain, which are essential for sustaining life on Earth, thereby highlighting God's perfect organization of the natural world and His provision for humanity through means that appear simple yet are profoundly purposeful.

translation: And the swimmers swimming [in the sky]
interpretation: This verse refers to the celestial bodies, particularly the stars and planets, which move through the heavens in their appointed orbits. The term 'swimmers' (al-sabihāt) uses the metaphor of swimming to describe the graceful, continuous motion of these heavenly bodies through space, emphasizing the wonder and order of divine creation and the cosmic system established by Allah.

translation: By those that race ahead in a race
interpretation: This verse, which begins Surah Al-'Adiyat, refers to horses or warriors racing swiftly forward. The interpretation emphasizes the concept of striving and exertion toward goals - whether in worldly pursuits or spiritual endeavors. It serves as an oath to invoke reflection on human effort, ambition, and the drive that propels creatures (and people) toward their objectives, setting the stage for the subsequent verses which contrast human ingratitude and heedlessness with the divine knowledge and judgment that observes all actions.

translation: By the scatterers dispersing [as a command]
interpretation: This verse refers to the angels or divine forces that execute God's commands throughout creation, emphasizing that all events in the universe occur by divine decree and the agency of these forces working to fulfill God's will.

translation: The Day when the Rajfah (the first blast of the trumpet) will shake (everything).
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment when the trumpet will be blown, causing a violent shaking and upheaval of all creation. The term 'Rajfah' (the shaker) refers to the first trumpet blast that will cause universal trembling and the destruction of the existing world, signifying the momentous and overwhelming nature of that divine event when all earthly order will be disrupted and souls will be seized by terror before their resurrection.

translation: The following one will pursue it.
interpretation: This phrase refers to the successive catastrophes or calamities that will follow one another on the Day of Judgment. The 'Radifah' (the following one) represents the second blast of the trumpet which will bring about resurrection after death. This conveys the idea of inescapable divine punishment and the certainty of the consequences of one's deeds, emphasizing that just as one disaster follows another, so too will the stages of the Day of Judgment unfold inevitably, with no escape or respite for those who rejected God's signs.

translation: Hearts on that Day will be terrified
interpretation: This phrase describes the state of human hearts on the Day of Judgment when they will be seized with overwhelming fear and anxiety due to the magnitude of that day's events. The word 'واجفة' (trembling/palpitating) emphasizes the intensity of this fear, which will be inescapable as people face the reality of divine judgment and accountability for their deeds. This conveys the Qur'an's message about the certainty and terrifying nature of the afterlife, meant to motivate believers toward righteous conduct in this life.

translation: Her eyes cast down in humility
interpretation: This phrase describes a state of profound awe and spiritual submission before Allah. The lowering of the eyes (khushu') signifies not merely a physical gesture, but an inward condition of the soul—one of deep reverence, humility, and complete awareness of standing before the Divine presence. It reflects the believer's recognition of their smallness before Allah's majesty and their heart's surrender to His will.

translation: They say, 'Are we indeed to be returned in the footsteps [of our former state]?'
interpretation: This verse reflects the deniers' rhetorical mockery and disbelief in resurrection. The phrase 'in the footsteps' (al-hafira) suggests returning to their previous condition of life and worldly existence. The verse emphasizes their arrogant incredulity toward the divine promise of the afterlife, indicating that they find the concept of resurrection absurd and laughable. Their use of the interrogative form with the particle of doubt ('a) demonstrates their stubborn rejection of this fundamental Islamic belief, treating resurrection as an impossibility rather than an inevitable reality ordained by Allah.

translation: What! When we are bones that have decayed?
interpretation: This verse expresses the skepticism of the disbelievers regarding the resurrection. They are questioning God's power to resurrect them after death, implying that once their bodies have decayed into dust and scattered bones, it would be impossible to bring them back to life. The interpretation reveals humanity's tendency to rely solely on their limited sensory perception and material understanding, failing to recognize God's infinite power and ability to recreate what has been destroyed. It serves as a rhetorical challenge that showcases the arrogance and doubt of those who deny the afterlife.

translation: They said, 'That then would be a losing return.'
interpretation: The disbelievers reject the concept of resurrection and the afterlife, dismissing it as a return that would result in total loss and ruin. This phrase reflects their denial of accountability and the divine judgment awaiting them on the Day of Resurrection, as they fail to comprehend or accept the value and reality of the eternal life to come.

translation: So it is only a single blast
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment when Allah will cause all creation to perish through one mighty sound or trumpet blast. The emphasis on 'only' (إنما) and 'single' (واحدة) underscores the absolute ease with which Allah will end the world and bring about the resurrection, requiring merely one command or sound. It demonstrates the insignificance of the entire creation in relation to Allah's power and will, and serves as a reminder of the certainty and swiftness of the Day of Judgment.

translation: Then suddenly they will be on the Plain (of Resurrection).
interpretation: This verse depicts the swift and sudden awakening of humanity on the Day of Judgment at a place called 'al-Sahirah' (the Plain or the Awakening Place). The word 'fa-idha' (then suddenly) emphasizes the instantaneous transition from death to resurrection, highlighting the overwhelming surprise and shock of that moment when people will find themselves standing before Allah. The verse conveys the certainty and inescapability of the resurrection, showing that despite any doubts people may have entertained during their earthly life, they will inevitably be confronted with the reality of the Day of Judgment.

translation: Has there come to you the story of Moses?
interpretation: This opening phrase serves as a rhetorical device to engage the listener's attention and draw them into the narrative that follows. It invites reflection on the profound lessons and divine guidance exemplified through Moses's life, emphasizing the importance of receiving and contemplating the historical accounts of the prophets as a source of spiritual instruction and moral guidance.

translation: When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa
interpretation: This verse marks the moment of divine calling to Prophet Moses, emphasizing the sanctity of the place through the mention of 'the sacred valley of Tuwa.' The act of calling by God Himself underscores the direct and personal nature of Divine communication, establishing Moses' unique status as a messenger chosen by God. The specification of location and the formal invocation of the Lord's call highlights the solemnity and significance of the mission about to be entrusted to him.

translation: Go to Pharaoh, indeed he has transgressed.
interpretation: This verse represents Allah's command to Moses to undertake his prophetic mission by confronting Pharaoh and calling him to monotheism. The phrase 'he has transgressed' establishes the moral justification for the mission—Pharaoh's rebellion against divine law and his oppression of the Children of Israel make him a target for prophetic guidance. This signifies that confronting tyrants and despots with the message of Allah is not merely permissible but a sacred duty entrusted to the prophets, and that excessive arrogance and violation of divine limits characterize those most in need of being called back to the truth.

translation: So say: 'Would you like to purify yourself?'
interpretation: This verse challenges the listener to willingly embrace spiritual purification and moral reform. The question posed is rhetorical, inviting reflection on whether one is genuinely willing to undertake the difficult work of cleansing oneself of spiritual impurity, vices, and worldly attachments in order to draw closer to God. It emphasizes that purification is ultimately a choice that requires individual will and commitment, not something that can be imposed externally.

translation: And I will guide you to your Lord so that you will fear [Him]
interpretation: This verse expresses the spiritual journey of drawing near to Allah through divine guidance, wherein proximity to the Divine naturally cultivates reverence and God-consciousness (taqwa). The phrase suggests that true fear of Allah is not born from coercion or mere instruction, but from experiential knowledge of one's Lord through guidance, implying that genuine piety emerges when the soul encounters divine reality and becomes aware of its own standing before the Almighty.

translation: So We showed him the greatest sign.
interpretation: This verse refers to the revelation of one of the greatest miracles of Allah to the Prophet Moses (Musa), most likely referring to the transformation of his staff into a serpent or the splitting of the sea, demonstrating Allah's absolute power and authority over creation as a confirmation of Moses' mission as a messenger, instilling certainty and conviction in his heart before his confrontation with Pharaoh.

translation: So he denied and disobeyed
interpretation: This phrase expresses the consequences of rejecting divine guidance through both intellectual denial (tashdib) and behavioral disobedience (isyan), depicting a person's comprehensive rejection of God's message through thought and action together. The conjunction of these two actions emphasizes the totality of the rejection, showing that refusing the truth is not merely a intellectual matter but must be accompanied by defiant action against God's commands.

translation: Then he turned back, hastening [away]
interpretation: This phrase describes a person's sudden retreat and swift departure, conveying the urgency and anxiety that compels someone to flee from a situation. The dual action of turning away and hurrying indicates not merely a calm withdrawal but an agitated flight driven by fear, shame, or distress, emphasizing the psychological state of someone overwhelmed by circumstances beyond their control.

translation: Then he gathered [them] and called out
interpretation: This verse describes a decisive moment where someone (typically understood as Pharaoh or a king) assembles his people and makes a proclamation. The action conveys authority and urgency, suggesting the speaker is addressing a matter of significant importance to his community or kingdom. The gathering and calling forth implies both power and a desire to communicate something of consequence to those assembled.

translation: Then he said, 'I am your Lord, the Most High.'
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 79:24) records the blasphemous claim of Pharaoh when confronted with the signs of Allah through Prophet Musa. Pharaoh's declaration of being the 'most high' lord represents the ultimate rejection of divine truth and the extreme arrogance of one who denies Allah's existence and oneness. This statement exemplifies how power and worldly dominion can delude a human being into believing themselves divine, and it serves as a warning against the destructive nature of pride, tyranny, and the refusal to submit to the absolute authority of the true God.

translation: So Allah seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and this world
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine justice of Allah in punishing those who transgress and reject His signs. The punishment encompasses both immediate consequences in this life and eternal punishment in the Hereafter, demonstrating that Allah's accountability is comprehensive and inescapable. This serves as a warning that defiance of Allah's commands results in total loss and suffering across all dimensions of existence.

translation: Indeed, in that is a lesson for those who fear (Allah).
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that spiritual lessons and guidance are only absorbed by those who possess God-consciousness and reverence. The phrase highlights that intellectual understanding alone is insufficient; moral and spiritual awareness (khashya) is the prerequisite for extracting beneficial lessons from events, signs, and teachings. Those who fear Allah approach knowledge with humility and openness, enabling them to perceive divine wisdom, whereas those without this reverence remain heedless despite clear evidence.

translation: Are you more difficult to create, or is the heaven? He built it.
interpretation: This verse invites reflection on the grandeur of creation, using the comparison between human creation and the celestial heavens to humble the listener and strengthen conviction in Allah's infinite power. By questioning whether humans—who often forget their fragility—are more difficult to create than the vast, structured heavens, the verse emphasizes that if Allah can construct the cosmos with such majesty and precision, then resurrecting humans on the Day of Judgment is far less difficult. This serves as a powerful argument for belief in the Hereafter and the omnipotence of the Creator.

translation: He raised its canopy and made it level.
interpretation: This verse describes Allah's creation of the heavens as a roof, raised high and perfectly proportioned over the earth. The phrase conveys divine artistry and precision in cosmic design, emphasizing that the heavens are not merely created but crafted with deliberate symmetry and balance. This imagery reinforces human awareness of being sheltered under a well-ordered, divinely-structured cosmos, meant to inspire reflection on the creator's wisdom and power.

translation: And He made dark its night and brought forth its forenoon light.
interpretation: This verse describes Allah's creation of the day-night cycle as a manifestation of His divine power and wisdom. The phrase emphasizes the alternation between darkness and light as a fundamental design of creation that sustains life and provides rhythm to existence. This alternation symbolizes the cycles of rest and activity that are essential to human and natural existence, demonstrating Allah's perfect ordering of the cosmos for the benefit of creation.

translation: And the earth after that He spread it out
interpretation: This verse describes Allah's creation of the earth by spreading it out flat and making it habitable. The word 'daha' conveys the sense of stretching, extending, and flattening the earth to provide a stable foundation for life. The phrase 'after that' indicates the sequential nature of creation, where the earth's spreading came after other acts of creation. This demonstrates Allah's power and wisdom in preparing the earth as a suitable dwelling place for His creation, establishing it with the proper form and dimensions necessary for human and animal life to flourish.

translation: He brought forth from it its water and its pasture
interpretation: This verse refers to Allah's creative power in providing the essential resources for life on Earth. The mention of water and pasture together represents the fundamental necessities for sustaining both human and animal life. The verse emphasizes Allah's role as the ultimate provider who has structured the earth with inherent potential to yield what is needed for survival and livelihood, demonstrating His wisdom in creating a balanced system where earth naturally produces the means of subsistence for all creatures.

translation: And the mountains He has firmly established them
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's power in creating and stabilizing the mountains, depicting them as anchors or pegs driven into the earth. The metaphor of 'establishing firmly' (irsa'a) suggests that mountains serve as stabilizers for the earth itself, preventing it from shaking or tilting, and conveys the purposeful design in creation where everything has a divine function in maintaining the balance and stability of the physical world.

translation: Enjoyment for you and for your livestock
interpretation: This verse refers to the provision and sustenance that Allah has granted to humanity and their animals in this worldly life, emphasizing that these material blessings and comforts are temporary provisions meant for use and benefit during our lifetime on earth, which serves as a reminder that all worldly possessions are transient and should not be the ultimate focus of human existence.

translation: So when the greatest catastrophe comes
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment, the ultimate overwhelming calamity that will befall humanity. The 'greatest catastrophe' (al-Tammah al-Kubra) represents the moment when the established order of creation is shattered and all souls are brought to account before God. It signifies the end of worldly life and the beginning of eternal accountability, emphasizing the certainty and magnitude of Divine judgment that no human power can prevent or escape.

translation: The Day when man will remember all that he strove for
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment when every soul will be confronted with the full reality and consequences of their deeds and efforts in life. The verse emphasizes human accountability and the inescapable nature of this reckoning, suggesting that on that Day, all pretense and forgetfulness will be stripped away, and people will have a clear and complete awareness of everything they pursued, worked toward, and achieved during their earthly existence, whether good or evil.

translation: And Hell will be exposed/revealed to those who see.
interpretation: This verse refers to the unveiling of Hell on the Day of Judgment, when it becomes visible and manifest to all creation. The phrase 'for those who see' emphasizes that Hell's reality will be unmistakable and apparent to every observer, serving as a tangible manifestation of divine justice and consequence for those who rejected faith and lived in heedlessness. The exposure of Hell demonstrates the ultimate truth that believers warned of throughout their lifetimes, making evident the reality of the afterlife that many had denied.

translation: As for one who rebels/transgresses
interpretation: This phrase introduces a conditional statement that distinguishes between two types of people based on their spiritual state. 'Tughyan' (طغى) refers to exceeding bounds and rebelling against divine guidance, describing those who arrogantly reject truth and indulge excessively in vice. The verse is setting up a contrast to show the consequences of choosing arrogance and disobedience, emphasizing that human choice and accountability are central to one's destiny in the afterlife.

translation: And he preferred the life of this world
